FOREWORD 

"All procedure is merely a methodical means whereby the court reaches out to restore rights and remedy wrongs. It must never become more important than the purpose which it seeks to accomplish." 

Crane, J., in Clark v. Kirby, 243 N. Y. 295.

The revision of this Second Compact Edition has not been allowed to become more important than the purpose which it was designed to accomplish. Obsolete passages have been stricken out. Archaic ones have been revitalized. Citations, foot-notes, case-digests and statutes have been kept abreast of the times. A chapter on Appeals has been added, and. 

Problems, Charts, Suggested Reading Assignments, and forty new Forms have been included in the interest of greater practical utility. The nucleus, however, remains the finished product of the gifted hand of Professor Carmody, as supplemented in 1929 by the genius of Professor John T. Loughran, who has since been called to the bench of the Court of Appeals. 

Wherever we have found it necessary to discuss procedural policy, we have endeavored to keep focal in consciousness the spirit of the "Credo" formulated by ex-Justice Proskauer in an address delivered to the Association of the Bar of the City of New York: 

"I will join with my adversary in waiving a jury trial wherever and whenever it can possibly be done without the sacrifice of a fundamental right. "I will join with my adversary in supporting a trial justice in fair comment upon the evidence and reasonable direction to a jury on the facts. "I will join with my adversary in fair concession of undisputed 

"I will not put an adversary to his proof in respect to facts whose existence my client admits. "I will refrain from merely formal or technical objection to the admission of evidence. "I will co-operate with the trial justice and my adversary to secure a speedy, prompt and complete presentation of the facts of the case. "I will neither make nor oppose interlocutory motions unless they are of real and practical importance. "I will take no appeal unless I am satisfied that substantial error has been committed and that a new trial should reasonably give a different result." 

New York, N. Y. 

September, 1934.

EDWARD Q. CARR JOHN F. X. FINN

1. As an applied working system, the substantive law is classified under a variety of heads sometimes corresponding to the nature of different legal rights and duties, and sometimes to the respective persons who may assert or deny them (e. g., crimes, con- 

Criminal

§ 2. Adjective and Substantive Law. 

Substantive law defines the rights which men have and the duties which they owe to others. Adjective law outlines the method by which these duties and rights are enforced and protected. The distinction is between the right or obligation and the remedy. A borrows $100 from B. B now has a right to its return. This is defined by the substantive law. If, however, A refuses to return the money, B must invoke the adjective law to compel A to return it. We are not concerned with substantive law in this book. It is presumed that the reader knows something of this. Adjective law alone shall engage our attention.¹ 

Common Law Equity

Civil Practice 

Act. tracts, torts, property; infants, executors, corporations). Likewise, the adjective law is similarly classified under a number of topics (e. g., action, process, pleading, trial, evidence, judg ment, execution). [3]

INTRODUCTION. 

§ 3. Evidence and Procedure. 

The facts which establish a right must be adduced before the final compulsory processes for its enforcement are set in motion. The principles by which these facts are ascertained and the manner of bringing them forward and establishing them constitute the law of evidence. The compulsory processes themselves are termed procedure. For example, the conversation or correspondence by which the loan from B to A was effected contains the evidence necessary to establish the right which B has to the return of the money; the process, pleadings, motions, orders, etc. and the rules governing their issuance and service constitute the procedure by which B's is protected and A's obligation enforced. We are not concerned with the law of evidence in this book. Procedure alone shall be the subject of our study. 

§ 4. Civil and Criminal Procedure. 

The procedure by which crimes are established and the criminal punished is called criminal procedure. Public rights and public wrongs are involved here. When private rights and private obligations are concerned, the procedure invoked for their protection and enforcement is called civil procedure. 

This book treats of civil procedure only and does not consider criminal procedure, except in occasional instances, for purpose of comparison. 2 

§ 5. Systems of Procedure. 

There are three systems of civil procedure still in use in the United States: common law, equity and statutory procedure. These are not the only systems of civil procedure, but they are the only ones which shall concern us. And of these three systems, statutory procedure, which in New York is found in the Civil Practice Act and the Rules of Civil Procedure, shall be our principal concern. Nevertheless, a 

2. A criminal offense is punished by a proceeding prosecuted in the name of the people of the state, as plaintiffs, against the party charged with the crime, as defendant (Code of Criminal Procedure, §§ 5, 6), to impose upon him some form of penal disci pline. (Penal Law, § 2.) The remedy for a civil injury is a proceeding brought in the name of the injured private person, as plaintiff, for the purpose of enforcing or protecting his right or redressing or preventing the defendant's wrong. (Civil Practice 

Act, 88 4, 6, 9; Code of Criminal Procedure, § 5-a.)

INTRODUCTION. 

5 hasty glance at the other two systems will enable us more easily to understand the procedure under the Civil Practice 

Act. 

§ 6. Common Law Procedure. 

The common law system is the oldest of the three systems of procedure. Its boast is its antiquity. It grew up in 

England with the development of that nation and has been in process of perfection and refinement for many centuries. 

Tradition assigns its origin to custom and not to statute. The king decided disputes among his followers and formulated his own rules for hearing their claims. With the growth of the state and the consequent increase in the number of differences, the king appointed representatives to hear the parties and settle their controversies. These representatives, who came to be known as judges, made their own rules and in time their rules became uniform throughout the realm and were known as Common Law Procedure.

Under this system a person who had a grievance against another and wished to sue him, had to go to one of the common law courts and give the essential facts to the clerk or officer of the court who then went to the chancellor's office, which Blackstone calls "the shop or mint of justice" and there procured, on payment of the fee, what was called an Original Writ. This was a paper directed to the sheriff and under the great seal of the king. The following is the form of one of these original writs:

WRIT OF COVENANT. 

George the Fourth, by the grace of God, of the United Kingdom of

Great Britain and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, and so forth, to the sheriff of Middlesex, greeting:

Command C. D., late of Essex, gentleman, that justly and without delay he keep with A. B., according to the force, form and effect of a certain indenture in that behalf made between them, as it is said. 

And unless he shall so do and if the said A. B. shall make you secure of prosecuting his claim, then summon, by good summoners, the said C. D., that he be before us, in eight days of Saint Hilary, wheresoever we shall then be in England, to show wherefore he hath not done it; and have you there the names of the summoners, and this writ. day of 

Witness ourselves at Westminster, the in the . year of our reign. ..... ....

INTRODUCTION. 

Pursuant to the directions contained in the writ the sheriff gave notice to the party named in it, to appear before one of the common law courts, Common Pleas, King's Bench or Exchequer. The notice was called a summons and was given by sheriff's messengers called summoners, and thereafter the case was heard and determined in one of these courts before a jury.

The writ set forth above is the writ of covenant and was the form used to begin an action for the breach of a covenant or agreement contained in a deed. If the contemplated action was for trespass the clerks in the office of the chancellor would give the suitor a different writ, and for every form of action there was a special form of writ. As, however, the commercial relations of the people became more complicated, occasionally a suitor would come to the chancery clerks with a situation in which he felt himself aggrieved but for which none of the forms of writ seemed suitable, and many a suitor was turned away by the clerks because there was no writ to fit his case.

This led to the statute of Westminster II, passed in the 13th year of the reign of Edward I (1285 A. D.), providing in chapter 24 that "Whensoever from thence forth in one case a writ shall be found in the chancery and in a like case falling under the same writ and requiring like remedy, no precedent of a writ can be produced, the clerks in chancery shall agree in forming a new one; and, if they cannot agree, it shall be adjourned to the next Parliament, where a writ shall be framed by the consent of the Learned in the Law, lest it happen in the future that the Court of our Lord the King be deficient in doing justice to the suitors." By reason of this statute some new writs were issued. 

They were known as writs of "Trespass on the Case" or simply "Case." The statute thus enlarged materially the common law jurisdiction and thereafter there was a writ for every one of the common law actions found in the following

1. The following note on common law actions was prepared by Professor 

John T. Loughran of Fordham Uni versity prior to his elevation to the 

Court of Appeals of the State of New 

York. It is printed here for the benefit of those readers who may desire an analysis of the common law causes of action which is something more than a bare outline and yet remains a terse and lucid summary: 

arose. "At the early law, litigation was commenced by what was called an original writ. This was a written mandate issued in the name of the king to the sheriff of the county where the case It directed the sheriff to summon the defendant to appear in court to answer for his failure to satisfy the plaintiff's demand. A writ had been sanctioned for each of a recognized list of forms of action (remedies), precedents for which were kept in an office called the Registra Brevium. 

Trover Damages for converting to one's own use the goods of another. A form of trespass on the case now separately classified.

Many forms illustrated by deceit, negligence, defamation of character, etc.

In the Detinet Where wrongfully detained. Same as detinue.

Clerks in this office would prepare a writ only for a plaintiff who presented a case conforming to one of these established writs. Originally, a writ had been sanctioned for each of the forms of action known as ejectment, covenant, debt, trespass, detinue, replevin. These forms of action were classified as real, personal and mixed. A real action was one for the specific recovery of real property, without damages; a personal action one for the specific recovery of personal property or one for damages; a mixed action one for the specific recovery of real property with damages. (N. Y., O. & W. R. Co. v. Livingston, 206 App. Div. 589, 593, 201 N. Y. S. 

629, 238 N. Y. 300.)

Ejectment. This was the form of action for trying titles to real property. It superseded a number of earlier real actions. Originally itself a real action, it became of a mixed

INTRODUCTION. 

nature, and is a mixed action today.

(Civil Practice Act, §§ 990, 1011; 

Willis v. McKinnon, 178 N. Y. 451.)

Covenant. Contracts are usually separated into two classes: (1) contracts under seal; (2) simple contracts. A contract under seal is sometimes called a covenant. The action of covenant was the remedy for breach of a contract under seal (Smith v. Kerr, 3 

N. Y. 144), except where debt could be brought.

Debt. Originally, this was the appropriate form of action for the recovery of a liquidated sum of money which the defendant had undertaken to pay in exchange for a loan, a sale or services; or which he was bound to pay by a promise under seal or by a record (e. g., a judgment); or for which he was made liable by a customary, official or a statutory obligation.

Trespass. As a form of action, trespass was the remedy for a direct and immediate interference by wrongful act with a natural person or tangible property. (Hay v. Cohoes Co., 2 N. Y. 159; 

Sullivan v. Dunham, 161 N. Y. 290; 

Gordon v. Ellenville & Kingston R. R. 

Co., 195 N. Y. 137.) There were three types of this form of action: trespass trespass to the person; trespass for a trespass upon real property (quare clausum fregit); trespass for a trespass to personal property (de bonis asportatis). for Detinue. As its name implies, detinue was an action to recover personal property wrongfully detained. (Graves v. Dudley, 20 N. Y. 76, 79.) The plaintiff could recover his goods or their value at the option of the defendant.

Replevin. This form of action "was extended to nearly all cases of unlawful caption or detention of chattels where it was sought to recover the chattels in specie. In many cases where the plaintiff was unable to obtain the return of the chattels he could recover in the action their value. Still the action remained essentially one to recover the possession of chattels." (Sinnott v. Feiock, 165 N. Y. 444, 445446.) [In New York, the common law actions of detinue and replevin have been fused in the statutory action to recover a chattel. See Chapter

XXXIII.] 

The foregoing forms of action constituted originally a complete list of the injuries for which alone civil redress was afforded. Unless the facts of a plaintiff's claim squared with one of these established forms of action, he had no remedy. A breach of contract was not actionable unless the bargain created a technical debt or had been reduced to a written instrument under seal. "For damage to the person the sole remedy was trespass, and trespass did not lie in the absence of aggression, and that direct and personal.” (Palsgraf v. Long Island R. R. Co., 248 N. Y. 

339, 346.) For damage to property the remedy also was trespass, but only when interference with the property had been direct and immediate. 

To supplement this rigidly exclusive catalogue of remedies, there was enacted in the reign of Edward I (1285 

A. D.) a statute which provided: "Whensoever from henceforth it shall fortune in chancery that in one case a writ is found, and in a like case falling under like law and requiring like remedy is found none, the clerks of the chancery shall agree in making the writ, or the plaintiff may adjourn it into the next Parliament, and let the cases be written in which they cannot agree, and let them refer themselves to the next Parliament, and by consent of men learned in the law a writ shall be made, lest it should happen after that the court should long time fail to minister justice unto complainants." (13

Edw. I, Chap. 1, § 24.) 

The common law courts refused to recognize the spirit of this legislation.

§ 7. Equity Procedure. 

The common law writs were issued out of the chancellor's office, but it must not be inferred that the chancellor was at first a judicial officer. The chancery was not presided over by a lawyer but usually by an ecclesiastic, who was the keeper of the king's conscience. It was really nothing but 

Interpreting the statute literally, they insisted that a new remedy created thereunder should be a "like remedy" to the old. The statute did, however, beget a new form of action known as trespass on the case, or "case," which in turn produced the distinct actions of trover and assumpsit.

The Action on the Case. This be came the remedy for torts for which trespass did not lie, and so for torts committed without force, actual or implied, and for forcible injuries where the damage resulted not immediately but consequentially. "In all the books, the invariable principle to be collected is, that where the injury is immediate on the act done, there trespass lies; but where it is not immediate on the act done but consequential, then the remedy is in case." (Percival v. Hickey, 18 Johns. 257.)

Trover. This became the remedy for the tort conversion-an exercise of dominion over a chattel without the authority, express or implied, of the person immediately entitled to posses sion thereof. (Industrial & General 

Trust Co. v. Todd, 170 N. Y. 233; 

Casey v. Kastel, 237 N. Y. 305.) "In the action of trover, the plaintiff does not seek to recover his property, but its value as a substitute for the property. He abandons the property to the defendant, preferring to pursue him for its value. He makes a kind of forced sale of it, without any expectation or intention of retaking it. * * But in the action of replevin, the plaintiff seeks to recover the property and is, in all stages of the case to final judgment, in pursuit of that, and not its value." (Allen v. Fox, 51 N. Y. 562, 564; Civil Practice Act, § 1120.) 

Assumpsit. This became the remedy for breach of simple contract. Simple contracts are classified as (1) express; (2) implied in fact; (3) implied in law (quasi contracts). Both express contracts and contracts implied in fact are true contracts created in accordance with the intention of parties. 

The difference between them is an evidentiary distinction, a difference in methods of proof. An express contract is proved by the language, oral or written, of the parties to he bargain; a contract implied in fact by their conduct. The contract implied in law, or quasi contract, is not a true contract. "It is an obligation which the law creates, in the absence of any agreement, when and because the acts of the parties or others have placed in the possession of one person money, or its equivalent, under such circumstances that in equity and good conscience he ought not to retain it, and which ex aequo et bono belongs to another." (Miller v. Schloss, 218 N. Y. 400, 407.)

There were two branches of the action of assumpsit. Special or express assumpsit was the remedy for breach of an express contract. General or implied assumpsit became concurrent with debt and superseded that action, became the remedy for breach of a contract implied in fact, and finally was extended to actions upon quasi contracts to compel restitution of an unjust enrichment. (Roberts v. Ely, 113 

N. Y. 128.)"

an administrative office of the king. The theory was that the king was the fountain head of all justice and those who had a grievance came to him and were attended to by his representative, the chancellor, and the issuance of these common law writs was merely the custom of the chancellor in referring certain matters that came before him in this way to the common law courts for adjustment. 

In the reign of Richard II, the then chancellor, John Waltham, who was a bishop, became dissatisfied with the way the common law courts adjusted certain matters that were referred to them by the writs out of the chancery. The matters concerned the uses of land. For example, a decedent would leave his land to A for the use of B. Now the common law courts would give no effect to such a use while the chancellor, who kept the king's conscience and was an ecclesiastic, felt that in conscience he was bound to give effect to the wishes of the decedent. Waltham, dissatisfied with the common law courts' handling of such matters, resorted to the statute of Westminster II, and devised a new writ for such a case called a Writ of Subpoena. The writ was not returnable at all before the common law courts but before the chancellor himself, and he heard such cases and gave effect to a devise of land for the use of B. 

This writ of subpoena opened the door, and soon many other matters were made returnable before the chancellor, and thus grew up what we speak of as the Court of Chancery. 

The common law courts resisted this encroachment upon their jurisdiction and a struggle between them and the Court of Chancery ensued which lasted for centuries and culminated in the notable conflict in 1616 between Lord Chancellor

Ellesmere and Sir Edward Coke, the then chief justice of the common law court of the King's Bench. 

A judgment had been obtained in the court of the King's Bench, the highest common law court in England, through gross fraud and imposition. Relief was sought by the injured party through a petition to the chancellor, Lord Ellesmere.

He entertained the petition and issued a subpoena returnable before himself to have the matter reviewed. Sir Edward 

Coke, chief justice of the court of the King's Bench, was much wrought up because the chancellor sought to review a judgment of his court, and started a sort of contempt proceeding against the suitors in the case, the solicitors, the

INTRODUCTION. 

11 counsel, and even against a master in chancery. This conflict between the common law and equity courts came before the king, James the First, who decided the case in favor of the chancellor, and to add to the humiliation of Coke, instead of deciding the case on precedent, based his decision on the plenitude of the royal prerogative. This was one of the causes which led to Coke's subsequent removal from office.

§ 8. Common Law and Equity Procedure in America. 

These two systems of procedure existed and were used side by side in England and came to America with the English colonists. As the amount of litigation here did not warrant the existence of two systems of courts presided over by two sets of judges, it was usual to have the same judges sit now as a court of law and again as a court of chancery. Sometimes a judge sitting as a court of law would give judgment, and then donning the ermine of the chancellor would solemnly sign a decree restraining the enforcement of his own judgment rendered but shortly before. Many absurd situations wherein the common-law courts either could give no redress at all, or could not give adequate redress; and any one coming to Chancery with a case which did not need its extraordinary jurisdiction, but could be adequately dealt with in the common-law court, was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Thus, side by side, there existed the Court of Chancery and the common-law courts, each with a distinct jurisdiction, the test of Chancery's jurisdiction in any given case being that the suitor could either get no relief, or could not get adequate relief in a court of common law. And, therefore, necessarily, there also grew up, not only two distinct systems of practice in these courts, but also two distinct systems of substantive jurisprudence, that in the Court of Chancery being the system which we call equity.' (Dalton v. 

Vandervere, 8 Misc. 484, 486-487; 29 

N. Y. S. 342.)

There are thus two distinct classes of cases within the jurisdiction of courts of equity. In the first class, the substantive right asserted is traditionally a purely equitable right; a right enforcible only in a court of equity. 

In cases of this class, the jurisdiction In of equity is generally exclusive. the second class, the right asserted is a legal right, and the basis to the equity jurisdiction is the absence of an adequate remedy at law. In cases of this class, the jurisdiction of equity is usually concurrent with that of the law courts. (Fur & Wool Trading Co., 

Ltd. v. Fox, Inc., 245 N. Y. 215.) Equitable remedies differ radically from legal remedies in their operation and effect. "What are the distinctions between actions at law and suits in equity? The most marked distinction obviously consists in their different modes of relief. In the one, with a few isolated exceptions [ejectment and replevin] relief is invariably administered, and can only be administered, in the form of a pecuniary compensation in damages for the injury received; in the other, the court has a discretionary power to adapt the relief to the exigencies of the case. 

Another leading distinction between common law actions and suits in equity consists in their different modes of trial. The former are to be tried by a jury, the latter by the court." (Rubens v. Joel, 13 N. Y. 488, 493.) A court of equity may exact personal obedience to its directions. Equity in most cases acts directly against a party or in personam. But it is not to be assumed that the difference between jurisdiction at law and in equity is solely a difference of remedy. There are substantive rights in equity not cognizable at common law,"

13 grew out of the attempt to make use of these systems of procedure, so far removed from the original setting in which they developed, and after the colonies severed their political relations with Great Britain and set up a government of their own, republican in form, these absurdities were intensified. 

The basic maxim that the king was the fountain of justice was at the foundation of both systems; but here in America there was no king and the entire system seemed like an effort to develop a plant in a soil not adapted to its growth. 

§ 9. The Introduction of the Statutory System of Procedure. 

The first serious attempt to create and introduce a new system of procedure in America was made in New York state. 

The Constitution of 1846 provided that three commissioners should be appointed by the next legislature "to revise, reform, simplify, and abridge the rules and practice, forms and proceedings of the courts of record." Accordingly, in 

1847 commissioners were appointed to carry into effect this constitutional provision.

The commissioners, of whom David Dudley Field was the principal figure, reported to the legislatures of 1848 and 1849 the "Code of Procedure." The provisions contained in this report were enacted into law and the code system of procedure was thus inaugurated. This Code is often referred to as the "Field Code." It was considerably enlarged by amendments in the years 1877-1880 but, by the Consolidated Laws of 1909, about six hundred sections which should have been classified as substantive law rather than as the law of procedure were taken out of the Code and inserted in the 

Judiciary Law. 

§ 10. The Passing Away of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

The Code of Civil Procedure has become inoperative, and the Civil Practice Act and a number of allied acts have taken its place. Some of the acts which have replaced the Code of 

Civil Procedure are the following: The Civil Practice Act, The New York City Court Act, The Surrogate's Court Act, The Court of Claims Act and The Justice's Court Act. 

For many years past a prolonged effort was made to simplify the Code of Civil Procedure. A radical change in practice from that contained in the Code was first proposed by the board of statutory consolidation, but the legislature

INTRODUCTION. 

rejected the proposal. The proposal was revolutionary, and the legislature favored evolution as the principle of revision. 

A joint legislative committee was appointed with J. Henry 

Walters as chairman, and after four years of consideration, this committee in the year 1919 reported to the legislature a series of separate acts, referred to above, which, taken together, were to supersede the Code of Civil Procedure. 

These acts, with some modifications, were adopted by the legislature in 1920, and became operative on October 1st, 

§ 11. The Civil Practice Act. 

Of the acts enumerated in the preceding section, the Civil Practice Act is the basic one." This act "except as otherwise expressly provided shall apply to the civil practice in all the courts of record of the State."" Such act and the Rules of 

Civil Practice will be the subject of special consideration throughout this book. Many of its provisions are identical with corresponding provisions of the Code of Civil Pro cedure, and many other of its provisions are, in substance, the same as the corresponding code provisions. When, therefore, decisions of the courts are cited in support of the position taken in regard to the meaning of the sections of the Civil Practice Act and these decisions relate to sections of the Code of Civil Procedure, such decisions are considered authoritative because of the substantial identity of the sections of the Civil Practice Act and the Code. In cases where there is a substantial difference in the language of the corresponding sections of the Civil Practice Act and the Code, either the decisions relating to such Code sections will not be cited, or if cited, such difference will be discussed in connection with the decisions.

INTRODUCTION. 

15 

§ 12. Changes in the Common Law and Equity Procedure Effected by the Code and Civil Practice Act Generally Considered. 

Section 8 of the Civil Practice Act' provides that 

"There is only one form of civil action. The distinction between actions at law and suits in equity, and the forms of these actions and suits, have been abolished." 

The language here used led many to think immediately after the adoption of the Code that the principles of law and equity which were at the foundation of the old systems and were enforced by them were abolished, but no such change was contemplated by the framers of the Code provision nor was any such change made. It was not the principles of law or equity but the mode of enforcing them that was abolished. 

It is the procedure that is new and not the principles. The rights, whether legal or equitable, which were formerly protected and enforced by actions at law and suits in equity, are now protected and enforced by a form of procedure called in the Civil Practice Act a "Civil Action.""" The Civil Prac tice Act does not, therefore, make unnecessary the study of common law and equitable principles, but it does largely dispense with the necessity of studying the common law and equity procedure formerly used to give them effect.

The Court of Appeals § 13. Courts and Judges. 

A court is a tribunal organized according to law and sitting at fixed times and places for the administration of justice. 

A judge or justice is an individual holding a judicial office.¹

There is a distinction between a court, as such, and a judge or justice thereof out of court, or at chambers. Sometimes the judicial function may be exercised only by the court, as such; sometimes only by a judge or justice of the court as distinguished from the court itself; sometimes by either.² 

A court of General Jurisdiction is one having the power or competency to take cognizance of all classes of litigable controversies, e. g., the Supreme Court of New York State. A + Throughout this chapter the term jurisdiction is used in the sense of jurisdiction of the subject matter of a controversy unless another sense is

court of Limited Jurisdiction is one having the power or competency of taking cognizance only of particular classes of judicial proceedings and of no others,-usually only those classes expressly specified in the statute creating or defining the powers of the court. The Municipal Court of the City of 

New York, for instance, is a court of Limited Jurisdiction which would never have jurisdiction of a divorce action, for example. A court of Original Jurisdiction is a court which hears cases in the first instance, e. g., the City Court of the City of New York. Such a court hears the testimony of witnesses which is taken down by stenographers as the witnesses testify from the witness stand. A court of Appellate 

Jurisdiction is one which ordinarily has no original jurisdiction at all,—e. g., the Court of Appeals of New York State. 

Such a court ordinarily has no witness stand and rarely hears witnesses orally. It considers only arguments by lawyers based upon a printed "record" of the testimony in the court below, and on printed briefs.

Justices of the Peace.10 § 16. The Municipal Court of the City of New York. 

The Municipal Court Code divides the City of New York into twenty-eight municipal court districts wherein the justices of the court are elected and its sessions are held.¹¹ 

The power and authority of the court (except as otherwise expressly prescribed) extends to the whole of the City of New York, and its process may be served and executed in any part of that city.12 Except as the statute creating it or its own rules provide otherwise, practice in the court conforms to that of the Supreme Court in like cases. 13 14 The court has no inherent competency. It is a court of limited original jurisdiction, and possesses no powers other than those conferred by the statute creating it. It may not give general affirmative equitable relief, but may entertain and give effect to equitable defenses.15 

The jurisdiction is fully defined by Section 6 of the Municipal Court Code. It includes actions on contract, express or implied (except actions on contracts to marry), and actions for torts (except actions for assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, defamation, criminal conversation, seduction or loss of society of husband or wife), when the amount claimed in the summons does not exceed One 

Thousand Dollars, exclusive of interest and costs. Actions may be brought in the court to recover a chattel or chattels of an aggregate value not exceeding One Thousand Dollars, with or without damages for the taking or detention thereof.

§ 19. Courts of Justices of the Peace. 

Justices of the Peace are elected by the electors of the several towns as directed by the legislature.28 They have only the original jurisdiction expressly conferred upon them by statute.29 This jurisdiction is fully defined by Article I of the Justice Court Act. It includes actions for breach of contract (except actions for breach of contract to marry), where the sum claimed does not exceed Two Hundred Dollars.30 They may not take cognizance of actions for assault, battery, false imprisonment, libel, slander, criminal conversation, seduction or malicious prosecution, nor of an action wherein the defendant sets forth in his answer facts showing that the title to real property will come in question. 

An appeal from a Court of Justice of the Peace is taken to the County Court of the county where the judgment was rendered.81

§ 20. The County Courts Outside the City of New York. 

There is a county court in each county of the state except the County of New York.32 The county courts of the counties of Kings, Bronx, Queens and Richmond have no civil jurisdiction.33 County courts outside the City of New York have a limited original jurisdiction in equity and at law defined by 

Article VI, Section 11 of the Constitution and Section 67 of the Civil Practice Act.34 

The equity jurisdiction extends to the following actions relating to real property situated within the county: Actions for the partition of the real property, for dower therein, for the foreclosure, redemption or satisfaction of a mortgage thereon, for the foreclosure of a lien arising out of a contract for the sale thereof, for specific performance of a contract relating thereto, and for the enforcement of a mechanic's lien thereon.35 It includes also actions to foreclose a lien not exceeding One Thousand Dollars upon a chattel found within the county. 86 The jurisdiction of actions at law is subject to two limitations: (1) In actions to recover money only (except actions on judgments rendered in the same court) the complaint may not demand judgment for a sum exceeding Three Thousand Dollars, and in actions to recover chattels, with or without damages for the taking or detention thereof, the aggregate value of the chattels may not exceed One Thousand Dollars. (2) It must appear that all the defendants are residents of the county when the action is commenced, or that the defendant has an office for the transaction of business within the county and that the cause of action arose therein. § 22. The Court of Claims. 

The State of New York, being sovereign, may not be sued in its courts without its consent. The Court of Claims has five judges who have jurisdiction to hear, audit and determine private claims against the state where the state consents to be sued thereon in that court.48 The jurisdiction and practice of the court are defined and regulated by the Court of Claims Act. Three judges usually sit in each case. An appeal from the court is taken to the Appellate Division of the 

Supreme Court in the Third or Fourth Departments." § 23. The Supreme Court; Its Unlimited Jurisdiction. 

The Constitution provides that the Supreme Court shall have "general jurisdiction in law and equity.""50 The Court of Appeals has said of this constitutional provision: “The terms used are so comprehensive that they include all cases of every description in law and equity, from the most important and complicated to the most simple and insignificant, and they imperatively and positively establish the court with that extended jurisdiction 

If a claim is made litigable at all, that is to say if made the subject of a suit or litigation in a court of law, then under the express provision of the Constitution the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court attaches at once. It is true that the prosecution of small claims in the 

Supreme Court may be made unprofitable by provisions as

60 Any justice of the court may, in general, perform the duties of his office or hold court in any county.50 The original jurisdiction of the court is exercised at its Trial Terms and Special Terms, which must be held by one justice at the times and places fixed therefor according to law. A Trial Term is a term for jury trials. Matters not triable by jury (including equity cases) are heard at a Special Term. A Trial Term or a Special Term may be divided into parts, each part being held by one justice. The number of parts in which a Trial 

Term or a Special Term is held in a particular county, and the allocation of business to the respective parts, are matters regulated by the rules adopted by the court in the particular county. 61

§ 27. The Supreme Court; Its Appellate Terms. 

Article VI, Section 3, of the Constitution empowers the Appellate Divisions in the first and second judicial departments severally to establish an Appellate Term of the Supreme Court in its department to be constituted of not less than three nor more than five justices of the Supreme Court designated by the Appellate Division from the justices who are residents of the department. The Appellate Term in either department may hear and determine appeals to the Supreme Court from the Municipal Court of the City of New York and the City Court of the City of New York. No more than three justices of an Appellate Term may sit in any case; two of the justices shall constitute a quorum, and the concurrence of two is necessary to a decision."2 

§ 28. The Court of Appeals. 

"The jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals is designated and created by law, and it has no other,””3 This jurisdiction is conferred in part by the Constitution, and in part by 

69. Const., Art. VI, § 2. Cf. Judici ary Law, § 71. The official terms of justices of the Supreme Court shall be fourteen years from and including the first day of January next after their election. Const., Art. VI, § 4. 

70. Const., Art. VI, § 2; Judiciary Law, § 81. 

71. Const., Art. VI, § 2. 

72. For the history of the Appellate Terms prior to the present Article 

VI, § 3, of the Constitution, see Dick son v. Manhattan Ry. Co., 45 Misc. 

572, 91 N. Y. S. 36, and C. P. A., § 627. 

73. Croveno v. Atlantic Ave. R. R. 

Co., 150 N. Y. 225, 228.

statute. The court has no original jurisdiction, but is limited to the review of the determinations of other courts." 74 Restrictions are placed upon the jurisdiction of the court by the Constitution, which also empowers the legislature further to restrict that jurisdiction, subject only to the limitation that the right of appeal to the court shall not depend upon the amount involved.75

In all cases the jurisdiction is limited to the review of questions of law, with two exceptions." Not all civil cases may be brought to the court as matter of right. In many cases the Appellate Divisions of the Supreme Court have final appellate power. The reason for the limited jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals is "the theory of the court's function in our judicial system, which the Constitution reveals. That function the court itself has defined. It is, briefly stated, the function, not of declaring justice between man and man, but of settling the law. The court exists, not for the individual litigant, but for the indefinite body of litigants, whose causes are potentially involved in the specific cause at issue. The wrongs of aggrieved suitors are only the algebraic symbols from which the court is to work out the formula of justice.""77

The composition of the court is defined by Article VI, Section 5, of the Constitution. The court consists of a Chief 

Judge and six associate judges, chosen by the electors of the state, and such justices of the Supreme Court (not more than four) as may be designated by the governor for service in the Court of Appeals when the court shall certify that the causes pending therein have so accumulated that they may not otherwise be disposed of with reasonable speed. 

Five members of the court constitute a quorum, and the concurrence of four is necessary to decision, but no more than seven judges shall sit in any case.

An appeal may be taken directly to the Court of Appeals from an inferior court of record (e. g. not from a Court of a 

Justice of the Peace, however, since such court is not a court of record) where the only question involved is a constitutional one.77a

Problems 

1. X, a resident of Montana, sues Y, a resident of Suffolk county, for $3,000 for breach of promise of marriage. The action is brought in the County Court of Nassau county, and although Y works in Suffolk county, he was served with the summons while watching polo matches in Great Neck, Nassau county. The promise of marriage was made in Nassau county and later repudiated there. Is the forum chosen proper one? If so, why? If not, why not? 

2. All the above facts appearing in the complaint, Y serves an answer counterclaiming for damages for $10,000 for breach of promise. X moves to dismiss on the ground that the court has no jurisdiction of the subject matter of the counterclaim. Motion granted or denied? Why? 

3. Suppose that the facts are the same as in Problem No. 2, except that X's motion to dismiss is based on the ground that the court has not jurisdiction of the parties to the action. Motion granted or denied? Why? 

4. A, a resident of Montana, sues Y, a Suffolk policeman residing in Suffolk county, for $10,000 for breach of promise of marriage, serving Y with a summons in Manhattan. The action is brought in the City Court of the City of New York, New York county. Is this a proper forum? If so, why? If not, why not? 

5. A, resident of New York county, was wilfully and unlawfully punched by the doorman of B's apartment house in New York county because A parked six minutes in front of the house. Both B and his doorman reside in New York county and never leave the limits of the city of New York. A spent $200 for medical services and wants to sue for $500 damages. (a) In what courts could you bring the action? (b) In what court would you bring the action? Why? 

6. X, a resident of New York county, has a $2,500 mortgage on 

Y's house at No. 2000 Jarvis place in Nassau county. The scrivener erroneously made the mortgage read No. 200 Jarvis place. X wants to reform the mortgage and foreclose it because it is past due. In which of the following courts could the action properly be brought: (a) City Court of the City of New York, Queens county; (b) County 

Court, Nassau county; (c) Supreme Court, Nassau county; (d) 

Supreme Court, New York county. 7. X sued his former partner Y in the City Court of the City of 

New York, New York county, for an "exact accounting of the $500 to $800 due to plaintiff." Both reside in Manhattan. (a) Is the forum a proper one? Why? (b) Assuming that the forum was proper, if Y was served with the summons at the races in Saratoga,

would the service be valid? (c) Would the Municipal Court of the 

City of New York have jurisdiction if the summons was served in 

New York city? 

8. Could actions in the following courts be properly started by the service of a summons on a defendant in Albany, if both plaintiff and defendant reside in New York county: (a) Supreme Court, New York county. (b) County Court, Nassau county. (c) City Court of the City of New York, New York county. 

(d) Municipal Court of the City of New York, Borough of Man hattan, ninth district. (e) Action between two Seneca (N. Y.) Indians involving Indian lands where complaint shows Peacemaker's Court has no jurisdiction. 

9. (a) Replevin of a $900 automobile. County Court, Suffolk county. Plaintiff and defendant both reside in New York county. 

Has the court jurisdiction? If so, why? If not, why not? (b) Answer the same or different if automobile worth $2,000?

Blackacre for $900. (d) A taxicab company for $900 for personal injuries when four people with her at the time join with her in the complaint, separately state their injuries, and each demand $900, for a grand total of $4,500.

§ 29. Introduction. 

The courts of the state and the general scope of the matters over which they may acquire jurisdiction have been considered. Before any court, however, may exercise its authority in this general field, it must be given jurisdiction in the particular case in question. It cannot acquire this jurisdiction on its own initiative. Even though the court may know the nature of the difference between two parties it cannot, upon its own responsibility, adjudicate the matters involved. Its authority must be invoked by the parties themselves, or, at least, by one of them. 

§ 30. Actions and Special Proceedings. 

When the authority of a court is once invoked it proceeds to act in one or the other of two general ways. It has but two modes of operation. If it proceeds along one of these lines, its proceedings are styled "an action;" if along the [41]

THE SUMMONS. 

other line, they are called "a special proceeding." The distinction is arbitrary. Both civil actions and special proceedings are brought for the same purpose, viz: the enforcement or protection of a right or the redress or prevention of a wrong. The difference between them is that the action is the ordinary prosecution for such a purpose; the special proceeding is not. An action is commenced by the service of the summons. Unless a civil prosecution can be so commenced, it is not an action. A special proceeding is commenced otherwise than by service of a summons. An action terminates in a final judgment, a special proceeding in a final order or decree.2 

1. Civil Practice Act, §§ 4, 5, 6. 

2. Civil Practice Act, §§ 218, 472; 

Matter of Gibson, 195 N. Y. 466, 469. 

§ 31. The Summons in Reference to Jurisdiction. 

In the ordinary case, a court has no power adversely to affect the right of a defendant in an action until the summons has been served upon him. There are situations, however, in which it is essential to protection of a plaintiff's right that he invoke the aid of the courts before an action is commenced in the usual way. The Civil Practice Act defines the provisional remedies arrest, temporary injunction, attachment, and temporary receivership. Replevin, too, partakes of the nature of a provisional remedy. The object of a provisional remedy is to make ultimate relief to the plaintiff effective by assuring the presence of the defendant's person or property for satisfaction of final process against him in the action. An order of arrest or of temporary injunction, or a warrant of attachment, may be granted before an action is commenced; and a chattel may be replevied before the summons is served in an action to recover a chattel (replevin). If a provisional remedy is allowed before service of the summons in an action, the court acquires conditional jurisdiction of the action and has control of all the subsequent proceedings, unless the conditional jurisdiction is divested. A similar situation exists where a summons is delivered to the sheriff for service under Civil Practice Act, Section 17.

§ 32. The Rules of Civil Practice and the Summons. 

Section 218 of the Civil Practice Act provides that "Rules may be made respecting the requisites and form of a summons and notice and indorsements thereon." There are many other provisions of the Civil Practice Act, which like section 218, require supplemental regulations too detailed for insertion in the act itself. The justices of the Supreme 

Court comprising the appellate divisions thereof in all four departments are charged with the duty of formulating rules of practice to supply these details," and they meet in alternate years or oftener, in Albany, for this purpose. However, in order to formulate the initial set of rules to accompany the Civil Practice Act, the legislature created a convention of judges and lawyers and empowered it to formulate rules to supplement the provisions of the Civil Practice Act. This convention met and adopted three hundred rules called the 

Rules of Civil Practice. Of these rules 45 to 53 inclusive relate to the form and requisites of the summons and must be read in conjunction with the Civil Practice Act sections on this subject. 

§ 33. Form of Summons-In General." 

The requisites of a summons are stated in rule 45 of the 

Rules of Civil Practice. A form of summons which complies with the requirements there laid down, follows:

JOHN DOE, against

RICHARD ROE, Plaintiff, Defendant. 

To the above-named defendant:

You ARE HEREBY SUMMONED to answer the complaint in this action and to serve a copy of your answer, or, if the complaint is not served with this summons, to serve a notice of appearance, on the plaintiff's attorney within twenty days after the service of this summons, exclu-

Naming parties in the ordinary case. 

In naming the parties their full names should appear. 

Middle names are not necessary, but the given name and the surname should be inserted in full. Abbreviations such as “ Wm.” for “ William," while not illegal, should be avoided.

Initials are not sufficient.10 If a married woman is a party to an action, her name should be inserted and not the given name of her husband. "Mrs. William Jones " is not proper; it should be "Mary Jones.''11 In case a corporation is a party, the name by which the concern is incorporated is the proper one to insert in the title.12 If a partnership is a party, the names of the partners should appear in the title and not merely the firm name under which the partners do business.13 

Parties suing in a representative capacity. 

Sometimes a person brings an action or is prosecuted not in his individual capacity, but as a representative of some other party. Such would be the case where a trustee in bankruptcy wishes to bring suit or is prosecuted. In a case of this kind the word " as " with a description of the capacity in which the party is suing or defending should follow the name of the party in the title. For example "John Doe as 

Trustee in Bankruptcy of the Rosedale Manufacturing Company," would be the proper way to express the name of the party in such a case. The same rule applies where an administrator or an executor is suing or being sued in his representative capacity. In the case of an unincorporated association (consisting of any number of persons), suit may be prosecuted or defended in the name of the president or treasurer thereof. Moreover, any partnership or any company of persons which has a president or treasurer is deemed an association within the meaning of this law. The word 14

An infant as a party. (6 Persons under twenty-one years of age may sue and be sued, but a guardian ad litem must sooner or later be appointed for them.16 In the case of an infant plaintiff, the following would be the form used in naming him as a party: 'George Brown, an infant, by Edgar Tilden, his guardian ad litem." The reason for this is that in the case of an infant plaintiff the guardian is appointed before the summons is served, while in the case of an infant defendant the appointment usually takes place afterward.18 But failure to appoint a guardian ad litem for an infant defendant renders any judgment against such minor defendant improper.10

§ 35. The Body of the Summons. 

The form of the body of the summons is given in rule 45. 

The form there given applies to actions in the Supreme Court and in the county courts. If the action is begun in the city court of the city of New York, the word "twenty" in the form should be changed to "six" in the usual case.

If the summons in a City Court action is served by publication, the defendant must always be given ten days to answer;21 and where an order of arrest is granted in certain marine cases in that court, the defendant must be summoned to answer forthwith.22 Otherwise the form is applicable to the city court.28 The date at the end of the form should be filled out as of the date when the summons is issued. In municipal courts the summons may be issued out of the court by the clerk on forms provided for that purpose, or by an attorney on the form prescribed in the Municipal Court Code," and the wording of these forms differs somewhat from the form contained in rule 45. the defendants. § 36. The Subscription of the Summons. 

The summons must be subscribed by the plaintiff's attorney but this subscription may be in typewriting or print.25 The office and post office address of the attorney should follow the signature as appears on the form given above.26 Section 

236 of the Civil Practice Act permits a party to prosecute his own suit, and in such case he may sign the summons himself.27 Attorneys however are forbidden to allow others to sue out process in their name merely to give it validity and therefore, if a party has an attorney in an action he cannot act in person except with the consent of the court.28 

After a summons which is signed by an attorney is served, a party who desires to act for himself must obtain the consent of the court to conduct any of the subsequent proceedings in the action.

§ 39. Defects in a Summons, Void and Irregular Process. 

The summons is not always drawn to conform strictly with the foregoing rules and it is necessary now to consider the legal effect of the failure of the summons to conform to such requirements. Defects in the summons are of two general classes. Certain defects make the summons absolutely void, others make it merely irregular. If the defect is of such a character that the court does not get jurisdiction in the case, the summons is absolutely void and has no legal value whatever; but if the mistake is of such a character that it does not defeat the purpose of the summons in giving the court jurisdiction, the summons is not void but merely irregular, and as the court has jurisdiction it can correct the mistake." 

The function of a summons is to give notice to a defendant that an action is begun against him and to warn him of the consequences of a failure on his part to pay heed to the notice. 

If the paper in question does not perform these functions it will be void, for in that case the court does not get jurisdiction of the defendant; but if it does perform these functions even though it does not comply in all respects with the requirements of the statute and rules, it will not be void, but merely irregular.

In the case of Stuyvesant v. Weil, 167 N. Y. 421, which involved foreclosure, the defendant named in the summons was Emma J. Stockton. The real name of the defendant, however, was Mary J. Stockton. The summons was served on the proper person. After the summons was served the attorney for the plaintiff discovered the mistake and corrected it with the approval and direction of the court. The action proceeded to judgment and the property was sold. 

The purchaser, however, refused to take title contending that the mistake in the summons defeated the jurisdiction of the court. In holding that the summons was good, the court 

Elder v. Morse, 214 A. D. 632; 212

§ 42. Notice of No Personal Claim Served with Summons- Municipal Court Endorsement as to Ownership and Control. 

Sometimes it is necessary to make defendants of parties against whom the plaintiff has no personal claim whatsoever. 

Tenants in a building which is the subject matter of a mortgage foreclosure action would generally illustrate this kind of case. To prevent such defendants from defending the action and getting costs against the plaintiff, it is provided that a plaintiff may serve with the summons upon such defendants" a notice subscribed by plaintiff's attorney setting forth the general object of the action, a brief description of the property affected by it, if it affects specific real or personal property, and that a personal claim is not made against" such defendant. If such defendant thereafter unreasonably defends the action, costs may be awarded against him.50

In the Municipal Court of the City of New York, in a negligence action, if plaintiff's" endorsement" on the summons states the registration or license number of a vehicle, ownership and control is deemed admitted unless the answer contains a specific denial in that regard.5¹

§ 43. Ways of Serving a Summons and Order of Treatment. 

To give the court jurisdiction, the summons must not only be correctly drawn, but it must be properly served. There are three kinds of service.¹ Personal service, substituted service and service by publication. We shall consider here, personal service and later² service by the other methods. In treating of personal service of the summons we shall consider first, who may make personal service, second, where it must be made and when, and third, how it must be made.

§ 44. Who May Make Personal Service. 

Any person may make personal service of the summons excepting (a) a party to the action, and (b) a person under eighteen years of age. Failure to observe these requirements, however, does not make the service void, but only irregular.* 

§ 45. Where Personal Service Must Be Made and When. 

Personal service must, as a rule, be made within the territorial limits of the court's authority. As the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is co-extensive with the boundaries of the state, the service of a Supreme Court summons may be made anywhere within the state. Service of it, however, outside of the state gives the court no jurisdiction. A summons or other process out of a county court may likewise be served anywhere in the state, but this is by special statutory authority. A summons issuing out of the city court need not be served within the limits of the former city of New York which includes the boroughs of Manhattan and The Bronx, but may be served anywhere within the Greater City of New York. In the municipal court a summons must be served within the city limits."

B. Service on an infant.

To serve a summons upon an infant it is sometimes necessary before service is complete, to deliver a copy of the summons to three different people. (a). In all cases of infancy a copy of the summons must be delivered to the father, mother or guardian if any one of them be within the state, and if not within the state to the person having the care and control of him, or with whom he resides, or in whose service he is employed.17 (b). In case the infant is fourteen years or over another copy must be delivered to the infant. This is not required where the infant is under fourteen. (c). The court may in its discretion require in all cases of infancy that a copy of the summons be delivered to a person designated by it, e. g. where both parents are incurable drunkards. 

C. Service on an incompetent.

If the natural person is judicially declared incompetent to manage his affairs on account of lunacy, idiocy or habitual drunkenness, service upon him is made in the ordinary way, with the additional requirement that an extra copy be served upon the committee appointed by the court to take charge of his person or his property.18 The court, however, may in such case dispense with service upon the incompetent and if it believes that the interest of the incompetent's committee is adverse, or that he is not fit, it may designate a person on whom service must be made.10 If the person has not been judicially declared of unsound mind the service is made in the usual way. The court may, however, in such a case, direct a copy to be served upon some person whom it will designate.20 This may be done also in the case of habitual drunkards and others if the court believes for any reason, that the person upon whom service has been made is not a fit person to protect the defendant's interest.21

§ 47. Personal Service on a Domestic Corporation.23 Section 228 of the Civil Practice Act clearly states the method of serving a summons upon a domestic corporation. 

Subdivision 1 shows how service may be made on the city of New York; subdivision 2 shows the method of service upon any other city, and subdivision 3 provides a method of service upon a domestic private corporation. Service is made under any of these subdivisions by delivering a copy of the summons to the officer or person named in the subdivision. Those persons in the case of a private domestic corporation are the president, vice-president, secretary, assistant secretary, " clerk, " cashier, treasurer, assistant treasurer, director or managing agent. The obvious purpose is to serve someone connected with the corporation of sufficiently high rank to render it reasonably certain that the corporation will be apprised of the commencement of the action.25

The only one of the persons named in the section about whom doubt is likely to arise is the managing agent of a domestic private corporation. Judge Cardozo in Tauza v. 

Susquehanna Coal Company, 220 N. Y. 259, at page 269, lays down the following rule for determining who is a managing agent: "If the persons named are true agents, and if their positions are such as to lead to a just presumption that notice to them will be notice to the principal, the corporation must submit." In Barrett v. The American 

Telephone Co., 31 State Reporter, 465, which was affirmed

§ 49. The Same Classification of Foreign Corporations. 

In applying the method of service outlined in section 229 of the Civil Practice Act (formerly section 432 of the Code) and now interpreted with substantial accord by state and federal courts, a classification of foreign corporations into those doing business in the state and those not doing business in the state must be made. To the latter class of foreign corporations the provisions of the section do not apply. 

The personal service of a summons upon such corporations cannot be made. To extend the provisions of section 229 of the Civil Practice Act to such corporations would render the section unconstitutional.30

1. Sec. 218 Gen. Corp. 3. Sec. 224 Gen. Corp. Law provides that a foreign corporation may always be sued by a resident of New York. It was formerly held that if a summons was served upon an officer of a foreign corporation while he was passing through the state or temporarily within the state, even though the corporation was not doing business here, such service would give our courts jurisdiction over the corporation, since the provisions of the section (229 of the Civil 

Practice Act, 432 of the Code) were literally complied with.³¹

But the federal courts held otherwise and insisted that to sustain judgments obtained after such service would be to deprive the foreign corporations of their property without due process of law in violation of the fourteenth amendment of the Federal Constitution, and our courts finally adopted the federal rule and agreed that personal service cannot be made on such corporation." 32 It is, therefore, of extreme importance that we be able to distinguish between those two classes of corporations, since if we place the foreign corporation in the class not doing business in the state it is useless to attempt to serve the summons personally upon it. Moreover, it is not safe. simply to write to the secretary of state and ascertain from him whether the corporation has filed a certificate pursuant to section 210-212 of the General Corporation Law authorizing it to do business here. Of course, if such a certificate is on file, it is safe to assume that the corporation is doing business here, but if there is no certificate on file, it is not safe to infer that the corporation is not doing business here. 

Many foreign corporations are doing business here which ought to have procured such a certificate but have failed or neglected to procure one. Many other foreign corporations are doing business here which are not required to procure any such certificate. The corporation which is engaged in interstate or foreign commerce may do business in this state without any such certificate. The test which determines whether a foreign corporation is or is not doing business in the state is the following: are its activities within the state casual and occasional, or are they systematic and regular. If the former it is not, but if the latter it is doing business within the state.³*

§ 50. The Same-Suits Against Foreign Corporations Not Doing Business Here. 

It is not to be inferred, however, that suits may not be maintained in the courts of this state against foreign corporations which are not doing business here. This is not the fact. Such suits may be maintained, but jurisdiction over corporations of this class must be secured by publication which is a means other than by the personal service of the summons upon them. The ways of obtaining jurisdiction over these corporations will be considered later. (Chapters VI and VII, post.)

It should also be noted here that even though a means be found for obtaining jurisdiction over this class of foreign corporations they may not be sued in our courts by nonresidents or other foreign corporations except in cases specified in the first three subdivisions of section 225 of the General Corporation Law. Generally speaking, those subdivisions limit such actions to 1. Actions on contracts made within the state or relating to property situated within the state when the contract was made; 

2. Actions for the recovery of real property within the state or a chattel replevied within the state; and 

3. Cases where the cause of action arose within the state.35 siery Mills, Inc., 247 N. Y. 592. The 

Court of Appeals has also decided, on the other hand, that the question whether a foreign corporation is doing business in this state, in the sense of the statutes requiring a license therefor by foreign corporations not engaged in interstate commerce turns on a different test. International Text 

Book Co. v. Tone, 220 N. Y. 313;

Inter. Fuel & Iron Corp. v. Donner 

Steel Co., 242 N. Y. 224. 

35. General Corporation Law, § 225. 

The section follows: 

"Section 225. Action against foreign corporation by another foreign corporation or non-resident. An action against a foreign corporation may be maintained by another foreign corporation, or by a non-resident, in one of the following cases only: 

1. Where the action is brought to recover damages for the breach of a contract made within the state, or relating to property situated within the state, at the time of the making thereof. 

2. Where it is brought to recover real property situated within the state, or a chattel, which is replevied within the state. 

3. Where the cause of action arose within the state, except where the object of the action is to affect the title to real property situated without the state. 

4. Where a foreign corporation is doing business within this state." 3

On the other hand, foreign corporations which are doing business here may be sued by non-residents and other foreign corporations without restriction." 

§ 51. The Same How Personal Service Is Effected on Foreign Corporations Doing Business Here. 

The personal service of a summons upon a foreign corporation doing business in this state is ordinarily effected by delivering a copy thereof to one of the officers mentioned in subdivision 1 of section 229 of the Civil Practice Act or by delivering it to one of the persons designated in subdivision 

2 thereof. If service cannot be effected under subdivision 2, or an officer specified in subdivision 1 cannot with due diligence be found within the state, a copy of the summons may be delivered to the cashier, a director, or managing agent of the corporation within the state. 

The order in which you proceed is of importance here.

§ 52. Exceptions to the General Rules Respecting Personal Service of the Summons - Privileged Persons. 

In certain privileged cases service made in conformity with the above regulations will not be effective to give the court jurisdiction. A non-resident who comes voluntarily into the state to attend a court as a suitor or witness or to assist in the administration of justice in almost any capacity is privileged from service while he is prosecuting that purpose, the theory being that this will encourage the attendance upon our courts of those whose attendance cannot be compelled.39 He is also privileged while he is coming to the court or returning home therefrom provided he returns with reasonable dispatch ier, a director or a managing agent of the corporation, within the state."

The statute now reads: 

"3. To the cashier, a director or a managing agent of the corporation, within the state, if service cannot be effected under subdivision two of this section, or an officer of the corporation specified in subdivision one of this section, with due diligence, cannot be found within the state."

Whether this change signifies a legislative intent to permit resort to subdivision 3 after resort to either subdivision 1 or subdivision 2 must await interpretation by the courts.

The requirement found in the subdivision of the Code that "the corporation has property within the state or the cause of action arose therein" is not found in the Civil Practice Act.

§ 54. Proof of Service. 

While personal service is now complete, the court is, of course, not informed as to the manner in which it was made. 

The paper containing information on this point is called the proof of service and rule 53 of the Rules of Civil Practice states the manner of making such proof. If the sheriff serves the summons, subdivision 1 (a) of that rule provides that the certificate of the sheriff will suffice as proof of service. Subdivision 1 (b) of the rule provides a second method of proving service by a written admission signed and acknowledged by the defendant served, but as it is seldom or never used it may be disregarded, except to comment that the admission is insufficient proof if it is not acknowledged or accompanied by an affidavit as required by the rule, or if it fails to state the place and manner of service, as required by subdivision 3. The principal method of proving service provided by rule 53 is by means of the affidavit of the person who has made the service. § 55. Affidavits Generally and an Affidavit of Service. 

An affidavit is a sworn statement of facts made before a person authorized to administer oaths.15 The persons so authorized are specified in section 357 of the Civil Practice Act. A notary public and a commissioner of deeds are found in the list and are the persons most commonly used. The affidavit is a very important tool used in law offices and intimate acquaintance with it is required. After serving a summons, therefore, the person who makes the service should sign a statement of facts in affidavit form, sufficient to show that he has complied with the law and the rules of the court in making the service and swear to the same before one of these officers. A form for such an affidavit in a very simple case follows:

(Sd.) 

EDGAR BAXON, Notary Public, Kings County, 

New York County Clerk's No. 93, Commission expires March 30, 1923.

The above is a very simple form of an affidavit of service. 

If service of a summons were made, however, on a foreign corporation by serving a director thereof, the affidavit of service would have to be quite elaborate, since, as we have seen, service on a director is authorized only after a diligent effort has been made, and without success, to serve some one of the persons mentioned in subdivisions 1 or 2 of section 

229 of the Civil Practice Act. The affidavit must show what efforts have been made to serve such persons. Whether the efforts which have been made show "due diligence" which the statute requires is a question for the court, in case the court is ever called upon to pass on the matter, and the affidavit must show the facts in the case to enable the court to determine whether legal service has or has not been made. 

The following form has been tested in court and held insufficient for the above reason:

Sworn to before me this day of August,

Deponent further says that he knew the person he served as aforesaid to be an officer in said defendant corporation.

§ 57. The Same-Requisites of an Affidavit and the Parts Thereof. 

After the summons is served all papers used in an action should begin with the title. Hence, the affidavits used in the preceding section begin with the title. § 58. The Same-In Matrimonial Actions. 

In addition to the facts required in the ordinary affidavit of service, if the action be a matrimonial one, the affidavit "shall state what knowledge the affiant had of the identity of the person served with the defendant named and how he acquired such knowledge." This is even required when the sheriff makes the service in addition to the sheriff's certificate of service, otherwise the officer who made the service must appear at the trial and testify in court as to such knowledge.50 The affidavit in such cases must also show affirmatively, if the complaint was not served with the summons, that the required notice specified in section 1167 of the Civil Practice Act was written or printed on the face of the copy of the summons delivered to the defendant.5¹ 

§ 59. Filing of Summons. 

The summons and each pleading in an action must be filed with the clerk by the party in whose behalf it is served within five days after notice from the adverse party requiring such filing, and upon failure to comply with such notice the court or a judge, in its or his discretion, may order that the summons or pleading be deemed abandoned either absolutely or upon failure to file within a time, if any, permitted by the order.52
