§ 60. Introduction. 

It was stated in section 39 that a summons which was not properly drawn was sometimes void altogether, in which case the court does not acquire jurisdiction at all over the defendant, and sometimes the defect in the summons only made it irregular, in which case the court acquired jurisdiction and might correct the mistake. The same thing is true with reference to the service of a summons. Failure to follow the law and rules with reference to this may result in void service or merely irregular service, depending, as above, on the question as to whether the court acquired jurisdiction over the defendant or not.

At first blush one would think that if the defect in either the summons or its service rendered the process void, it would be unnecessary to do anything, since a void process is no process at all. A little reflection, however, will show that such process may not be regarded by any one, except the defendant, as void. No one is likely to view the summons or its service very critically except defendant and it is entirely possible that a judgment might be entered against the defendant as a result of a failure on his part to heed even a void summons or a void service thereof. Of course, the judgment, too, will be void and may be declared so by a court if the matter is properly brought to the court's attention, but if this is not done, the judgment stands as a matter of record and might impair defendant's credit or defeat the sale by him of his real property, or become the basis of a levy by the sheriff on his goods. Even a void judgment may be very annoying. It will be seen, therefore, that it is not wise to ignore a void process, and whether void or merely irregular, it is generally wise for one to avail himself of his rights in the premises and enforce the remedies afforded by law in such cases. It is the defendant's right to have a void process or void service thereof set aside by the court and an irregular process or an irregular service corrected. Such a right is enforced by means of a motion.¹ 

1. In the Municipal Court of the 

City of New York, there is a special procedure in this connection, whereby a notice of special appearance is filed with the clerk, after which the "traverse" of service is set down for a hearing and the "traversing" party is automatically absolved from further pleading until directed to do so by the court. Mun. Court Code, §§ 78, subd. 

8; 88.

§ 61. Motions: General Nature of. 

Motions are subordinate and incidental steps in the progress of an action. The main steps in an action are the process, the pleadings, the trial and the judgment. These will be taken up in order in this book. Generally speaking, process gives the court jurisdiction in the particular case; pleading is the step in the action where the parties state their respective positions with reference to the matter in litigation and thereby disclose the differences between their contentions, or the "issues,' as they are called; the trial is the part of the action where these issues are determined; and the judgment is the instrument embodying the results of the trial or other determination of the action. If each of these main steps were taken just as the law and rules direct, there would be little need for motions; but if error creeps in anywhere along the main line of an action's progress, a motion is resorted to for its correction. So, where there are defects in the summons or its service, a motion must be made to correct the mistake. It consists of an application to the court or to a judge or justice thereof for the incidental relief sought." When the application is decided the court or judge will embody his determination in the form of a paper called an order.³

In connection with the other main steps in the action, motions are necessary also and such motions will be considered where the main step to which they are incident and subordinate is under discussion.* 

2. Civil Practice Act, § 113. 

3. Civil Practice Act, § 127. 

4. A motion is not a principal rem edy. The Civil Practice Act describes two principal remedies: (1) an action; (2) a special proceeding. (§ 30 ante.) The right to apply to a court for relief by motion is not an independent right. The right to relief by motion depends upon the relevancy of that relief to the principal remedy in connection with which the motion is made. It follows that in the ordinary case the object of a motion is to procure relief collateral to the main purpose of the action or special proceeding in which the motion is made, and that the subject of a motion is usually some matter of procedure. Matter of Jetter, 

78 N. Y. 601, 605; Matter of Dietz, 138 App. Div. 283, 122 N. Y. S. 1063.

The Civil Practice Act defines a mo tion as an application for an order 

(Civil Practice Act, § 113). The reason for this definition is that the determination of a motion is usually embodied in a paper called an order. 

This definition should be understood to include oral motions made to a court during the trial of a litigation before it. Motions so made are not strictly applications for orders, and are deter-

§ 62. Motion Papers. 

Two things are usually necessary before a court will act. (a) Facts must be brought officially to its attention, and (b) The other interested party or parties must be given an opportunity to be heard.

To bring, the facts to the court's attention officially they must be sworn to, and in the case of motions, an affidavit or petition is the usual paper required for this purpose. The form of an affidavit has already been considered, and the form of a petition will be given later. Both forms, moreover, may now be used interchangeably." There are two ways of giving the opposing side an opportunity to be heard: (a) by means of a notice of motion, and (b) by means of an order to show cause.s 

Sometimes one of these ways must be resorted to, and sometimes the other. The usual way is by means of the notice of motion, but if the time is short, the order to show cause is used. The details relating to the use of these two means of giving notice will appear as we proceed. 

The two papers, therefore, that are necessary in making a motion are: (a) a notice which may take either the form of what is called a notice of motion, or the form of an order to show cause, and (b) an affidavit or affidavits setting out the necessary facts in official form. These papers are furnished by the party making the motion." 

There are some motions which, unlike so-called "contested" or " litigated "motions do not require a notice at all. They are unilateral applications for orders and are called ex parte motions. These are the exception and not the rule, but they are not uncommon.10 The reason and necessity for such motions will also be seen later in this chapter. mined by oral rulings of the trial court entered upon the stenographic record of the case. The motions discussed in this chapter are motions in the sense of section 113 of the Civil Practice Act, viz., applications for written orders.

§ 63. Form of Affidavit and Notice of Motion in a Particular Case. 

Suppose a situation arose like that stated in the following facts. Plaintiff's attorney went to the place of business of Richard Roe, the defendant, to serve a summons upon him. The attorney asked a man in the outer office who answered the description of defendant, if he was Richard Roe, and the man replied, "No." The attorney then put the summons upon a table before the man and went away. 

This man was not Richard Roe. He was a clerk in Roe's office and the next day this clerk took the summons to Richard Roe. Richard Roe comes to his attorney and tells him that he does not wish the action to proceed to judgment, but desires that steps be taken to set aside the service of this summons. He shows his attorney the summons which is entitled in the Supreme Court, New York county. Consider first The affidavit. The title, venue and formal opening come first. The form of these was shown in section 56, but of course, the facts will vary in each case. The following affidavits would suit the purpose here indicated. notice of any motion for an order that will affect his substantial right. "There are many applications for orders as to which no special provision exists under the law or the Gen eral Rules of Practice requiring notice to be given. When applications are made ex parte for such orders much depends upon the particular facts presented and the circumstances under which the application is made, whether notice is necessary to be given to the adverse party or not. * * The real test of the necessity of giving notice in a case not specifically provided for by law or the General Rules of Practice, is whether the adverse party is affected by the order." Matter of Salmon, 34 Misc. 251, 253; 69 N. Y. S. 215. 

When the motion is made and determined ex parte in a case where from the nature of the application the adverse party was entitled to notice, the order is irregular and may be vacated.

The notice of motion requires some explanation. Like all other papers after the service of the summons, it begins with the title.

All papers intended to be used on the motion by the party who makes it should be referred to in the notice.15 In the instant case the affidavits of Martin and Roe are recited in the notice. Papers not thus referred to should not be considered on the motion.16 Affidavits are best referred to by naming the affiant and giving the date when they were sworn to.

The place is fixed by rule 63, except where the law provides that a motion may be made where the applicant or other person to be affected thereby resides (subdivision 3). A motion must be made within the judicial district in which the action is triable or in a county in any other district adjoining the county where it is triable (subdivisions 1 and 6); but in the first and eighth districts the motion must be made where the action is triable and a motion on notice cannot be made in the first district in an action triable elsewhere (subdivision 2). In New York and Kings counties and in other parts of the state where the volume of business warrants it, there is a special term of the court (Part I) for the hearing of litigated motions, that is, those motions made on notice where both sides have an opportunity to be heard, and such motions must be brought on there (subdivision 5), unless the special rules of the district otherwise provide. There is also a special term (Part II) for the hearing of ex parte motions in New York and Kings counties. The special rules of the court in each district must be consulted for minute details such as these. In stating the time and place it is customary to insert the phrase "or as soon thereafter as counsel can be heard” since many motions are often brought on for the same time and they are heard in their order.17

Generally speaking, these sections make the following provisions: When a party is represented by an attorney, the paper must be served on the attorney.22 Service is made by simply delivering the paper to him personally,23 or at his office by leaving it with any one in charge, or in a conspicuous place if no one is there. If his office is not open, he may be served by enclosing it in a sealed wrapper directed to him and depositing it in his letter-drop or box.25 Throwing through the transom above the entrance is improper, 20 as is also pushing under the door, or having a janitor unlock the door.28 27 The paper may be served also by mail instead of personally. This method is accomplished by depositing the paper properly enclosed in a post-paid wrapper addressed to him in a post-office or in any post-office box regularly maintained by the United States Government.29 Other details are found in rule 20 regarding service on the clerk of the court and at the attorney's residence.

Where papers are served personally on an attorney, the person serving them usually takes with him an original and a copy of the paper or papers to be served. The attorney upon whom service is made keeps the copy and signs a statement on the original papers admitting due and proper service thereof upon him. This admission of proper service is proof thereof for all subsequent purposes, but if the attorney does not so admit service, it will be necessary for the person who made the service to draw an affidavit showing such service and file the same for subsequent use.

§ 67. Filing of Motion Papers. 

Motion papers in the Supreme Court are to be filed in the office of the clerk of the county specified in the summons as the place of trial.40 Motion papers are usually handed up to the clerk of the particular part of the court which hears the motion. This is in compliance with the rule requiring papers to be filed with the county clerk since the clerks of the several parts of the court are special deputy county clerks, although they are appointed by the Appellate Division."

In other courts of record, papers shall be filed in the office of the respective clerks thereof.42 

§ 68. Note of Issue for Motions, Hearings Thereof, Etc. 

In New York and adjoining counties a calendar of the motions scheduled to be heard for each day is made up in advance by the clerk and published in the New York Law Journal. In order that this may be done it is necessary for each attorney who has a motion coming on for argument to give the clerk notice of that fact. A paper called a note of issue furnishes the information needed. This paper simply consists of the title of the action, the nature of the motion, as for instance" Motion to set aside the service of a summons, the names of the attorneys for and against the motion with their addresses and the date when the motion is returnable. 

This paper is filed with the clerk of the part of the court where the motion is to be heard.43 

On the return day this calendar of motions is called off, and when this motion is reached it is argued before the court and disposed of then or later.

§ 71. The Requisites of a Court Order and an Explanation of the Forms. 

There are two kinds of orders - judge's orders and court orders. The distinction between these is shown in section 

84, post. The forms of orders shown in the preceding section are court orders. The main parts of a court order are: the caption, the recital part, the directory part and the signature. There is very little difference between the short and long form of order except by way of abbreviation. 

§ 72. The Same - The Caption. 

The caption contains the title and gives the time and place where the court was sitting when the order was issued. It also gives the name of the judge who presided. The short form does not state the time in the caption but at the bottom of the order. 

§ 73. The Same - The Recital Part. 

This part of the order specifies the papers read in determining the motion. This is the main function of the recital part of an order. If an appeal be taken from any order, the papers here specified constitute the record read by the appellate court in reviewing the decision of the court below. The short form consists of a printed form and in the blank spaces opposite the printed part which refers to papers, numbers are inserted to indicate that a paper or papers of that sort were used on the motion. Each paper used is numbered serially. The number 4 opposite the words "answering affidavits" does not mean that four answering affidavits were used, but merely that the one answering affidavit used was the fourth paper read in connection with the motion and was given the number four for that reason.

The recital part should also show whether both sides appeared on the motion or one side only, the other side defaulting. This is important since there is no appeal from a default order as a general rule.50 The long form shows 

49. Rule 234. 

50. Civil Practice Act, § 557, subd. 1.

the appearances clearly, and in the short form a phrase indicating the default, if there is a default, and which party defaulted is inserted. In the case of default, if the party making the motion defaults, the motion should be denied. If the adverse party defaults, the motion is granted unless the court otherwise directs.51 

§ 74. The Same - The Directory Part. 

This part states the disposition made of the motion. In the short form the court often simply writes in the words "motion granted" or "motion denied" and a reference to the notice of motion is necessary to see what relief has been granted or denied. If the determination is long and involved the short form of order is not likely to be used at all. In such cases the court indicates in a general way the disposition of the motion which it desires to make, causes a memorandum to that effect to be published in the Law Journal, or sent to the attorneys and requires the attorneys to settle the order on notice. In that event the long form of order is used. The attorney in whose favor the motion is decided prepares a form of order in conformity with the judge's memorandum, serves a copy of it on his adversary with a two days' notice of the time when it will be submitted to the court. The opposite party may submit a different form or file a statement opposing any feature of the proposed order which he thinks is not warranted by the judge's disposition of the motion. 

§ 75. The Same - The Signature. 

The signature on an order is generally made with the initials of the judge who presided but he may sign his name in full.52 

§ 76. The Same The Word "Enter." 

The word "Enter" appearing on the long form order just above the signature is a direction to the clerk to enter the order in the files of the court. Rule 71 requires all the papers used or read on the motion on either side to be filed with the clerk; otherwise the order may be set aside as irregular. § 79. Requisites of the Affidavit to Support an Order to Show Cause. 

The affidavit used in this form of bringing on a motion. must contain all the facts found in the affidavit used in bringing on the motion in the ordinary way, and in addition must contain facts which may be classified into the following three groups: 

1. Facts showing the shortness of time or other reason which indicates the necessity for proceeding by way of an order to show cause."1 

2. Facts showing the present state of the action."2 

3. A statement that no previous application for the order herein sought or any similar order has been made, or if one has been made, to whom made, the determination thereof, and what new facts, if any, exist, which warrant a renewal of the application.68

If a previous application has been made and the affidavit failed to show that fact on the application, the order obtained may be vacated.

§ 81. Requisites of an Order to Show Cause and an Explanation of the Form.

An order to show cause is usually a judge's order though it may be either a court order or a judge's order. It is always, of course, obtained on an ex parte application. Its main function is to cut down the time required for bringing on a motion. The parties cannot shorten this time but the court or a judge of the court may.65 It is, therefore, a short notice of motion. 64 It may contain a stay of proceedings pending the hearing and decision of the motion brought on by it. Judges are rather careful about granting stays especially when the 

64. Rule 60. 

65. Rule 60.

application is made ex parte. The power to grant stays is found in sections 167 to 169 inclusive of the Civil Practice Act. Considerable confusion has been caused among practitioners in this connection by the recent amendment to section 882 of the Civil Practice Act, which prohibits "injunctions" except on notice. How far this amendment affects stays contained in orders to show cause cause must await judicial determination.

The order to show cause must contain a direction relating to the time and manner in which it shall be served.GG 

The main parts of the order are: 

The title is as shown on the form given in the preceding section. If the order had been made by the court, however, it would begin with a caption as in the form given in section 70.

The recital part comes next and refers to the papers upon which the application is made. 

The directory part follows. It contains the short notice of motion, the stay, if any is asked for and granted, and the direction relating to the time and manner of service. 

If made by a judge, it is then dated and signed usually with the judge's full signature." 

§ 82. Procedure After the Order to Show Cause Is Obtained. 

A copy of this order and the affidavit on which it was based must be served within the time stated in the order to show cause upon the attorney for the plaintiff.68 In serving the order it is desirable, but not necessary to exhibit the judge's signature on the original order." The note of issue must be filed as in the ordinary case except that in this instance it is not necessary that it be filed prior to the return day of the motion. In other respects the procedure is the same as in the ordinary case.

§ 84. The Same Court Orders and Judge's Orders Distinguished. 

The forms of orders given in sections 70 and 80, ante, illustrate the distinction running all through the Civil Practice Act and the rules, between judge's orders and court orders. 

That distinction should be kept clearly in mind. A court order is one made by a judge or justice while he is actually sitting as a court and performing the functions of a court. 

Such sittings must be public" and are held at times and places fixed by law." Orders thus made are formal ones and are entered in the files of the clerk's office and made a matter of record. ________________ 

A judge or justice, however, may do many things of a judicial character while he is not sitting as a court at all. 

He may sign orders at his home or on the street, for that matter, and they will be judge's orders but they are not court orders. Orders signed when a judge is not acting as a court are said to be signed at chambers. 

§ 85. Same When Motions Are to Be Made to the Court and 

When to a Judge or Justice Thereof. 

70. Rule 60. 

71. Judiciary Law, § 4. 

When the Practice Act refers to a motion made to the court, the order obtained on the determination thereof should be a court order, and when it requires the motion to be made to a judge or justice of the court, the order obtained thereon should be a judge's order. When it provides that the motion may be made to the court or a judge or justice thereof, the order may be in either form in the discretion of the party making the motion. A motion must be made to a court or judge or justice thereof. The general rules which determine when a motion should be made to the court and when to a judge or justice of the court may be stated as follows: 78 

72. Judiciary Law, § 84. 

73. Civil Practice Act, § 115.

1. 

When the defendant has made default in appearing in an action or proceeding," any application or motion therein may be made to the court or to a judge or justice thereof out of court. 

2. Where any of the defendants in an action or proceeding have appeared, all motions or applications thereafter made in such action or proceeding, with certain exceptions, must be made to the court. 

The exceptions are: 

a. A motion made for an additional extension of time to plead. 1 b. Where the defendant consents to the making of a motion before a judge; and c. Where it is otherwise authorized by law.75

In these exceptional cases, the motion may be made to a judge.

While the above states the general rule for the distribution of motions between those made to the court and those made at chambers, it should be noted that the court can make any order which a judge is empowered to make.” The reverse of the proposition is not, however, true. The power of a judge or justice of the court to make orders which the statute requires the court to make is limited. A judge may make some orders which the statute requires the court to make but not all of such orders. The power of a judge to make court orders is authorized in the first judicial district excepting in the case of a motion for a new trial on the merits."

§ 87. Summary of Distinctions Between Court and Judge's Orders as to Form. 

1. The caption or heading of the judge's order is simply the title, while in the caption or heading of the court order there should be found, preceding the names of the parties, the words" Special Term, Part I, etc. and Present, Hon.... 

Justice." This is called the special term caption. Under the long form of court order the caption would read as in the form found in section 70, ante. 2. The statement of the papers upon which the order is based differs in the two forms. Under the long form of order, the recital part of the court order begins as follows: "Upon reading and filing" etc. enumerating the papers read upon the motion, while in the case of a judge's order, the recital part would be as follows: "Upon reading the affidavit " etc., followed by a recital of the papers read on the motion. The reason for this distinction is that the judge's order is not generally filed but taken away by the attorney who has it signed. The court order is filed and may not be taken away. 

3. Another distinction between a judge's and a court order is that the word "Enter" appears at the end of a court order and does not so appear at the end of a judge's order. The word "Enter" is a direction to the clerk to file the paper. It does not appear on the judge's order for, as stated, a judge's order is not filed at the time it is signed. (The short form court order in use in New York county, however, does not use the word.) 

4. A judge's order is dated at the end. So is a short form court order. In a long form court order the date appears in the caption. 

5. In a judge's order the signature is usually written out in full while in a court order the initials of the judge alone usually appear. 86 

86. This distinction is made immaterial by Rule 70 of the Rules of Civil 

Practice. The custom of making the distinction, however, is likely to continue for some time. See Rule 3 of the

General Rules of Practice.

§ 88. Introduction. 

The personal service of the summons has been considered, and it was stated in section 43 that there were two other methods of serving a summons: substituted service and service by publication. The discussion of these two methods of service was deferred for the reason that they involve motions and orders and it was necessary before they could be intelligently discussed, to discuss first the details of making motions and procuring orders. Chapter V dealt with these matters and now substituted service and service by publication will be discussed in order. 

Although sections 2 and 3 of the Civil Practice Act provide that "this act shall be liberally construed," and that "the rule of the common law that a statute in derogation of the common law is strictly construed does not apply to this act," the Court of Appeals of this State said in a recent case" respecting substituted service and service by publication: "Whenever it is necessary to determine whether jurisdiction has been obtained over a defendant in an action by service of the summons in some way other than by personal service thereof, it must be remembered that the general rule in regard to the service of 

1. Erickson v. Macy, 231 N. Y. 86. 

Cf. Korn v. Lipman, 201 N. Y. 404 (mail box). [106]

process established by centuries of precedent, is that process must be served personally within the jurisdiction of the court upon the person to be affected thereby. Substituted service when provided by statute is in derogation of such general rule, and, consequently, the directions thereof must be strictly construed and fully carried out to confer any jurisdiction upon the court. (Korn v. Lipman, 201 N. Y. 404.) ''2

This emphasis on the fact that constructive service of process is in derogation of the common law and that its statutory authority must be strictly construed continues to be made by the courts, despite an occasional case in which the court's discretion has been invoked to cure procedural defects in such service which have been merely unsubstantial.* 

§ 89. Substituted Service: When Possible. 

An order of a court or judge is necessary before service of a summons can be made by substitution. Such an order is secured ex parte, but before it will be signed the supporting affidavits must show two things: First, the defendant must be a resident of the state, and second, proper and diligent effort must have been made to serve the defendant personally and such effort must have resulted in failure." Private domestic corporations, (other than municipal corporations) joint stock and other unincorporated associations which have a president or treasurer residing within the state are treated as residents under this section. 6a

§ 90. The Same-Necessary Papers: The Affidavit. 

The papers necessary to effect substituted service of the summons are, in addition to the summons, an affidavit and an order. The complaint may accompany the summons if the applicant wishes. The affidavit must set forth the facts showing a case within the requirements of the preceding section, and as this application for an order for the substituted service of a summons is necessarily made ex parte, the affidavit must also contain the statement required by rule 61 of the Rules of Civil Practice to the effect that no previous application for the relief therein sought or for any similar relief has been made, etc. In showing that proper and diligent effort has been made, it is desirable first to make that broad statement, and then it is necessary to state in the affidavit the details of the efforts made to serve the defendant personally. The mere statement that one has made proper and diligent effort to serve the defendant will not suffice. 

This would be a statement of a conclusion on the part of the affiant. The affidavit should contain the facts upon which his conclusion is based. What he may consider due and diligent effort may not be considered so by the court. He must state the evidentiary facts in the affidavit and the court will draw its own conclusions. If the affiant can show attempts at evasion of service, the court will probably be prompt to grant his application for an order.

If the sheriff has attempted to make personal service of the summons his certificate to that effect may be used to aid in showing proper and diligent effort to serve personally,¹º and place of his sojourn. Ottman v. Daly, 7 N. Y. S. 897. The language of the

Code section which made this restriction on substituted service is eliminated. 

9. Nichols v. Emmett, 56 Misc. 321; 

107 N. Y. S. 663; Bank v. Gregory, 139 A. D. 93; 116 N. Y. S. 309. In showing diligent effort to serve a domestic corporation facts must appear which demonstrate that one cannot with diligent effort serve personally any of the officers or persons enumerated in § 228, subd. 3, since if one can serve the summons on any of these with diligent effort one cannot have substituted service. Section 435 of the

Code specifically so provided, but such a detailed statement was unnecessary. 

The Code section also specifically provided that substituted service might be made upon a resident upon showing "if he is within the state, that he avoids service so that personal service cannot be made." Such language, however, added nothing to what had already been said, since under such circumstances a case of inability to serve with diligent effort would appear.

The affidavit as to attempts to serve must be made by one who is over eighteen years of age and who is not a party to the action, since one under eighteen years of age or who is a party to the action cannot make personal service of the 12 summons." 

§ 91. The Same - Necessary Papers: The Order. 

An order is necessary before substituted service can be made. This order is based, of course, upon the affidavit of the person who has attempted to serve the defendant and upon such other affidavits as may be submitted in connection therewith. It may be made by the court or by a judge thereof.13 The title of the order will depend upon which of these forms of order is made use of. (See section 70, ante.)

The recital part of the order will, of course, refer to the affidavit and to the certificate of the sheriff if the sheriff had anything to do with it. In addition to this, it is better in the recital part of the order to add the following: "And it appearing to my satisfaction (or if made by the court to the satisfaction of the court) that the defendant is a resident of the state (or a private domestic corporation, or a joint stock or other unincorporated association having a president or treasurer residing within the state as the case may be) and cannot with proper and diligent effort be served personally with the summons within the state. 

This process is jurisdictional in its character and the two facts referred to in this recital are the ones upon which jurisdiction is based. It is desirable, therefore, to have the order show that these points were in the judge's mind when he signed the order. The body of the order will follow the language of section 231 so far as that language may be made applicable to the situation.¹

§ 92. The Same - Procedure When the Papers Are Secured. 

After the order is signed there are two ways to effect the service under this method, both of which are specified in the order. By the first method one simply leaves a copy of the summons and of the order itself at the defendant's residence, or in the case of corporations, joint stock and other unincorporated associations, at their place of business with a person of proper age¹5 if one can find such person who will receive it. 

The second way is used where one cannot find such a person. In that case the process server affixes a copy of the summons and of the order upon the door of defendant's residence or place of business, as the case requires and then deposits another copy of the same papers in a postpaid 

ing orders as nearly as may be in the language of the Civil Practice 

Act section which authorizes the order. "Now, on the motion of attorney for plaintiff, it is ordered: "That the service of the said summons be made by leaving a copy thereof and of this order at the residence of the defendant, with a person of proper age, if upon reasonable application admittance can be obtained and such person found who will receive it, or if admittance cannot be so obtained nor such person found, by affixing the same to the outer or other door of defendant's said residence, and by depositing in a post office another copy thereof, properly inclosed in a post-paid wrapper, addressed to the defendant at his said place of residence.

After the process server has served the summons in either one or the other of those two ways, his next step is to file the original order and the papers upon which it was granted, together with proof of their service with the clerk. Service by either method must be made within ten days from the time the order is signed, otherwise it will be ineffective. Rule 49 of the Rules of Civil Practice states that on the filing of these papers service by this method is complete." By the reasoning of a recent decision of the Court of Appeals, however, it would seem that Rule 49 is void in this respect, because the convention which formulated the Rules of Civil Practice had no power to make rules inconsistent with the Civil Practice Act, and this provision of Rule 49 is inconsistent with Section 231 of the Civil Practice Act, which states that substi tuted service must be made either by "leaving a copy with a person of proper age" or alternatively by "affixing and depositing in a post office." § 93. Observations on This Mode of Service. 

It has been questioned whether this method of service is constitutional under the due process of law clause of our state and federal constitutions. The question was whether an action thus begun which resulted in a personal judgment against a defendant would not be taking his property without due process since the defendant may not have had any notice at all of the action. It was held that a personal judgment thus obtained is in compliance with the due process of law clause.10 It is doubtful, however, whether this method of and 233 of the Civil Practice Act to conform with section 235 in this respect. In the meantime, the practitioner is confronted with the problem of remembering that service of a summons is complete as indicated in the following tabulation: 

(a) Personal service within state. 

Upon delivery to the defendant of a true copy and leaving it with him. (b) Publication. On the 42nd day after the day of first publication. (Rule 51.) (c) Outside the state in lieu of publication. Upon delivery of a copy of the summons, complaint and notice to the defendant. (C. P. A., § 233; 

Winter v. Winter, supra; 256 N. Y. 113.) (d) Outside the state without an order.-Ten days after filing proof of service. (C. P. A., § 235.) (e) Substituted service.-Either upon "delivery" to a person of proper age and or upon "affixing depositing in a post office." (C. P. A., § 231. Cf. Winter v. Winter, supra; 

256 N. Y. 113.) 

19. Continental Bank v. Thurber, 74 

Hun 632; 26 N. Y. S. 956; affd. in 143 

N. Y. 648, held: "A citizen of a State is bound by its laws, both substantive and those regulating judicial proced- Acquiring jurisdiction of resident defendants by constructive service of process is a proceeding according to the course of the common law. * ure. 

All countries having judicial systems provide modes by which resident citizens can be bound by the judgments of its courts without personal service of the process."

The case of a nonresident of the state is a different case.

The person of a nonresident may be subjected to the power of a court of this state only by personal service of a summons upon him (Garfein v. McInnis, 248 N. Y. 

261, 264), or by his voluntary general appearance before the court (Chapter 

VIII.) No service of process other than personal service thereof can bring before our courts the person of a nonresident of the state. Grubel v. Nassauer, 210 N. Y. 149, 152. 

Where, however, there is situated within this state a specific res (e. g., property), a court of the state may adjudicate the status of that res, although it has no jurisdiction of the person of a nonresident party having an interest therein. Pennoyer v. Neff, 95 U. S. 714, 724.

The principles just stated underly the whole system of constructive service of process, and necessarily limit the provisions of the Civil Practice Act and the Rules of Civil Practice summons regulating all service of a other than personal service thereof.

§ 94. Service by Publication: When Possible. 

Section 232 of the Civil Practice Act enumerates all the cases where the service of a summons may be made by publication. There are eight subdivisions of this section and each one of them specifies a case or group of cases where resort may be had to this method of service. 

The first subdivision authorizes a resort to service by publication upon a. Foreign corporations. b. Unincorporated associations whose president and treasurer are both non-residents,21 and the possibility of substituted service is thus excluded.

C. Domestic corporations where personal service can not after due diligence be made. In such case service by sub. stitution is also possible.

Excepting in the case of a domestic corporation it will be seen that the general idea running through this class of cases found in subdivision 1 of section 232 is non-residence.

The second subdivision is intended to reach such residents as have a. Departed from the state with the intention either of x. Defrauding their creditors, or y. Avoiding the service of a summons, or such as have b. Kept themselves concealed therein, with like intent.

As the defendant is a resident in the contemplation of this subdivision, it will be seen that the summons may be served by substitution whenever a situation develops which would call into use the provisions of this subdivision. 

The third subdivision also applies to residents of the state and substituted service is therefore possible in cases contemplated by it. In this subdivision, however, the question of fraud is eliminated. Six months continuous absence from the state by an adult without an effective designation of a person upon whom a summons may be served after diligent effort, is all that is necessary here. A traveling man or a person who is visiting abroad would illustrate a case where this subdivision might be invoked. 

The fourth subdivision relates to infants and incompetents.

In these cases it is necessary if personal service is attempted, to serve one or more persons other than the defendant before such service is complete.22 If, for any reason all of the persons required to be served cannot be served after due diligence, the order for service by publication may be procured. 

It is immaterial in this case whether the infant be a resident or a non-resident.23

§ 95. The Same-Necessary Papers. 

Three papers must be prepared in addition to the summons before service by publication may be had. They are required by section 232 of the Civil Practice Act and are the following: 

(a) A verified complaint. (b) An affidavit. (c) An order, except where one is prosecuting an equity action under section 235, where an order is not required,20 e. g., in a matrimonial action, an action for money only where a warrant of attachment, granted in the action, has been levied on property of the defendant within the state, or in an equity action under subdivision 6 of section 232. 

We shall discuss each of these three papers in succession. 

§ 96. The Same - The Complaint.s 

Actions may usually be begun by the service of a summons merely. But service of the summons by publication is so objectionable when personal service may be had and it might be the means of so frequent acts of fraud that its use is circumscribed by many safeguards and the requirement that a complaint accompany the summons is one of these safeguards. The complaint is the paper in which the plaintiff's cause of action is set forth. This complaint must be verified, that means sworn to, and this is a further safeguard against unwarranted prosecutions. The law realizes that a person served by publication only, may never get actual notice that a cause of action is started against him. Publication may be

Accordingly, it was held that the statement in the affidavit, "That the defendant resides at 242 

Elwood avenue, city of Newark, State of New Jersey, and the name of the defendant duly appears in the telephone records of the New Jersey division of the Bell Telephone Company," was insufficient to establish the nonresidence of the defendant. An examination of these excepted cases, where the affidavit used does not show inability to serve personally, will reveal however, that the exceptions are more apparent than real. 

For example, the excepted cases in subdivision 1 are joint stock or other unincorporated associations having a president and treasurer "neither of whom is a resident "; a domestic corporation" where after diligent effort service cannot be made within the state " upon the persons necessary to effect personal service;" where after diligent inquiry the defendant remains unknown," etc. In such cases as in the cases contemplated under the second, third and fourth subdivisions, where one has shown the facts required to bring the case within the subdivision in question he will already have shown facts as a general thing demonstrating that personal service cannot be made with due diligence. Under the seventh subdivision due diligence to serve personally need not be shown and yet when this subdivision is read in conjunction with section 17 of the Civil Practice Act there is little likelihood of a resort to service by publication where personal service is possible with diligent effort.

In drawing this part of the affidavit it is desirable to state generally that the plaintiff has been and will be unable, with due diligence, to serve the summons personally within the state upon the defendant and then follow this general statement up with detailed facts showing the efforts to make personal service. The omission of the general statement may be as fatal to the affidavit as the omission of the detailed statement.33

§ 99. Perfecting Service by Publication. 

After the order is signed there are two methods of perfecting service under it. The normal way to perfect service would be to follow the directions contained in the order. 

Section 233 of the Civil Practice Act, however, authorizes as an alternative way for carrying out these directions the service of the papers personally upon the defendant outside the state. This makes possible two methods of complying with the order. Under both methods certain steps must be taken prior to others and we shall therefore state in order what these steps are under both methods.

§ 102. The Same - When Service Is Complete. 

The summons is served with the delivery of the same to the defendant outside of the state, despite the fact that Rule 51 attempts to provide that service without the state is complete ten days after proof thereof is filed. In case of service by publication in the newspapers designated in the order, service is complete on the forty-second day after the day of the first publication.55 The twenty days referred to in the summons within which the defendant must appear or answer does not begin to run until after service is complete by the appropriate lapse of time as above indicated.

The section has been amended to include also matrimonial actions and actions where a warrant of attachment, granted in the action, has been levied on property of the defendant within the state. § 104. Introduction. 

Now that we have considered the statutory requirements for the service of the summons in the three ways provided for such service, it is important that we discuss the effectiveness of these ways of serving the summons to give jurisdiction to the court. Process is the main step in an action through which the court acquires jurisdiction and the fundamental principles relating to jurisdiction set limits to the application of the statutes relating to process. We shall consider a concrete case first, then discuss the general principles governing jurisdiction, and finally apply those principles to the statutes governing the service of the summons. 

§ 105. A Concrete Case Involving Service by Publication. 

Suppose that Mr. Doe is a resident of this state and has a good cause of action for breach of a contract against Mr. [128]

Roe, but that Mr. Roe is a non-resident and cannot with due diligence be served with the summons within the state. 

Now Mr. Doe has all the facts which the Civil Practice Act and the rules require to entitle him to an order for the service of a summons by publication upon Roe. So he proceeds, let us suppose, and gets his order and serves the same by publication or personally without the state as the case may be. Suppose further that Mr. Roe defaults in the action. 

Now he should be in a position to enter up a judgment against Mr. Roe by reason of his default. 

§ 106. Provisions of the Civil Practice Act and Rules Relative to the Entry of Judgment in Such a Case. 

Section 493 of the Civil Practice Act and rule 192 state the provisions which must guide him in entering up a judgment in the case of a default after the summons was served by pub lication or by substitution. Section 493, subdivision 1, requires that he make application to the court or a judge for the judgment demanded in his complaint. Rule 192, subdivision 1, provides that upon this application he must file proof that the service is complete and that the defendant is in default. This he can do. Now subdivision 2 of section 493 provides that judgment shall not be rendered for a sum of money only excepting in actions specified there. Doe's case is one of these, and, therefor he can comply with the first requirement contained in that section. The last part of section 493 requires in the case of a non-resident defendant or foreign corporation that the plaintiff, upon his application for judgment, must file "proof that a warrant of attachment granted in the action has been levied upon property of the defendant." Rule 192, subdivision 2 further requires in such case that there shall be filed "a description of the property so attached with a statement of the value thereof according to the inventory." 

Now Doe has obtained no warrant of attachment. This was not referred to in the supposed case, nor was it referred to when we were discussing the service of a summons by publication. Therefore, it will not be possible for him to file such proof and as a consequence he will not be able to enter up a judgment against the defendant.

This seems rather hard. He has faithfully followed the 

Civil Practice Act all along, and now he is forbidden to reap 1

the fruits of his labors. Orders for the service of a summons by publication in common law actions are sometimes obtained but which are insufficient to support a judgment because prior to the entry of the judgment a warrant of attachment was not secured and a levy under it made upon property of the defendant.¹ 

§ 107. Jurisdiction in Rem and in Personam. 

Mr. Doe's surprise at this outcome of his labors to procure a judgment against Roe in the supposed case is occasioned, however, only by his failure to understand fully the principles of jurisdiction. Our attention, therefore, must be directed to a discussion of this subject. There are two kinds of jurisdiction: Jurisdiction over the person and jurisdiction over the thing. Where the court has jurisdiction over the person of the defendant it may enter what is known as a personal judgment against him and a personal judgment imposes a personal obligation upon the defendant. This obligation will follow the defendant wherever he may go and may be enforced against him out of any property which he possesses. It may follow him to another state and be the basis of an action against him there. Its peculiar character is that it clings to the person of the defendant and imposes a duty upon him from which it is difficult for him to escape. 

On the other hand, jurisdiction over the thing may be defined as the power which a court has to appropriate a piece of land or article of personal property and apply the same to the satisfaction of a claim which the plaintiff may have against the defendant or upon the property in question. The marriage relation is also considered by some a thing over which the court may acquire jurisdiction. The court in such case 

1. Haase v. Michigan Steel Boat Co., 148 App. Div. 298; 132 N. Y. S. 1046;

German-American Coffee Co. v. John ston, 168 App. Div. 35; 153 N. Y. S. 866. Cit

An order for the publication of the summons under the circumstances stated in the problem will not be granted and if granted may be vacated. 

Proof is required before granting the order for publication that a warrant of attachment granted in the action has been levied on property of the defendant. Dimmerling v. Andrews, 236 

N. Y. 43; Van Mater v. Post, 147 

App. Div. 111; 131 N. Y. S. 805; 

McLaughlin v. McLaughlin Real Estate Co., 162 App. Div. 644; 147 N. Y. 

S. 959; Westbrook v. Ward, 171 App. 

Div. 547; 157 N. Y. S. 755. 

2. Jurisdiction in rem is in a strict sense limited to actions or proceedings against property where the owner of the property is not a party to the

has no jurisdiction over the defendant's person whatever, but its jurisdiction is simply over the property which belongs to the defendant, or over the marriage status. Its power in the premises is exhausted when the property is exhausted, or the status determined. It cannot pursue the defendant personally. The court's activity must cease when the property under its control has been disposed of. A judgment entered in such a case may result in a levy upon the property and a sale thereof but cannot follow the person of the defendant.2a

These two kinds of jurisdiction are sometimes called jurisdiction in personam, and jurisdiction in rem, and they give rise to two kinds of judgments, judgments in personam and judgments in rem. There are, moreover, two classes of actions which correspond to these two kinds of jurisdiction and of judgments. They are actions in personam and actions in rem. An action in personam is one in which the jurisdiction is over the person and which may result in a personal judgment. An action in rem is one where jurisdiction is over the marriage relation or the property, but not the person of the defendant, and may result in a judgment in rem, that is, against the property or upon the status. 

If the court has neither of those two kinds of jurisdiction in any particular case it has no jurisdiction at all and is powerless to enter a valid judgment of any kind. If it has jurisdiction in any particular case the character of the judgment which it may direct will be determined by the kind of jurisdiction it has. action at all. A libel against a vessel would illustrate what is meant but the term is now quite generally used in the sense stated in the text. The following quotation from the opinion of Mr. Justice Field, in the case of 

Pennoyer v. Neff, 95 U. S. 715, at page 

734, would illustrate what is meant: "It is true that in a strict sense, a proceeding in rem is one taken directly against property, and has for its object the disposition of the property, without reference to the title of individual claimants; but, in a larger and more general sens, the terms are applied to actions between parties, where the direct object is to reach and dispose of property owned by them, or someone interested therein. Such are cases commenced by attachment against the property of debtors, or instituted to partition real estate, foreclose a mortgage, or enforce a lien. 

So far as they affect property in the state, they are substantially proceedings in rem in the broader sense which we have mentioned." 

2a. Cf. C. P. A., § 520.

Take for example an action to foreclose a mortgage upon real property where the summons is served by publication upon a non-resident defendant who is the owner of the property. The court may acquire jurisdiction over the property but it has no personal jurisdiction. Suppose now the property is sold but does not bring enough to satisfy the mortgage indebtedness, may the plaintiff have judgment for the deficiency against the defendant? No, for this would be asking a judgment in personam where jurisdiction in rem alone existed. Similarly a court may have jurisdiction over the marriage status through service of the summons by publication and enter a decree dissolving the marriage but it could not grant alimony in such case as this would be a judgment in personam.* 

§ 108. The Same - The Case of Pennoyer v. Neff." 

A lawyer named Mitchell sued in the courts of the state of Oregon a man named Neff for the sum of three hundred dollars claimed to be due him for professional services. 

Neff was a non-resident of the state of Oregon. The summons was served upon him by publication and judgment was entered against him upon his default. There was no warrant of attachment granted and no levy made. 

The law of the state of Oregon relating to the publication of the summons was similar to our own statutes on the subject but there was no provision in the law of Oregon forbidding the entry of judgment against a non-resident defendant upon his default such as there is in our section 493 of the Civil 

Practice Act and rule 192 of the Rules of Civil Practice. A 

judgment, was, therefore, entered by Mitchell against Neff. 

3. Schwinger v. Hickok, 53 N. Y. 280. 

4. Baylies v. Baylies, 196 App. Div. 

677; 188 N. Y. S. 147. 

5. 95 U. S. 714. The decisions of the United States Supreme Court are controlling here for the reason that judicial action in any state without jurisdiction in the court, even though sanctioned by the statute of the state, is in conflict with the requirements of due process of law. (Twining v. 

New Jersey, 211 U. S. 78.) And the

Fourteenth Amendment of the Fed eral Constitution forbids any state to make or enforce any law which shall deprive persons of life, liberty or property without due process of law. The 

United States Supreme Court is the court of last resort and highest authority on all questions involving the construction of the United States Con stitution. (United States Constitu tion, Art. VI.) And the question of jurisdiction in the court to pronounce a judgment affecting life, liberty or property is a constitutional question.

Now Neff was the owner of a piece of land in the state of Oregon from a time prior to the commencement of the action and when Mitchell got his judgment the sheriff of Multnomah county where the land was situated, sold this land under an execution and Pennoyer bought it. Later Neff came into the state of Oregon and brought an action against 

Pennoyer for the recovery of the possession of the land, claiming that the judgment obtained by Mitchell against Neff was void for lack of jurisdiction of the court which pronounced it, and that in consequence the sale to Pennoyer under such judgment was likewise void and Pennoyer got no title. The court sustained this view, saying: "Except in cases affecting the personal status of the plaintiff, and cases in which that mode of service may be considered to have been assented to in advance, as hereinafter mentioned, the substituted service of process by publication, allowed by the law of Oregon and by similar laws in other States, where actions are brought against nonresidents, is effectual only where, in connection with process against the person for commencing the action, property in the state is brought under the control of the court, and subjected to its disposition by process adapted to that purpose, or where the judgment is sought as a means of reaching such property or affecting some interest therein; in other words, where the action is in the nature of a proceeding in rem. * * It follows from the views expressed that the personal judgment recovered in the State Court of Oregon against the plaintiff herein, then a non-resident of the state, was without any validity, and did not authorize a sale of the property in controversy.'

§ 110. How Jurisdiction in Rem May Be Obtained. 

In determining how jurisdiction in rem may be obtained, it is necessary to classify actions into those which have a specific subject-matter and those which have not. Actions to foreclose a mortgage on real property, or to partition it, or to enforce specifically a contract to convey it, or to foreclose a lien on specific chattels have as their subject-matter the property to which they relate. The common law actions for a money judgment have on the other hand no specific subject-matter. Money derived from any source will satisfy the judgment. The claim is not in such cases a demand for a specific fund or the proceeds thereof. It is really a personal claim that defendant answer the demands of the plaintiff out of any money he has or may acquire.

Now in actions which do not have a specific subject-matter, such as common law actions for money, before the court can acquire jurisdiction in rem, property must be seized under the direction of the court and this is constructively bringing the property before the court. A warrant of attachment is the usual means adopted for this purpose. A warrant of attachment is simply a direction to the sheriff made by a judge commanding him to seize property of the defendant and hold it pending the litigation. When the sheriff has made the levy, jurisdiction is acquired over the property seized and the court may proceed to adjudicate upon it. It makes no difference whatever in this class of cases whether the property of the defendant over which jurisdiction is sought be real or personal, tangible or intangible; a seizure thereof is necessary to give the court jurisdiction in rem. 10 In actions, however, which have a specific subject-matter, 9. No cases have been found supporting this proposition which is based on the reasoning in Continental Bank v. Thurber, supra. Cf. Karchman v. 

Karchman, 224 A. D. 773, 230 N. Y. S. 856. 

10. Pennoyer v. Neff, 95 U. S. 714. 

In this case as shown above, the action was one at common law for a money judgment and though the defendant had real property in the jurisdiction all the while, the court acquired no jurisdiction over it because no seizure by warrant of attachment or otherwise was had. Dimmerling v.

The presence within the state of the property constituting the subject-matter of the action combined with service of the summons by publication or otherwise, will give the court jurisdiction in rem. No question of jurisdiction arises in such actions except where the summons is served by publication upon a non-resident, for where personal or substituted service is had, jurisdiction in personam is obtained, and the same is true where service by publication upon a resident is obtained. But where the defendant is a non-resident and the summons is served by publication, no personal jurisdiction is obtained, and unless jurisdiction in rem is secured the court will have no jurisdiction at all.

Nevertheless the presence within the state of the specific property to which the action relates, coupled with service by publication, even where the defendant is a non-resident, gives the court jurisdiction in rem. § 111. The Same In Matrimonial Actions. 

Up to this point in the discussion of jurisdiction in rem, property constituted the res over which jurisdiction was sought. In a divorce action, however, no property interests need be involved. If the summons is served personally upon the defendant in such an action, of course, the court has jurisdiction over the parties, and if the defendant be a resident and the summons is served upon him by publication, a court has jurisdiction over the parties and its judg ment will be entitled to recognition and enforcement throughout the United States under the full faith and credit and due process clauses of the Federal Constitution. The validity of such judgment may not be questioned with reference to the due process clause of the Federal Constitution since the state is supreme in dealing with the marriage relation of its own citizens.17 But if the defendant be a non-resident and the summons is served upon him by publication so that the court cannot acquire jurisdiction over the person of the

The answer to that question is that the res in a matrimonial action is the status of the parties and the court may acquire jurisdiction in rem in such a case if the locus of the res is within the territorial boundaries of the state.18 The determination of the locus of the res in a matrimonial action is the test of jurisdiction and the principles governing the matter have been defined with reasonable clearness by the adjudicated cases on the subject.19

If, thereafter, the husband moves to another state for business or other justifiable reasons, the res will follow him to his new domicile whether the wife accompanies him or not, for the reason that it is the duty of the wife to accompany her husband. Therefore, if she deserts him before such removal or remains behind and refuses to accompany him and he in his new domicile brings an action against her for divorce, serving the summons upon her by publication, the courts of the state where the husband has his domicile will thereby acquire jurisdiction in rem and a judgment dissolving the marriage in such case will be valid and enforcible in every state of the Union.22 On the other hand, if the husband abandons his wife and moves to another state and takes up a domicile there, the res in matrimony will not follow him to his new domicile but will remain behind in the state where the wife is domiciled, and if, under such circumstances, the husband in his new domicile brings an action for a divorce against his wife and the summons in such action is served by publication, the court in such a case will neither have jurisdiction over the person of the defendant nor over the res, and a judgment of divorce pronounced by a court under such circumstances will not be enforcible in any other state of the Union under the full faith and credit clause of the United States Constitution.28

Again, if the wife unjustifiably departs from the state of the domicile, the husband remaining, the res in matrimony will remain with the husband, and if he begin an action for divorce against his wife, serving the summons by publication, the courts will have jurisdiction over the res and a judgment of divorce pronounced in such an action will be valid and entitled to obligatory enforcement under the full faith and credit clause of the United States Constitution.24

§ 112.

Procuring Orders for the Publication of the Summons as 

Affected by the Principles Relating to Jurisdiction. 

One may satisfy all of the statutory requirements found in the Civil Practice Act for the publication of the summons and still not be entitled to an order for the publication thereof. In addition to these statutory requirements the fundamental principles relating to jurisdiction must be satisfied before one becomes entitled to an order for the publication of a summons.

Where either kind of jurisdiction exists or is assured at the time of the application for the order for the publication of the summons, there is, of course, no question of the right or power of the court to grant such an order, provided the statutes governing its issuance are complied with. Therefore, in all the cases contemplated in section 232 of the Civil Practice Act where the defendant is a resident, there is no question of the power or right of the court to grant an order for the publication of the summons when the statute is followed, since jurisdiction in personam exists in such cases. Nor is there any question of the right or power of the court where the defendant is a non-resident to grant such orders, where the subject matter of the action affects real or personal property situated within the state. Foreclosure of mortgages on real or personal property situated within the state, or the partition of such real property, or actions for dower, illustrate the type of action here contemplated. The order may be granted in such cases since jurisdiction in rem exists. Likewise there can be no question of the right and power of the court to grant an order for the publication of a summons on a non-resident defendant, even though the action have no specific subject-matter but is an ordinary common law action for money, provided in advance of the application a seizure of defendant's property is had under a warrant of attachment, for then juris-

She intended after the rendition of a decree, immediately to return here, (N. Y.) and consequently she never became a resident of that state." Followed in Lefferts v. Lefferts, 263 N. Y.

diction in rem as to the property seized is obtained by the seizure.

The real question is, has the court any power to grant an order for the publication of the summons where it does not appear on the application that the court will acquire any jurisdiction on the service of the summons by publication. 

If, for example, the action relate to specific personal property, but the moving papers show such property to be outside the state, or fail to show that it is within the state, should the court grant the order, realizing that the publication of the summons will give it no jurisdiction? 

In Bryan v. University Publishing Co.26 the Court of

Appeals vacated an order for the publication of a summons where the defendant was a non-resident, and the property which was the subject of the action was not within the state. The prevailing opinion (the court divided four to three) uses this significant language in giving the reasons for its decision: "The court can give no relief, and the impropriety of issuing an order which, if it leads to a judgment, 'would operate on nothing in the state and be regarded by nobody out of it,' becomes apparent. 

It offends every principle by which the jurisdiction of a court can be vindicated, and should not be allowed to stand."

The rule laid down in the Bryan case, supra, has been universally followed, and in all actions which relate to a specific subject-matter, the moving papers on the application for an order for the service of a summons by publication must show the presence within the state of the property constituting the subject-matter of the action.27 Nor can it be said that the statute (Civil Practice Act, § 232, subd. 6) requires this. It is true that if subdivision 6 of section 232 of the Civil Practice Act furnishes the necessary grounds upon which the plaintiff may apply for the order of publication, the

It should be borne in mind that the decision of Dimmerling v. Andrews was one involving attempted service by publication on a non-resident in an action for money only. The decision would not apply to an action having a specific subject-matter, even where the defendant is a non-resident, since seizure of the property in such a case is not necessary to give the court jurisdiction in rem,-e.g. in a foreclosure action. It would also seem that no attachment would be required for valid service by publication on a resident under subdivision 3 of section 232, for instance, even though the action were for money only.³¹ 31 30

§ 115. Appearance. 

The defendant's appearance in an action may be made in three different ways: (a) By serving upon plaintiff's attorney a notice of appearance. (b) By serving on him a copy of an answer, and (c) By serving on him a notice of motion raising an objection to the complaint in point of law.¹

The first of these ways must be used if the summons is served without a complaint. The other two ways are not available under such circumstances since a defendant cannot answer a complaint or raise an objection to it until he has seen it. § 116. The Same - Form of Notice of Appearance. 

No particular form for a notice of appearance is prescribed. Its function is to advise the attorney for the plaintiff that an attorney makes his appearance, in the action by authority of the defendant and as his representative and to furnish plaintiff's attorney with the name and address of such attorney so that subsequent papers in the action may be served upon him at such address. The attorney is an officer of the court, and his statement that he has authority so to represent the defendant is sufficient in the usual case."

§ 117. The Same - The Demand for the Complaint. 

In the form given above the complaint is demanded. This is not a necessary part of the notice, and the notice is effective without it, but a notice without such demand entitles the defendant only to copies of all subsequent papers and notice of all subsequent proceedings as its language indicates. A complaint, however, is not a necessary subsequent paper. The action may proceed to judgment without it and unless specifically demanded, the notice of appearance entitles a defendant only to notice of such proceedings as ensue.' Of course, if the complaint is served with the summons no demand is necessary and defendant's appearance in such a case is effected either by answer or by motion. The demand for the complaint may be incorporated into the notice of appearance or served separately. 

§ 118. Time of Service. 

The language of the summons and of section 237 of the Civil Practice Act requires the notice to be served within twenty days after the service of the summons. This means within twenty days after the summons is completely served.¹º 

In City Court actions, if the defendant is arrested before answer, except in certain marine cases, he has ten days within which to appear, regardless of the shorter time limited in the summons in such actions." While the language used in the summons and in section 237 of the Civil Practice Act seems mandatory, a notice of appearance subsequently served will, nevertheless, be effective in so far as it will require notice to be given of all proceedings after its service.12

Even if no summons were served on the defendant at all the service of a notice of appearance upon plaintiff's attorney would make unnecessary the service of a summons since all the jurisdiction which the proper service of a summons could give is obtained by service of the notice. Many corporations, such for example as street railway corporations which have a great number of actions against them begun almost daily, avoid the annoyance to their officers, which would be occasioned by the frequent service of process upon them, by having their legal department submit to the jurisdiction in this way.

Parties, however, cannot in this way confer upon courts jurisdiction which the statutes deny them. Jurisdiction over the parties can thus be given to the court but jurisdiction over a subject-matter outside the statutory jurisdiction of the court cannot thus be conferred. A municipal court could not, for example, be given jurisdiction to try a divorce action even though the parties were willing. 

13. A defendant who appears in an action for any purpose other than that of raising the question whether the court has obtained jurisdiction of him personally or through his property, appears generally therein, even though he characterize his appearance as special. A general appearance gives jurisdiction of the de fendant's person. (Civil Practice Act, § 237.) The nature and effect of a special appearance have been defined as follows: "When a summons has been served on a defendant who does not intend to submit himself to the jurisdiction of the court over his person, he may elect to remain out of court but he need not wait until the entry of judgment against him by default. He may appear specially. The special appearance is recognized only for the purpose of raising the question whether the court has obtained jurisdiction over the defendant personally or through his property."

§ 120. The Same - Case of Reed v. Chilson, 142 N. Y. 152. 

This was an action begun in New York upon a judgment obtained in Michigan for a deficiency arising upon a foreclosure sale. When the action was commenced in New York, the plaintiff and one of the defendants were residents of Michigan and the other defendant was a resident of North Dakota. The summons in the New York action was served upon both defendants without the state pursuant to an order of publication. A warrant of attachment had been issued but no property was levied upon. 

It will be noted that under the principles governing juris diction discussed in chapter VII, the New York courts at this point had no jurisdiction of any kind. The defendants, not understanding, of course, the principles of jurisdiction, engaged an attorney in New York to protect their interests. 

He served upon plaintiff's attorney a notice of appearance. 

Later an answer was served by the same attorney in which he alleged that neither of the defendants were residents of the state, or had any property therein, and that the court had no jurisdiction. Of course, it was held that the court did have personal jurisdiction over both defendants since the service of the notice of appearance was equivalent to the personal service of a summons upon them in the state.¹5 

§ 121. Accidental Appearance. 

Since there is no prescribed form for a notice of appearance, and its main function is to apprise plaintiff's attorney that defendant is now represented by counsel and to furnish plaintiff's attorney with the name and address of such counsel, there are cases which hold that any paper used in an action and signed by an attorney as "defendant's attorney,' giving his address, is a notice of appearance.¹º 99 

15. It is not uncommon for attorneys in states where divorce colonies are found to seek to cure by means of the notice of appearance defects in the jurisdiction of the courts where the divorce action is prosecuted. The ac tion is begun and the summons served by publication. Thereafter another attorney, often working in conjunction with plaintiff's attorney, writes to the defendant in the action and offers for a nominal sum to represent her or him as the case may be. The defendant without knowing the effect of the notice of appearance often authorizes the attorney to appear in the action. 

This gives the court jurisdiction over the parties in personam and the divorce obtained after such appearance is good anywhere. 

16. Ayres v. West R. R. Co., 48 

Barb. 132; Baxter v. Arnold, 9 How. 

Pr. 445.

The trend of modern decisions, however, is to the effect that a general appearance can be effected only in the manner prescribed by statute."

As there is danger here it is advisable, if one wants to put in an appearance, to do so in the manner prescribed in section 237 of the Civil Practice Act, and if no appearance is desired, to avoid signing papers used in the action as "defendant's attorney." It was for this reason that the motion papers used for the purpose of illustration in section 63 ante, were signed "defendant's attorney, appearing specially for the purpose of this motion only." Such an appearance as this is not a general appearance but a limited one. If a general appearance were effected in making a motion to set aside a summons one might give the court jurisdiction in the very act of seeking to escape it. 

§ 122. Appearance by Defendant in Person. 

18 As a plaintiff may prosecute his own action in person, if he is of full age and not judicially declared incompetent,' so a defendant may defend the action in person under like circumstances and in addition may serve upon plaintiff's attorney a notice of appearance, or any other paper in the action just as an attorney could.¹9

If, however, an attorney once appears for a party the party thereafter cannot, except with the consent of the court, act in person in the action.20

§ 127. Pleadings Generally and the Complaint as to Form. 

The second main step in the action is the preparation of pleadings. Pleadings are the papers wherein the parties formulate and state their differences. These differences when formulated are called the issues, and they are of two kinds, issues of fact and issues of law.¹ An issue of fact results when a material allegation of fact is asserted by one and denied by the other party to the action; and an issue of law is evolved when a proposition of law is asserted by one and controverted by the other party. 

There are but three pleadings under the Civil Practice Act: the complaint in which plaintiff states his cause of
