§ 130. The Same - The Title and Formal Opening.* 

The title of the complaint does not differ from the title of the summons, although the requisites for it are found in section 255 of the Civil Practice Act while the requisites of the title of the summons are stated in rule 45. Those requisites were discussed in section 34, ante, and need not be repeated here. The formal opening consists of the words "Plaintiff alleges" with such embellishment as the attorney may desire to give them. There is no rule or Civil Practice section relating thereto. 

§ 131. The Same-The Connecting Words. 

The words in capital letters immediately after the formal opening and the similar words likewise in capital letters reading "For a second, separate and distinct cause of action " disclose an effort to comply with the part of rule 90 which requires each separate cause of action, counterclaim or defense to be separately stated and numbered." The obvious purpose in this part of rule 90 is to require each cause of action to be complete in itself. An allegation from one cause of action in a complaint cannot be borrowed to piece out a deficiency in another. This regulation has not always been rigorously enforced by the courts but it is required by the rule. It is not necessary, however, that allegations found in one cause of action, when required in another, should be repeated therein in extenso. It is permissible to incorporate such allegations in succeeding causes of action by reference.' 

Paragraph fifth in the form of complaint given in the last section illustrates this method of incorporating allegations.

§ 142. The Same-Explanation of the Form-The Petition. 

A petition, when it is sworn to, differs from an affidavit only in the matter of form. These papers may be used inter-

changeably to effect the same purpose.13 An affidavit therefore might have been used here instead of a petition, but it is desirable to become acquainted with the form of a petition as well as with that of an affidavit. 

The title of this petition deserves attention. Since this petition is framed in advance of the commencement of the action and is a necessary precedent step before the action can be commenced, there is no title. The title begins with the summons and the summons is not yet issued. After the commencement of the action a petition, if used, would begin with the title the same as an affidavit, but this petition is a special proceeding and has a caption appropriate to special proceedings rather than to actions.

Next follows the address to the tribunal from which relief is sought. A petition is defined as a written address to a tribunal stating facts entitling the petitioner to relief or to some direction or order and asking therefor.13 The address here is to the Supreme Court of the State of New York. 

The body of the petition is the place where the facts relied upon should be stated. In regard to the statement of facts, the petition does not differ in any respect from the affidavit. 

The "wherefore clause" found at the end of the petition is a statement of the relief sought. Since petitions and affidavits have become interchangeable, it is not uncommon to find this "wherefore clause" used to close an affidavit, although originally it was appropriate only for the petition. 

The signature follows. This completes the petition but it will be noticed that the facts stated here are not thus far made under oath. It is necessary, therefore, when a petition is used as a basis for judicial action to have the petition verified, that is, sworn to. A verification is nothing more than a short affidavit attached to petitions, complaints or other papers in which the petitioner or other affiant swears that the allegations stated in the petition are true. The form of it is prescribed by rule 100 of the Rules of Civil 

Practice.

Commission expires April 1, 19... § 144. The Same - Explanation of the Form- The Acknowledgment.

The only part of the form of consent which requires explanation is the acknowledgment. It is simply a statement made by a notary public to the effect that he knows the person whose signature is attached to the paper or instrument and that such person acknowledged before him the genuineness of the paper or instrument. It has a venue which has to be made in a place where the notary public is authorized to administer oaths. Whenever the genuineness of a signature to a written instrument must be established with certainty, an acknowledgment or more accurately, the notary's certificate of acknowledgment, is the means made use of for that purpose. It is, therefore, attached to deeds, contracts and other instruments where the persons who read the deeds, contracts, etc., may not know anything about the person who signs the instrument nor whether the signature attached to it is genuine. The court, for example, in this case will not know whether George Doe actually does consent to act as the guardian ad litem or whether the signature is a mere forgery. George Doe will not be before the court when the application is made and the court must, therefore, before it will act, have some proof of the genuineness of the signature attached to the consent. The same is true with recording officers. Before they may record in their offices deeds 

14. Rule 40, subd. 5. 12:1

or other instruments they must have proof of their genuineness and this is obtained through the instrumentality of the certificate of acknowledgment.

A paper duly acknowledged is admissible in evidence without further proof of the genuineness of the signature.15 

§ 145. The Same - The Form of Affidavit and the Order. 

The form of an affidavit and order has already been discussed. All that it is necessary to state here, therefore, is what the affidavit should contain. Rule 40 of the Rules of 

Civil Practice states what the qualifications of guardians ad litem must be. The affidavit of the proposed guardian ad litem, therefore, should show that he possesses the qualifications required by that rule. 

§ 146. Methods of Procuring Guardians Ad Litem for Infant Defendants. 

There are two distinct ways of procuring the appointment of a guardian ad litem for an infant defendant.18 

15. C. P. A., §§.384, subd. 1, 386. 

16. Under the Code there were two distinct ways provided for procuring such appointments. The first way was stated in § 471 of the Code and the second way in § 473. The provisions found in these two sections were not exclusive of one another but overlapped each other and few sections of the Code were more confusing. The sections were amended by successive legislatures beginning in 1849, sometimes by addition and sometimes by subtraction, and did not reach a settled condition until the year 1889. 

Eight changes in the law took place between 1849 and 1889, an average of a change every five years. Decisions of the courts handed down within this transitory period were often cited in support of an interpretation of the section long after the legislature had changed the language so that the decision was no longer applicable.

history of these changes and a discussion of the opinions relating to them is found in Taylor v. Emmet, 137 App. Div. 202; 122 N. Y. S. 66. 

Decisions prior to this one should be read with caution since the language to which such opinion applies may not be the same as the language of the Civil Practice Act, or the Code sections as they existed just prior to the adoption of the Civil Practice Act. 

The following quotation from the opinion of former Presiding Justice 

Dowling, in Taylor v. Emmet, clears up the confusion in reference to the two methods of procuring the appointment of guardians ad litem for infant dedefendants: "The Code recognizes two methods for procuring the appointment of a guardian ad litem of a non-resident infant defendant. The first method is under § 471, which applies both to resident and non-resident infants. As to the former the application may be made within a specified time after personal service, either by the infant himself if he is fourteen years of age or upwards, or if he is under that age, or neglects to apply within the time limited, then the ap-

plication may be made by any other party to the action, or by a relative or other friend of the infant, in which case notice thereof must be given to his general or testamentary guardian, if he has one within the State, or, if he has none, then to the infant himself, if he is of the age of fourteen years or upwards and within the State, or if he is under that age and within the State, then to the person with whom he resides. As to non-resident infants. under § 471 the summons may be served without the State or by publication pursuant to the provisions of §§ 438 to 444, inclusive, and the time within which the infant, if fourteen years of age, may apply for the appointment of a guardian, begins to run from the completion of service under § 441; if he is under fourteen years of age or neglects to apply within the time fixed by the section, then the application may be made by any party to the action or by a relative or friend of the infant, but no notice of such application need be given to the infant, unless he has a general or testamentary guardian within this State or is within the State when the application is made. 

It is clear that § 471 provides for the procedure only where the summons has been served either personally or by publication. The second method is that prescribed by § 473 and is entirely separate and distinct from the first. The summons need not be served, either personally or by publication, to give the right to apply for the appointment of a guardian. When nonresidence or temporary absence from the State of the infant defendant is shown, then the right to the order of designation arises, and the reference in § 473 to §§ 471 and 472 is solely to prescribe the means to be followed by the infant in case he or some person in his behalf desires to apply for the appointment of a guardian of his own selection." 

Now, the Civil Practice Act has not in the writer's opinion changed the law thus stated. A rearrangement of the sections of the law has taken place but the provisions of the law remain unchanged excepting in the few places indicated. 

The following statement showing a distribution of the Code sections with reference to the Civil Practice Act will support this view: Code § 468.

§ 149. The Same - Notice - When Necessary and to Whom. 

Notice of the application is necessary where any one other than the infant or his general or testamentary guardian makes the application, provided the infant or his general or testamentary guardian is within the state. If the infant or his guardian makes the application no notice is required nor is any notice required where any other person makes the application unless the general or temporary guardian or the infant is within the state, in which case notice must be given to such guardian if within the state, but if not, to the infant if over fourteen years of age, and if under that age to the person with whom he resides.19 Any other party to the action may make the application if it has not been made on behalf of the infant within twenty days after the completion of service on him.20

The provision requiring that it must affirmatively appear in the affidavit presented upon the application of a guardian ad litem whether or not a person had been designated under section 225 of the Civil Practice Act to receive the summons was inserted in that section of the Practice Act by chapter 199 of the Laws of 1921. The purpose of the provision is obviously to prevent duplication of persons acting on behalf of infants and to give the court opportunity if it choose to exercise it, of appointing the same person who was previously designated to receive the summons, as guardian ad litem. Compensation for the person designated to receive the summons is provided for by rule 44 of the Rules of Civil 

Practice. 

§ 151. The Same The Second Method. 

This method applies only to non-resident infant defendants, or to resident infant defendants who are temporarily absent from the state.22 It may be resorted to before the service of the summons,23 and when a guardian ad litem is thus appointed the summons is served upon such guardian instead of upon the infant," and such guardian has twenty days to appear on behalf of the infant.25 

By this method an affidavit or petition is presented to the court by some other party to the action, usually the plaintiff, showing a situation to exist within section 206 of the Civil Practice Act, and on this the court will sign an order providing that a person named therein will be appointed guardian ad litem unless within a time specified after service of a copy of the order, the infant or someone on his behalf procures such guardian to be appointed by the first method. 

The order will also give special direction respecting the service thereof which may be upon the infant. 

The order so obtained is then served as its provisions direct. Thereafter if the infant defendant or anyone on his behalf so desires, he may make application by the first method for the appointment of a guardian ad litem. If he fails to do this within the time specified in the order, the court on an affidavit by the plaintiff or other party showing a failure on the part of the infant or anyone on his behalf

§ 152. Court Appointment of Guardian Ad Litem Without Appli cation. 27 The Supreme Court may appoint a guardian ad litem or a special guardian for an infant or an incompetent person at any stage in an action or proceeding when it appears to the court necessary for the proper protection of the rights and interests of such infant or incompetent person, and it may do this for an incompetent person who has been judicially declared incompetent and has a committee appointed to take care of his person and property if the court feels that the committee is not a fit person to protect the rights of the defendant.28 Compensation of the guardian is taken from the estate of the infant or incompetent.20 

§ 153. Duties, Compensation, Etc., of Guardians Ad Litem. 

Rule 43 provides that the guardian ad litem shall be compensated for his services in an amount which the court deems reasonable. Rule 42 prescribes the duties of the guardian ad litem and rule 41 requires security to be given by the guardian ad litem against misuse of funds which may come into his hands in the discharge of his duties. 

§ 154. Leave to Sue and Defend as a Poor Person. 

A poor person is one who is not worth one hundred dollars besides his wearing apparel and furniture necessary for himself and family, and the subject-matter of the action. If such a person has a cause of action which he desires to prosecute, he may make an application by petition to the court in which he shall state the nature of the action which he intends to bring and that he is not worth one hundred dollars, and the court will assign an attorney to him to conduct his action. Similarly, if such person is prosecuted, he may, on a similar application to the court by petition, procure leave to defend the action as a poor person and have an attorney assigned to conduct his defense. 2 He is not obliged to pay

§ 155. In General. 

In every case certain facts must exist before the plaintiff has any right of action at all. These are the essential facts without which no good complaint can be drawn because no cause of action exists. These usually consist of (a) A fact or group of facts showing a right in the plaintiff ; (b) Another fact or group of facts showing an invasion of that right by the defendant; and in legal actions where damages are sought, (c) A third fact or group of facts showing the damages suffered by the plaintiff.

In contract. actions where the rights of the parties grow out of the agreement that exists between them, the first group of facts showing the right of the plaintiff would require that the plaintiff show the existence of the contract, the consideration therefor and the performance by him of the [178]

PLEADINGS-COMPLAINT STATEMENT OF CAUSE OF ACTION 179 

obligations which it requires him to perform, if any, before the obligations it imposes on the defendant emerge. In tort actions where the law of the land rather than the agreement between the parties determines their respective rights and duties, the situation out of which the law spells the duty owing to the plaintiff by the defendant must be shown. The invasion of plaintiff's right will consist in a statement of the facts showing a failure or refusal by the defendant to perform the duties imposed on him by the agreement between the parties or by the law of the land. A single sentence may be all that is necessary to show the right or its invasion, but in more complicated situations many typewritten pages may be required. 

§ 156. A Knowledge of Substantive Law Necessary. 

To determine what the essential facts are which constitute the cause of action requires a knowledge of the substantive law applicable to the case, e. g. that in an action for fraud and deceit there must exist the five elements of misrepresentation, scienter, intent, reliance and detriment. What the essential facts are cannot be determined by a knowledge of the Civil Practice Act alone. All that act requires is that the complaint must contain "a statement of each cause of action "" and that "every pleading shall contain a plain and concise statement of the material facts, without unnecessary repetition, on which the party pleading relies, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved."" What the "material facts" are can be ascertained only from the substantive

§ 157. Election of Remedies. 

It is at this point that consideration must be given to the remedies afforded by the law. The same facts often give the plaintiff a choice of remedies. A breach of contract for the purchase of land may offer as remedies an equitable action for specific performance and a common law action for damages. A hires B's horse and while he has him in his possession sells him to X. This gives rise to three possible courses. 

B may sue A for converting his horse or for the money received on the sale or he may sue X in replevin. 

It is important that consideration be given here to the choice of remedy since sometimes a choice made at this point is final. The principle is that where the remedies are inconsistent with each other a deliberate choice of one with knowledge or the means of knowledge of the facts which would enable the party to resort to the other, will preclude such party thereafter from retracing his steps and pursuing the particular case, except that where the right asserted is a personal right (a plaintiff's right to security in his physical person or in his reputation) the facts giving rise to the right are judicially noticed and need not be stated.

When the right asserted arises out of contract or is a right of property, the fact of the contract or of the plaintiff's interest in the property must be stated. A written contract may be pleaded by making a copy thereof part of the complaint. Any contract may be pleaded according to its legal effect. Grossman v. Schenker, 206 N. Y. 466.) "In any real property action, plain. tiff must, as the pleading phrase goes, show his title, that is he must state some fact or facts which give him the right to possession, as that he is the owner of the fee or of a term of years or otherwise

If plain- tiff's title comes to him [by deed] by devise or by descent, the facts may be pleaded. But ordinarily it is neither permissible nor necessary to go + * back and set forth the entire chain of title in the grantor, devisor or an. cestor." (Crook v. Licourt, 216 App. 

Div. 237, 214 N. Y. S. 774; Rule 240).

An allegation that the plaintiff is the owner of a chattel, or that the chattel is his property, is a sufficient statement of title therein, unless a special property in the chattel is asserted 

(Wagman v. Raynor, 163 App. Div. 

68; 148 N. Y. S. 471; Rule 270).

Where, by the substantive law, actual damage is of the gist of the defendant's wrong, the facts showing such damage must be stated (All 

American Securities Co., Inc. v. Foun dation Co., 211 App. Div. 684, 686; 

208 N. Y. S. 328; Copolla v. Kraushaar, 102 App. Div. 306; 92 N. Y. S. 

436), but the plaintiff need not allege in terms that he has suffered damage 

(Ketchum v. Van Dusen, 111 App. 

Div. 332; 97 N. Y. S. 658). If special damages are claimed, the facts occa sioning such damages must be stated (Keefe v. Lee, 197 N. Y. 68; Kurak v. 

Traiche, 226 N. Y. 266).

other remedy. If, for example, a party to a contract has a right to rescind it because of the fraudulent acts of the other party thereto, but instead of pursuing that right he sues to enforce the contract, he has made an election between inconsistent remedies and such election is final." 

If the remedies, however, are not inconsistent, a choice of one will not preclude the plaintiff from later abandoning it and following the other. In an action on contract, for example, alternative remedies might be pursued where they are both in affirmance of the contract. Again an action for replevin and an action for damages in obtaining goods under false pretenses are consistent.'

If there is an inconsistency, the election is made when the complaint is served. It is the commencement of the action and not the result of it that constitutes the election. Of course, the service of the summons without the complaint is not an election since the summons is the same whichever course is adopted. Ignorance of the facts relieves one of the effect of an election between inconsistent remedies."

§ 159. First Rule For Stating Facts. 

The ultimate facts which constitute the cause of action should be stated in the complaint and not the evidentiary ones. There are two classes of facts, evidentiary and ultimate. Evidentiary facts are those acquired by the senses. 

They are perceived by sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell and muscular resistance. They warrant an inference respecting the existence of an ultimate fact. Ultimate facts are statements of conclusions or opinions acquired by reflection on evidentiary facts. The distinction is psychological. For example, we notice that the hull of a ship first disappears, then the masts or smoke stacks. These are evidentiary facts. They are perceived by us by means of our sense of sight. Reflection may cause us to wonder why these smaller parts of the ship should not disappear from sight first and the great body of the ship last. Such reflection may lead us to state later the ultimate fact that the earth is round. Again, I hear A and 

B talking together. I note what each says to the other. This is evidence. I reflect upon the conversation and conclude that A and B entered into an agreement. This is the ultimate fact, i. e. one from which a party's right to relief follows by operation of law. Still again I see X drive an automobile down the street. I see him drive rapidly through a con-

The distinction between "ultimate " facts and " evidentiary facts is difficult to apply, since "evidence" is always a relative term.

It has always been a rule of pleading facts that the ultimate facts should be stated and not the evidentiary ones which tend to establish them. This rule, however, under the Code did not find expression in any statute or rule of practice.

§ 160. The Same Case of deCordova v. Sanville.10 

The complaint in this case, after alleging the death of the plaintiff's testator and the issuance of letters to the plaintiff, alleged that plaintiff's testator delivered to the defendant a check for the sum of five thousand dollars; that said check was paid and the defendant received the proceeds thereof; that the plaintiff's testator did not owe the defendant any money and was not indebted to the defendant at said time; that the plaintiff has duly demanded payment of said sum of five thousand dollars, but no part thereof has been paid. There was no allegation that plaintiff's testator loaned five thousand dollars to the defendant.

It will be seen here that the facts alleged are evidentiary ones for the most part. The allegation that plaintiff's testator delivered the check to defendant is evidentiary. So is the allegation that the check was paid and the defendant received the proceeds thereof. The ultimate fact which these facts tend to establish is that plaintiff's testator loaned five thousand dollars to the defendant. This was not alleged and 

Mr. Justice Ingraham whose dissenting opinion in the Appellate Division was adopted unanimously by the Court of 

Appeals says: "What fact is it that constitutes the cause of action? Clearly it is the fact of a loan by the plaintiff to the defendant. The plaintiff alleged the evidence which would make out a prima facie case on the trial of an action to recover a loan of money." 

16. 214 N. Y. 662, reversing 165 A. 

D. 128, on the dissenting opinion of 

Mr. Justice Ingraham. See also Hall v. Torrey, 196 A. D. 804; 188 N. Y. S. 486.

PLEADINGS-COMPLAINT STATEMENT OF CAUSE OF ACTION. 

And later he continues "In this case as was said by Judge Andrews in Nay v. Curley (supra) 'a check may represent a loan or a gift, or money of the drawer, to be applied by the drawee to the use of the former as his agent or otherwise,' or it also may represent a loan of money by the drawer of the check to the payee. Upon the mere proof of the delivery of the check by the drawer to the payee there is a presumption of fact that the check was delivered in payment of a debt. That presumption can be rebutted by showing that no debt existed, and the triers of the fact are authorized to presume that there was a loan, but that presumption is one that is rebuttable by proof that there is no loan. It is not at all a presumption of law but a mere deduction of a fact from other facts that were proved and which presumption is for the jury or the triers of the fact. The distinction, I think, is clear between a presumption of law which is not rebuttable and a presumption of fact which the trier of the fact is authorized to draw from a proved state of facts. Of course the presumption of law need never be alleged in the complaint, for the only purpose of the complaint is to state the facts upon which by operation of law a liability is created, but a mere inference which a trier of the facts may draw from a certain state of facts is not a proper subject of pleading at all. It is the ultimate fact which is to be proved or which must be alleged as the fact 'constituting each cause of action.' 

The language of the Code (Sec. 481) is that a complaint must contain 'a plain and concise statement of the facts constituting each cause of action without unnecessary repetition,' not the facts from which by inference or deduction the facts which constitute a cause of action can be inferred. That fact the plaintiff herein has not seen fit to allege in this complaint. This objection is one of substance and goes to the very foundation of pleadings, and with all the irregularity and confusion incident to the pleadings under the Code, I think we should hold to this one requirement: that the plaintiff should state the facts which constitute the cause of action and not sustain a pleading which only states the evidential facts from which the trier of the facts is authorized to infer or deduce a liability. (See Emery v. 

Pease, 20 N. Y. 62, 64; Van De Sande v. Hall, 13 How. Pr. 458; 

Bliss Code Pl., 3rd ed., Sections 175, 175a).” 

§ 161. The Same-Three Exceptions to First Rule for Stating Facts. 

In three cases, the facts pleaded must be sufficiently proximate to the evidence to apprise the adverse party of the general nature of the evidence relied upon to sustain them. 

The cause of action may be stated in such a general way as to make it impossible for an opponent to anticipate the character of the proof which may be adduced at the trial in support of it. To illustrate, first, plaintiff alleges that he and the defendant entered into a contract, a copy of which he

PLEADINGS COMPLAINT STATEMENT OF CAUSE OF ACTION. 185 

attaches to his complaint. He then alleges that defendant prevented him from carrying out his part of the contract and asks for damages.

It will be seen here that nowhere is the defendant advised of the nature of the acts of prevention complained of. They may be any one or more of a hundred different preventive measures and if defendant had to go to trial under such a condition in the pleadings, he would not know what witnesses to bring to contradict plaintiff's contentions and proofs." 17 The purpose of the pleadings is to develop issues of fact, and such issues emerge only when specific acts or omissions are asserted by one and denied by the other party to the litigation.18 

As Mr. Justice Laughlin said in a recent case.¹º "The specification of various agreements on the part of the defendant, followed by a general allegation of a breach thereof, presents a pleading precisely the same as if the plaintiff had set forth in haec verba the contract and alleged performance on its part and a failure. on the part of the defendant to perform its obligations thereunder. 

It is well settled that in an action to recover damages for the breach of a contract the facts constituting the breach must be pleaded, and that it is insufficient to plead generally that the defendant failed to fulfill his obligations under the contract, or that he has been guilty of a breach of the contract. (Citing numerous cases.) 

Second, the same principle is further illustrated with great frequency in pleading the truth as a defense to a libel or 17. The time of the occurrence of a fact, when material, should be stated (Peo. ex rel. Crane v. Ryder, 12 N. Y. 

433; Barlow v. Pease, 5 Hun, 564).

In tort actions, the time of the occurrence of the alleged wrong is generally immaterial (Critelli v. Rodgers, 87 

Hun, 530). 

A complaint for negligence must state some fact from which an inference of negligence is permissible (Schweitzer v. Mindlin, 248 N. Y. 560). 

A mere allegation of negligence disassociated from a stated act or omission is not sufficient, and the stated act or omission must be alleged as the cause of the injury or damage (Pag nillo v. Mack Paving & Construction 

Co., 142 App. Div. 491; 127 N. Y. S. 

72; Wasmer v. Town of Brant, 222

§ 162. Second Rule for Stating Facts. 

Legal conclusions must not be stated and if stated will be disregarded in determining the sufficiency of the pleading. 

An ultimate fact may be drawn from the evidence by a layman without any, knowledge of legal principles whatever, but a legal conclusion requires the application of a legal principle to the ultimate fact before it can be reached. 

A says to B "I am in need of money. Can you lend me one hundred dollars." B says "Certainly" and delivers to A a check for one hundred dollars which A cashes at his bank. These are evidentiary facts. Reflection will condense all this into the statement B loaned A one hundred dollars. 

This is an ultimate fact. Now by operation of the law of con. tracts we may say A owes B one hundred dollars or is indebted to him in that amount. This is a legal conclusion."¹ 

A few illustrations will help to clarify the principle, but it would require a work exclusively devoted to pleading to furnish anything like a complete list of allegations that have been held to be legal conclusions.22 An allegation that a pertion of the particular acts constituting the wrong done the plaintiff by him, so as to enable him to plead and prepare his defense, and the court to properly control and guide the trial of the action." (a) Pleading an account. Suppose a person from time to time buys goods from another who keeps an account of the purchases made and the buyer refuses to pay for them. 

Now each purchase is in reality a separate and distinct transaction and strictly speaking should constitute a distinct cause of action. To avoid such prolixity as a formal statement of the details of each transaction would require, the Civil Practice Act provides that it is not necessary for a party to set forth in a pleading the items of an account therein alleged. 

The pleader may state generally that between certain dates the defendant bought goods, wares and merchandise of the plaintiff aggregating in reasonable value the total of the several transactions. Such grouping of items is convenient for the plaintiff, and to prevent the possible injustice to the defendant which might result from lack of opportunity to examine the items claimed by the plaintiff, it is provided in the Practice Act that the party who avails himself of this short cut in pleading the facts must furnish to the adverse party within ten days after a written demand therefor a copy of the account, which, if the pleading be verified must also be verified.38 The account contemplated here is more comprehensive than a mere running account for the purchase of goods. It applies to almost every demand made up of items. It should be remembered, of course, that if a plaintiff wishes to do so, he may in certain actions, pursuant to section 255a of the Civil Practice Act, attach to his verified complaint an itemized and numbered schedule; and defendant must then specifically indicate by verified answer the items which he disputes in respect of delivery, performance, reasonable value or agreed price. Failing specifically to the reasonable value. Either must be alleged. (Sparks v. Ducas, 123 App. 

Div. 507; 108 N. Y. S. 546.) When both are alleged, proof of one or the other is sufficient. (Rubin v. Cohen, 129 App. Div. 395; 113 N. Y. S. 843.)

"In pleading the performance of a condition precedent in a contract, it is not necessary to state the facts constituting performance, but the party may state in general terms, that he, or the person whom he represents, duly performed all the conditions of such contract on his part. Were it not for this provision a person suing on a contract would have to show in detail what he did, so that from such allegations it would appear that he had performed his part under the agreement." If plaintiff pleads performance generally under the Rule and in addition sets out specifically the facts which he claims constitute performance, but which nevertheless do not show performance, the general allegation of performance will not suffice. This rule permits an exception to the rule of pleading requiring ultimate facts that are proximate to the evidence to be stated.

(d) Pleading judgment or determination. "In pleading a judgment or other determination of a court or officer of special jurisdiction, it is not necessary to state the facts conferring jurisdiction, but the judgment or determination may be stated to have been duly given or made." The intention here was to make the rule which always applied to courts of general jurisdiction applicable to courts of special jurisdiction. It is, therefore, not necessary, in suing upon a judgment or other determination of a court of limited jurisdiction, to state the facts showing jurisdiction in the court to pronounce the judgment or other determination of such court. The word "duly" is equivalent to saying that the judgment was rendered according to law and is in this sense a legal conclusion.48

It would not satisfy the requirements of this rule to say that the judgment was recovered and duly entered. The word "duly" must qualify the judgment, not its entry.* 49 (e) Pleading in libel or slander. "In an action for libel or slander, it is not necessary to state in the complaint any extrinsic fact for the purpose of showing the application to the plaintiff of the defamatory matter, but the plaintiff may state in general terms that such matter was published or spoken concerning him.""50 Without this provision it would be necessary to set out in the complaint extrinsic facts which would show that the defamatory matter referred to the plaintiff. Public statutes do not have to be pleaded at all, as the court takes judicial notice of them, but it is otherwise with a private statute or the statutes of a foreign state which under the general rules of pleading would have to be stated as any other facts. § 164. Manner of Stating Facts as to Form. 

As to form, statements of facts are made either (a) absolutely, or (b) on information and belief." One may not know of his own knowledge the facts required to be pleaded. In such case he alleges them on information and belief. These two forms of stating facts are illustrated in the form of complaint given in section 129. If facts are stated on knowledge in a verified pleading, and are false, the party verifying may be prosecuted for perjury, although not for contempt of court. 54

§ 166. In General. 

We have considered the manner of commencing an action.' 

This involved the naming of the parties thereto as a part of the title in the summons. Ordinarily there is no difficulty in determining who should be the plaintiff and who the defendant, but in exceptional cases, now much more common than under the Code, some confusion may arise on this point. 

§ 167. The Real Party in Interest. 

1. Section 31, ante. 

The Civil Practice Act provides that "every action must be prosecuted in the name of the real party in interest."" 

This rule was adopted in the Code to clear up the difference that existed between the common law and equity practice [ 200 ] 

2. Civil Practice Act. § 210.

in reference to plaintiffs. It reconciled the practice by adopting the equity rule.³

There are four classes of persons who, while not the real party in interest, may nevertheless be plaintiffs in an action. 

They are: (a) An executor or administrator; (b) A trustee of an express trust;* .4 (c) A person with whom or in whose name a contract is made for the benefit of another, or (d) A person expressly authorized by statute.®

In the case of an executor or an administrator the law requires the executor to be the plaintiff," but in other cases, either the person referred to in the section may be the plaintiff, or he may join with him as co-plaintiff the real party in interest.8 

§ 168. Joinder of Parties Proper and Necessary.10 

The discussion thus far concerns for the most part cases where there is but one plaintiff and one defendant. We are 

3. Brownson v. Gifford, 8 How. Pr. 

389, 395; Cummings v. Morris, 25 N. 

Y. 625; Morrison v. Schmeman, 166 

A. D. 264; 151 N. Y. S. 607. In the case last cited, the assignee of a mortgage was held a party in interest in a foreclosure action. In Clark v. Dado, 

183 A. D. 253; 171 N. Y. S. 205, an overdue note was transferred for the purpose of allowing the transferee to bring the action. It was held that the trausferee was not the real party in interest and could not maintain the action. In Karczag Publishing Co. v. 

Shubert Theatrical Co., 181 A. D. 529, 

169 N. Y. S. 1, it was held that an agent interested only in a percentage of the collections made for his principal, was not a real party in interest. 

An assignee is the real party in interest even though the legal title only passed and he must account to the assignor in case of recovery. Sheridan v. Mayor, 68 N. Y. 30. However, if X gives to Y only a formal power of attorney to sue in X's name, that is not an assignment and Y cannot sue in his own name either as the real party in interest or as a trustee.

now to consider briefly the law governing those cases where there are more parties than one. A distinction must be made at the outset between proper and necessary parties. 

Necessary parties are those without whom the court cannot, if proper objection be made to their omission, proceed to a decree. Proper parties are those whose absence will not prevent the entry of a binding judgment but whose presence may make that judgment more complete. Partners, for example, suing in an action at law to recover a partnership debt are necessary parties. They must be joined as plaintiffs, and when sued on a partnership contract they must be joined as defendants." On the other hand, where partners are sued for a tortious act, all need not be joined, because, although they are all liable, they are severally liable; but the joinder of them all is not objectionable. They are proper but not necessary parties in such case;¹2 because although called "joint" tort feasors, they are severally liable in such cases, or as it is sometimes said, " jointly and severally" liable. 

§ 169. Necessary Parties Plaintiff.13 

In actions at law and in equity if several parties have a joint interest they must join as plaintiffs. This is true not only in the case of partnerships where the partners have a joint interest in actions at law, but it is true in joint contract ventures generally." It is likewise true in tort actions that parties having a joint interest must join in the complaint.' 15 rially changed the law on the joinder of parties. It has adopted the English rule which is much more liberal than the former Code rule.

In equity, all parties entitled to have a deed executed¹ or to have a contract rescinded" are necessary parties.

§ 170. Proper Parties Plaintiff Under the Code. 

The common law rule was that the proper parties plaintiff were the necessary ones and none other. Persons having several interests had to sue separately. The Code relaxed this rigidity in the single case where the plaintiffs sought to be joined had a community of interest in the subject of the action and in obtaining the judgment demanded.19 (a) Thus in an action on a note reading as follows: "On demand after 30 days we promise to pay to the order of 

John F. Nagle, Seven Hundred and Fifty ($750.00) Dollars; also to Chas. H. Callahan the sum of Seven Hundred and 

Fifty $750.00) Dollars with interest," Nagle and Callahan sued the maker. Such plaintiffs had no joint claim and, therefore, were not necessary parties under the common law rule, and though they had a community of interest in the subject of the action, they had no community of interest in the relief sought since each sought his own individual damages in the judgment.20 (b) And in a tort action where, for example, the defendant says, "your boys stole my corn," each boy has an interest in prosecuting the action for slander, but the interests are distinct, and separate suits would be necessary although the proof, except for the matter of damages, would be the same in each case.21

-COMPLAINT JOINDER OF ACTIONS. 

"All persons may be joined in one action as plaintiffs, in whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions is alleged to exist whether jointly, severally or in the alternative, where if such persons brought separate actions any common question of law or fact would arise. 7725 Joinder is proper now under the above language where the two following requisites appear: (a) The parties joined as plaintiffs must have some right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions. 

(b) If they brought separate actions a common question of law or fact would arise.

The language here used is taken from the English Practice Act, order XVI, rule 1, which was enacted in England in 1896, and its interpretation by the English courts is very liberal. Joinder would have been proper under this language in every one of the cases cited under the last section.2

It must not be thought, however, that the Civil Practice Act is so liberal in permitting the joinder of proper parties plaintiff that one can join any parties one chooses. 

For instance, in Olsen v. Bankers Trust Co. 205 App. Div. 

669, 199 N. Y. Supp. 700, a drawee bank had made payment to a forger, who had forged an endorsement of the payee's name on a check which had been certified at the request of the maker. The payee sued to collect on the bank's certification. The maker attempted to join as a co-plaintiff with the payee against the drawee bank and sought to compel a withdrawal of the certification made by the bank. Joinder was not permitted, because, the court said: "The claims of these plaintiffs are not co-ordinate, alternative or complementary. They are not joint, nor several, nor common. They are mutually destructive. There is no common question of law or fact."

247 N. Y. 551, on grounds of public policy, an assignor under section 29 of the Workmen's Compensation Law was not permitted to join as a co-plaintiff with the insurance carrier-assignee even though the assignee had attempted to reassign to the assignor a portion of the chose in action.28

§ 172. Practical Considerations on Joinder of Plaintiffs.29 

While great liberality is now allowed in joining plaintiffs, practical considerations will often make it inexpedient to join plaintiffs too freely in actions. The possibility of joint liability of co-plaintiffs to successful defendants, for costs, where an unsuccessful plaintiff is included, the possibility of conflicting interests arising in the course of the action among plaintiffs, the possibility of a defendant setting up a counterclaim against some plaintiff, the danger of delay in the prosecution of the action occasioned by adjournments, death, bankruptcy, etc., may make a possible joinder unwise. 

§ 173. Necessary Parties Defendant. 

The necessary parties defendant are the same under the Practice Act as under the Code. The change in joinder under the Practice Act is in connection with the proper parties defendant. The general rules on the subject may be stated as follows: 

(a) In the contract actions those jointly liable must be joined as defendants.30 In tort actions, since joint tort feasors are liable both jointly and severally, they are not necessary defendants.31 (b) Where a person is a necessary party plaintiff but his consent to act as plaintiff cannot be obtained, he becomes a necessary party defendant.32 The reason for making him a defendant must be stated in such case in the complaint.33 

§ 174. Proper Defendants Under the Code and Under the Practice Act.

To make the joinder of defendants proper in such cases, however, the several liability of the defendants had to be for the entire amount. Liability of each defendant for part of the sum claimed was not sufficient, and joinder in such case was improper. Hence in an action upon a policy of marine insurance where the policy rendered each of the underwriters separately liable for a specified part of the loss only, the joinder of all the underwriters as defendants was held improper.35

The provision quoted above from the Code is continued under the Practice Act36 but now defendants who are liable for a fractional part only of the loss and not for the entire amount specified in the contract may properly be joined.

§ 175. Proper Defendants Under the Practice Act - Alternative Relief Where Plaintiff Is In Doubt As to Who Is Liable. 

Section 213 of the Civil Practice Act provides: 

"Where the plaintiff is in doubt as to the person from whom he is entitled to redress, he may join two or more defendants, to the intent that the question as to which, if any, of the defendants is liable, and to what extent, may be determined as between the parties.' 

The report of the Joint Legislative Committee on this section states, quoting the notes to the English Practice 

Rules: 

"The typical case for the application of the rule which is of most frequent occurrence in practice is where a person, assuming to act as agent for a disclosed principal, makes a contract with plaintiff, the breach of which gives right to the action. The principal denies the agent's authority. Plaintiff is in the dark as to the authority of the agent. He may join both principal and agent under this rule claiming against the principal such relief as he may be entitled to upon the footing that the agent had the authority which he seemed to have, and alternatively claim against the agent damages for breach of warranty of authority."

This section has been construed to apply to the case suggested by the note quoted above. It has been applied also to a case where plaintiff was in doubt as to which of two defendants with slightly different names was liable to him, rules 1, 4 and 7 must be construed liberally, and where there is a substantial and bona fide allegation of joint or several tort in respect of what is in effect the same transaction or series of transactions, all parties alleged to have participated in the tort may be made defendants to the action."

213 This section seems to give almost absolute power to the court to correct errors growing out of non-joinder or mis joinder. Rule 102 of the Rules of Civil Practice supple ments it. The power of substituting one party for another is also included. A substitution of parties under this section is permissible only, however, where one has lawfully succeeded to the rights and interests formerly held by another party.49

The manner of adding or dropping parties by order of the court is stated in section 193 of the Civil Practice Act as 

1. The court may determine the controversy as between the parties before it where it can do so without prejudice to the rights of others or by saving their rights; but where a complete determination of the controversy cannot be had without the presence of other parties the court must direct them to be brought in. 

2. Where any party to an action shows that some third person, not then a party to the action, is or will be liable to such party wholly or in part for the claim made against such party in the action, the court, on application of such party, may order such person to be brought in as a party to the action and direct that a supplemental summons and a pleading alleging the claim of such party against such person be served upon such person and that such person plead thereto, so that the claim of such moving party against such person may be determined in such action, which shall thereupon proceed against such person as a defendant therein to such judgment as may be proper. 

3. Where a person not a party to the action has an interest in the subject thereof, or in real property the title to which may in any manner be affected by the judgment, or in real property for injury to which the complaint demands relief, and makes application to the court to be made a party, it must direct him to be brought in by the proper amendment. 

4. The controversy between the defendants shall not delay a judgment to which the plaintiff is entitled, unless the court otherwise directs.50

§§ 178-a. Abatement and Continuance. 

If a party to an action dies, the cause of action sometimes "abates" or ceases, e. g. where a plaintiff, whose leg had been broken by a taxicab, was suing the owner of the taxi, and while the action was pending the plaintiff was killed by an airplane. Other causes of action do not abate with the death of a party,-e. g. a cause of action by a storekeeper against a customer for goods sold and delivered in the storekeeper's lifetime. In such cases the Civil Practice Act in sections 82-95 specifically provides for the steps to be taken after the death of the party. Such sections are self-explanatory and will not be treated in detail here.

§ 180. The Same-First Limitation on Joinder.78 

It must appear upon the face of the complaint that all of the causes of action united in it belong to one and the same subdivision of section 258 of the Civil Practice Act. If every cause of action in the complaint cannot be lodged under some one subdivision of that section, the joinder is prohibited. Thus a cause of action for false imprisonment may be joined with one for malicious prosecution as they are both for personal injuries and fall under subdivision 2." So also a cause of action on a note, and one for services may be joined as they both fall under the first subdivision. 

But an action for slander cannot be joined with one for false imprisonment since they fall under subdivisions 3 and 2 respectively" nor can a cause of action against an attorney for negligence in conducting a lawsuit be joined with a cause of action against him for statutory treble damages under Penal Law, section 273. Again, a cause of action on contract cannot ordinarily be joined with one on tort since the former falls under subdivision 1 and the latter either under subdivisions 2, 3, 4 or 6 of section 258.77 76 The word," ordinarily " is used here because it is possible that the tort and contract causes of action might be so related in their origin or otherwise that it could be said of them that they arose out of the same transaction, in which case they would fall under subdivision 9 and thus satisfy the requirements of this limitation that they fall under some one of the subdivisions. In an automobile accident, for example, the owner may be injured personally and his machine may be damaged. He could sue defendant for both causes of action and join them in the same complaint although the first cause of action would ordinarily be classified under subdivision 2 and the second under subdivision 6. It is not always easy to say what causes of action arise out of the same transaction or transactions connected with the same subject of action. Careful analysis is usually required to determine whether the causes of action may or may not be grouped under subdivision 9 of section 258. A plaintiff who was injured by the explosion of a gun bought by him from the defendant joined in his complaint a cause of action for a breach of warranty made by the defendant at the time he purchased the gun, with a cause of action for negligence in placing upon the market a gun constructed of such defective material and in such a careless manner that it was unsafe for use and endangered the community. The court held this joinder bad. The warranty and the construction of the gun occurred at different times and have no necessary connection with one another." The mere fact, however, that the actions arise at the same time does not establish a connection between them. An action for an assault, for example, joined with one for slander because of words spoken at the time the assault was administered, are not properly joined and do not arise out of the same transaction. The assault could easily have been administered without the slander, and the slanderous words spoken without the assault.80 So also, a cause of action for wrongful death which the complaint alleged was caused "solely" by negligence of the owner of a picket fence upon which a boy fell was not joinable with a cause of action for malpractice against the physician who treated the boy, even though in the action against the owner one element of damages is the damage done by the physician.' 81 But a defendant who attempts to get property, which he claims, from a plaintiff who also claims it, and assaults the plaintiff by way of removing an obstruction to a forcible entry of plaintiff's house in order that he might get the property and take it away, may be sued in the same complaint for an assault and trespass, though these actions ordinarily would fall under subdivisions 2 and 6 respectively, 78. PLEADINGS COMPLAINT—JOINDER OF ACTIONS. 

§ 182. The Same Third Limitation on Joinder.92 

It must appear on the face of the complaint that the causes of action joined do not require different places of trial. The Civil Practice Act states the proper place for the trial of different types of actions. Conflict with the law regulating the proper place for the trial of actions is what is contemplated in this limitation. Thus where plaintiff sued to recover damages for the loss of a barn located in another state and also for loss of its contents of grain, charging defendant with wilfully and wantonly burning them, the joinder was held improper under this restriction. The loss occurred prior to 1913, at which time our courts did not have jurisdiction of an action for injury to real property lying without the state. In 1913, a statute was enacted giving such jurisdiction, and the joinder would now be proper."*

Under section 17 of the Municipal Court Code an action for rent or to dispossess a tenant must be brought in the district where the property is located. If rented premises were in the ninth district the joinder in an action in the first district of a claim for rent of such premises, while the tenant was still in possession, with a claim for goods sold and delivered in the first district would be improper. 

§ 183. The Same A Limitation on Joinder Under the Code Abolished. 

Under the Code there was a fourth limitation on the joinder of causes of action. It was required by section 484 that each cause of action "affect all the parties to the action." Thus if A had a cause of action against X alone, and another cause of action against X and Y, he could not join them for the reason that the cause of action against X alone did not affect Y.95 This limitation which was found under section 484 of the Code has been omitted from section 

258 of the Civil Practice Act. The omission makes a consid erable change in the law on joinder of causes of action and must be read in connection with sections 209, 211, 212 and 213. These sections have already been discussed so far as they affect joinder of parties plaintiff and defendant. 

92. This limitation is the same under the Civil Practice Act as it was under the Code. 

93. See Civil Practice Act, 88 182, 183, 184, 185 and 186. 

94. Jacobus v. Colgate, 217 N. Y. 235. 

95. O'Connor v. Virginia Passenger 

& Power Co., 184 N. Y. 46.

Section 212 of the Civil Practice Act provides: 

"It shall not be necessary that each defendant shall be interested as to all the relief prayed for, or as to every cause of action included in any proceeding against him."

It therefore follows that if, under the Practice Act, A has one cause of action against X and still another against X and Y, there is nothing to prevent him from joining them in one complaint." Now, of course, Y is not interested in the cause of action against X and might be inconvenienced by attending the trial of that action. To meet this situation the section continues: "but the court may make such order as may appear just to prevent any defendant from being embarrassed or put to expense by being required to attend any proceedings in which he may have no interest.”

By way of further illustration, if several persons were injured in the same accident and claim damages against the common defendant on the ground that its negligent conduct caused the accident, we see no reason under section 209 of the Civil Practice Act why they could not all join as plaintiffs, each claiming his separate damage. Each plaintiff claims a right to relief and there would be a common question of law or fact. See also sections 171 and 174 ante.⁹7 97

The section in the Civil Practice Act relating to such consolidation of actions is new, and is general and broad in its terms. It reads as follows: 

(* * Actions may be consolidated whenever it can be done without prejudice to a substantial right.''99 

Even under this statute, however, causes of action which could not have been joined in the first instance, can not be later joined by an order of consolidation. This section must be read and applied in connection with the sections relating to joinder of causes of action; for it is to be inferred that a code of statutes was intended to be consistent and harmonious in its several parts and provisions.¹ And a construction of this provision which would allow a party to consolidate actions which could not have been originally prosecuted as a single action, would render ineffectual the limitations already discussed relating to joinder of causes of action. 

Where the actions are such as might be joined in one complaint, and could be consolidated without prejudice to a substantial right, the consolidation is within the discretion of the court. But such discretion will not generally be exercised in favor of the motion to consolidate unless it is shown either that no defense is intended, or that the questions which will arise in both of the actions are substantially the same." 2

Consolidation under the code was not permissible where the plaintiff in one action was the defendant in the other," but the language of section 817 of the code which required that the actions to be consolidated should be "in favor of the same plaintiff against the same defendant” is not repeated in the Practice Act and such limitation no longer exists." 

The regulations, therefore, governing the consolidation of actions are as follows: 

1. As a general rule, any causes of action which could have originally been prosecuted together as a single suit, but which are being prosecuted as individual actions, may be consolidated. Actions which could not have been originally prosecuted as a single action can not be consolidated. 

2. Even actions coming within the foregoing rule can not be consolidated where a substantial right would be prejudiced thereby. 

3. Otherwise the consolidation is within the discretion of the court; but the court in its discretion will seldom grant such a motion unless it is shown that no defense is intended or that the questions which will arise in both of the actions are substantially the same.

There is no longer a divergence of authority as to whether a court of limited jurisdiction can consolidate two or more actions where the aggregate amount would carry the demand beyond the monetary jurisdiction of that court. It can."

§ 185. The Same - When Actions are Pending in Different Courts. 

The Civil Practice Act provides that when one of the actions so consolidated is pending in the supreme court, and another is pending in another court, the supreme court may, by order, remove to itself the action in the other court and consolidate it with that in the supreme court. It likewise provides that where one of the actions is pending in the county court and another is pending in the justice's court, the county court may by order remove to itself the action in the justice's court and consolidate it with that in the county court. Although this section applies in terms to the supreme court and the county court alone, it is extended by another statutory provision to all courts of record.15 So any court of record has this power to remove to 14

§ 186. The Same-Actions in Behalf of the People. 

Where two or more actions brought in behalf of the people upon the same mortgage or contract are pending against separate defendants claiming or defending under the same title, the attorney-general, upon the request of the defendants, must cause them to be consolidated into one action; and only one bill of costs can be taxed against the defendants."

§ 188. The Same - Where There Are Two or More Defendants.23 

In an action against two or more defendants alleged to be severally liable, if some but not all of such defendants have been served with the summons, the action may be severed and continued against those served as if they were the only defendants named therein. In such an action, if the summons is served upon all of the defendants the plaintiff may take judgment against one or more of them where he would be entitled to judgment if the action was against that one or them alone. When such judgment is taken, the clerk, upon application of the plaintiff, must enter an order severing the action and directing that the plaintiff may proceed against the other defendants. As regards the other parties to the action, persons jointly liable are regarded as one party for every purpose contemplated by this section."" 

In an action against two or more defendants, if a several judgment is proper, the court may render judgment or require the plaintiff to take judgment against one or more of the defendants, and direct that the action be severed and proceed against the others as the only defendants therein.25 This is true not only in cases of joint and several liability, but authorizes a separate judgment, when a separate liability of some of the defendants is established on the trial although the cause of action, as alleged in the complaint was joint only.20

§ 190. In General. 

After a complaint is served the defendant must decide what course he shall pursue with regard to it. He may, of course, answer it and we shall consider that course in the next two chapters. However, there may be many objections to it which should be urged before answering because unless so urged, they are waived. Other objections may be urged before answering but are not waived by deferring them till later. We shall consider in this chapter all the objections which may be taken to a complaint before answering and indicate which of them are waived unless so urged and which [231]

are not. In all cases the objections are taken by motion and these motions are some of the motions incidental to pleading. The other motions incidental to pleading will be specifically considered in their proper order as the occasions for their use are presented. Generally speaking, they are all covered by the following

Rule 90 authorizes the first motion and Rule 102 the second. (a) To state separately and number. If there are two causes of action in a complaint, but the allegations containing them are commingled, it is the right of the defendant to have the allegations relating to one cause of action separated from the allegations relating to the other, and set up in consecutive order and numbered." A complaint, for example, which seeks to recover money earned under a contract, the performance of which was prevented by the defendant, and also damages suffered and prospective profits lost by the defendant's breach, states two causes of action and they must be separately stated and numbered." Likewise, in an action for the price of goods delivered under a contract, and damages for refusing to take the remainder of the goods sold by the same contract.Ⓡ

If the recovery on one of the alleged causes of action would not bar a recovery upon the other, there is more than one, cause of action and the motion should be granted,¹¹ but if recovery on one would bar a recovery upon the other, the motion to compel a separate stating and numbering should be denied, since the same facts may give rise to more than one remedy and these remedies may or may not be set out as different causes of action in the complaint. This motion like the last is intended primarily to aid the opposing party to plead. A defendant should not be required to answer a complaint that he does not clearly understand. The complaint in the case of the U. S. Printing and Lithograph Company v. Powers was before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, First Department, twice upon this motion,16 and the motion was granted both times. 

The first time the complaint alleged that the defendant guaranteed a certain indebtedness" by various agreements in writing " without alleging the substance of any of them, and the second time the complaint attached a copy of one of the agreements but the agreement itself so attached was ambiguous and the complaint did not state any definite construction of it that would resolve the ambiguity. If, however, the meaning of the pleading is clear even though additional details regarding the allegations thereof would be helpful to the defendant to enable him to prepare for trial, though not necessary to enable him to plead, the motion should be denied." When, however, the details sought are necessary to enable the defendant to plead even though the general meaning of the pleading be clear the motion will be granted. For example, the time when services alleged in the complaint were performed or materials furnished, or whether the contract alleged was oral or in writing, though ordinarily mere matters of detail, may, at times, be necessary to enable the defendant to determine whether he should plead the statute of frauds or the statute of limitations. In such cases the general rule is that the motion will be granted.' 18

§ 193. Motion to Compel an Amendment by Adding New Parties or Dropping Parties or Causes of Action. 

"If there be a misjoinder of parties plaintiff or a defect of parties plaintiff or defendant, or if causes of action be improperly united, the court may order the party to serve such amended pleading as the nature of the case may require.''¹9 

The principles relating to necessary and proper parties plaintiff and defendant and joinder of causes of action were stated in chapter XII, ante. If a necessary party to an action is omitted there is a nonjoinder and if a person is made a party defendant in an action who is neither a necessary nor proper party there is a misjoinder. A nonjoinder of parties is also called a defect of parties. It is so called in Rule 102. These terms were used under the Code but as the Civil Practice Act has increased the number of proper parties, the likelihood of a misjoinder of parties has been correspondingly diminished. 

Under the Code the remedy for nonjoinder and misjoinder of parties was by demurrer. A defendant could demur for a defect or nonjoinder of parties plaintiff or defendant and for a misjoinder of parties plaintiff.20 This remedy does not exist under the Civil Practice Act. The remedy now provided is a motion to amend the summons and complaint by adding the necessary parties in case of a nonjoinder, and dropping parties defendant who are found to be neither necessary nor proper. Complete power is given to the court at any stage of the cause to order such amendment and the court is warned that no cause shall be defeated for nonjoinder or misjoinder of parties, and that where a complete determination of the controversy cannot be had without statute of frauds or limitations would be a good defense, to apply for leave to amend the answer by setting up such defense. This would cause great delay.

It is true that a motion for a bill of particulars has been granted even though made before the answer is in as there is nothing in the statute requiring such motion to be deferred until after the answer is in. (Bracken v. Toland, 153 A. D. 57; 137 N. Y. S. 

1043.) But the purpose of the bill of particulars is best effectuated if made after the answer is in and the issues framed and there seems no good reason for making an exception in regard to the latter motion to enable it to do the regular work of the former (Royle v. McLaughlin, 195 A. D. 513; 

186 N. Y. S. 356), especially since the motion to make more definite is made on the pleading alone and the motion for a bill of particulars is pased on an affidavit showing necessity therefor.

21. Civil Practice Act, §§ 192 and 

193. Subdivision 1 of section 193 provides that where a complete determination of the controversy cannot be had without the presence of other parties, the court must direct them to be brought in.

It has been held that this provision applies to equitable actions, and that it was not intended to change the rule that the plaintiff in an action at law need not sue any other than the parties he chooses (Chapman v. Forbes, 123 N. Y. 532; Fox v. Western, 257 

N. Y. 305).

In equitable actions the rule is not simply one of practice or convenience. 

The court should refuse to proceed in the absence of a party whose presence is necessary to a complete determination of the controversy (Mahr v. N. U. 

F. Ins. Soc., 127 N. Y. 452; First Nat. 

Bank v. Shuler, 153 N. Y. 163.) 

Under subdivision 2 of section 193 a defendant who can show that some third person not then a party to the action is or will be liable to him for, the claim made against him in the action, may bring in such person as a defendant. The original defendant must make the application, unless there is a counterclaim in the answer, when the plaintiff would make the application to bring in any such third person who might be liable over to plaintiff on the counterclaim. It is discretionary with the court to grant or deny the application. To invoke the discretion of the court on his behalf, a defendant must present an affidavit on notice to the plaintiff which "shows that some third person, not then a party to the action, is or will be liable" to the defendant "wholly or in part for the claim made against" him in the action. If the court grants the application, an order must be made which will "direct that a sup- plemental summons and a pleading alleging the claim of such party (the defendant) against such person (the person sought to be included) be served upon such person and that such person plead thereto."

The pleading to be served on such third party is the answer of the orig. inal defendant which must not only set out defendant's answer to the complaint but the claim of the defendant against the third party which will be in the nature of a complaint by the defendant against such third party. It would seem that the defendant should serve the supplemental summons with such answer upon the third party. The plaintiff ought not to be required to do so. 

It would seem that a copy of the order of the court, directing the supplemental summons and the pleading to be served upon such third party, should be served with them. Where this is done, the third party is required to plead to the claim set out against him in defendant's answer. It is not clear what would happen if such third party has a counterclaim which he wants to assert against the defendant. He ought not to be compelled to forego asserting it if it is otherwise proper. To allow it, however, might complicate the issues and delay the trial and accordingly provision is made that "The controversy between the defendants shall not delay a judgment to which the plaintiff is entitled unless the court otherwise directs" (Civil 

Practice Act, § 193, subd. 4). The third party brought in may only plead to defendant's answer, and he may not plead to the allegations in the com plaint. (Municipal Service Co. v. D. 

B. & M. Corp., 257 N. Y. 423.)

Subdivision 3 of Civil Practice Act, 

§ 193, applies to actions at law and actions in equity (Rosenberg v. Salo-

a party but who has an interest in the subject of the action or in real property, the title to which may in any manner be affected by the judgment, or for injury to which the complaint demands relief, may make application to the court to be made a party and the court must direct him to be brought in by proper amendment.22

If two or more causes of action are improperly joined the remedy is also by motion to compel an amendment by which the plaintiff must elect which of the causes of action he will retain. 

§ 194. Motion to Strike Out Unnecessary and Improper Matter. 

"If any matter, contained in a pleading, be sham, frivolous, irrelevant, redundant, repetitious, unnecessary, impertinent or scandalous or may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action, the court may order such matter stricken out, in which case the pleading will be deemed amended accordingly, or the court may order an amended pleading to be served omitting the objectionable matter. 1928 This rule is a compound of parts of former Code sections 

537, 538, 545 and the New Jersey rule numbered 25. The decisions which have interpreted these Code sections apply in a limited way, at least, in interpreting the rule. There are difficulties in the way of applying these decisions fully, partly because of the new language introduced and also partly because practice under former Code sections 537, 538 and 545 was not uniform. mon, 144 N. Y. 92). The application thereunder to be made a party must be that of the omitted person. 

It seems that Civil Practice Act, § 105, empowers the court in its discretion, either in an action at law or an action in equity, to direct that any person, who could have been joined as a party at the commencement of the action, be brought in as a party defendant upon motion of the plaintiff, if a satisfactory reason is shown for failure to join such person originally and the rights of the parties have not changed since the commencement of the action. It was held in Gittleman v. Feltman, 191 N. The word "sham" here used relates to matter so demonstratively false as to leave no reasonable doubt in the mind of the court as to its falsity.24 

The matter in a pleading which may be characterized as "frivolous" must be not only useless in point of law but so obviously so as to indicate bad faith on the part of the pleader. 

The words "irrelevant," "" 'redundant' and "scandalous" were used in the Code.26 They have, of course, the same meaning here as there, and in both places they are used in connection with the motion to strike out. They are used in their ordinary sense. Irrelevant matter has no bearing on the subject matter involved in the litigation and can have no effect on the ultimate decision of the court.27 An illustration of redundant as distinguished from irrelevant matter is seen where one entire cause of action is incorporated by reference in another. This matter might not be irrelevant in its proper place but some of it, at any rate, must be redundant where found, otherwise a motion to state separately and number should apply.28

The additional words repetitious, unnecessary and impertinent, not found in the Code but adopted from the New 

Jersey Practice Rule 23 carry out the same obvious purpose by additional synonyms and make more emphatic the insistance of the law makers that 25 "Every pleading shall contain a plain and concise statement of the material facts, without unnecessary repetition, on which the party pleading relies, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved. 20

Under the Code, the mere fact that matter contained in a pleading was irrelevant, etc., did not entitle the adverse party to have the same stricken out. In addition to its irrelevancy the presence of the matter contained in the pleading had to aggrieve or injure in some way the adverse party before the motion would be granted." The Code language clearly required the moving party to be aggrieved but the 

Civil Practice Act uses the disjunctive "or" to introduce the phrase "or may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action." The rule can scarcely mean that every unnecessary word or phrase may be stricken from the pleading by this motion and it is to be observed that the court is given discretion to determine when the motion should be granted, for the rule says 

"The court may order such material stricken out.'

It has been held that the sufficiency of the pleading technically should not be tested on a motion to strike out, and when alleged unnecessary matter sought to be stricken out would, if the motion were granted, so emasculate the pleading that the part remaining would be obviously insufficient in law, the motion should be denied.³2 The apparent reason of these decisions is to encourage the raising of questions of sufficiency by motions under Rules 106 and 107, which are especially designed for that purpose. This was the Code rule and the same reasoning applies to the rule under the Practice Act where a special motion is provided to test the sufficiency of the pleading itself."
