§ 198. The Time for Making Motions Contemplated in this Chapter. 

"a. A motion under Rules one hundred and two, one hundred and three or one hundred and four must be noticed within twenty days from the service of the pleading to which the motion is addressed. 

The time to make such motions shall not be extended unless notice of at least two days of an application for such extension be given to the adverse party. 1958 This rule applies to all the motions of the first class discussed in this chapter except the motion to state separately and number for the making of which no time is prescribed. 

Its nature is such, however, that it should be made before answering the complaint." The law regulating extensions of time for making these motions as well as for other purposes is considered in chapter XX, post. The intention is to require such motions to be made before answering, and if the answer is served during the pendency of such motion the motion is deemed abandoned."1

§ 204. Objections to Separate Causes of Action in a Complaint. 

If a complaint contain more than one cause of action, the motions herein considered may be addressed to one or more of the causes of action stated and need not be addressed to the entire complaint.82 If addressed to the entire complaint, the motion will be denied if the complaint contains one cause of action which is good.88 

§ 205. Effect of Service of Answer Pending Motion - Pleading After Disposition of Motion. 

84 The service of an answer to a complaint after such motion was made and before its determination, was formerly construed as an abandonment of the motion, but this is no longer the case since the repeal of $ 282 of the Civil Practice Act in 1932. An answer may now be served during the pendency of such a motion without prejudice to the rights of the moving party. The motion is no longer "killed" thereby. Pleading after disposition of a motion to take an objection to a pleading in point of law is regulated by Civil Practice Act, § 283. This section does not apply to the corrective or regulatory motions.85

Rule 108. Some of the matters which this rule seems to permit the court to dispose of were under common law pleading issues triable by a jury and 

Art. I, 2 of the Constitution of the state preserves trial by jury in all cases where it has been heretofore (meaning at common law) used and says that the right to this mode of trial shall remain inviolate forever.

If, therefore, the court should undertake to dispose of these objections, especially those urged under subds. 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 of Rule 107 without the aid of a jury the question of conflict between this rule and the practice it authorizes with the article of the state Constitution above referred to would be presented. At common law even temporary issues of fact presented by dilatory pleas were tried by a jury. 

Such pleas included pleas to the jurisdiction, to the disability of the person, and in abatement. Res adjudicata, statute of limitations, release and the statute of frauds were not dilatory pleas, but pleas in bar and issues of fact thereon were triable by a jury. 

See Chitty Pleading, p. 490, and chap. 

V of Gould's Pleading, p. 159.

The courts may, however, so construe the rule as to require the trial of such issues by a jury, which construction might save it. It is proper to give a statute such a construction as will save it from a constitutional inhibition. The court in Dollar v. 

Canadian Car Co., 220 N. Y. 270 so construed § 432 of the Code. 

82. Civil Practice Act, § 281, Rule

§ 206. Waiver of Objections. 

Leaving aside the recent broad provisions of sections 192 and 193 of the Civil Practice Act with respect to the right to add or drop parties at any stage of the cause, it may be stated as a general rule that if the objections to a complaint appearing on its face are not taken by motion they are all waived except (a) that the court has not jurisdiction of the subject of the action, and (b) that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. These objections are never waived whether appearing on the face of the complaint or not so appearing. They may be raised at the trial or even for the first time on appeal. Other objections not appearing on the face of the complaint may be taken by motion or answer. If not so taken they, too, are waived.88 The only apparent exception to this general rule is the motion to dismiss the complaint under Rule 107, subdivision 1, on the ground that the court has not jurisdiction of the person of the defendant. Such objection is usually waived by answering, so that defendant's only remedy is by a proper motion, appearing specially. 88a 

86. Civil Practice Act, § 278, subdivision 1 and § 279. Under the Code 

(88 488, 498, 499) these objections to a complaint had to be taken by demurrer if they appeared on the face of the complaint, otherwise they were waived except (a) where the court had not jurisdiction over the subject of the action, or (b) where the complaint did not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. Where, however, the defendant is a foreign government, the objection that the court has no jurisdiction over the person of the defendant is not waived by failing to raise it by motion, since service of a summons on such a defendant gives the court no personal jurisdiction over it. Problems. 

1. Defendant is a resident of Suffolk county and is served with a complaint in an action for $2,500, brought in the County Court of Nassau county. The complaint states that the defendant resides at 55 Blank street, Riverhead, Suffolk county, L. I. No answer has yet been served, because defendant's time to serve the answer was extended by the plaintiff without prejudice. 

Thirty days after the complaint was served, defendant moves to dismiss it on the ground that it appears on the face thereof that defendant is a resident of Suffolk county and that therefore the court has no jurisdiction of the subject matter. Motion granted or denied? Why? 

2. In 1930, X, a dentist, sued Y for $5,000 for dental services rendered in 1920 and 1921 as itemized in a numbered schedule annexed to the complaint as Exhibit A. Eleven days after service of the complaint Y moves, on a notice of motion without affidavits, to dismiss the complaint on the ground that it appears on the face thereof that the cause of action is barred by the statute of limitations. 

Motion granted or denied? Why? 

3. R is the receiver of The Michigan Corporation, appointed by a court in Michigan, the state in which the corporation was organized. 

He sues D in the New York Supreme Court for a $60,000 claim owing from D to The Michigan Corporation. (It was recently held in New York that a foreign receiver of a foreign corporation has legal capacity to sue in New York, on principles of comity. Assume this to be sound law.) 

Nineteen days after the complaint was served, D moves "for judgment dismissing the complaint under Rule 106 of the Rules of Civil Practice on the ground that it appears on the face of the complaint that plaintiff has not legal capacity to sue and that the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action." 

R points out that in fact it does not appear on the face of the complaint that R is a foreign receiver or that The Michigan Corporation is a foreign corporation. These are truly the facts, however, and they appear in D's moving affidavit. 

R opposes the motion on the grounds that it is not timely and that D should have moved under Rule 107 and again used affidavits under that rule, instead of moving "on the face of the complaint.' 

Motion granted or denied? Why?

Now taking each allegation of the complaint separately, the attitude of the defendant toward it must be either (a) he knows that it is true, or (b) he knows that it is false, or (c) he has information which leads him to believe that it is true, or (d) he has information which leads him to believe that it is false, or (e) he has not sufficient knowledge or information to form a belief either way. Beside all this and considering the complaint or a cause of action in it, as a whole, (f) the defendant may know some fact or group of facts not referred to in the complaint which should, even if the allegations in the complaint are true, prevent plaintiff from recovering. The debt sued on may be voidable because, for example, defendant has been discharged in bankruptcy.

These positions of the defendant are the only ones which it is possible for him to take and the problem confronting him in preparing his answer is, what shall he say in his answer under each contingency. 

§ 209. Defendant's Answer Under Each Contingency Stated in Last Section. 

If the defendant's position is that represented in cases (a) or (c) in the last section, he says nothing in his answer about the allegation in question and this is an admission of its truth. In (d) the denial will be on information and belief and in (e) the denial will take the form "defendant denies that he has any knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to" the allegation. § 211. Denials, Defenses and Counterclaims Distinguished. 

A denial is a contradiction of one or more material allegations of the complaint. It introduces into the case no new facts. It merely denies that facts already stated in the com plaint are true. Defenses and counterclaims introduce new matter not referred to in the complaint. The new matter introduced by a defense is of such a character, that if established, it would undermine or defeat in whole or in part the cause of action stated in the complaint. It shows for example that the plaintiff released the defendant from the claim sued on, or that the contract for the breach of which the plaintiff claims damages was not in writing and not enforceable under the statute of frauds, or brings out facts which excuse or justify in law, the things complained of. The new matter which constitutes a counterclaim does not seek to undermine the complaint, but sets up a counter cause of action against the plaintiff which may offset the claim of the plaintiff in part or altogether, or may even result in an affirmative judg- (1) Positive. (2) On information and belief. (3) Of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief. (1) Positive. (2) On information and belief. (3) Of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief. 

9. A mere averment of facts inconsistent with those alleged in the complaint raises no issue. Place v. Bleyl, 45 A. D. 17; 60 N. Y. S. 800.

PLEADINGS 

ment against the plaintiff after satisfying plaintiff's demands. The test which will determine whether the new matter is matter for defense or for a counterclaim is this: could you with such new matter draw a complaint in which the defendant would be the plaintiff and the plaintiff the defendant, and start an action thus independently of the one being prosecuted by the plaintiff. If you could, the new matter is matter for a counterclaim; otherwise, it is defensive matter. A defendant who knows that the statute of limitations has run on the claim which the plaintiff is prosecuting against him, may be able with such new matter to undermine and defeat plaintiff's cause of action but he could by no means start with those facts an action against the plaintiff. 

Such facts, if used at all, must be used in the action already begun by plaintiff. They are matter of defense and not of counterclaim. 

§ 212. Joinder of Denials, Defenses and Counterclaims. 

"A defendant may set forth in his answer as many defenses or counterclaims or both as he has, whether they are such as were formerly denominated legal or equitable.'"10

The causes of action joined in a complaint must be consistent as we have seen," but in an answer, consistency is not a virtue. Inconsistent grounds of defense are permissible. 

A defendant sued for an assault may, for example, deny that the assault took place and justify the assault on the ground of self-defense.12 A defendant sued by a corporation for an unpaid subscription to its capital stock may set up that the plaintiff has never been incorporated as one defense, and that it was incorporated for illegal purposes, as another," And a defendant sued for the purchase price of goods sold, may deny the sale, plead breach of warranty and also a rescission of the contract sued on.¹4 14

Problems. 

1. Dictate the answer in the case of Lindbergh v. Casey, Problem 1,

Chap. III. 

2. Action for wrongful death by administrator of a workman against a foreman. "D denies that D directed the decedent to go down and work in a hole that D had constructed." Is the denial good? (Stuber v. McEntee, 142 N. Y. 200.) 

3. Replevin. D (1) Admits P's demand; (2) Denies on information and belief every allegation of the complaint not hereinbefore admitted or controverted. Is the denial good? (Griffin v. L. I. R. R., 101 N. Y. 348.) 

4. Action for breach of employment contract. P alleges D discharged P "without cause". D enters a general denial and alleges that P was discharged for six specified causes. On the trial D desires to offer proof of two additional causes. P claims that the testimony about to be offered is not within the issues raised by the pleadings, and therefore inadmissible. D claims that in any event the testimony is admissible under D's general denial of P's allegation that D discharged P "without cause". Whose argument prevails? (Linton v. Unexcelled Fireworks Co., 124 N. Y. 533.) 

5. "D denies that D wrongfully discharged P." Does Section 275 of the Civil Practice Act make this equivalent to an allegation of justified dismissal? (Browne v. Empire, 44 A. D. 598.) 

6. Contract of employment provided P was to serve D to D's satisfaction. P sues for wrongful discharge. General denial interposed by D, with no affirmative defense of justified dismissal. Is an issue raised? (Burns v. Lipson, 204 A. D. 643, 198 N. Y. S. 810.) 

7. (a) "D has no information sufficient to form a belief as to the allegations contained in paragraphs 3 and 4 of the complaint. 

Valid? (Steinback v. Diepenbrock, 52 A. D. 437, 65 N. Y. S. 118.) (b) "D denies that he has any knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the allegations in paragraph 5 of the complaint. Valid? 

8. "D states that he denies." Valid? (Kirschbaum v. Eschmann, 205 N. Y. 127; Jones v. Ludlum, 74 N. Y. 61.) 

9. (a) P sues D and C for negligence. "D, answering the complaint, alleges (1) that P was contributorily negligent; (2) that P released 

D; (3) admits the copartnership between D and C but denies each and every other allegation in the complaint not hereinbefore specifi cally admitted, qualified or denied." Is the denial good? (Clark v. 

Dillon, 97 N. Y. 371.) (b) "D denies all the allegations contained in paragraph 2 of the complaint except as hereinafter admitted." Valid? (Thompson v. Wittkop, 184 N. Y. 117.) 

10. P's complaint in the New York Supreme Court alleges that P is a resident and sets forth a cause of action for negligence against D, a foreign corporation, in connection with a collision that occurred in New Jersey. D, "on information and belief denies that it has any knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to whether or not P is a resident of New York." Does this raise an issue as to

§ 217. In General. 

As was shown in the last chapter, the answer of the defendant consists of denials and new matter. The new matter may take the form of defenses or counterclaims or any combination of these. We shall in this chapter take up denials first, then defenses and finally counterclaims. An answer which does not contain any of these three forms is not an answer at all. Therefore, if a paper purporting to be an answer simply admits the allegations of the complaint, it is not regarded as an answer at all for there is no authority for it in the Civil Practice Act.¹

§ 218. What Constitutes a Good Denial. 

(a) The denial must be express and direct and must not be left to inference. A version of a transaction inconsistent. with that expressed in the complaint is mere argumentativeness, is not a denial of the complaint and will not put its allegations in issue. The allegations in the complaint in such case stand admitted." 2 (b) The denials to raise an issue must be directed to a material allegation of the complaint. In an action in the 

Supreme Court where jurisdiction is presumed, the complaint alleged that the plaintiff was a resident. The answer denied. this. The court held that such denial raised no issue since the allegation was immaterial.* as immaterial. Again the denial of a legal conclusion stated in the complaint raises no issue, as a legal conclusion is disregarded in construing the complaint. If the complaint, for example, alleges that the defendant is indebted to the plaintiff, the denial of such allegation will not put the matter in issue."

§ 221. Form of Specific Denial to Be Avoided-Negative Pregnant. 

In drafting a specific denial it is often difficult to avoid repeating in the denial some of the language of the complaint. In Baker v. Bailey," the case most often cited to illustrate the vice now under discussion, the denial was that the defendant "on December 18th committed an assault from which death resulted on December 25th." The plaintiff had alleged the assault in this language and the defendant merely substituted "denies" for "alleges" and repeated the language. Such a denial is called a negative pregnant. It is a denial pregnant with an admission of the truth of the allegation so denied.18 In the above case the pleader might easily mean that he did not commit the assault on the particular day or that the victim did not die on the exact day specified. 

The general rule is that denials in haec verba of allegations of the complaint where the denials may be fairly construed to apply to incidental matters, such as dates, adjectives, conjunctives or disjunctives, etc., are negatives pregnant and are treated as admissions.19 A denial of the allegations of the complaint "as alleged" was so construed.20 In some

§ 222. Evidence Admissible Under a General Denial. 

Proof at the trial is confined to the issues raised by the pleadings. A defendant whose evidence warrants advising him that he will win his case will be justly incensed if the answer does not permit him to present his evidence at the trial. It is important to know what evidence a general denial will make admissible. The general rule is that "under a general denial the defendant may controvert by evidence anything which the plaintiff is bound to prove in the first instance to make out his cause of action, or anything which he is permitted on the trial to prove for that purpose under his complaint."22

In Griffin v. Long Island Railroad Co.28 a replevin action was brought to recover the possession of two railroad cars. 

The complaint alleged that defendant took them from the possession of the plaintiff, that the cars were the property of the plaintiff, that defendant had them in its possession and refused on demand to give them up. The defendant admitted the demand but denied the remaining allegations of the complaint. On the trial the plaintiff gave evidence tending to show that it owned the cars, then it showed their value and rested. The defendant offered to show a sale of the two cars to it by the person who owned them before they were claimed to have been sold to the plaintiff. The trial court sustained an objection to this evidence on the ground that title in a third party was not raised by the pleadings. This ruling on appeal was held error, for since the plaintiff was bound to show title in itself to succeed, evidence tending to show knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to "the" allegations of the complaint should be stricken as bad. § 223. The Same-Proof of Payment. 

The peculiar thing about proving payment is that often the plaintiff is bound to plead non-payment but he does not have to prove it. A denial by the defendant in such case will not permit defendant to prove payment. Actions on contracts for the payment of money only, illustrate this proposition. The plaintiff in such actions must allege nonpayment since the breach of the contract consists in the nonpayment. But a denial of non-payment will not enable the defendant to introduce at the trial proof of payment.28 

The rule here stated was applied in an action on a judgment,29 on an account stated,ºº and also in an action for a specific amount originally due where the complaint admits partial payments thereon," and in an action for rent where installments have been paid,2 To prove payment in such cases the defendant must plead it as a defense.

Thus where promoters and directors of a corporation fraudulently cause the corporation to buy land at a price in excess of its value and with an understanding between them and the grantor, that the grantor will return to them the excess, the minority stockholders in an action against the grantor and the directors and promoters must not only allege that the grantor has received this excess but that he has not paid it out. In such case under a general denial proof of payment is permissible. 

Likewise in an action for damages for the breach of a contract for the sale of real estate, an allegation that defendant failed to pay, as the contract required, one-half of the purchase price and failed to secure the balance of the purchase price by a bond and mortgage on the tender of the deed, will enable the defendant under a general denial to prove payment. § 228. Denials as Part of a Defense. 

Rule 90 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that: 

"Denials of facts alleged in the complaint or in an answer and denied by reply must not be repeated or incorporated in a separate defense or counterclaim. Any fact once denied shall be deemed denied for all purposes of the pleading."

This rule removes from consideration a very vexatious question which existed under the Code. The question was, when is a denial a necessary part of a defense? The answer to that question now is, never. never.56 If an allegation in the complaint is to be denied, insert a denial in the answer but do not make it a part of a defense. 

54. Scarboro v. Health Dept., 26 A. 

D. 177; 49 N. Y. S. 1033; N. Y. Tel. 

Co. v. Simon, 77 Misc. 192; 137 N. Y. 

S. 542. 

55. Civil Practice Act, § 241, and see 159, ante. 

56. Blackwell v. Columbia Trust Co., 199 A. D. 759; 192 N. Y. S. 226.

Under the Code it was often necessary to make a denial a part of a defense or to incorporate a denial previously set out in an answer into a defense. The theory was that each defense had to be complete in itself and in construing it no other part of the answer could be considered. (Douglass v. Phenix Ins. Co. of Brooklyn, 138 

N. Y. 209.) Since, therefore, every allegation of the complaint was deemed admitted unless denied within the four walls of the defense under consideration the defense itself might be nullified by such admissions. If for example the complaint in an action for libel alleged damages of $100,000 and a defense in the answer pleaded matter in mitigation of damages, unless such defense contained a denial of the allegation of the complaint in question such allegation was deemed admitted in construing the defense and the defensive matter pleaded in mitigation of damages was nullified in advance by such admission. (Haffen v. 

Tribune Association, 126 A. D. 675; 

111 N. Y. S. 225.) To obviate this result it was necessary to incorporate the denial of such allegation into this defense even though another part of the answer contained such denial.

There is a long line of cases of this tenor (see Mendelson v. Margulies, 157 

A. D. 666; 142 N. Y. S. 825) and it became a highly technical matter in pleading to determine when a denial was a necessary part of the defense. 

Nice distinctions were often required (Oishei v. New York Taxicab Co., 136 

A. D. 683; 121 N. Y. S. 472) and attorneys fell into the habit in alleging defenses, of incorporating all the denials into every defense by reference.

Motions often followed to strike out and much time of the court was thus wasted. Rule 90 manifestly discloses an effort to do away with all this and we trust that it may be successful.

§ 229. The Defense of Payment. 

Payment is a matter of defense in actions on contract for the payment of money only. For a discussion of this subject see previous section 223. 

§ 230. Dilatory Defenses. 

58 These defenses do not go to the merits of the cause of action and are not defenses in bar. They raise questions of jurisdiction, disability of parties and defects in the proceeding. The fact that a plaintiff is an infant who has had no guardian ad litem appointed, lack of jurisdiction in the court, or another action pending would illustrate them. If these objections appear on the face of the complaint they must be taken by motion or they are waived," except lack of jurisdiction in the court over the subject of the action." If the objections, however, do not appear on the face of the complaint, they are not waived by failing to take them by motion, because section 278 of the Civil Practice Act is inapplicable.

Such objections may in the discretion of the court, at least in the cases specified in Rule 107, be pleaded as a defense.59

The rule at common law was that defendant had to furnish the plaintiff in such cases with the correct form or a better writ, otherwise his plea was bad. We have already seen that the answer containing a dilatory defense must be verified.61 60

Matter of defense which occurred subsequent to the commencement of the action may be used. Anything that has occurred up to the time that the answer is served may be used as a defense,62

63 directed, and the new matter contained in a defense is deemed to be controverted by traverse or avoidance, as the plaintiff may elect. The word traverse as here used, means denial, and the word avoidance means by way of defense. For example, if the complaint is one in ejectment and the defense is that the defendant has title to the premises by deed from a prior owner of the property, such allegation would be deemed controverted by a denial if the plaintiff wanted to prove that such deed did not exist, and it would be deemed controverted by avoidance, if the plaintiff undertook to show that the defendant procured such deed through fraud and undue influence.64 

§ 233. Counterclaims-In General. 

The defendant's answer may contain "a statement of any new matter constituting a defense or counterclaim. """5 To constitute à counterclaim the new matter must be of such a character that with it the defendant could draw a complaint in which he would be the plaintiff and in which his adversary would be the defendant; or if, in the principal action the plaintiff is suing on an assigned claim or as trustee for another, the assignor of such claim or the one for whom such trustee is acting, would be the defendant. In the city court, however, a defendant may sometimes interpose a counterclaim of such a nature that he could not have originally brought an action thereon in that court. Thus, there is no monetary limitation upon the amount of a counterclaim which may be set up, and judgment upon a counterclaim may be rendered in favor of the defendant for any sum.66 

The defendant, however, cannot use as a counterclaim every cause of action which he may have against the plaintiff or against plaintiff's assignor or cestui que trust. The defendant's right to set up a counterclaim in his answer is a privilege given by law and is limited to specified types of actions. It must, therefore, possess certain requisites which may be stated as follows:

§ 234. The Same The First Requisite. 

The counterclaim "must tend to diminish or defeat the plaintiff's recovery. If, for example, the action is for the specific performance of a contract to convey real property, the defendant would not be permitted to set up as a counterclaim an action on a promissory note, since even if defendant succeeded, the plaintiff's right to recover would not be affected thereby. In an action on behalf of infant beneficiaries under a will for the construction thereof, in which no other relief is asked, which action is brought against trustees appointed to execute a trust, a counterclaim for an accounting on the ground that plaintiff's general guardian who administered the estate for some time had never accounted is not a proper counterclaim for it does not in any manner tend to diminish or defect the recovery or the relief which the plaintiffs seek. The construction of the will should be had irrespective of whether or not plaintiff's general guardian should account. 68 In an action to foreclose a mortgage a man who had a mechanic's lien on the property was made a party defendant. 

Plaintiff asserted no personal claim against that defendant whatever. The lienor, as it happened, had a claim against the plaintiff for ten thousand dollars and set it up as a counterclaim in this foreclosure action. The counterclaim was held improper under this restriction."⁹ 

But where plaintiff sues to recover back money he paid the defendant on the execution of a contract for the conveyance of land, on the ground that the defendant cannot give a marketable title to the land, the defendant may counterclaim in an action for the specific performance of the same contract since the equitable counterclaim would, if successful, entirely defeat plaintiff's recovery."

§ 235. The Same-The Second Requisite.72 

The second thing to be especially remembered in connection with counterclaims is that you can only counterclaim contract against contract, and not tort against tort or contract against tort unless the latter two arise out of the same transaction." 

The counterclaim "must be one of the following causes of action 1. A cause of action arising out of the contract or transaction set forth in the complaint as the foundation of the plaintiff's claim or connected with the subject of the action; 

2. In an action on contract, any other cause of action on contract existing at the commencement of the action." 

In an action for rent the tenant could not counterclaim in an action for trespass on the leased premises since such counterclaim falls within neither of the subdivisions stated."

Likewise in an action for conversion begun by a trustee in bankruptcy against a pledgee of property of the bankrupt, a counterclaim based on the endorsement of notes by the bankrupt does not come within the classes enumerated." But where the plaintiff sues for an alleged breach of his contract of employment by the defendant in that he was dismissed before the end of his term, a counterclaim based on the fraudulent representations of the plaintiff which induced the defendant to purchase the assets of a corporation and employ the plaintiff by the very contract of employment upon which the plaintiff is now suing, is a proper counterclaim for it falls within the first class of cases enumerated in this restriction.76

Again where the action is on a contract and a counterclaim states a cause of action also on contract, which cause of action existed at the commencement of the action upon

§ 236. The Same - The Third Requisite. 

The counterclaim must be "in favor of the defendant or one or more defendants between whom and the plaintiff or the plaintiff and another person or persons alleged to be liable a separate judgment may be had in the action. ""79 

This language is rather obscure. A few illustrations may help to clarify it. (a) If A sues X and Y on a joint obligation, as would be the case where X and Y are co-partners, and the action is one at law, X may not interpose as a counterclaim an action he has individually against A since in the action a separate judgment may not be had between A and X.80 (See Diagram I(a), p. 283.) (b) If A sues X and Y on a several liability, as in the case of a joint and several note of which they are the makers, X may then interpose his individual claim against A as a counterclaim since in such case a separate judgment may be had between A and X,81 X could not, however, interpose as a counterclaim in such a case a claim that X had jointly with Y and Z against A.82 (See Diagram I(b), p. 283.) (c) If A sues X, and X has a several claim against A, B and C, he may interpose it as a counterclaim under the

§ 237. The Same-The Fourth Requisite. 

The fourth requisite of counterclaims is really a combination of three rules of substantive law, viz. (1) That the assignee of a chose in action takes it subject to all defenses that existed against it at the time of the assignment, (2) subject also to any defenses accruing against it thereafter at any time before notice to the debtor of the assignment, and (3) subject also, in some cases, to defenses accruing thereafter at times subsequent to notice to the debtor of the assignment. 

If the action is founded upon a contract which has been assigned by a party thereto other than a negotiable promissory note, or bill of exchange, and if the cause of action which it is desired to use as a counterclaim is not an offset "arising out of the contract or transaction set forth in the complaint as the foundation of the plaintiff's claim or connected with the subject of the action," 85 the counterclaim must conform to the following regulations: (a) It must be a cause of action on contract,s (b) Which existed at the time of the assignment," (c) Belonging to the defendant in good faith before notice of the assignment,s 88 (d) And possessing all of the first three requisites discussed in sections 234, 235 and 236 immediately above.""

It is then good as a counterclaim, but only up to the extent of the plaintiff's demand."⁰ In other words, if an assignee takes a claim which at the time of the assignment had no outstanding defenses to it, the defendant against whom it

§ 238. The Same-Equitable Recoupment. 

The statutes allowing counterclaims were intended to enlarge the opportunities of defendants in adjusting their

differences with plaintiffs and not to cut them down. Therefore, where on a contract for the delivery of goods on installments to be paid for separately within a time specified after delivery, the vendor assigns to plaintiff the money due on one installment, and the assignee sues the vendee upon it, the vendee may set up as a counterclaim a breach of warranty growing out of a subsequent delivery, although such cause of action arose subsequent to the assignment. This is not contrary to the requirement found in subdivision (b) of the last section, since it was permitted in equity as an equitable recoupment, and is continued in section 266, subdivision 1 of the Civil Practice Act under the principle herein stated. If allowing such a counterclaim seems to violate the express requirements of section 267, subdivision 1 of the Civil Practice Act, just remember that that section by its very terms does not apply to counterclaims embraced within section 266, subdivision 1.°° 93 

§ 239. The Same - New Parties Summoned to Appear. 

In such a case as is found in section 236 (c), supra, where the counterclaim sets up a cause of action against the plaintiff along with others, he shall set forth the names of all the persons who, if such counterclaim were to be enforced by cross action, would be defendants to such cross action. The new parties thus introduced into the action "shall be summoned to appear by being served with a copy of the answer. 

Such parties become defendants in the action the same as if they had been served with the summons. It has been held that 9994

§ 240. In General. 

The motions which must be made promptly after the answer is served may be classified under four headings: (a) To correct defects by amendment (Rules 90, 102, 103), (b) To treat as a nullity and give judgment accordingly (Rule 104), (c) To strike out a defense therefrom as insufficient in law, (Rule 109, subd. 6), and (d) For judgment dismissing a counterclaim contained therein. (Rules 109, 110).

There are other motions by which an answer may be attacked, (e. g., motions for summary judgment, judgment on the pleadings, and similar motions), but these are the only ones upon which the rules place a time limit. They will be considered in order. A general outline of these motions follows:

§ 244. The Motion to Treat the Answer as a Nullity. 

"If an answer or reply be sham or frivolous the court may treat the pleading as a nullity and give judgment accordingly, or allow a new pleading to be served upon such terms as the court deems just. 712 There are two motions of this class: (a) the motion to treat the answer as a nullity because it is frivolous, and (b) the motion to treat it as a nullity because it is a sham. 

These motions are quite distinct from each other. The papers used in making them differ and they are intended to reach different vices in the answer. (a) To treat an answer as a nullity because it is frivolous. 

A frivolous pleading is one which, assuming the truth of its allegations, is so clearly and palpably bad as to require no argument to convince the court thereof, and which would be pronounced by the court, on a mere inspection, to be indicative of bad faith in the pleader.18 It denies no material allegation of the complaint and sets up no defense. If argument is necessary to convince the court of the bad faith of the pleader or the insufficiency of the plea, it cannot be held to be frivolous. Cases where this motion has been granted are so scarce that illustration is difficult.15 In the cases cited from which the above language was taken, the Court of

§ 245. The Motion to Strike Out a Defense as Insufficient in Law On Its Face.82 

The sufficiency of a defense as a matter of law was formerly reached by demurrer. This motion is a substitute for that procedure, and the principles applicable to the demurrer in such cases apply to this motion. On this motion, therefore, the facts stated in the defense and all that can by reasonable and fair intendment be implied from them, must be deemed true. This motion relating to the defense is in this respect exactly like the corresponding motion for judgment dismissing the complaint for insufficiency of facts. It challenges the sufficiency of the complaint, as well as of the defense.95 

§ 246. The Same - This Motion Searches the Record. 

At common law the pleadings were often quite numerous. 

The plaintiff and defendant might alternately plead with a declaration, a plea, a replication, a rejoinder, a surrejoinder, a rebutter and a surrebutter. If for example the declaration were for trespass to land, and the plea was that defendant had title by descent, and the replication was a lease from defendant since defendant came into possession, and the rejoinder of defendant was that he was an infant when he made the lease, and the plaintiff in his surrejoinder alleged ratification of the lease after defendant reached his majority, and the defendant in his rebutter said that the lease was cancelled by mutual consent after ratification, and the plaintiff traverses this latter allegation, you would have a line of common law pleadings counting up to seven. Now, anywhere along this line, either party might demur to his adversary's pleading on the ground that it was insufficient in law upon its face to effectuate the purpose for which it was intended. 

31. Monica v. Bleecker, 229 A. D. 

184 (First Dept.-affidavits may not be used). So also Bland v. White, 138 

Misc. 715, 246 N. Y. S. 532; contra,

Liberty v. Huntington, 224 A. D. 184 (Second Dept.).

33. Berg v. Bates, 153 A. D. 12; 137

35. Trenkman v. Smith, 226 A. D. 

774. But cf. Bernard v. Chase, 233 

A. D. 384, 253 N. Y. S. 336.

When such a demurrer was interposed, the court would examine not merely the pleading to which the demurrer was directed, but would examine the entire line of pleadings, commencing with the declaration, and the first pleading found defective would receive the court's condemnation, and judgment would be entered for the adverse party. If, therefore, a declaration were bad and the defendant interposed a plea to it which was also bad, and the plaintiff demurred to the plea, the court rendered judgment in favor of the defendant on account of the defective character of the declaration. plaintiff complained that the plea was bad and that defendant ought not to have judgment, the answer was that defendant's plea was good enough for the declaration. The principle was stated in the words a demurrer searches the record.

If This principle applied under the Code as at common law, but its application was limited to the single case where a complaint which did not state a cause of action was served and the defendant set up in his answer thereto a defense which in law did not amount to a defense. Plaintiff could not demur to a denial in an answer, for a demurrer to a denial would mean that even if it were true that the allegations of the complaint were false, the plaintiff ought nevertheless to recover. While the plaintiff might demur to a counterclaim contained in an answer, the principle that a demurrer searches the record would not on such demurrer reach back and test the sufficiency of the complaint. There was no counterclaim at common law and the principle in question never had such application. Moreover, it would be inequitable and unjust to test the sufficiency of the complaint on a demurrer to a bad counterclaim.86

Leaving aside for the moment a motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 112, this left the principle a demurrer searches the record applicable under the Code to the single case where a demurrer was interposed to a defense, either in an Answer or a Reply. As this motion is the substitute for the demurrer under the Code, this principle should apply in its determination as it did on the deter-

§ 247. Motion for Judgment Dismissing a Counterclaim for Defects Appearing on Its Face. 

There are five grounds upon which this motion may be based. Four of these grounds are the same grounds upon which a motion for judgment dismissing the complaint may be made.38 It will not be necessary, therefore, to discuss these grounds of objection here." The reader is referred to the discussion under section 196, ante, for their meaning and application. Cases especially applicable to counterclaims are cited in the notes.40 The objection to the complaint that the court has no jurisdiction over the person of the defendant is here omitted, since if the defendant is interposing a counterclaim he has already submitted to the jurisdiction. The fourth ground of objection to the counterclaim has no counterpart under Rule 106 and needs some consideration. The requisites of a counterclaim were discussed in chapter XV, sections 234, 235, 236 and 237. Now if the counterclaim interposed does not possess these requisites, the proper way to raise the objection to it is by motion for judgment dismissing it under this subdivision.* 41

§ 249. Time of Making Motions Discussed in This Chapter. 

The motions contemplated in the first two classes, viz., motions to correct defects in the answer and to treat it as a nullity must be made within twenty days after the service thereof, and extensions of time to make the motion cannot be obtained except on two days' notice to the adverse party." 

The motions contemplated in the last two classes, viz., to strike out a defense and for judgment dismissing a counterclaim must be noticed within ten days from the service of the answer. 45 Extensions of time to make these motions must be had under the general rules relating thereto, as stated in chapter XX, post. Three of these grounds of objections which may be urged to a counterclaim are waived if not thus taken by motion where they appear on the face of the answer." § 252. The Same - The Complaint and Answer. 

These papers are both necessary in passing upon these motions. Whether the answer needs amendment, or is a nullity, or a defense therein is good in law, or a counterclaim therein is proper, cannot be well ascertained or ascertained at all, in most cases, without the complaint. 

§ 253. The Same - The Affidavit. 

In all these motions except possibly (a) to strike out sham matter from the answer, (b) to treat the answer as a nullity because it is a sham, and (c) for judgment dismissing the counterclaim for defects not appearing on its face, the only function the affidavit can have is to show that the motion is made within the time fixed by law and the rules. 

In the three cases just mentioned, the affidavit, if permitted, must show, in addition to the fact that the motion is made on time, (a) The falsity of the matter sought to be stricken out, or (b) The falsity or sham character of the entire answer, and (c) The facts relative to the particular objection as the occasion requires.

§ 255. The Appropriate Motion to Reach Defects Connected with 

Denials of Knowledge or Information Sufficient to Form a Belief.

As was shown in section 224, ante, denials of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief are often defective. 

The remedies for curing the defects connected with such denials are not uniformly resorted to nor are the decisions of the courts uniform with reference to the appropriate remedy to meet a particular defect. The following seems to be the practice now most favored by well considered decisions. 

When such form of denial results in ambiguity, as where it is followed by the phrase "as to all of the allegations of the complaint or a particular paragraph, the motion to make the answer more definite and certain would be the appropriate one." Where such denial is directed to a personal transaction about which the defendant must unmistakably have knowledge, the motion to strike out such denial as a sham would be proper.56 Where the whole answer is in this form and of this character, the motion to treat it as a nullity because it is frivolous and for judgment accordingly, would be the proper one." Where, however, such denials are used in relation to a personal transaction about which the defendant may have no knowledge, as where a corporation is a defendant and the acts complained of may have been performed by its agents, or where the matter toward which the denial is directed is a matter of public record which may have been mutilated or temporarily removed from the files, the motion to treat the answer as a nullity because it is a sham, is the appropriate one to make.58 

The reason for this is that this motion, in some departments, at least, permits the use of affidavits on the substance of the objection and would thus give opportunity to the defendant to explain why he may not have the knowledge which one

§ 256. In General. 

Usually the pleadings end with the answer. The aim of the Code was to correct the delay often occasioned in common law pleading by reason of the number of pleadings there allowed. An effort was made therefore under the Code to limit the number of pleadings to two, and usually two pleadings were all that were required. Under certain circumstances, however, a third regular pleading was necessary. 

When it was used, it was called the reply. The practice thus introduced by the Code is continued under the Practice Act.2 1 

§ 257. When a Reply Is Necessary. 

Other than in the Municipal Court, the reply is always necessary where there is a counterclaim set up in the answer, but the counterclaim which thus requires a reply must be distinctly called a counterclaim. If the answer contains facts which would, if properly entitled, amount to a counterclaim, but they are not set forth as a counterclaim no reply is necessary. Plaintiff may, however, reply to such counterclaim if he chooses to do so. Facts in an answer which constitute a counterclaim but are not so designated may be effectual at the trial as a counterclaim and if the defendant proves them he may have the relief which they demand, but the defendant will have to prove such facts. 

1. In the Municipal Court of the 

City of New York, a reply to a counterclaim is not necessary unless the court orders one. The counterclaim is deemed denied. Municipal Court Code, § 87.

Failure of the plaintiff to reply to them will not amount to an admission of their truth. It is not a sufficient denomination of the new matter thus set up in the answer that affirmative relief is asked therein." 

§ 258. When a Reply May Be Required. 

Where the answer contains a defense, though no counterclaim be stated therein, the court may in its discretion require a reply to the defense. The plaintiff has no choice in the matter, nor can he apply to the court for permission to reply to a defense. The court's discretion in such case can be, exercised only on the application of the defendant." 

The matters which will influence the court's discretion in requiring a reply are: (a) The prevention of surprise at the trial, (b) To expedite the trial, (c) To narrow the issues, and (d) The interests of justice.

Thus in an action for malicious prosecution where the defendant alleges, as a complete defense, the immediate subsequent indictment of the plaintiff for the identical offense charged in the complaint, the court should exercise its discretion by requiring a reply. Again where the action is for personal injuries and the defense is a general release, an order requiring a reply may be granted.10 So where the statute of frauds is pleaded as a defense in an action on contract required to be in writing by the statute, and the complaint does not state whether the contract sued on was or was not in writing, a reply may be directed." § 259. What the Reply Should Contain. 

"The reply must contain a general or specific denial of each material allegation of the counterclaim controverted by the plaintiff, or of any knowledge or information thereof sufficient to form a belief; and it may set forth new matter not inconsistent with the complaint constituting a defense to the counterclaim. A reply may contain two or more distinct avoidances of the same defense or counterclaim. 7914

The reply is exactly like the answer to the complaint so far as denials and defenses are concerned, but of course it may contain no counterclaim. One particular requisite of a reply stated in the language quoted above should be noted. 

It must not be inconsistent with the complaint. Such inconsistency was forbidden in common law pleading where it was called a departure.15 

§ 260. Effect of a Reply or a Failure to Reply.

§ 261. Form of Reply. 

The reply in form follows the general scheme of an answer. 

The formal opening and the prayer for relief differ. The following shows a form of reply: 

(Title) 

The plaintiff, replying to the counterclaim contained in defendant's answer, denies each and every allegation therein and demands judgment as in the complaint prayed for, in addition to judgment dismissing the said counterclaim. 

(Verification when necessary.) (Signature.) 

The verification of the reply follows the rules for verification of the answer. If the complaint is not verified the defendant, as has already been said, need not as a rule verify his answer. He may, however, if he chooses do so, or he may confine his verification in such case to the counterclaim. If he thus verifies his answer such verified answer will require a verified reply."

§ 266. The Amendment of Pleadings-In General. 

We have already discussed certain motions by which a party compels his adversary to amend his pleading for the purpose of correcting errors or defects contained therein.21 

The amendments which we wish to discuss now are those not forced upon a party, but those which are made or sought at his own instance. Often a party finds it desirable to amend his pleading. There are two classes of amendments to pleadings: (a) amendments before trial, and (b) amendments at or after trial. Of the amendments before trial there are two subdivisions: (1) amendments of course and (2) amendments by leave of court. The authority for amendments of course is found in section 244 of the Civil Practice Act. The authority for all other amendments is found in section 105 of the Civil Practice Act, although the Supreme Court has inherent power apart from that section to make amendments.22 We shall consider amendments at or after trial when we are discussing trials. Amendments before trial will be discussed now. 

§ 267. Amendments of Course. 

"Within twenty days after a pleading, or the answer or reply thereto is served, or at any time before the period for answering it expires, or within twenty days after the service of a notice of a

motion addressed to the pleading, the pleading may be once amended by the party, of course, without costs and without prejudice to the proceedings already had. But if it is made to appear to the court that the pleading was amended for the purpose of delay and that the adverse party will thereby lose the benefit of a term for which the cause is or may be noticed, the amended pleading may be stricken out, or the pleading may be restored to its original form, and such terms imposed as the court deems just. 2723 This provision makes possible the service of an amended complaint as of course within twenty days after the original complaint is served, within twenty days after service of a notice of motion addressed to the original complaint, or within twenty days after the defendant's answer thereto is served.²* It likewise would permit the service of an amended answer as of course within twenty days after the service of the original answer or within twenty days after the service of a notice of motion addressed to the answer, or within twenty days after the service of a reply to a counterclaim contained therein. It would, as of course, permit the service of an amended reply within twenty days after the service of the original reply or within twenty days after the service of the notice of motion addressed to the reply.25 The phrase "or at any time before the period for answering expires" was in the Code section and means that if time of a defendant to answer is extended by stipulation or otherwise, such extension automatically extends plaintiff's time to amend his complaint as of course.26

The right thus to make a motion addressed to a pleading or to amend one's pleading once is absolute, and even though the court order a pleading amended on the motion of an adverse party, the service of such amended pleading does not cut off this right, and a further amended pleading may be served within the twenty day period.28 The fact that a motion is addressed to a pleading does not cut off this absolute right.

The only limitation upon this absolute right to serve one amended pleading as of course, is found in the last sentence of section 244 of the Civil Practice Act which is the same as it was in the code and which reads as follows: "But if it is made to appear to the court that the pleading was amended for the purpose of delay and that the adverse party will thereby lose the benefit of a term for which the cause is or may be noticed, the amended pleading may be stricken out, or the pleading may be restored to its original form, and such terms imposed as the court deems just.' 

The motion addressed to a pleading falls in the event that an amended pleading is served.20

§ 268. The Amendment of a Pleading Before Trial by Leave of 

Court.

When the right to amend a pleading of course has been lost either by exercise or by lapse of time, the pleading may be amended by leave of the court and in its discretion. The power of a court of general jurisdiction to amend a pleading is inherent. The statute, however, gives to all courts such power. It follows: 

"At any stage of any action, special proceeding or appeal, a mistake, omission, irregularity or defect may be corrected or supplied, as the case may be, in the discretion of the court, with or without terms, or, if a substantial right of any party shall not be thereby prejudiced, such mistake, omission, irregularity or defect must be disregarded. ''81

The principal distinction between an amendment of course and one obtained before trial by leave of the court is that the right to the former is absolute and the latter is discretionary with the court. The court exercises this discretion liberally allowing an amendment "unless something has taken place intermediate the service of the original pleading and the application to amend, which will work to the prejudice of the adverse party if the amendment be allowed, or that the trial will be delayed by reason of it.''32

§ 275. Motion to Dismiss Complaint for Failure to Serve the Same 

After Demand.

If the complaint is not served with the summons, the defendant may serve upon the plaintiff's attorney a written demand for a copy thereof at any time within twenty days after the service of the summons is complete. The language of the Civil Practice Act, which states this penalty for noncompliance with the demand is "if he fails to do so he is precluded from giving evidence of the account.' Court of Appeals said, referring to the power of the court to order bills of particulars and the character of the actions in which they apply: "There is no restriction upon the power; it extends to all descriptions of actions, where justice demands that a party whether plaintiff or defendant should be apprised of the particulars of the facts his adversary expects to prove; and the scope of the order must ordinarily be a question of discretion to be governed by circumstances.' 

In that case, the answer to an action for conversion of certain securities set up an account stated between the parties after full consideration and discussion, whereby the defendant should be considered indebted to plaintiff in a certain sum. Plaintiff demanded a copy of the account, thinking that the pleading of an account stated required him to demand a copy of the account rather than a bill of particulars. But, as there are no items in such an account, the demand for a copy of the account was held not to apply¹ and the Court of Appeals allowed a bill of particulars in the case. 

It is distinguished from the motion to make more definite and certain¹ in that it is not intended to correct ambiguities or other similar defects in a pleading for which purpose the motion to make the pleading more definite and certain was designed, but it is intended to supplement the allegations of a clear pleading with details of the claim stated there." 

A bill of particulars is not a pleading, and it cannot enlarge a cause of action or perfect an improper pleading. § 278. Purpose of Bill of Particulars. 

There are two main purposes which a bill of particulars is intended to effectuate. These are (a) to limit the proof and scope of the inquiry at the trial, and (b) to prevent surprise thereat.20 

Thus where the answer claims that the merchandise delivered by the plaintiff is not up to sample and not of standard quality, the particulars of the defects and of the failure to come up to standard and sample should be furnished in a bill of particulars, since they would prevent surprise to the plaintiff at the trial respecting the line of attack upon the merchandise, and when the defects claimed to exist are specified, the proof at the trial will be limited to such defects, and thus the scope of the inquiry will be narrowed.21 

In an action on a promissory note the complaint, anticipating the statute of limitations, alleged a new promise by the defendant to pay which was denied by the defendant in his answer. The defendant is entitled in such case to a bill of particulars stating when and how the new promise was made, and whether in writing or oral, and if in writing, a copy of the writing.22 The two purposes referred to above are conserved in such case.

Again, where in an action to recover damages to plaintiff's building in the construction by the defendant of a subway in front thereof, the plaintiff claims that his building was rendered dirty, dangerous and unsanitary by reason of the careless, negligent, unnecessary and unreasonable manner of placing and operating a derrick in front of the property, the defendant is entitled to be informed by a bill of particulars

trial, if carried too far, might work an injustice. It would, of course, help to prevent a party from being surprised at the trial if his adversary were compelled to furnish in advance a list of the witnesses he expected to use and a statement of the testimony which he expected each of them to give. 

Yet such a rule might work an injustice and, except in extraordinary cases, the right to particulars ceases to exist at the point where the particulars demanded begin to draw upon the evidence of the adverse party.29 In an action for damages for a breach of the contract of employment, the defendant set out fourteen grounds as constituting justification for plain tiff's discharge. The plaintiff demanded a bill of particulars of the grounds which would give minute details concerning each ground. The court in discussing the matter said: "Bills of particulars should be required when necessary for the purpose of preventing surprise and needless preparation, but the discretion of the court should be so exercised as to avoid an undue disclosure of the evidence of the adverse party by which he may estab lish the facts at issue. (Taylor v. Security M. Life Ins. Co., 73 App. 

Div. 319; Baltimore Machine Works v. McKelvey, 71 id. 340; Mussinan v. Willner Wood Co., 69 id. 448; English v. Westchester Electric 

R. Co., id. 576; Bell v. Heatherton, 66 id. 603.)

In the case at bar the plaintiff's demand for a bill of particulars is altogether too broad. It is alleged in the answer that the plaintiff failed to devote his entire time, energies and intelligence to the business; that he did not use his best efforts to make the business profitable; that he was not attentive to business, remained away all day on Saturdays and frequently stayed away on other business days, claiming that he had been detained by private matters; that he arrived after office hours in the morning and departed before the close of business hours for the day. We think that the defendants should not be limited in their evidence on these subjects by a bill of particulars, and that the answer apprises the plaintiff of all that is essential for him to know to enable him to defend against the charges. This defense, though stated in general language, is sufficiently definite, and more cannot be required without unduly calling for the evidence itself. But in many cases the general purposes of the bill of particulars can be achieved only by requiring the evidence of one's adversary. Where greater injustice is likely to occur through the surprise resulting from withholding the evidence than would result to the adverse party by compelling its disclosure, evidence may be required by a bill of particulars. 31 The names of persons, for example, are not usually directed to be given in a bill of particulars since as a usual thing this is a disclosure of the evidence of the adverse party. But where a failure to have. the names will result in unfair surprise they may be required in a bill of particulars. Where, for example, in a defense to an action for damages for a discharge of an employee, the defendant alleges as a defense that plaintiff accepted for his own use from various persons money and other benefits as a consideration for approving and passing merchandise purchased by him for the defendant, the names of the persons from whom the plaintiff received such consideration was ordered to be furnished in the bill.32

This argument is, however, usually specious. The information sought cannot be required to enable a defendant to deny the allegations of the complaint since he may put such allegations in issue by denying that he has knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief thereof. The most plausible case for such argument is where the defendant claims that he needs information to enable him to plead an affirmative defense, as where he does not know whether the contract sued on was in writing, or when the cause of action accrued, and needs the information to enable him to determine whether he has the affirmative defense of the statute of frauds or limitations. Bills of particulars have been allowed to defendants before answering under such circumstances. The better motion for such situation, however, is the motion to make the complaint more definite and certain, for while indefiniteness and uncertainty of time, place or form do not as a rule make the pleading indefinite and uncertain, yet where such details go to the essence of a defense the uncertainty and indefiniteness in connection with them may be said to make the pleading itself indefinite and uncertain.³ 35 

§ 281. The Procedure - A Demand Not Necessary. 

Under the Code, a demand was not necessary as a preliminary step prior to the making of a motion for a bill of particulars, and the practice of making demands for particulars before a formal motion was made fell somewhat into disuse. Of late years, a motion usually began the procedure. 

It is under the Civil Practice Act still unnecessary to make a demand before making the motion for the bill, but costs. may be imposed in the order granting a bill where a demand has been made and not complied with. If no demand is made, or having been made is not complied with, a motion is necessary.

§ 282. The Same - Motion Papers for Bill of Particulars. 

The papers required for making a motion for a bill of particulars are: (a) a notice of motion, (b) the pleadings, and (c) an affidavit.

The notice is the usual one except that the particulars sought are stated in it. 

The pleadings, or at least the pleading for which particulars are sought, must be before the court, since only from an inspection of them can the court determine what particulars should be furnished, if any at all. If the original pleadings are on file and may be requisitioned before the court on the hearing of the motion, such pleadings may be made use of for the motion and it will then be unnecessary to incorporate them among the papers used in making the motion. If, however, the pleadings are not on file and cannot thus be brought to the attention of the court on the motion, copies of them, or the principal parts of them about which particulars are sought should be attached to the affidavit in making the motion.

The affidavit should be made by the party. The affidavit of the attorney alone is insufficient unless some good reason exists for a departure from the rule," and while the stringency of this rule has been relaxed to some extent, it is not abandoned.38

It is not necessary as a general rule that the affiant should state that he has no knowledge concerning the particulars which he seeks, as the purpose of the bil¹ is to set forth what the party claims and not what the adverse party may know about such claims," but it would seem that knowledge of the facts by the party seeking the bill should have some bearing on the question of surprise and it is therefore better to state lack of knowledge in the moving affidavit for the bill of particulars if that be the fact. In a case, for example, where the bill of particulars will not limit the issues, and the one function it could serve would be to prevent surprise at the trial, the fact that the adverse party

Under the former procedure, Rule 23 of the General Rules of Practice required all applications for orders which were allowed or disallowed in the discretion of the court to show merits, but that requirement has been omitted from the Rules of Civil Practice, and it is now probable that such requirement will no longer be insisted upon in the affidavit used on the motion for a bill of particulars. An affidavit of merits in most cases seems useless anyway, since the party who brings an action undoubtedly will swear that his attorney advises him that there is merit in it, and a defendant who interposes through his attorney a defense to an action in his answer, would likewise swear that there was merit in it and that he was so advised by his counsel. 

It would be well to end the affidavit with a prayer that the particulars stated in the notice of motion should be ordered.

§ 284 Penalty for Failure to Comply with Order. 

The penalty for failure to comply with the order is the same as where the demand for a copy of an account is ignored. The party refusing will be precluded from giving evidence at the trial in support of the allegations for which he has failed to furnish the particulars ordered.** A preclusion order is required for the same reason that it is required after failure to comply with the demand for a copy of the account, but it follows as a matter of course since the provision authorizing it is mandatory.*

Sometimes the order granting the bill of particulars contains a provision precluding the party from giving evidence if he fails to furnish the particulars required, but such provision is premature and unauthorized.*

If a party required to furnish particulars serves a bill of particulars which does not comply with the requirements of the order, the adverse party may move for a further bill of particulars,8 or he may return the bill of particulars within a reasonable time which is considered to be within twenty-four hours," with a statement showing the reasons for its return. He can then move for a preclusion order. 

He cannot keep the bill of particulars which he deems inadequate and move for a preclusion order.50 The party who has served a bill of particulars which has been returned may move to compel his adversary to accept the bill, in which case on the motion the question of its sufficiency will be determined; or he may wait until his adversary moves for a preclusion order when the sufficiency of the bill will be determined on this motion."¹

§ 285. Motions for Judgment on the Pleadings. 

"Judgment may be rendered by the court in favor of any party or parties, and against any party or parties, at any stage of an action or appeal, if warranted by the pleadings or the admissions52 of a party or parties; and a judgment may be rendered by the court as to a part of a cause of action and the action proceed as to the remaining issues, as justice may require. ''53 "If either party be entitled to judgment on the pleadings, the court may, on motion, give judgment accordingly, and without regard to which party makes the motion. ''54

The language of Rule 112 is identical with that of Code section 547 except for the last clause of the rule beginning "and without regard" etc., which was not found in the 

Code section. The adjudicated cases under Code section 

547 will, therefore, apply in the interpretation of the rule except as such decisions are modified by the addition of this last clause. Under the Code section, if the plaintiff made a motion for judgment on the pleadings and the defendant failed to make a cross motion of the same kind, the court could not give judgment to the defendant even though the complaint was bad, since there was no motion before him asking for such relief. He could only deny plaintiff's motion for judgment.55 If on the denial of plaintiff's motion the defendant brought on a new motion for judgment it would, unless the situation changed in the meantime by amendment of the complaint, be granted. To avoid the two motions where one would do as well, the last clause was added to Rule 112 and now on a motion for judgment by either party, the court may give judgment to any party entitled thereto. 

52. See Civil Practice Act, §§ 322, 323. 

53. Civil Practice Act, § 476. This section is new. It replaces both Code 

S$ 547 and 511 which are omitted. 

The part of § 476 relating to the admissions of the parties was under Code § 511 limited to the admissions of defendant in his answer (Burgess v. 

House, 49 A. D. 383; 63 N. Y. S. 512).

It seems now that admissions outside the answer and by either party will lay the foundation for a motion for judgment, but if such motion is based on admissions it would not be, strictly speaking, a motion for judgment on the pleadings. See note 25 to section 368. 

54. Rule 112. 

55. Dahm v. O'Connell, 179 A. D. 363; 

166 N. Y. S. 450; Rieser v. Prager, 157 N. Y. S. 118; Lobsitz v. Lissberger, 157 N. Y. S. 117.

The use for this motion is materially lessened by the new procedure. Under the Code it was possible to test the sufficiency of a complaint by interposing a demurrer to it and then moving for judgment on the pleadings. This enabled the defendant to test the sufficiency of the complaint without answering it. Now the demurrer is abolished and if the defendant wants to test the sufficiency of the complaint before answering, he must do so on a motion to dismiss the complaint under Rules 106 and 107. The same thing is true when the plaintiff desires to test the sufficiency of a counterclaim contained in an answer before replying thereto. He can no longer demur and move for judgment on the pleadings. He must make a motion under Rules 109 or 110 for judgment dismissing the counterclaim if he desires to test its sufficiency before replying to it. 

§ 286. The Same The Purpose and Application of. 

Since this motion can be made only after the joinder of issue, and that requires an answer under the Practice Act, the demurrer having been abolished, the only objections which can be raised to a complaint by the motion are the insufficiency thereof to state a cause of action, and the lack of jurisdiction in the court over the subject-matter. All other objections to the complaint in point of law are waived by answering, except possibly the objections with respect to defect and misjoinder of parties.57 Under the Code all objections to a complaint in point of law, save the two above mentioned, were likewise waived by answering.58 Under the Code, however, it was possible to join issue by the service of a demurrer and thus avoid the waivers which the service of the answer would cause. The motion for judgment on the pleadings where issue was thus joined might, therefore, attack the complaint for any objection appearing on its face.59 The Practice Act has thus cut down materially the occasions for resorting to this motion so far as the complaint is concerned. 56 If the answer contains no counterclaim, its sufficiency as a matter of law may be tested on this motion." § 289. Summary Judgment and Partial Judgment. 

"Rule 113. Summary Judgment. When an answer is served in an action, 1. To recover a debt or liquidated demand arising on a contract express or implied in fact or in law, sealed or not sealed; or 

2. To recover a debt or liquidated demand arising on a judgment for a stated sum; or 

3. On a statute where the sum sought to be recovered is a sum of money other than a penalty; or 

4. To recover an unliquidated debt or demand for a sum of money only arising on a contract express or implied in fact or in law, sealed or not sealed, other than for breach of promise to marry; or 

5. To recover possession of a specific chattel or chattels with or without a claim for the hire thereof or for damages for the taking or detention thereof; or 

6. To enforce or foreclose a lien or mortgage; or 

7. For specific performance of a contract in writing for the sale or purchase of property, including such alternative and incidental relief as the case may require; or 

8. For an accounting arising on a written contract, sealed or not sealed.

The complaint may be dismissed or answer may be struck out and judgment entered in favor of either party on motion upon the affidavit of a party or of any other person having knowledge of the facts, setting forth such evidentiary facts as shall, if the motion is made on behalf of the plaintiff, establish the cause of action sufficiently to entitle plaintiff to judgment, and if the motion is made on behalf of the defendant, such evidentiary facts, including copies of all documents, as shall fully disclose defendant's contentions and show that
