If upon such motion made on behalf of a defendant it shall appear that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment, the judge hearing the motion may award judgment to the plaintiff, even though the plaintiff has not made a cross-motion therefor. 

If the plaintiff or defendant in any action set forth in subdivisions 3, 4 or 5 hereunder shall fail to show such facts as may be deemed, by the judge hearing the motion, to present any triable issue of fact other than the question of the amount of damages for which judgment should be granted, an assessment to determine such amount shall forthwith be ordered for immediate hearing to be tried by a referee, by the court alone, or by the court and a jury, whichever shall be appropriate. Upon the rendering of the assessment, judgment in the action shall be rendered forthwith. 

When in any actions in cases set forth in subdivisions 6, 7 and 8 hereunder the judge hearing the motion has been convinced that there is no preliminary triable issue of fact, the court shall forthwith render an appropriate judgment or order and thenceforth the action shall proceed in the ordinary course. 

Where an answer is served in any action setting forth a defense which is sufficient as a matter of law, where the defense is founded upon facts established prima facie by documentary evidence or official record, the complaint may be dismissed on motion unless the plaintiff by affidavit, or other proof, shall show such facts as may be deemed by the judge hearing the motion, sufficient to raise an issue with respect to the verity and conclusiveness of such documentary evidence or official record. 

This rule shall be applicable to counterclaims, so that either party may move with respect to the same as though the counterclaim were an independent action. The court in its discretion may provide for the withholding of entry of judgment until the disposition of the issue in the main case.

This rule shall be applicable to all pending actions. 

Rule 114. Partial Judgment. If it appear that such defense applies only to part of plaintiff's claim, or that any part be admitted, the plaintiff may have final judgment forthwith for so much of his claim as such defense does not apply to or as is admitted, on such terms as may be just, and the action may be severed. 

These provisions are found in the rules only. There is no reference to summary judgment in the Civil Practice Act or to partial judgment except in section 476 which is very broad in its scope and possibly lays a foundation for the procedure stated in the rules. In New Jersey, where a similar

provision is found in the rules of the Supreme Court," there are two sections in the New Jersey Practice Act relating to the matter. Both the New Jersey provisions and the New 

York provisions were originally based upon similar provisions in the English Practice Act which has been in operation since the year 1855. It has been held that Rules 113 and 114 do not infringe upon the right to trial by jury guaranteed by the constitution.74 

§ 290. The Same - The Purpose and Scope of. 

The purpose of the provisions relating to summary judgment is to give a more expeditious way for obtaining a judgment, either in favor of the plaintiff or the defendant in the various kinds of actions referred to in the rule, than the previous practice afforded. The provisions undertake to accomplish this purpose by providing for a preliminary inquiry into the good faith of and probable merit in one party's claim and the other's resistance. The law is not intended to abolish trial by jury in lawsuits arising in the different classes of cases mentioned in the rule," but it is calculated to prevent delay in reaching judg-

S. 43, it was held "that the power to make rules of practice is a judicial power inherent in and not expressly conferred upon the Supreme Court; that the act creating the convention to adopt rules of Civil Practice merely provided a method and means whereby the court could conveniently and expeditiously exercise its judicial duty and was in no sense a delegation of legislative power by the legislature."

§ 291. The Same - Distinguished from the Motions for Judgment on the Pleadings and the Motion to Strike Out an Answer as a Sham,86

The motion under consideration is distinguished from a motion for judgment on the pleadings in that its determination does not depend upon the pleadings alone but upon the evidence relied on by the parties to support the ultimate facts stated in their pleadings, the "evidence" being contained in affidavits. It will not suffice for a party therefore to rest on a formal allegation in his pleading, no matter how posi-

The purpose of the motion for summary judgment is to test out whether a pleading which is sufficient in form is so in substance and this is ascertained by requiring the party to show in support of his pleading enough of his evidence to satisfy the court of his good faith. The substance of a jury trial required by the Constitution in the determination of issues at law is preserved here since the constitutional provision preserves the right of trial by jury not for fictitious but for real issues. As stated by the late Mr. Justice Page in the case of Dwan v. Massarene: "A fictitious denial, the effect of which was merely intended to force the plaintiff to prove his cause before a jury has no place in the code system of pleading. It was a relic of the artificial commonlaw pleading, which had persisted because of the resistance of the courts to the expressed will of the Legislature. 

With the intention of doing away with this technicality and fruitful source of delay and expense to the enforcement of a just and legal claim to which there was no defense in fact, the convention adopted rules 113 and 114."

The motion for summary judgment is distinguished from the motion to strike out an answer as a sham and from a motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 112 in that it is limited to the particular kinds of actions specified in the rule (113) while the motion to strike out a sham answer applies to all kinds of answers and the motion for judgment on the pleadings applies to pleadings in all kinds of actions. 

A further distinction seems to be that on the motion to strike out an answer as a sham the burden rests upon the plaintiff to establish the falsity of the answer beyond doubt, while on the motion for summary judgment the plaintiff's burden consists in showing the evidence that will sustain his complaint" and stating beyond this his belief that there is no defense to the action. By so doing he casts the burden upon the defendant of coming forward and showing by evidence an arguable defense."¹ Likewise, where the motion is by the defendant for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, the burden is on the plaintiff to show that from an evidentiary standpoint he has an arguable cause of action. $292. § 293. Partial Judgment. 

The provisions relating to partial judgments should be read in conjunction with those relating to summary judgments, and such remedy can be granted only in a case in which a summary judgment may be entered. Rules 113 and 114 supplement each other."

Many situations might arise from the New York practice for the application in connection with summary judgments of the provision relating to partial judgments. There may be more than one cause of action in the complaint and it may be found that the defendant is entitled to defend as to one of the causes of action but not as to the other. It may be that even in a single cause of action a part of the claim is conceded by the defendant and only a portion of the entire claim is in dispute. In such cases, judgment may be ordered for the part which is admitted, and the action continued for the purpose of determining the disputed part of the claim or the disputed cause of action. Authority for the procedure contemplated by this rule is found in the provisions of the Civil Practice Act relating to severance and to the entry of judgment based on admissions." 

§ 294. The Same-Peculiar Wording of Rule 114.

8. True-False Problem. 

X sued Y in the Supreme Court of New York County on a judgment for $10,000 obtained by X against Y in New Jersey on a promissory note. Y's answer admitted all the facts, but set up as an affirmative defense that after Y had appeared generally in the New Jersey action, no further steps had been taken by Y and that X's judgment was merely a judgment by default. Y also counterclaimed for $3,000 on a New Jersey judgment, which Y had secured against X.

X moved for judgment on the pleadings and his motion was denied. 

X then moved for partial judgment of $7,000 against Y under Rule 114 and this motion likewise being denied, X appeals from both orders. Answer the following "Yes" or "No": 

1. X's motion for judgment on the pleadings was properly denied. 

2. On such motion the Court had the right to consider facts stated in X's bill of particulars. 

3. If such motion was brought by X more than twenty days after the service of the last pleading, it was untimely. 

4. The order denying such motion was appealable. 

5. The order denying X's motion for partial judgment under Rule 114 was appealable. 

6. Disregarding all other elements, the very nature of X's action was such that a valid partial judgment would be impossible. 

7. Y's affirmative defense was insufficient in law. 

8. Y's counterclaim was properly interposed in the action. 

9. The presence of Y's counterclaim in Y's answer of itself prevented any partial judgment being granted on motion without a trial. 

10. X having first moved for judgment on the pleadings, he thereby waived his right to move for partial judgment. 

11. X's motion for $7,000 partial judgment on motion was properly denied.

§ 295. Extensions in General.2 

Statutes and rules often place a maximum period of time within which an act must be done or commenced, and often too they provide a minimum time before an act is done or commenced for giving notice to the adverse party. It is often desirable to enlarge the maximum time limits and cut down the minimum. A pleading may not be ready to serve when the rule requires its service and an extension of time is then needed. A motion may have to be brought on in less than five days and an abridgment of time is required. 

There are two methods of procuring extensions and abridgments of time: (a) By stipulation, and (b) By order. 

§ 296. Extensions and Abridgments by Stipulation.

§ 301. In General. 

The trial is the third main step in an action. The pleadings formulate the issues; the trial determines them. In considering this main step we shall notice in this chapter how a cause is brought on for trial, and in subsequent chapters the trial itself and the incidental practice relative [361]

THE TRIAL BRINGING A CAUSE FOR TRIAL 

thereto. In discussing the manner of bringing a cause on for trial, we shall first determine the proper place of trial, then the appropriate tribunal to try the cause, and finally the details of practice necessary in bringing the cause before that tribunal.

2 (a) Generally speaking, actions affecting real estate must be tried in the county where the real estate is situated. Actions affecting land in more than one county, such, for example, as an action for the specific performance of a contract contemplating the exchange of two parcels of real property located in different counties, may be tried in either county. § 305. Tribunals for the Trial of Issues. 

There are three tribunals for the trial of issues: (a) a court and jury, (b) a court alone and (c) a referee. In some cases the parties have an absolute right to a trial by jury. 

In other cases they may have a jury trial, not however as a matter of absolute right, but in the court's discretion. In some cases, too, the court must direct the trial to proceed before a referee. A consideration of the principles which govern a distribution of causes for trial among these three tribunals is now in order. 

§ 306. Jury Cases -In General. 

There are four classes of cases which may proceed before a court and jury. The first class consists of all actions which were triable by a court and jury at common law. The second consists of cases which have been made triable by a jury through statutory enactment. The third class consists of cases which are normally triable by the court without a jury, but where a jury is called in to aid the court in the trial of the case. The fourth class consists in cases where a jury trial does not exist as a matter of right nor is it invoked by the court's discretion; it proceeds more by accident than by design. We shall consider these cases in order. 

§ 307. The Same - First Class Common Law Actions. 

In section 6, ante, will be found an outline of common law actions. These actions were all tried by a court and jury. 

They are still so tried. Section 425 of the Civil Practice 

Act 18 provides: 

"In each of the following actions an issue of fact must be tried by a jury unless a jury trial is waived or a reference is directed: (1) an action in which the complaint demands judgment for a sum of money only (2) an action of ejectment; for dower, for waste, for a nuisance; or to recover a chattel.'

This section of the Civil Practice Act is declaratory of the common law with respect to the cases where the parties were entitled to trial by jury. It adds no new cases to that list and it takes none away. It is a comprehensive statement in general terms of common law jurisdiction. If, therefore, a case be found which answers the literal requirements of the 

18. Former Code § 988 without change.

THE TRIAL 

section but which was not under the old procedure entitled to the right of trial by jury, the language of this section will not give it that right.

When, therefore, the complaint demands a money judg ment, but sets out a cause of action which constituted under the old procedure an action for a partnership accounting, triable by the court alone, no right to a jury trial exists." 

Again, although subdivision 2 of this section includes actions for a nuisance, yet the word nuisance so used is limited in its application to actions seeking an abatement of the nuisance and damages;20 and when it is sought in the action to enjoin the continuance of the nuisance, although it may be said still to be an action for a nuisance, the right to a jury trial ceases since the injunction is distinctly equitable in its nature.21

Moreover, where an action was brought for an injunction to restrain the continued operation of a nuisance adjoining the premises which plaintiff had leased, and plaintiff joined with this action one for damages suffered by reason of the past operation of the nuisance the action was held to be triable by the court without a jury. In such case the action for damages is considered a mere incident to the equity action and under the ancient procedure, when equity once acquired jurisdiction as it had here by the injunction action, it gave complete justice and disposed of all incidental matters whether legal or equitable to avoid multiplicity of suits.22 

But when in such case before the trial was reached plaintiff's lease of the premises expired so that he could no longer maintain an action for an injunction but could maintain the action for damages, the action thus stripped of its equity features became an ordinary common law action for damages and a jury trial became a matter of right.23 It has been held, however, that in an ordinary case if a plaintiff joins an equitable cause of action with a legal cause of action in the same complaint, he thereby waives his right to a jury trial." 24

§ 308. The Same-Constitutional Provisions. 

The right to trial by jury in this class of cases is protected against legislative change by constitutional provision. Article I, section 2, of the state Constitution says: "The trial by jury in all cases in which it has been heretofore used shall remain inviolate forever; but a jury trial may be waived by the parties in all civil cases in the manner to be prescribed by law."

A similar provision is found in every Constitution which the state has had. It was stated in the first Constitution, being that of the year 1777, as follows: "Trial by jury in all cases in which it hath heretofore been used in the colony of New York shall be established and remain inviolate forever."

The general types of actions, therefore, that were triable by jury in the procedure that existed prior to the year 1777 must continue to be so tried now. 

It will now be further apparent why section 425 of the Civil Practice Act is declaratory of the common law. It could not be other than declaratory of it for if it sought to change the common law in this respect it would be unconstitutional and void. The section helps materially to make clear the cases that are thus protected by the Constitution and such help constitutes its need and its justification. 

§ 309. The Same-Second Class-Statutory Jury Trials. 

While the legislature cannot, because of this constitutional inhibition, remove any case from the first class of jury trial cases and make it triable by the court without a jury, without giving plaintiff a reasonable opportunity to demand or waive his right to a jury trial, there is nothing to prevent the reverse of that process. The legislature can take a case which formerly was triable by the court or otherwise than by a jury and make it a case triable by a jury. 

The Constitution does not prevent this. The legislature accordingly has from time to time since the year 1777 made a number of cases jury cases which at first were not such. 

The following cases have been made triable by a jury through legislative intervention:

THE TRIAL 

(a) Actions for divorce where the answer puts in issue. the allegation charging adultery and either party applies therefor.25

Ta (b) An action to annul a marriage, except where it is founded upon an allegation of physical incapacity, where either party applies therefor." (c) An issue of fact in an action for partition." 

(d) An action against an alleged usurper of an office, franchise or corporate right.28 (e) An action by the attorney-general to annul a corporation.20 (f) An action by the attorney-general to vacate letters patent. 80 (g) An issue of fact in an alternative mandamus order.

82 Of course, the article in the first Constitution of the state, preserving the right to trial by jury in all cases where "it hath been heretofore used," referred to the cases triable by jury prior to that time. Now while this process was going on a new Constitution was adopted from time to time, the last one being adopted in 1894. In each of these the phrase quoted from the first Constitution or a similar phrase was continued and the effect of such phrase in the latter Constitutions seems not only to continue the right to trial by jury in old common law cases, but to seal up as constitutionally protected jury trials the cases to which jury trials were given by the legislature prior to the adoption of the Constitution in question. Originally, for example, divorces were granted by the legislature; but in the ordinance of 1787 the legislature turned that work over to the chancery court. § 311. Jury Trials Third Class In the Discretion of the Court. 

In equity actions where neither party has a right to a jury trial, the court may in its discretion call in the aid of a jury.34 

It has always been the practice of courts of equity in their discretion to call in the aid of a jury on the application of either party or on their own initiative," but the court in such cases is not bound by the verdict of the jury and may adopt it or disregard it as its judgment directs.36 

§ 312. Jury Trials Fourth Class-Accidental Cases. 

It has happened that cases were tried before a jury where neither party had a right to such mode of trial but either through accident on their part it was brought on for trial before a jury, or through accident on the part of the court it was allowed to be tried before a jury. A determination of an action reached in this manner is binding on the parties, who have no right to complain of the result.87

§ 313. Trials by the Court Without a Jury — In General. 

Actions in which the parties are not entitled to a trial by jury pursuant to the foregoing regulations are, as a rule, tried before a court without a jury. Litigants in such cases, however, have no constitutional right to a trial by the court.38 The court can, as already seen, call in the aid of a jury to assist it, and when this is done a case exists falling within the third class of jury trial cases. In an action triable by a jury, however, if the parties waive a jury, the action must be tried by the court, unless a reference is directed in a case prescribed by law.38a For convenience, cases triable by the court without a jury are classified in the manner indicated in the following sections. 

§ 314. The Same First Class. 

All cases not falling within one of the classes of jury trials discussed in the foregoing sections of this chapter are triable by the court alone unless they are sent before a referee for trial. Equity cases are the ones contemplated in this class except the equity cases where a jury trial has been allowed by statutory enactment." 39 

§ 315. The Same-Second Class. 

Actions for a breach of contract are normally triable by a jury since they are common law actions. They must be tried by the court, however, if the parties waive their right to a jury trial. The same thing is true with all other actions triable by jury, with the reservation that in such other actions the court is not bound by the waivers of the parties and may refuse to try the action without a jury."¹ 41

While the five modes of waiving one's right to a jury trial are the only ones mentioned in the Civil Practice Act, they do not exhaust the ways in which a party may waive such right. Any conduct on the part of a party which under reasonable rules of construction amounts to an expression of indifference regarding the mode of a trial will be considered a waiver. Thus the joinder of a legal with an equitable cause of action has been held to be a waiver. The failure to appeal from an order directing the trial of the action before a referee and proceeding with the trial before that tribunal has been held to be a waiver;48 but failure to appeal from an order transferring the cause from the Jury Term to the 

Special Term is not a waiver.49 47

§ 318. References by Consent. 

When the parties to an action consent to the trial thereof or to the trial of any issue therein before a referee the same must be sent to a referee for trial.56 The consent must be given by written stipulation." The referee may be named in the same stipulation and if so named, the cause must be referred to him.58

This regulation applies to all kinds of actions whether legal or equitable except the three following: (a) Matrimonial actions, (b) An action against a corporation to obtain a dissolution thereof, to appoint a receiver of its property, or to distribute its assets. But if such action is brought by the attorney-general it is not an exception to the rule. (c) An action where an infant defendant will be affected by the result of the trial.

In these excepted cases a consent by the parties is not binding on the court which may designate or refuse to designate, in its discretion, a referee to try the cause, and if it decides to designate a referee it must name the referee."

With the present liberal rules for joining causes of action and the interposition of counterclaims, the application of the rules for distributing trials between the court and the court and jury has become difficult. It is possible now to join legal and equitable causes of action in the same complaint, and it is likewise possible to interpose equitable defenses to legal causes of action and legal counterclaims to equitable causes of action. Some special attention must be given, therefore, to such cases. (a) Where the complaint sets forth a legal cause of action and the defendant sets up an equitable defense or an equitable counterclaim, the rule is that the complaint alone determines the proper tribunal for the trial." A defendant, therefore, cannot by interposing an equitable defense or an equitable counterclaim to plaintiff's legal cause of action, defeat the plaintiff's right to a trial by jury. In common law actions the notice of trial was for a trial term. In actions, however, which are triable by a jury through statutory enactment, that is, those referred to in section 309 of this chapter, the proper practice was to notice such actions for trial at special term the same as in equity actions.

By chapter 504 of the Laws of 1934, amending section 433 of the Civil Practice Act, this procedure was drastically changed. The Commission on the Administration of Justice in New York State had previously made the following recommendation:82 "With slight additions, the note of issue can be made to serve the purpose of the notice of trial, thereby dispensing with the necessity for two different notices. A copy of the note of issue [under the new practice] is served upon the adverse parties and performs the function of the notice of trial.' ے کا رام الله The amendment to the Civil Practice Act is not in itself sufficient to carry out the change in practice. The commission has recommended a proposed substitute for Rules 150 and 151 of the Rules of Civil Practice, which refer to notices of trial and of issue. This amendment must be adopted by a majority of the justices of the Appellate Division and published in accordance with the Judiciary Law before it can take effect. The suggested amendment reads as follows: 

"At any time after the joinder of issue, and at least twelve days before the commencement of the term or the opening of an adjourned term, any party may file a note of issue with the clerk, stating the title of the action, the names of the attorneys, the time when the last pleading was served, whether the action is triable by a jury or by the court without a jury, the term at which the trial of the case is desired, and the particular nature and object of the action. In any county in which the clerk has published a comprehensive list of types of actions, the note of issue shall specify the classification into which the action falls. The clerk shall thereupon enter the cause upon the calendar. The clerk must prepare the calendar and have the necessary copies made for distribution at least five (5) days before the commencement of the term. "A copy of the note of issue shall be served upon the attorneys for each of the adverse parties who have appeared in the action at least twelve (12) days before the commencement of the term. "No new note of issue shall be required upon the subsequent amend- 

82. N. Y. Legislative Document 50D, (1934) at page 37.

ment of the pleadings or upon the bringing in of any new parties, but a supplemental statement shall be filed within five (5) days thereafter, with the clerk advising him of the change in the title of the action, the names of the new parties and of their attorneys, and a copy thereof shall be served upon the attorneys for each of the parties, and the case shall retain its place on the calendar unless the court shall otherwise direct. "If any party subsequently joined in the action shall not have had adequate time to prepare the case for trial, when it is reached, a suitable adjournment shall be granted."

It will, of course, be necessary to amend various local court rules to make them conform with the new amendment. 

In actions triable by a jury through statutory enactment (section 309, supra), after a note of issue has been served, a motion may be made to the court on notice for an order directing all the questions arising upon the issues to be distinctly and clearly stated for trial by jury. In such cases the court must cause the issues to be distinctly and plainly stated.83 

When such an order is made directing the issues to be tried by jury and distinctly and plainly stated, a certified copy of the same is filed with the calendar clerk of the trial term of the court and it then becomes his duty to put the cause upon the trial term calendar.84 When the case is reached for trial and the issues therein determined at the trial, the verdict must be certified by the trial term clerk back to the special term clerk for the attention of the court. Formerly a general rule of practices required the party who desired a jury trial in such cases to give notice of motion stating the issues he desired thus to have tried to the adverse party within twenty days after issue was joined. Such rule has been declared unconstitutional because it unduly cuts down the right of the party to a jury trial contrary to the constitutional provisions relating thereto.86

Certain civil actions have a right to a more speedy trial than others and such right is called a preference. Actions in which the state seeks to recover money, funds, credits or other property from a defendant obtaining, receiving, paying, converting or disposing of the same is given preference over all other actions. Generally speaking, other actions are entitled to preference among themselves as follows: (1) Actions by or against the state. (2) Actions where one of the cities of New York, Buffalo or Rochester is a party." (3) Actions where a public board or body exercising powers for the protection of public health or public or private property is a party." (4) Actions in which an executor, administrator or mostly any other person acting in a representative capacity is a party."

THE TRIAL § 325. Practice When the Case is Reached on the Calendar. 

There are five possible contingencies when a case appears upon the calendar that may present themselves: (a) neither party may appear, (b) defendant may appear and the plaintiff may not, (c) plaintiff may appear and the defendant may not, (d) both parties may appear, and (e) both parties may appear but the attorneys of one or both may be actually engaged in another trial. (a) If neither party appears the judge marks the cause off the calendar. In such case a motion will be required to restore it to the calendar. (b) If the defendant appears and the plaintiff does not, the defendant may make a motion that the complaint be dismissed.30 If the complaint is thus dismissed, judgment is entered for the defendant and that ends the matter. Such a judgment, however, is not a judgment on the merits and does not bar another action for the same cause.81 31 (c) Where the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not, the plaintiff may take what is called an inquest. An inquest is a proceeding whereby evidence upon one side only is presented. It is a trial of issues of fact where one party alone introduces testimony. In this case the party would be the plaintiff. If there were a counterclaim in the answer, the specific sum of money, or upon a bond or undertaking on appeal, or upon a negotiable instrument, or for goods sold, delivered and accepted, or upon a policy of insurance, or upon an account stated, or for wages, salary or compensation for services, or for rent or hire of real or personal property, or for money had and received, or for moncy loaned, or on a statute wherein the sum sought to be recovered is a sum of money other than a penalty, or on a guaranty, or in an action of replevin, or in an action wherein an attachment has been issued and has not been discharged, either party may, upon five days' notice of motion returnable not earlier than the term for which the cause has been noticed for trial, apply to the justice holding

Trial Term, Part II, for an order plac ing said cause on the Reserve Calendar for a day certain. "The papers on which the application shall be made and the answering affidavits, if any, must be filed with the calendar clerk before 12 o'clock noon of the day for which the application is noticed, and no oral argument will be heard on such application unless so ordered by the justice holding Part II." 

Cf. also Trial Term Rule IV, which provides that where an action is brought by or against a receiver of a corporation it may be preferred for a day certain although no notice of application a preference may have been served with the note of issue as provided in

Section 141 of the Civil Practice Act.

32 defendant might take an inquest on the counterclaim in the situation presented by (b) supra. We shall discuss inquests a little more fully in the next section. (d) In case both parties appear the trial proceeds and that matter is taken up in the next chapter. (e) If both parties appear, but the attorneys of one or both of them are engaged in another trial, a representative of the engaged attorney will answer "ready, subject" to the engagement. As soon as the engagement in question is terminated, the trial will then proceed, subject to the discretion of the calendar judge. If the excuse given for not being ready is something other than a recognized "engagement" the court may grant a short adjournment, or in its discretion it may mark the case off the calendar, dismiss the complaint or order an inquest. § 326. As noted in the preceding section, the plaintiff usually takes an inquest where the defendant fails to appear at the trial. 4. True-False Question. 

X sues Y for an absolute divorce in the Supreme Court, New York County. Y's answer puts in issue the material allegations of the complaint. Answer "Yes" or "No": 

1. The entire action is triable of right by jury. 

2. The action should be noticed for trial at trial term. 

3. A motion must be made to frame issues for a jury if a jury trial is desired thereon. 

4. Assuming a trial by jury, X and Y each have ten peremptory challenges. 

5. After the jury have been empanelled and sworn, X may move for judgment on the pleadings. 

6. A motion made by Y's attorney at the end of the plaintiff's case to dismiss the complaint for failure of proof, must ordinarily particularize the grounds of the motion. 

7. If the motion is denied and Y puts in his evidence, his attorney must renew the motion to dismiss at the end of the entire case, else it is waived. 

8. Unless an exception is taken to the judge's charge, no ground for reversal ordinarily exists in the Court of Appeals, even though the charge contained reversible error. 

9. The Court may reserve decision on the defendant's motion to dismiss the complaint until after the jury have brought in their verdict on the framed issues and then grant it. 

10. The verdict of the jury is a special verdict, and it must be in writing.

§ 327. Introduction. 

In the last chapter the proper tribunal for the trial and the practice in bringing the cause on for trial before such tribunal were considered. Before considering the trial proper, however, it will be necessary to consider the compulsory processes which are provided for the production of evidence at the trial. Witnesses will not always come voluntarily and if they are outside the state it may be impossible to compel their attendance. In this and the succeeding chapter the compulsory production of evidence at the trial will be treated.¹ 

§ 328. The Compulsory Production of Evidence at the Trial-In General. 

The processes by which a party may compel those who have evidence material to his cause to produce it at the trial are subpoenas and orders, the notice to produce, depositions and proceedings relating to admissions, discovery and inspection. The proceedings relating to these matters will be discussed in this and the following chapter.2 

1. The Civil Practice Act has changed materially the practice relating to preparation for trial. The changes are so numerous that a reference to the particular topics discussed in this and the succeeding chapter is required. 

§ 329. The Subpoena - Definition - Where to Be Served. 

A subpoena is a process in the name of the court, referee, 2. Generally speaking, the procedure relating to subpoenas is the same under the Practice Act as it was under the Code. The order to bring up a prisoner to testify as a witness supersedes the writ of habeas corpus to bring up a witness to testify which was provided for under the Code. The notice to produce is the same as it was under the Code. The provisions relating to depositions have been very generally changed and an examination of those provisions in detail is necessary to show the extent of the change. 

The provisions relating to admissions, [391]

A court of record has power to issue a subpoena subject to the limitations prescribed by law with reference to the territory in which it may be served. A subpoena issued out of the Supreme

New York counties." A Municipal Court subpoena may be served anywhere in the city of New York. A justice's court subpoena may be served in the county where the justice resides or in the adjoining county.⁹

There are two kinds of subpoenas. The first requires the attendance of the person named in it merely. This is called simply a subpoena. This is called a subpoena duces tecum.10 discovery and inspection have been enlarged and extended. § 331. Service of the Subpoena. 

The ordinary subpoena or the subpoena duces tecum is served by exhibiting the original subpoena to the witness, delivering to him a copy thereof or a ticket containing its substance, and paying him or tendering to him the travelling fees allowed by law and the fee for one day's attendance." 

The fee is fifty cents for each day's attendance and if the witness resides more than three miles from the place of attendance he must be given eight cents for each mile going to the place of attendance.18

§ 332. Special Provisions Relating to a Subpoena Duces Tecum. 

Records kept by the register of the counties of New York, Kings, Queens and Bronx shall not be removed by virtue of a subpoena duces tecum. To procure such records an order of the court is necessary.20 Moreover any other record, a certified copy of which may be read in evidence, cannot be removed by virtue of the subpoena duces tecum outside of the city or town where the office of the custodian of the record is situated.21

Original hospital records need not be produced under a subpoena duces tecum without an order of the court.22 And an order will not be granted requiring the New York City Department of Health to produce records of treatment of a clinical patient for a communicable disease. To do so would be to violate public policy and the privilege of physician and patient.22a

A subpoena duces tecum for the production of a book of account must be served at least five days before the day when the person subpoenaed is required to attend and if time does not permit of such service an order of the court is necessary to compel the production of such book of account.23 A person whose book of account is subpoenaed or required to be produced under an order may, upon motion, be relieved wholly or partly from the obligations imposed upon him by the subpoena or order upon such

A subpoena duces tecum, for the production of a book or paper belonging to or under the control of a corporation must be directed to the president or other head of the corporation or to the officer thereof in whose custody the book or paper is.25

When a subpoena duces tecum requires an officer of a corporation, or a public officer to attend and bring a book or paper under his control, it is not necessary that the officer himself attend and bring the book or paper, but a subordinate officer or employee who possesses the requisite knowledge to identify it and testify respecting the purposes for which it is used may appear in the place of such an officer. If a party desires the attendance of the officer in person, an ordinary subpoena without the duces tecum clause must be served upon him in addition.26

In all cases where a subpoena duces tecum is directed to a library association or corporation, a public officer, a department of a municipal corporation, or other public officer or department, the same shall be signed by a justice of the Supreme Court in the district in which the library or department is situated or the public officer is employed, or by a judge of the court in which the action is pending and upon one day's notice to the interested party and to the opposing attorney.27

A prisoner may also be brought up to give testimony in an action pending in an inferior court provided he is confined in a jail in a county where the action is to be tried or in an adjoining county. In such case a justice of the Supreme Court or county judge residing within the county where the officer resides may make the order.30

After testifying, the prisoner must be remanded to the prison from which he was taken. Any officer upon whom such order is served must obey the same, and if he refuses or neglects so to do he forfeits to the party on whose application the order was made the sum of five hundred dollars.32 

§ 334. Notice to Produce. 

Where books, papers or documents are in the possession of the adverse party and an attorney desires their production for use at the trial, he may serve upon the attorney for the adverse party a notice called a notice to produce. 

There is no form prescribed for this notice and indeed it may be given orally" but it is usually in writing, entitled in the action, directed to the attorney for the adverse party and signed by the attorney for the party issuing it. It should, however, be very specific in identifying the papers to be produced. The following would do as a form of a notice to produce:

(Title.) 

SIR:

You are required to produce at the trial of the above entitled action the following: (here follows a description of the papers desired, sufficiently definite to identify them) together with all other papers, books, documents, checks, memoranda, etc., in your possession or under your control in any wise, relating to the issues involved in this action and for a failure to produce the same, secondary evidence of their contents will be given. 

(Date.) To: 

(Name and address of opposing attorney.) (Signature and address of attorney.)

It will be seen from the form that the only penalty involved in disobeying a notice to produce is that secondary evidence of the contents of the papers may be offered instead of the originals at the trial. It follows that if the party does not possess knowledge or information of the contents of the papers sought, the notice to produce may be ineffectual since the party will not be able to give secondary evidence of their contents. A subpoena would be necessary under such circumstances.

The notice to produce should ordinarily be served a reasonable time before the trial. There is no particular time required for its service.84

There is no provision in the Civil Practice Act nor was there any in the Code, relating to the notice to produce. This notice is incident to the trial of an action and is provided for in the law of evidence rather than in the rules of practice.

§ 335. Depositions - Introduction. 

Much evidence would be unavailable if there were no other ways of securing it than by subpoena, order or a notice to produce. The subpoena cannot ordinarily reach a person outside the state; it cannot bring the sick and infirm to the court room; it would be inadequate to ascertain in advance that which an adverse party alone knew and which would be material and necessary in establishing a cause of action or defense. A notice to produce is of value only when you know what you want and can introduce secondary evidence in case, after a notice to produce, the adverse party fails to produce the primary evidence. To meet the needs created by the above and other situations, provision is made in the Civil 

Practice Act for taking such testimony by deposition. 

§ 336. Classes of Persons Whose Deposition May Be Taken. 

There are two classes of persons whose depositions may be taken. These are (a) persons in the nature of parties and (b) other persons. The first class includes actual parties, expected parties, the original owner of the claim which the party now has, and when the party or original owner of the

claim is a corporation, joint stock or other unincorporated association, this first class comprehends the officers, directors, managing agents and employees of such entities." 

The second class contemplates witnesses other than those mentioned in the first class. 

§ 337. Grounds for Taking Depositions of Persons in the First Class. 

The only grounds required, so far as the bare language of the statute is concerned, to authorize the taking of the deposition of a person in the first class are that the testimony sought shall be "material and necessary in the prosecution or defense of the action."" Rule 124 indicates that an attack may be made upon a party's right to examine an adverse party in advance of the trial not only on the ground that the testimony sought "is not material or necessary," but also states that the court may prevent the examination where it shall deem "for any reason that the interests of justice would not be subserved by such an examination." 

Indeed, it would seem strange if each of the parties could examine the adverse party in advance of the trial on a simple showing that such an examination is "material and necessary" for the prosecution or defense of the action; and such a rule might result in great annoyance to honest business enterprises. It would be a great weapon in the hands of unscrupulous plaintiffs for they could on a mere suspicion or less, frame a cause of action and then annoy the adverse party by subjecting him to an examination which would in reality be nothing more than a "fishing excursion" in the hope of finding something that might embarrass the adverse party if known and which might force a settlement if it did not prove plaintiff's cause of action. 

1. Civil Practice Act, §§ 288, 289 

and 295. The Code provisions included in this class were the parties and expected parties. They did not include the original owner of the claim sued on (Sheff v. Lewis, 191 App. Div. 30: 

180 N. Y. S. 831). In the case of corporations, the Code provisions in- 

Icluded the officers, directors and managing agents but did not include the employees. Cf. Code §§ 870 and 872, subdivision 7 with §§ 288 and 289 of the Civil Practice Act, Section 290 

of the Civil Practice Act has extended the scope of these examinations to cover the "matters" which are material and necessary, rather than the mere "issues," as previously. 

2. Civil Practice Act, § 288.

§ 338. The Same-Historical Background. 

So much confusion exists in relation to depositions of persons in the first class, commonly referred to as examinations before trial, and there are so many conflicting decisions regarding the circumstances which will authorize such an examination, that a more fundamental consideration of the subject seems needed to show what the law on the subject really is.

At common law a party had to rely on third persons as witnesses to prove his case. He could not place his adversary on the witness stand and interrogate him. Blackstone characterizes this as one of the defects incident to jury trials. 

Equity came into existence to correct defects in the common law and to cure this particular defect, equity gave the right to a litigant in a common law action to begin a proceeding in equity solely for the purpose of subjecting his adversary to an examination under oath and the action at law might be stayed until such examination could be had." 

The same proceeding gave a party the right to an inspection of the books, papers and documents of his adversary." 

This method of getting at information needed by a party, and in the possession of his adversary was slow and expensive, and the Code of Civil Procedure made changes in the interest of expedition and economy. The Civil Practice Act has continued these changes made by the Code.

Code Changes Continued by the Civil Practice § 339. The Same 

Act. 

By section 1914 of the Code' the procedure by way of an equitable bill of discovery was abolished and at the same time other Code provisions, now found in the Civil Practice Act, were enacted by which the benefits of the bill of discovery were to be secured. 

Section 828 of the Codes provided that parties might be compelled to be witnesses. This replaced the old proceeding so far as the trial itself was concerned but left yet to be

§ 340. The Same - Interpretation of the Changes Made by the Code. 

The case of Glenney v. Stedwell10 declared that in abolishing the right to a discovery the intention was not to destroy the right but to change the remedy by which it was to be enforced, and that therefore the new Code provisions replaced and secured the benefits given by the former procedure. 

The Civil Practice Act sections have the same effect. They merely change the procedure by which a right "conferred upon the Supreme Court by the Constitution of the State of 

New York in 1846 is to be exercised.""" They are to be interpreted in the light of the history out of which they emerge and of which they form a part. The principles governing the exercise of the right to a bill of discovery under the old equitable procedure give definition to the right to examine an adverse party before trial under the Code and under the 

Civil Practice Act.

Bishop's criticism, and we assured the members of the association during the debate that we would urge the Joint 

Legislative Committee to make the two suggested amendments. Subsequently both amendments were accepted by the Joint Legislative Committee and enacted by the Legislature in chapter 926 of the Laws of 1920. 

Thus section 288 defines the right to an examination. The original sugges tion that it should not be necessary to show the materiality of the expected testimony or the necessity for the examination is not adopted. The provision of section 288 in chapter 925, that the testimony must be 'material' is amended by chapter 926 by making it read 'material and necessary.' "The reform attempted by the Joint 

Legislative Committee, particularly as set forth in Civil Practice Act, sec. tions 288, 290 and 291, consisted in incorporating into our statutes the convenient practice which has worked so smoothly in the federal courts and in the hope that most depositions will eventually be taken without opposition, and that the courts will be troubled only in cases where the moving party is really proceeding beyond his rights. 

On the other hand, while the number of instances in which a party may have an examination is increased, the right to an examination is still to be limited, upon objection, to cases where the moving party can show that the testimony is both material and necessary."

THE TRIAL PREPARATION FOR-DEPOSITIONS, ETC. 405 § 341. The Same - Principles Governing the Old Procedure of Discovery Must Be Examined to Circumscribe the Application of the Civil Practice Act Provisions. 

The Civil Practice Act provisions merely define the right and do not circumscribe its exercise. The only words of limitation found in the act are the words "material and necessary." Considered apart from the historical setting and seeking to interpret these words "material and necessary" merely, a party would seem to have the right to examine his adversary to any extent in any case, and some of the decisions of the courts relative to these Civil Practice Act provisions or rather the Code provisions which they replace apparently made without reference to the historical background would seem to indicate that such is the law.¹2 

However, the limitations connected with the bill of discovery attach substantially to the new statutory proceedings and furnish the principles for their application.' 12

Litigations that presented the relation of principal and agent or the like, and the facts were peculiarly within the knowledge of the adverse party. Third: Litigations in which a defense, unanswered and established, would destroy the plaintiff's cause of action. But in cases of this third class the examination was limited properly to avoidance, and was not extended to disclosure." 

For example, the complaint in an action for an accounting alleged that the defendant was an attorney and the legal and confidential adviser of the plaintiff and invested her money for her, and from time to time paid her certain amounts of money and that he was in possession of her bonds, money and papers, and that he refused to furnish her with a statement of his account. The answer of the defendant denied that he was the confidential adviser of the plaintiff and alleges that he had fully accounted and settled with the plaintiff for all claims and demands existing between them with certain exceptions and also sets up as a defense the statute of limitations. The court allowed the plaintiff to examine the defendant with respect to the alleged accounting which he said in his answer that he had made, although this examination related to issues of which the defendant had the affirmative.27 The same situation would illustrate the second exception stated in the above quotation if the defendant were not a confidential adviser and attorney but simply an agent employed to do the same work which he was doing.28

The second exception which embraces the case where the facts are peculiarly in the possession of the adverse party, is illustrated where an executor sues to recover damages for the death of a decedent and the defendant sets up contributory negligence as a defense. The executor should be allowed to examine the defendant relative to the defense of 

26. 188 App. Div. 23; 176 N. Y. S. 406. 

27. Griffen v. Davis, 99 App. Div. 

65; 90 N. Y. S, 491. 

28. Whitman v. Kieley, 58 App. Div. 

92; 68 N. Y. S. 551; Kastner v. Kastner, 53 App. Div. 294; 65 N. Y, S. 756,

contributory negligence. Likewise where the executor sues on a contract between the defendant and the decedent and payment is set up as a defense.29

The third exception found in the quotation given above is more apparent than real. The fact is that it is not an exception at all but comes under the general rule. The defendant usually has the affirmative, of the issues presented by an affirmative defense but not always. Under the rules of pleading a defense is deemed controverted either by traverse or avoidance as the case requires.80 If controverted by traverse the defendant has the affirmative of the issues; if by avoidance the plaintiff has the affirmative. In the former case the examination of the defendant should not be allowed under the general rule while in the latter case it should. For example, where the plaintiff sued an insurance company on a policy of fire insurance and desired to examine the defendant company with reference to the affirmative defense that plaintiff had made false proof of loss, swore falsely, etc., in order, as plaintiff said, to void the effect of the defense, the examination was not allowed since the defendant himself had the affirmative of the issue upon which the examination was sought. 

But where the action was on contract and the defense was that the contract had been cancelled, the plaintiff should not be allowed to examine the defendant to show that the contract had not been cancelled but he should be allowed to examine the defendant to show that the cancellation was ineffective. On the issue of whether the contract had or had not been cancelled, the defendant would have the affirmative but on the issue as to whether the alleged cancellation was ineffectual, under the circumstances the plaintiff would have the affirmative.32 81

§ 344-A. Physician's Examination of Plaintiff in a Personal Injury Action. 

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, if the defendant shall present to the court satisfactory evidence that he is ignorant of the nature and extent of the injuries complained of, the court, by order, shall direct that the plaintiff submit to a physical examination by one or more physicians or surgeons to be designated by the court or judge, and such examination shall be had and made under such restrictions and directions as the court or judge shall deem proper. If the party to be examined shall be a female she shall be entitled to have such examination before a physician or surgeon of her own sex. § 346. Modes of Procedure for Procuring the Deposition. 

Whether the examination contemplated relates to persons in the nature of parties or to mere witnesses, there are two modes of procedure outlined in the Civil Practice Act and Rules for procuring and taking their depositions.

§ 348. Vacating or Modifying the Notice. 

If the adverse party questions in any respect the right of his opponent to proceed as indicated in the notice, he may make a motion to vacate or modify the notice.18 

The papers used to make such a motion, in addition to a copy of the notice of examination (or order for the examination as the case may be), are a notice of motion, the pleadings and, in the discretion of the mover, affidavits. The notice of motion must specify the grounds of the objections to the notice." The affidavit, if used, may state the facts showing the unfitness of the time, place or person named in the notice, or that the testimony is not material or necessary for the party, or such other facts as under the rules or law may defeat or tend to defeat the examination.5⁰ It is not necessary that an affidavit be used in support of the motion. Rule 124 uses the word "may" not "must" in referring to the use of the affidavit. It was not intended, seemingly, in formulating the procedure for instituting an examination by notice merely, to shift thereby the burden of showing the materiality and necessity for the examination from the party seeking it and cast upon the party opposing it the burden of proving the negative of such materiality and necessity."" P. A., § 290). Any question may be raised by motion to vacate or modify the notice. The moving party has merely to raise the question. The burden is then upon the party who has given the notice to sustain it, and the moving party may then present his affidavits in opposition. ENTER J. S. C. § 349.

Compelling Attendance of Witnesses in the Absence of an Order. 

It will be necessary to procure the presence at the place designated of the person to be examined. The service of the notice upon the attorney for the adverse party will not be sufficient to procure the attendance of any witness. The subpoena, however, may be resorted to to compel the presence of the party whose examination is sought.55 The manner of serving the subpoena, the fees to be paid thereon, and the penalty for disobeying it are the same as when the subpoena is served upon a witness to attend at a trial.56 

§ 350. Manner of Taking Testimony. 

Before proceeding with the examination, the officer or person before whom the deposition is to be taken shall have a copy of the notice, together with proof of service thereof before him. He shall also have before him a certified copy of the order, if there be one, by which the notice was modified. 

If he have the notice merely before him, he shall require the party at whose instance the notice was served, or counsel representing him, to make affidavit that to the best of his 55. It was formerly held that the court could not strike out the answer of a defendant for failure to appear for examination before trial in response to a notice served upon his attorney (Levine v. Moskowitz, 206 

App. Div. 194; 200 N. Y. S. 597; 

Rosenberg Holding Co. v. Berman, 214 

App. Div. 146; 211 N. Y. S. 900; Ungar v. Payne, 217 App. Div. 768); but that it could stay affirmative action by him on a counterclaim, just as it could stay affirmative steps in the action by a plaintiff who neglected to appear for examination before trial pursuant to a proper notice. It is now provided by C. P. A., § 299, that where a party has appeared in an action the order for his examination may be served upon his attorney, and for a wilful failure to appear for the examination the pleading of the party may be stricken out, upon application to the court, on notice.

The court has no inherent power to strike out a party's pleading as & punishment for contempt. (Peters v. 

Berkeley, 219 App. Div. 261, 264; 219 

N. Y. S. 709.) The court is author. ized to strike out the pleading of a party who disobeys a subpoena or order 

(Civil Practice Act, § 405). It seems that this authority is to be exercised, not as punishment for contempt merely, but as a punishment for the suppression of evidence (Feingold v. Walworth Bros., Inc., 238 N. Y. 446).

The officer or person shall then administer to the witness an oath in form as administered to a witness in court.58 The examination shall then be conducted in the same manner as on the trial, except that an objection to any question need not be noted and may be raised upon the trial unless it be an objection to form only, in which case it must be noted.59 

All questions and answers may be taken down unless the parties consent, or an order directs, that only the substance thereof be inserted." If the examination within the state be conducted before any one other than a judge of the court, and the witness refuses to answer a question, such refusal may be reported to the court or judge who shall determine if the witness should answer."1

If the court orders him to answer and he wishes to question such order, it is not the proper practice to have a formal order entered directing the witness to answer such question and appeal from that order and have the direction reviewed. 

Such a practice would result in too much delay. The same practice is adopted here as is adopted at the trial. If the witness is directed to answer he must answer or stand committed for contempt. All errors in the rulings of the court may be reviewed on appeal from a judgment entered after the trial.62 Although the statutes relating to the procedure for taking depositions have been changed since the decisions in these cases, the same reason for the principle exists under the present procedure as existed under the Code procedure, and these cases, therefore, apply.

§ 351. Filing of Deposition. 

The deposition and the papers required to be annexed thereto shall be filed within ten days after its completion and return, in the office of the clerk of the court in the county in which the action is triable unless such filing is waived by stipulation. The deposition must remain on file and it is always open to the inspection of the parties who are entitled to make copies of it." 

§ 352. Use Made of Deposition. 

A deposition thus taken may be read in evidence by either party at the trial or upon a motion," except that a deposition taken within the state other than one taken at the instance of the adverse party or in pursuance of a stipulation shall not be read in evidence unless it appears to the satisfaction of the court that the witness is dead or out of the state or at a greater distance than one hundred miles from the place where the court is situated, or for any other reason his attendance cannot be compelled by subpoena with the exercise of reasonable diligence."

§ 353. Effect of Deposition. 

When read at the trial the deposition has the same effect and no other as oral testimony of the witness would have. 

Any objection to the competency of the witness or to a question or answer may be made as if the witness were being then personally examined except only an objection to the form of the question which must be noted on the deposition or it is waived." One is not bound by the deposition of an adverse party to the action.72

If a party desires to make application to the court for an order directing an examination of the adverse party or of another witness instead of proceeding by a simple notice to · take the deposition he may do so. The motion for the order in such case must be upon notice and must be made before the court. He must, however, make application for an order in the cases specified in section 346, ante. When the is instituted by order instead of by notice, the moving party assumes the burden of showing the propriety of the examination at the outset, whereas if the proceeding is instituted by notice, the propriety of the application is assumed and the burden of showing the impropriety thereof is deferred until the adverse party objects to the examination by means of a motion to vacate the notice and if no such objection is made the propriety of the examination stands conceded. The moving party does not have to justify the examination unless the right to it is attacked by a motion to vacate the notice or modify the same.

§ 355. The Same-Necessary Papers. 

The necessary papers are a notice of motion and an affidavit or affidavits. If, however, the order is sought before the action is commenced there is, of course, no notice of motion." The notice of motion is the usual one. It should specify the matters which would be contained in the notice if the proceeding were instituted by notice instead of by order except that the time when and the place where the examination is sought may be left for determination upon the motion and fixed by the order. 78 The affidavit should set out facts showing that statutory grounds exist for taking the deposition."5 What these facts will be depends upon the ground relied on. If the person to be examined is a party or a person in the nature of a party,' the facts required must bring the case within the rules for the examination of such person as stated in sections 337 to 344, ante. If the person to be examined is of the second class" then the facts showing statutory grounds would be that such person is sick or about to depart from the state, or lives more than one hundred miles from the court room, etc.78 Then besides there are occasional statutory requirements that appear indirectly. The following matters should be considered in preparing the affidavit in order to satisfy the requirements of the statute and rules. a. The affidavit should state in all cases whether the person to be examined is a resident or a non-resident, and if a resident, it should show his residence or the place where he has an office for the regular transaction of business in person. 

This is necessary since a resident cannot be compelled to attend for examination outside these counties."⁹ b. The affidavit must show in all cases that the testimony sought is material and necessary for the party making the application in the prosecution or defense of the action.80 

This will require that the affidavit disclose the issues either by attaching copies of the pleadings or better, since the pleadings are deemed before the court,¹ by summarizing their contents and it will also require that facts be shown from which it may reasonably be inferred that the witness whose testi-

§ 357. Proceedings After the Order is Obtained. 

The proceedings after the order is obtained are substantially the same as in the case where the proceeding was instituted by notice, instead of by order.04 

Instead of serving upon the person who is to take the testimony a copy of the notice, he must be given a certified copy of the order.

Again, if books and papers are produced pursuant to the order, the examining party is not entitled to a general inspection of such books and papers. Such an inspection can be obtained only under sections 324 to 328 of the Civil Practice Act.95

In the proceeding now under consideration, the examination of the witness is had in connection with such books and papers to show that the books contain relevant entries, and then the inspection of these entries preparatory to offering them in evidence is had, and finally they may be offered in evidence. The inspection here provided for is a limited inspection and not a general one which is provided for elsewhere.98 

§ 358. Testimony Taken by Stipulation. 

The parties to an action may stipulate in writing that the testimony of a witness may be taken by deposition within or without the state or that an order be entered for that purpose. § 359. Testimony Taken by Commission. 

If testimony is to be taken within the state the examination is upon oral questions unless the parties stipulate otherwise. 

If testimony is to be taken without the state, the court in which the action is pending or may be brought, upon motion, may order the taking of testimony wholly or partly by written interrogatories to be settled as prescribed by the rules."" 

If on a motion to take the testimony of a particular person it appears that such person is outside the state' and the court may order the testimony to be taken by written interrogatories, it may do so in two ways. It may order that a commission issue to a person designated in the order² or it may order that the testimony be taken before an authorized officer or person. The persons so authorized are a judicial officer, notary public or an attorney of the state where the witness is. § 361. Procedure After Order for the Issuance of a Commission. 

After the order is entered and a copy thereof served on the adverse party, the attorney in whose behalf the order for the commission was entered prepares written questions or interrogatories which he desires to propound to the witness and serves them upon his adversary within ten days after the entry of the order. The adverse party then prepares, if he chooses to do so, cross interrogatories which he serves upon the attorney who procured the order within ten days after he has received the interrogatories. If a party shall fail to serve cross interrogatories within the time limited

Either party within two days after the service of the cross interrogatories, or within two days after the time to serve cross interrogatories has expired may serve on the adverse party a notice of not less than two nor more than ten days of the settlement of the interrogatories and cross interrogatories before a justice of the court or a county judge. If neither party serves such a notice within the time limited therefor, the interrogatories and cross interrogatories are to be deemed settled as served, and shall be allowed without notice. However, in city court actions, the interrogatories must be settled by a justice of the court. The settlement of the interrogatories is merely for the purpose of authentication and it is not a decision that they are competent or material."

§ 362. The Suppression of a Deposition. 

It is not an infrequent happening that the answers to the cross interrogatories found on the return of a commission are evasive or otherwise framed so as to deprive a party of his right to cross-examine a witness. If such is the case or if any other unfair or overreaching conduct is practiced by either party in respect to the deposition, the court may, on an application made by the party aggrieved and on notice to the adverse party, make an order suppressing the deposition.10 Such motion should be made before the trial if opportunity therefor exists," otherwise the objection thereto is deemed waived.¹ 12 

§ 363. Depositions Taken Within the State For Use Without the State. 

Other states and foreign countries often have need for the testimony of persons who are within the state of New York. In such cases the reverse of the process which has just been described in connection with the issuance of commissions on interrogatories takes place. In such cases the trial proceeds in some other country or state and someone within the state of New York is designated as commissioner to take the deposition of a witness located here and procure his answers to interrogatories and cross-interrogatories and return the deposition when it is complete to the state from which it is issued. Witnesses in this state may be subpoenaed to appear before such a commissioner and give their testimony. The subpoena is then issued out of the 

Supreme Court or by the county court or by a judge of either court on the presentation of a verified petition stating the situation.13 The subpoena should not issue unless the papers in support of the petition show that a real issue of fact is pending in the foreign court.18a

§ 364. Admissions-In General. 

It has been shown that an allegation in a complaint or counterclaim is admitted if the adverse party does not deny the allegation in his answer or reply. In addition to such admissions, which may be called voluntary admissions, the

Civil Practice Act provides for two kinds of admissions which are not strictly voluntary but are to a limited degree enforced. 

These are (a) admissions of the genuineness of papers, and (b) admissions of facts. 14 

§ 365. Admissions of the Genuineness of Papers. 

"The attorney for a party, at any time before the trial, may exhibit to the attorney for the adverse party, a paper material to the action and request a written admission of its genuineness. If the admission is not given within four days after the request, and the paper is proved or admitted on the trial, the expenses incurred by the party exhibiting it in order to prove its genuineness must be ascertained at the trial and paid by the party refusing the admission, whatever the result of the cause, matter or issue may be; unless it appears to the satisfaction of the court that there was a good reason for the refusal. § 368. The Same-Effect of. 

"Any admission made in pursuance of such notice is to be deemed to be made only for the purposes of the particular cause, matter or issue, and not as an admission to be used against the party on any other occasion or in favor of any person other than the party giving the notice. 1724 The admission, it will be seen, is limited to the particular action and may not be used apart from the action. An admission made for the purpose of one trial is not necessarily binding on a trial of a different action.25 

§ 369. The Same — Withdrawal of. 

"The court or a judge at any time may allow any party to amend or withdraw any admission so made on such terms as may be just. 926 An application must be made to the court or a judge thereof for leave to withdraw an admission once made and

In England it is provided that "any party may at any stage of a cause or matter where admissions of fact have been made, either on the pleading, or otherwise, apply to the court or a judge for such judgment or order as upon such admissions he may be entitled to, without waiting for the determination of any other question between the parties; and the court or a judge may, upon such application, make such order, or give such judgment, as the court or judge may think just." 

(English Practice, Order 32, Rule 4.) 

There is a somewhat corresponding provision in § 476 of the New York 

Civil Practice Act and it would seem that the intention of the legislature was that these admissions may be used at or before the trial. They may, it would seem, be used on a motion under 

Rules 112 and 113 for judgment on the pleadings. The use of them on such motion is no more outside the purview of a motion for judgment on the pleadings than is the use of a bill of particulars on such motion. In both cases matters outside the pleadings are resorted to on the determination of the motion.

In England the power to give judgment under this rule is a discretionary power and judgment under it cannot be claimed as a matter of right. Mel lor v. Sidebottom, (1877) 5 Ch. D.

§ 370. Discovery and Inspection. 

The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to discovery and inspections have been substantially retained by the Practice Act," but the right to a discovery and inspection has been materially enlarged. By the Practice Act new machinery has been provided by means of which a discovery of the documents in the possession of the adverse party and an inspection of them may be had. Sections 327 and 328 

of the Civil Practice Act and Rules 140-142 of the Rules of 

Civil Practice are new.

They have been taken from the Eng lish Practice, Order 31, Rules 15 and 19A. These extensions in the law with relation to discovery and inspection are discussed in the following sections. The application for a discovery and inspection is made by order to show cause.30 

§ 371. Distinction Between Discovery and Inspection and the Examination of the Adverse Party Before Trial or Pleading. 

The aim of the remedy known as discovery and inspection is to permit a party to inspect the books, papers and documents or articles of property belonging to his adversary in order that he may procure therefrom evidence to enable him to frame his pleading or to prove his cause. 

The general purpose is the same as in the case of an examination before trial of the adverse party but the two remedies should not be confused.31

It is true that on an examination of the adverse party before trial or pleading he may by order be required to pro duce his books, papers and documents and such books, papers and documents may be offered and received in evidence.32 

27. See Hollis v. Burton, (1892) 3 

Ch. 226. 

28. Sections 803-809 inclusive; General Rules of Practice, 14, 15 and 16. 

29. Sections 324–326 inclusive; Rules of Civil Practice, 140, 141 and 142. 

30. Rule 140. 

31. Proceedings for the discovery of documents and property are distinct from examinations of parties and wit nesses (New York City Car Advertis ing Co. v. Regensburg & Sons, Inc., 205 App. Div. 705; 200 N. Y. S. 152;

Singer v. National Gum & Mica Co., 

211 App. Div. 758; 208 N. Y. S. 1;

Citizens Trust Co. v. Prescott & Son,

In a proper case an order may now direct both an examination before trial and a discovery and inspection (Fey v. Wisser, 206 App. Div. 520; 202 N. 

Y. S. 30). 

32. Civil Practice Act, § 296; § 355g,

It is likewise true that now under the Practice Act the books, papers and documents of an adverse party may be ordered to be produced on an examination of an individual defendant as well as on an examination of a corporation defendant.33 31 On an examination of the adverse party before pleading or trial, however, the books, papers and documents produced are merely an incident to the examination of the adverse party. Their inspection and perusal is not the primary objective of the examiner. The party producing them retains control over them although he can be required to answer questions relating to their contents. In the cases cited in the notes reference is made to the necessity of serving a subpoena duces tecum to secure the production of the books at the time and place where the examination is ordered. This was the law under the Code except as to defendants who were corporations, joint stock or other unincorporated associations; but it is not required under the Practice Act since the order directing the examination may now require their production. On such examination the examining party may inspect any book or paper which the witness says contains entries relating to the subject-matter of the examination, but his inspection is limited to the specific entries or accounts to which reference is made by the witness, 36 and the examiner is not permitted to roam at will through the books, papers and documents thus produced.37 

Where a discovery and inspection is allowed, a more general perusal of the books, papers and documents is contemplated. Such perusal is had not as an incident to any examination, but as an end in itself. ante. On an examination before trial, however, the court in its discretion usually limits the examiner to offering in evidence only such books or documents or portions thereof as have refreshed the recollection of the witness.
