§ 372. Cases Where Discovery and Inspection Is Allowed. 

"A court of record, other than a justices' court in a city, by order, may compel a party to an action pending therein to produce and discover, or to give to the other party, an inspection and copy, or permission to take a copy or photograph of a book, document, or other paper, or to make discovery of any article or property, in his possession or under his control, relating to the merits of the action, or of the defense therein. The procedure for obtaining such order shall be regulated by rules. ''38

The cases where discovery and inspection has been ordered under the above statute may be classified under four headings. "First. Where the books, papers and documents are the foundation of the action, as for instance a written contract which a party desires but of which he has no copy. "Second. Where the applicant has a special interest in the books, papers and documents, such as that of a partner or that of one occupying a confidential relation.''40 "Third. Where the books, papers and documents contain evidence which the party desires to enable him to prepare his pleading or to prepare for trial, but in which he has no special interest. ''¹¹ 1939 

Fourth. Where the inspection sought does not relate to books, papers and documents but to an article of property the character of which may furnish evidence which will enable the party to prepare his pleading or to prepare for trial, 38. § 373. Limitations on Discovery and Inspection.** 

45 In the first two groups above enumerated an inspection is usually granted as a matter of course. The same is true of the fourth group. With relation to the third group, however, care has to be exercised lest in procuring the inspection of the books, papers and documents for the applicant an unwarranted invasion and search into the private affairs of the adverse party may not result. Care is taken in such cases to limit the inspection to the part or parts of the books, papers and documents where the information sought and to which a party is entitled may be found, and the order for the discovery and inspection is so circumscribed that the remedy may not be used for ulterior purposes. In Hoag v. Ulster and 

Delaware R. R. Co. for example, plaintiff was suing to recover for injuries resulting in death. The deceased had been a freight engineer in the employ of the defendant. His engine collided with a passenger engine of the defendant and he was killed. An order for discovery and inspection was allowed so far as it gave an inspection of the orders given to the engineers and conductors of both engines, but was disallowed with respect to an inspection and discovery of the bills of lading and manifests showing the points from which and to which the freight on the train was consigned. In fact most of the litigation under the sections of the Code which the above quoted section of the Practice Act replaces, is concerned with the limitation of orders for inspection and discovery which are too broad.""

A premature application for an inspection and discovery will be denied on the same principle that a premature examination before trial is denied. In an action for an accounting, for example, an inspection of the accounts will not be ordered until it is determined at the trial whether or not the plaintiff secures a judgment directing an accounting." But in a law suit where the plaintiff claims a share in the profits of the defendant's business as part of his compensation for his services, the application is not premature, since the issues are all determined in one action.48

The documents sought to be inspected must themselves be evidence. It is not enough that the documents suggest or may furnish a clue to evidence. Therefore, a discovery of the reports made by railroad employees to their employer will not be ordered unless they are of such a character that they may be introduced in evidence in support of the issues involved in the action."" 

§ 374. Other Remedies Introduced by the Practice Act. 

In addition to the remedy just discussed, two new remedies have been provided by the Practice Act, which may be invoked by a party to procure a discovery and inspection of documents in the possession of his adversary.

The first is effected by means of a notice merely. The second is a proceeding in aid of discovery, its object being to compel a party to disclose the location of specific documents so that discovery and inspection may be had if the disclosure shows the documents to be in the possession of the adverse party. These two remedies are taken from the 

English Practice Law and will be discussed in order.

§ 375. Discovery and Inspection on Notice. 

If a party to an action in his pleadings or affidavits refers to any document, the adverse party may by a simple notice in writing compel the party to produce such document for inspection and allow copies thereof to be made. If he refuses he cannot thereafter put any such document in evidence in such action unless he satisfies the court that his refusal was justified or excusable.50

The word "document" alone is used in the statute providing this remedy while in the section of the Practice Act which perpetuates the Code provisions" the words "book, document or other paper" are used. A recent decision, however, says "there is a document wherever there is a writing or printing capable of being read, no matter what the material may be upon which it is impressed or inscribed. """2 

It is to be observed that the document must be referred to in a pleading or affidavit. In English practice this would include a bill of particulars also.5 53 54 The document need not be one that is specifically described in the pleading or affidavit. It is sufficient if it is described or referred to in a general manner. The statute only applies to documents that are referred to and does not apply to copies of documents that are referred to though they may be in the possession of the party.55 Hence if a party refers to letters written by himself he cannot be ordered to produce copies of them.

While the word "document" as construed in England would include books, yet if a party refers to business books he will be required to produce only the entries referred to.56

§ 376. The Same - Form of Notices and Enforcement of Penalty. 

No form of notice is prescribed by the New York law. 

The following would answer the requirements of the statute: 

(Title.) 

TAKE NOTICE that the (plaintiff or defendant) requires you to produce for his inspection the following documents referred to in your pleadings or affidavits, namely, Dated, To: (Signature and address for the adverse party.)

The statute does not in terms require the party who receives such a notice to make any response thereto. It only prescribes the penalty for his refusal to produce the document. In England the party to whom such a notice is given is required promptly to give a notice when the documents in question may be inspected at the office of his attorney and prescribes a form of such notice given in response.58 If he refuses to give an inspection of the documents, it is for him to justify his refusal.59 It is not necessary for the party giving the notice to take any further steps in the matter." Under the Practice Act, there is no provision which specifically places the burden upon the party to whom the notice is given to furnish opportunity to inspect the documents. In case of his refusal, however, it would seem that before the penalty prescribed by section 327 of the act can be enforced, a preclusion order would have to be obtained in like manner as where a demand for a copy of an account is ignored.¹

§ 377. Disclosure by Party in Aid of Discovery. 

"The court, on the application of any party to an action, also may make an order requiring any other party to state by affidavit whether any one or more specific documents, to be specified in the application, is or are, or has or have at any time been in his possession or power, and if not then in his possession, when he parted with the same, and what has become. thereof. Such application shall be made upon an affidavit stating that in the belief of the deponent the party against whom the application is made has, or has at some time had, in his possession or power, the document or documents specified in the application, and that they relate to the matters in question in the case or matter, or to some of them.63 (Signature and address.)

The English cases construing the equivalent of this section, i. e. English Practice Order 31, hold that under this section no order can be made unless the applicant can name and specify certain specific documents and the order must be confined to those particular documents.6*

It is also held that the particular document or documents must be named and specified so that it or they can be identified.65

§ 378. Practice in Connection with Disclosure in Aid of Discovery or Inspection on Notice. 

A cursory reading of the two new sections of the Practice Act just discussed" might tend to make one believe that they should be used together. It might seem that an effective method for using them in conjunction would be to make the application for a disclosure first. This would require the adverse party to make an affidavit in which reference would be made to the specific documents to which the order for the disclosure related. Once having made such an affidavit the party might seem immediately to come under the operation of the section for discovery or inspection on notice. The next step would then be for the party to give the notice to produce such documents for an inspection, if they were within the control of the adverse party under section 327. It has been

71. English Practice, Order 31, Rule 

12, provides: “Any party may without filing any affidavit apply to the court or a judge for an order directing any other party to any cause or matter to make discovery on oath of the documents which are or have been in his possession or power relating to any matter in question therein. On the hearing of such application the court or judge may either refuse or adjourn the same, if satisfied that such discovery is not necessary, or not necessary at that stage of the cause or matter, or make such order, either generally or limited to certain classes of documents, as may in their or its discretion be thought fit, provided that discovery shall not be ordered when and so far as the court or judge shall be of opinion that it is not necessary either for disposing freely of the cause or matter or for saving costs."

It will be seen, therefore, that in 

English practice a disclosure may be ordered by the court without any affidavit on the part of the person who applies therefor. This order once obtained requires the adverse party to give an affidavit of the documents which are or have been in his possession or power relating to any matter in question in the cause. Such affidavit is called an affidavit of documents under Rule 12.

The practice in England is to get an order for an affidavit of documents under Rule 12 and on the affidavit being filed to give the notice to produce in the form referred to in Rule 16 which corresponds with the notice referred to in the text in connection with 376, ante, and thus procure an inspection of the documents in the possession of the adverse party in connection with the cause and make copies of them. § 379. In General. 

1 When the cause is actually called for trial and both parties are present and ready the trial proceeds. This chapter is devoted to jury trials. Trials by the court and by a referee will be treated in the following chapter. The principal purpose of the trial, irrespective of the tribunal before which it is conducted, is to determine the issues of fact presented by the pleadings. Issues of law, however, to a limited extent are determined at the trial. It has been shown that defendant's objection to a complaint on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action is not waived by him, though he fail to make a motion for the dismissal of the complaint on that ground. Likewise it has been shown that the plaintiff does not waive his objections to a counterclaim or affirmative defense contained in an answerby failing to make a motion for a judgment on the counterclaim or to strike out the defense. Such objections may be raised at the trial. If they are raised at the trial by motion, an issue of law is presented and must be determined by the court. Sufficiency of an affirmative defense contained in a reply may likewise be raised at the trial, and if so, the question presented is one of law. 3 The issues of fact which are to be here determined may arise by denials in the answer or reply of material allegations of the complaint or counterclaim or by allegations of new matter contained in the answer or reply which are deemed to

§ 381. Procuring the Jury-In General. 

The next step in the trial is the impanelling of the jury and the administration of the oath to them. Jurors will be found in the courtroom or the Jurors' Assembly Room for that purpose. The clerk of the court draws the names of the jurors present by lot until twelve prospective jurors fill the jury box. When the jury box is filled the jurors are examined to see if they are free from bias or prejudice or are otherwise fit. 

There are many situations which will disqualify a juror.¹º He may be related to a party or have formed an opinion in the case which will require evidence to remove, or he may be biased in one way or another with respect to the character of the action, and so on. The examination of the jurors by counsel is intended to afford opportunity for the disclosure to the court of the facts regarding such matters.

11. Civil Practice Act, § 453. This form of challenge is now seldom used.

Downey v. Finucane, 205 N. Y. 251, five persons were sued together for fraud and deceit for issuing a false stock prospectus. Each defendant claimed that he was entitled to six peremptory challenges. The court held 

Then there may be a challenge to the polls which is a challenge of individual jurymen. A peremptory challenge is one for which no cause need be assigned. A party in a civil action can have six such challenges in a court of record and three in a court not of record.12

A challenge for cause may be either for principal cause or to the favor. The distinction is one of law. The same ground may be used for a challenge under either heading. If you challenge for principal cause you practically assert that the condition of the juror is such that the legal presumption is that he would not try the case fairly, while if you challenge him to the favor your challenge amounts to an assertion that there is a suspicion - not a presumption now that the juror will be biased in the trial of the case. If, for example, a juror is related to a party within the sixth degree, there is a legal presumption that such juror will be biased and he may be challenged for principal cause.13 But if the relationship was in the tenth degree instead of the sixth, the challenge for principal cause should be overruled, but a challenge to the favor would be a proper challenge. If the court overruled the challenge when the juror was related to a party within the sixth degree it has committed reversible error, but otherwise on the ground that the answers of all the defendants were identical and that each defendant had a common interest. Cf. Code of Crim. 

Proc. 360 "Where there are several defendants, they must unite in their challenges."

§383. The Same-Limitations on Questions Asked of Prospective Jurymen.

§ 386. Preliminary Motions. 

At this stage of the trial it is possible for the parties to make certain motions. The action may not require that any motion be made, but when the circumstances warrant it there are eight possible motions which may be made after the jury is sworn in. These motions are: (a) The defendant may move to dismiss the complaint for failure to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. 

You will recall this as one of the grounds upon which a motion to dismiss the complaint might have been made."7 This motion you will also recall survived the failure of the defendant to make it promptly after the complaint was served and it may be availed of at the trial.28

Thus where an action was begun by the owner of the fee of a piece of land against a certain defendant as commissioner of the land office of the state and against another defendant as comptroller of the state for the cancellation of the record of certain tax sales, a motion was made at the trial to dismiss the complaint for insufficiency because the suit was one against the state and the state cannot be sued without its consent. The Court of Appeals held that the motion should have been granted.29 The motion was denied at the trial and the Appellate Division unanimously affirmed the decision of the court below, but the exception taken to the ruling survived all this and prevailed in the Court of Appeals.30 (b) The motion to dismiss may be made on the ground that the court has not jurisdiction of the subject of the action. 

This objection to a complaint likewise survives a failure to move on this ground for the dismissal of the complaint before answering, and may be made here.³¹ 31

§ 387. Opening Addresses to the Jury. 

If the case is still pending and not disposed of by the preliminary motions discussed in the last section, the next step in the progress of the trial is the opening addresses of counsel to the jury. Unless otherwise directed by the court, the opening addresses of both plaintiff and defendant are made at this time." This is considered an important matter in the trial principally because the person who addresses the jury first at this time has the right to address the jury last at the close of the case. 

§ 388. The Same Who Shall Open the Case to the Jury. 

42 The general rule is that the party holding the affirmative of the first issue raised by the pleadings is entitled as a matter of right to open the case to the jury at this time and to close it after the evidence is in. This will be the plaintiff if any material fact necessary to his recovery on any of the causes of action which he may have alleged in his complaint must be proved. If, for example, the action is on a promissory note and the answer admits the execution of the note but denies delivery thereof the plaintiff has the affirmative of the issue on the delivery and consequently the right to open. If, however, the delivery also is admitted and all that the answer contains is the affirmative defense of usury the affirmative of that issue must be sustained by the defendant and he, in such case, is entitled to open and close to the jury. The test is whether without any proof the plaintiff upon the pleadings is entitled to recover upon all the causes of action alleged in the complaint. If he is, the defendant has the right to open. The answer admitted the allegations of the complaint with respect to the note but set up as a defense that the note in question was given in payment for certain canal boats which the defendant purchased of the plaintiff under a warranty that they would be of a certain quality and capacity and that the boats were not as represented. The answer also contained a counterclaim for wages alleged to be due defendant for services rendered the plaintiff. The defendant further answering denied each and every allegation in the complaint not thereinbefore admitted. Plaintiff replied denying the new matter in the answer. Each party at the trial claimed the right to open to the jury. The cause of action on the note was admitted. The burden of proving the breach of warranty was on the defendant but plaintiff showed that the denial in the answer put in issue allegations of the complaint with reference to the overdraft and he had the affirmative of that issue. 

To meet this situation the defendant offered to admit the allegations of the complaint with respect to 'the overdraft. 

The court, however, ruled that the admission of the defendant at the trial did not change the issues which were framed by the pleadings. An admission is to be treated as evidence and the plaintiff was given the right to open to the jury. Had the defendant moved for leave to amend his answer by striking out his denials relating to the overdraft and got leave to amend the same, the ruling would have been different. If the party who has the right to open does not claim that right but allows the adverse party to open to the jury, he has waived it and cannot at the close of the trial claim the right to close to the jury.15

§ 390. Motion to Dismiss After Opening Address of Counsel. 

A complaint may be good as a pleading but the opening address of counsel may show that the evidence upon which counsel relies to support the pleading is wholly inadequate for that purpose. In such case a motion may be made based on the pleading and the opening remarks of counsel to dismiss the complaint. Such would be the case where a cause of action stated is conclusively defeated by something interposed by way of defense and clearly admitted as a fact. In 

Sweeney v. O'Dwyer the complaint in an action for false imprisonment based on a warrant signed by defendant who was a judge alleged: 48 "3. That the said warrant was void. 

4. That the said warrant appeared void on its face. 

5. That defendant knew at the time when he signed and allowed the said warrant that he had no power to sign or allow it and that it was void, and the arrest and imprisonment thereunder would be illegal.' 99 This sounds ominous enough and the complaint as such was good, but the counsel in his opening disclosed that the facts relied on to support this complaint were simply that an order which should have been signed by a judge but which was signed by the court was held good by the defendant and as plaintiff had disobeyed it the defendant had issued a warrant to punish plaintiff for contempt and had put him in jail. 

Here the opening of counsel disclosed merely an erroneous determination by the court in a matter over which the court had jurisdiction and this did not sustain the allegations of the complaint.50

§ 391. Putting in the Evidence — In General. 

When we were considering pleadings we learned the distinction between evidentiary and ultimate facts and that the pleadings should contain ultimate facts but not evidentiary ones.52 At the trial ultimate facts, except the opinion of experts, are as objectionable as evidentiary ones are in pleadings. We shall assume, for convenience, that the plaintiff opens to the jury and puts in his evidence first. 

§ 392. The Same - Manner of Introducing Evidence-Three Kinds of Evidence. 

From the point of view of the trial lawyer, evidence may be divided somewhat differently than it is divided in the study of evidence. We may classify evidence here from the point of view of the manner of introducing it. Some evidence may be introduced without the presence of any witness upon the witness stand whatever, while other evidence requires a witness under oath before it can be gotten into the case. As an example of evidence which requires no witness we may cite a certified copy of a public document or an exemplified copy of the record of a judicial proceeding in a foreign country.55

Evidence of this character may be introduced without the aid of any witness whatever. The seal or seals in such cases are sufficient proof of the authenticity of the document without further identification. Formerly nearly all manner of evidence required the presence of a witness upon the stand before it could be used but now certain statutes dispense with the necessity of calling a witness to lay a foundation for the introduction of the evidence outlined in them. 

The statutes in question and the documents, the introduction of which without witnesses is authorized by them are briefly described in the notes."

For the most part, however, evidentiary facts are introduced through the mouths of witnesses who are called to the stand, sworn57 and asked questions and the answers to these questions are the evidence relied upon to prove the allegations in the pleadings. Witnesses are thus used to testify to evidentiary facts which are within their own knowledge and which may be pertinent to prove the allegations of the complaint.

They may also be used to identify documents which would not be admissible of their own weight because not identified with the case but which nevertheless, if a proper foundation for their introduction be made by the testimony of witnesses, may be introduced and the facts contained in them made use of to establish the allegations of the pleadings. As examples of such documents may be cited ordinary letters, contracts, notes, books of foreign corporations,58 the records of meetings, copies of statutes of any state and many other documents and records.1 In such cases the witness must be shown the letter or note or other document and asked if he knows the signature on the note or letter and whose signature it is or otherwise connect it with the case on trial before the party may offer it in evidence. This is called laying the foundation and the manner of laying the foundation must be ascertained from the law of evidence. 59 Thus, we have, from the point of view of the trial lawyer, three classes of evidentiary facts: (a) documents requiring no witnesses for their introduction, (b) documents which have to be identified and the foundation laid by oral testimony before they can be introduced, and (c) oral statements of witnesses. population by the director of the census, and a certified record of a bill of sale, mortgage, hypothecation or conveyance of a vessel recorded in the office of the collector of customs. § 393. How Plaintiff Puts in His Case. 

Plaintiff may proceed as his discretion dictates on the introduction of the evidence which he has. Let us assume for convenience that he proceeds with the documentary evidence first-that which requires no witnesses. It is introduced by stating merely "I offer in evidence an exemplified copy of the judgment roll," etc., indicating the particular document which he wishes to introduce. That document is thereupon received in evidence if it is material and relevant and satisfies the rules of evidence applicable to the case, and the plaintiff may read it to the jury if he chooses to do so or leave it for future reference.

Plaintiff may then call his first witness who will be sworn by the clerk, and counsel will proceed to examine him. Only one counsel can examine or cross-examine a witness.62 The questions asked must conform to the general rules of evidence, that is, they must be relevant, competent, material, etc. 

It is not our province to point out these rules. Our work begins where the knowledge of evidence ends. To question a witness properly presupposes that the examiner knows the rules of evidence and seeks by his questions to elicit from the witness only such facts as are admissible under these rules.68

The witness, unless he is an expert, must generally be asked questions that will draw from him things he has seen or heard or felt or tasted or otherwise experienced through his senses. The best approach by way of questions is to ask if he was present at a particular place at a particular time, and after he says he was, ask him who else was present, and

If this approach is not followed the examiner will often be found asking leading questions, that is, questions which state in the form of a question what the witness will testify to and make it possible for the witness simply to say "yes" or "no" while the examining attorney carries on the story. 

This is likely to draw an objection from the opposing counsel and the court may in its discretion sustain such objection. 

Such questions are permissible on cross-examination but not on direct. 

§ 394. The Same — Objections to Questions - In General. 

It is the duty of the counsel examining a witness to ask questions which harmonize with the rules of evidence. If the opposing counsel thinks that the question is improper he has the right to object to the question and obtain from the court a ruling on the objection. Prior to the amendment of section 446 of the Civil Practice Act in 1934, it was customary for the party against whom the court ruled then to except to the ruling in order to save his right to review the ruling on appeal. 65 This formality is now unnecessary." a. Time of making objection. The objection should be made as soon as the question is asked and before it is answered. Counsel is not permitted to wait until he finds out whether the answer of the witness will be favorable or unfavorable to him before he objects to the question. If, however, the answer of the witness is cunningly made so quickly that opportunity is not afforded for an intelligent objection until after it is made, the objection will be timely and the answer will be stricken out."7 66 

64. Zilver v. Graves Co., 106 App.

A party for example, who objects to a question on the ground that it calls for evidence that is incompetent, immaterial and irrelevant has included within his protest almost any specific

465 objection that can be found in the whole subject of evidence since the three headings found in the objection constitute the main headings under which that subject is treated. A specific objection points out what the objector believes to be the precise vice in the question. The objection that the question calls for hearsay evidence or for a conclusion of the witness or that the testimony sought is outside the issues raised by the pleadings illustrates objections of a specific nature.

It is common in works on trials to find the statement that objections should be specific and not general, but the writer has not found such advice good in his experience. Objections are made not only to confine the testimony within proper bounds and prevent the jury from hearing improper matter that might influence them, but also to preserve a record for appeal purposes. A careful trial lawyer is seldom so sure of his jury that he may not desire to lay a foundation for an appeal if one becomes necessary, or to lessen his adversary's chances on an appeal if an appeal is taken by him. Now for appeal purposes, a general objection sustained is the best possible state of the record for the objecting party, and a general objection overruled is the worst possible state of the record for the objecting party. An attorney always likes to have his own general objection sustained and those of his adversary overruled. The reason is that a general objection which is sustained will not be disturbed on appeal if any specific ground of objection exists which would make the question improper. For example in Tooley v. Bacon it was alleged in the answer that the plaintiff placed the funds and property in controversy in the hands of the intestate for the purpose of delaying and defrauding his creditors. After the defendant had given some evidence tending to sustain this defense the plaintiff, as a witness in his own behalf, was asked if he had put any money in the hands of the intestate for the purpose and with the intent to delay or defraud his creditors. Counsel for plaintiff objected generally and the referee sustained the objection. Defendant excepted and on appeal urged this ruling of the court as a ground for reversal. The specific ground of objection to such testimony that the witness was incompetent to answer the question under section 829 of the Code of Civil Procedure (C. P. A., sec. 347), Bacon being dead, was not made. The court said:

JURY TRIALS 

"That no ground was specified is however immaterial now. When evidence is excluded upon a mere general objection the ruling will be upheld, if any ground in fact existed for the exclusion. It will be assumed, in the absence of any request by the opposing party or the court to make the objection definite, that it was understood and that the ruling was placed upon the right ground. ' '88 

And a general objection overruled will not be disturbed on appeal unless there is no ground on which the evidence sought might be justified no matter in what form the question might be put."⁹ 69 

Again in Donohue v. Brooklyn & Queens R. R. Co." the action was for personal injuries. On the trial plaintiff's sister was put on the stand and asked "Has your sister (the plaintiff) continued to complain of pains in her head ever since the accident up to the present day?" The objection was general; was overruled and defendant excepted. 

The answer was "Yes, sir." The verdict was for the plaintiff. Defendant on appeal urges his exception to the ruling as ground for reversal. Here the evidence elicited could not possibly be gotten into the record properly, no matter in what form the question was put for it consisted of a declaration of a party made subsequent to the accident and it was not made to a physician in course of treatment. The appellate court reversed here although the objection was general, since no recasting of the question would have enabled plaintiff to put in the evidence.

The reason for the rulings given above on general objections is that the party asking the question should be given the opportunity of meeting an objection to his question by reframing the question or by moving to amend his pleading or by other means, and a general objection does not afford him this opportunity. Therefore, if the court overrules the general objection the attorney who interposed it cannot complain if the appellate court will strain to sustain that ruling since if he had apprised his adversary of the specific objection which he had in mind the examining attorney might, by laying the necessary foundation or refram-

§ 395. Striking Out Testimony. 

Sometimes evidence gets into the record which is improper but to which no objection could have been taken when first given. This may happen in six ways: (a) The question may be proper but the witness' answer is not in fact an answer to the question asked but something which the witness volunteers and which is not admissible under the rules of evidence. 

In such case counsel may move to strike out the answer as irresponsive." (b) Where evidence is properly admitted when offered but subsequent testimony shows that the evidence should never have been admitted, as where a witness is asked to state what he saw at a particular time and place and he describes a situation as if he had seen it but later in answer to some other question, often on cross-examination, it is disclosed that all that the witness described was hearsay and that he never saw at all the things which he vividly described." (c) Where the answer to an improper question is given before an objection could reasonably be interposed thereto, a motion to strike out the answer is proper." (d)

§ 396. Cross-examination - Purposes of. 

After a party is through with the witness and has elicited from him all that he expects to prove by him, the witness is then turned over to the opposing attorney who proceeds to cross-examine him. There are three distinct purposes to be effected by cross-examination. The first of these is to weaken or destroy the effect upon the jury of the direct testimony of the witness by bringing out facts which will modify the force of the direct testimony of the witness. When prosecuting this purpose, there is no necessary effort at all to discredit the witness or the jurors' belief in his truthfulness. The second purpose of cross-examination has for its object the discrediting of the witness and the development in the jurors' minds of doubt as to his veracity. The third purpose is to lay the foundation for the impeachment of the witness. 84

The right to cross-examine in this connection is absolute. (b) to impeach the witness. This is within the court's discretion and ordinarily the crossexaminer can ask a witness whether he has done anything degrading or immoral during his entire lifetime.

Suppose that a witness had testified on direct examination regarding a street car accident in an action for personal injuries and had told with vividness the occurrences connected with the accident. The simple question on cross-examination "where were you when you witnessed the accident" might develop that he was too far away from the scene for accurate observation, or that the traffic in the street prevented him from getting anything but glimpses of the incidents while they were actually happening. This would illustrate the first purpose in cross-examination. As an illustration of the second purpose in cross-examining a witness, the question "were you ever in state's prison" is suggestive enough. 

§ 397. The Same-Right Absolute as to the First Purpose. 

If the cross-examination is directed to the first purpose alone, then the right to cross-examine along this line is absolute. If the court interferes with it and prevents such crossexamination it has committed reversible error. In Morley v. Castors plaintiff's attorney was cross-examining Mr. 

Charles S. Morley, one of the original defendants, and it became apparent to defendant's attorney that Mr. Morley's evidence was at variance with the defense pleaded by him. 

The defendant, therefore, moved to amend his defense so as to make it conform to the evidence which Mr. Morley had given. Plaintiff's attorney pleaded surprise and the court granted an adjournment to enable the defendant's attorney to make a motion at special term to amend his pleading. 

Before the case came up again Mr. Morley had died and the defendant sought to have read on the second trial the evidence that Mr. Morley had given at the first trial. The trial judge granted this but on appeal it was held error. The reasoning was that the plaintiff had an absolute right to cross-examine Morley; that he was deprived of this right by 

Morley's death; that the testimony of Morley on the first trial did not contain a complete cross-examination; that to admit the evidence on the second trial would be in effect to dispense with cross-examination of a material witness, which crossexamination was not aimed at the character of the witness but related solely to the facts in issue. 87

The Same - Prosecution of Second Purpose Discretionary with the Court. 88 But the right to cross-examine a witness is confined within the boundaries prescribed by the subject matter of the direct examination. Just as long as your examination pertains to the subject matter of the direct examination, your right is absolute; but when you seek to elicit new matter from the witness not connected with the subject matter of his direct examination, the right dies and the discretion of the judge is born and takes its place. The court usually permits cross-examination in prosecution of the second purpose to a limited degree but may stop it in its discretion, and unless it palpably abuses this discretion, its exercise of it would not be ground for reversing a decision. § 399. The Third Purpose of Cross-examination. 

The third purpose of cross-examination is to lay the foundation for specific impeachment. In case a witness has made statements which contradict the testimony he has given on his direct examination, he must be asked whether in substance and effect he did not at a given time and place in the presence of or to a person or persons specified, make the alleged contradictory statements. If he denies that he did, the foundation is laid for the testimony of the persons to whom such statements were made and they may testify. They could not testify to the alleged statements, however, unless the foundation described above were made. In case the contradictory statements of the witness were made in writing, the paper must be shown or read to the witness to lay the foundation for its introduction.96 

§ 400. Re-direct Examination. 

As the absolute right to cross-examine is confined within the scope of the direct examination, so the re-direct examination must be confined within the scope of the cross-examination. Its purpose is to bring out fully and completely any matter which was raised on the cross-examination; to explain seemingly contradictory statements or otherwise to minimize the effect of the cross-examination." If part of a conversation is brought out on cross-examination the remainder of it may be brought out on re-direct examination.98 If upon crossexamination it is brought out that the witness has been convicted of a crime, it may be shown on re-direct examination what the character of the crime was upon which the conviction was obtained. The credibility of a witness is affected less by conviction for some crimes than by conviction for others.99

JURY TRIALS § 401. The Rest of the Plaintiff's Case. 

After a party has finished with his first witness he puts on any other witnesses that he may have. They are similarly dealt with and thus the matter of putting in proof continues until all of the proof is in on the part of the plaintiff. It should be observed here that the plaintiff must put in all of his case before he rests. He cannot put in merely enough evidence to make out a prima facie case and reserve the rest for use if it seems to him to be needed after his opponent has put in the evidence which he has. The plaintiff must put in his whole case when he has the opportunity. He has no right to reopen his case after his opponent has closed his.¹ 

§ 402. The Withdrawal of a Juror. 

Sometimes, before the close of the plaintiff's case or at the close of it, or later, the plaintiff may discover that his proof is unsatisfactory. If this condition is caused without fault on his part and he is surprised by the situation which confronts him, he may move for the withdrawal of a juror. The failure of a material witness who has been subpoenaed, to attend, sickness of a party or a witness, or other similar situations which cannot well be anticipated, furnish illustrations for the use of this motion. If the court grants the motion, the jury is discharged and the case is for the time being terminated. 

When it comes on again for trial it will be necessary to go through with the proof from the beginning again. The withdrawal of a juror is not a matter of right but rests in the discretion of the court. As a condition of exercising its discretion the court may impose costs or other terms. This motion is equivalent to a voluntary submission to non-suit, and it cannot be resorted to after the case has been submitted to the jury.* 2 3

475 § 403.

Defendant's Motion for a Non-suit at the End of Plaintiff's 

Case. 

At the close of the plaintiff's case the defendant may make a motion to dismiss the complaint for failure of proof. This is a motion for a non-suit. It is based upon the theory that the plaintiff's proofs are insufficient to establish the cause of action alleged in his complaint. The complaint may stand against a motion to dismiss it at the outset for the reason that on such a motion every allegation of fact contained in the complaint is deemed to be true; but when the plaintiff has put in his evidence it may turn out that such evidence does not sustain every material allegation of fact in the complaint and in such case the motion for a non-suit should be granted. 

On this motion the evidence put in by the plaintiff is assumed to be true and plaintiff must have in addition, the advantage of every reasonable inference that can be drawn from the facts proven. 

On this motion the defendant's counsel must point out specifically the grounds upon which he relies, indicating the particular allegation or allegations of the complaint which he insists have not been proved by the evidence. A general motion to dismiss will be of no avail, except where the failure of proof is so manifest that he who runs may read it, and is not correctible, in which case a general motion will suffice." 

§ 404. The Same Variances and Amendments at the Trial. 

The reason for the requirement that the defendant must on his motion for a non-suit, point out the specific allegation of the complaint which he claims has not been proved, is that the plaintiff must have an opportunity to correct a discrepancy between his pleadings and his proof which he might be able to obviate if it were called to his attention. § 406. The Defendant's Case. 

The defendant's course follows the lines of the plaintiff's course. He must prove his defense or counterclaim as the plaintiff proved his cause of action. The rules for examination and cross-examination of witnesses are the same, the motion for the withdrawal of a juror is the same and the manner of dealing with a variance and a failure of proof is the same.15 

§ 407. Rebuttal. 

When the defendant has put in his whole case, the plaintiff may then put in rebuttal evidence. This is evidence which rebuts or contradicts the evidence produced by the defendant. 

The plaintiff cannot, however, open up his case and put in evidence tending to support the allegations of his complaint.16

JURY TRIALS § 408. Motions at the Close of the Evidence. 

After all the evidence on both sides has been put in, certain further motions may be made. There are two possible motions at this time. The motion for a non-suit may be renewed by the defendant and a motion may be made by either party for the direction of a verdict.

It is necessary for the defendant, who has moved for a non-suit at the close of the plaintiff's evidence, to renew his motion after all the evidence has been introduced on both sides. If he fails to renew his motion for a non-suit at this time, the motion which he made on the close of the plaintiff's evidence is waived." In resisting this motion, there is available to the plaintiff not only the evidence which was introduced up to the time that the plaintiff rested, but in addition, any evidence favorable to him which was put in while the defendant was putting in his evidence.18 'The court may reserve decision on this motion until after the jury's verdict is rendered," but an exception to the court's action in reserving its decision is sufficient and will bring up for review defendant's right to have the motion granted." 20 If this motion is denied and defendant move for the direction of a verdict, it is not sufficient for the defendant merely to take an exception to the ruling if he desires to have the case submitted to a jury. It is necessary in addition for him to move affirmatively that the case be submitted to the jury on the facts. The necessity for this affirmative motion here is the same as where a motion is made by defendant for a direction of a verdict, and to avoid duplication of discussion, reference is made to the succeeding sections for the reasoning.21

§ 409. Motions for Direction of a Verdict. 

The other motion which may be made at this time is the motion for the direction of a verdict. The meaning of the motion is that the moving party asks the trial judge to direct the jury to bring in a verdict in his favor. At first blush it would seem that such motion would be an invasion by the court of the constitutional right of the parties in a common law action to a jury trial, but a closer examination of the situation reveals that there is no invasion by the court upon this right. The province of the jury is to determine disputed questions of fact. The function of the judge is to pass upon the law of the case and all issues of law must be decided by him. If there is no dispute on the facts, there is nothing for the jury to do in the case. When the facts are admitted, the rights of the parties is a question of law to be determined by the court. If a group of facts tend to establish the existence of a contract between the parties and these facts are not contradicted by other facts, it is the province of the judge to decide whether there is or is not a contract between the parties. It is not the province of the jury to pass upon that matter at all.22 The same is true in tort actions as well as contract actions. If there is no dispute between the parties regarding the facts which one party claims show negligence on the part of the defendant and the other party claims do not show it, the jury has no function to perform and the question is one of law for the court.23 

In such cases where the only question to be determined is what is the legal effect of admitted facts, the jury has no function whatever to perform, and if the plaintiff or defendant thinks that the undisputed facts entitle him as a matter of law to a decision in his favor, he may make the motion for a direction of a verdict in his favor. Either party may make the motion and it often happens that both parties make the motion. If there is any serious dispute, however, with reference to any material issue of fact, the question is one 

22. Edison Elec. Ill. Co. v. Thacher, 229 N. Y. 172; U. S. Rubber Co. v.

Under the Code it was the law that a motion for a direction of a verdict could not properly be granted if any material fact was in dispute, even though the evidence on one side vastly preponderated over that on the other. It was held that the court might set aside a verdict in such case if one were rendered against a party whose evidence vastly preponderated, but that it was not permissible for the court to direct a verdict in such case. A dispute had to be resolved by the jury. If the court felt that the jury's verdict was against the weight of evidence, it could set aside the verdict and order a new trial. It could not direct a verdict because that would involve determination of the disputed fact by the court. The most it could do would be to set aside the verdict and let a new jury on a re-trial pass on the disputed fact.25 The Civil Practice Act provides, however, that "the Judge may direct a verdict when he would set aside a contrary verdict as against the weight of evidence. ''20

The result of this amendment in the Civil Practice Act is that there are two circumstances now which authorize the court to direct the verdict: first, where there is no dispute with regard to the facts and, second, where there is a dispute with regard to the facts but the evidence on one side so preponderates that the court would be warranted in setting aside a verdict against that side if the jury brought in such a verdict.27

N. Y. 259, 262; Gordon v. Ashley, 191 N. Y. 186.)

The result of setting aside a verdict and the result of directing one are widely different *. In the one case there is a retrial. In the other the judgment is final

JURY TRIALS § 410. The Same The Procedure with Reference to Motions to 

Direct a Verdict or for a Non-suit at the Close of the 

Evidence. 

There are three situations which may arise on the motions to direct a verdict: (a) either party may move for the direction of a verdict and the motion be granted, (b) either party may make the motion and the motion be denied and (c) both of the parties may make the motion and the motion of one be granted and the other denied. 

In the first case, after the motion is made and granted, it is sufficient for the party against whom the verdict is directed to except to the judge's determination of the motion or to rest content with the automatic exception given to him by section 446 of the Civil Practice Act. In the latter event, he should be sure that he says nothing which might indicate express acquiescence in the court's ruling. 824 In the second case, it is necessary for the party who made the motion, not only to register an exception to the trial judge's denial of his motion (either expressly or by silence), but he must in addition, affirmatively move that the case go to the jury on the facts. He does this by saying "I affirmatively move that the case be submitted to the jury on the facts." In the third case, where both parties move for a direction of the verdict it is likewise necessary for the party whose motion is denied to move affirmatively that the case go to the jury on the facts.34

The reason for this procedure is that when a party makes his motion for a direction of a verdict or where the defendant

If both parties move for a direction of a verdict it is held that such motions amount to a temporary submission of the whole case to the trial judge and the decision of the judge in favor of one or the other of the parties would have the same effect exactly as if the jury had found a verdict for such party after the case had been submitted to it.35 In such case, if the judge finds any dispute in the record with regard to the facts he may resolve it, as he is constituted by the motions of the parties the judge of both the law and the facts. If either party does not wish to make the judge the tribunal for the determination of any disputed facts that may be found in the case, it is necessary for him to move affirmatively as above stated or at the least to argue that the case be submitted to the jury on the facts. Such an affirmative motion relieves him of the effect of the position he placed himself in by his motion to direct a verdict and enables him to raise on appeal the question as to whether the verdict rendered is or is not contrary to the weight of evidence."6

§ 411. The Same-In Unliquidated Damage Cases. 

It would be difficult to direct a verdict for the plaintiff in personal injury actions or other actions where the damages are unliquidated, since the court would have to assess the damages to determine the amount for which the verdict should be directed. To meet situations such as this, when a motion is made to non-suit plaintiff or for the direction of a verdict, the court pending the decision of such motion may submit any question of fact raised by the pleadings to the jury or require the jury to assess the damage. After the jury shall have rendered a special verdict upon such submission or shall have assessed the damage the court may then pass upon the motion for a non-suit or direct such general verdict as either party may be entitled to.37 

The practice here indicated is most used in unliquidated damage cases but it is not limited to such cases by section 459 of the Civil Practice Act. It applies to all common law actions.

§ 414. The Judge's Charge. 

The next step in the progress of the action is the judge's charge to the jury. The main function of a judge's charge is to advise the jury with respect to the principles of law applicable to the case. Ordinarily it covers the following matters: 

First, it points out the issues of fact raised by the pleadings. 

This is important for it is upon these issues that the jury is to pass. Second, it advises the jury that the party holding the affirmative of these issues must establish them by a fair preponderance of evidence. Where the court charges the jury that an issue must be proved "by absolutely disinterested witnesses and established by the clearest and most convincing evidence" it has committed error, for "in civil cases a plaintiff is never required to prove his case by more than a preponderance of evidence."45 Much milder statements of the preponderance rule than the above have been held bad." 

Third, the judge may recapitulate the evidence grouping it with relation to the issues," but in doing so he must exercise care lest he usurp the function of the jury by drawing inferences from the evidence which may not be the only reasonable ones. When a judge says of a witness that he either told the truth or perjured himself, he commits error for the witness

Fourth, the judge instructs the jury on the points of law that may aid them in determining the facts. A brief excerpt from a particular charge will make this clear: 51 "It is very important in this case for you to give careful heed to what the law of this State is as applicable to this case so that you may not go astray. The law does not hold that in a contract of this kind, because there is a delay in payment or a delay in the delivery of goods, that that would necessarily give the other party a right to abrogate the contract at once. That is not the law. If that was the law, there would be nothing to submit to you, because it is here conceded there was a delay in the payments, and if that was the law, I would simply be obliged to dismiss the plaintiff's complaint and throw his claim out of court.

I shall presently read to you the text of the law applicable to this case so that you may understand it and fully grasp its meaning. 

Before reading it, however, let me state that, after understanding the law, it is your duty to consider the facts to which the law is applicable. The burden of proof is upon the plaintiff to establish every fact that it is necessary for him to establish by a fair preponderance of evidence. That means by evidence that is weightier than that of the other side. ''52

The part of the charge referring to the law applicable to the case under trial will, of course, differ with the case, and the above excerpt is intended merely to illustrate the character of this part of the judge's work.

§ 415. Exceptions to the Charge.5 

If, when the judge charges the jury on the law, the attorney for either side believes that the judge has incorrectly stated the law on any point, he may take an exception to the charge. Ordinarily, unless an exception is taken to a charge, no ground for reversal exists, even though the charge contained reversible error.54 The exception to a charge must point out the specific objection which the counsel has to the particular part of the charge which he deems to be erroneous.55 The reason for this rule is that the court must be given an opportunity to correct any erroneous charge which he makes, and if the error is not specifically pointed out to him he will not be given such opportunity. One exception to a particular point is enough, and though the court may repeat the objectionable part of the charge in substance or effect, it is not necessary for the counsel to repeat his exception.º 

Exceptions to a charge are not automatic, even under the newly amended section 446 of the Civil Practice Act, which 

"Sec. 446. Exceptions during the trial.

An exception shall be deemed to have been taken by the party adversely affected to every ruling of the court or of the referee during the trial, unless the said party shall expressly indicate that he acquiesces in the ruling. Exception to the charge given to the jury by the court and to the granting of requests to charge made by the adversary, shall not be deemed to have been taken unless expressly noted before the jury have rendered their verdict."

It is apparently permissible under this statute to register exceptions to the charge after the jury has retired, provided only that no verdict has yet been rendered.

It is necessary for the attorneys to make requests, for the judge is not obligated to charge further than his own judgment approves. If the charge is highly prejudicial, a motion for leave to withdraw a juror may be made. 

§ 417. Deliberation of the Jury. 

After the judge has charged the jury and any exceptions to the charge and requests to charge have been made, the jury retire to the jury room and deliberate. The old rule used to be that they would have to stay in the jury room without "meat or drink, fire or candle " until they reached a verdict. This rule has been relaxed. The essential thing regarding the jury's work is that they should arrive at a verdict by deliberation, not by flipping a coin or by adding together the sums which each juror thought should be the measure of plaintiff's recovery and dividing the aggregate by twelve. A verdict reached by the latter method is sometimes called a quotient verdict. Verdicts thus reached violate the rule that the verdict should be reached by deliberation, but while the jurymen may be punished for such conduct, the verdict cannot be set aside on the affidavits of jurymen showing the improper manner of reaching it, because public policy requires that jurors be not allowed as a general rule to impeach their own verdict.1

The jury may take, if the court permits, any paper which has been introduced in evidence into the jury room for examination and consideration when they are arriving at a verdict. If, after a reasonable time, in the discretion of the trial judge, the jury cannot agree upon a verdict unanimously, 60. E. Heller & Bro. v. Continental 

Mills, 196 App. Div. 7; 187 N. Y. Supp. 511. 

61. McDonald v. Pless et al., 238 U. 

S. 264, and cases cited. A verdict which is clearly a compromise is reversible error. Breymann v. Morris, 202 App. Div. 454; 195 N. Y. 6. 441.

1 they may be discharged. In such case the action must be re-tried by a new jury." 

§ 418. Kinds of Verdicts. 

If the jurors arrive at a decision, in their deliberations, such decision is called a verdict. Verdicts are of two kinds, general and special. In a general verdict the jury pronounces generally in favor of the plaintiff or the defendant. 

The form is "we find for the plaintiff for $. 

or 

we find for the defendant." A special verdict is one by which the jury finds the facts only, leaving the court to determine which party is entitled to judgment thereon."³ 

The court may direct and compel the jury to find a special verdict as well as a general verdict, or to bring in answers to one or more specific questions of fact which it submits,** even in common law actions, where heretofore it was entirely discretionary with the jury to bring in a special or a general verdict as it saw fit.65 In an action for damages for the refusal of the defendant to deliver goods under a contract requiring deliveries in instalments, where the defendant justified its refusal to deliver on the ground that prior deliveries had not been paid for as required by the contract, the trial judge submitted the following questions to the jury and required them to bring in a special verdict answering them: "1. Was the breach of contract on the part of the plaintiff so material as to justify the defendant in refusing to proceed further in delivering the goods under the contract on and after May 29th, 1919? 

2. Irrespective of your answer to the former question, and assuming that the plaintiff would be entitled to recover, what is the amount of the damages which the plaintiff is entitled to receive?''66 

The special verdict must be in writing; and must be filed with the clerk and entered in the minutes. If the jury bring in both a general and special verdict, the latter controls in case of inconsistency between them, and in case of ambiguity an appellant is entitled to the most advantageous construction of the inconsistent findings. § 419. Motions After the Jury's Verdict is Rendered. 

Three motions may be made at this time by the losing party. They are a. Where the party has taken one or more exceptions during the trial (or, presumably, where exceptions are deemed to have been taken by law), a motion may be made that these exceptions be heard in the first instance by the court to which an appeal could be taken from a final judgment in the action, and that the entry of the judgment upon the jury's verdict be suspended in the meantime." The language of the Civil Practice Act section makes this motion general. Under the Code it only applied in cases where the appeals were taken to the 

Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. If the trial judge feels doubt with respect to his rulings and the exceptions taken (or, presumably, deemed by statute to have been taken) thereon, and feels that a judgment should not be entered against the losing party until opportunity to pass upon his rulings by the appellate court has been afforded the loser, he may grant this motion, in which case a judgment cannot be entered upon the jury's verdict until the appellate court on a motion for a new trial has heard the exceptions.

§ 420. Introduction. 

A trial by the court without a jury is essentially the same as a trial by a court and jury with such modifications as the absence of the jury requires. The points of similarity and difference between jury trials and trials by the court without a jury follow.

The submission of a copy of the pleadings to the court is the same, but the procedure for procuring a jury is eliminated.2 

The preliminary motions are the same, but the opening addresses to the jury and the motion to dismiss after such opening address are modified. The court may hear from the attorneys an informal statement of their respective contentions but nothing like an opening address is usual. 

Putting in the evidence, the examination and cross-examination of witnesses, the objections to questions asked, the motions to strike out testimony and the redirect examination are the same. It should be stated in this connection, however, that as there is no jury to be affected by the testimony, the courts are much more liberal in the admission of testimony than they are in jury trial cases, although the rules of evidence are the same for both tribunals. It is assumed, however, that the court without a jury will know how to evaluate testimony which reaches it better than a jury would know. 1 There is no juror to withdraw, but the conditions which necessitated the motion for the withdrawal of a juror are as likely to present themselves in an equity action as in a law suit. Instead, therefore, of the motion for the withdrawal 

1. See § 380, ante. [ 497 ] 

2. See §§ 381-384 inclusive, ante.

TRIAL BY THE COURT OR REFEREE WITHOUT A JURY 

of a juror the proper motion where there is no jury, is for an adjournment. The rules regulating the motion to withdraw a juror are the same as those in equity cases governing the motion for an adjournment.³

The motion for a non-suit and for amendments at the trial are the same before each tribunal. At the close of the evidence, while a motion for judgment dismissing the complaint may properly be made, there can be no motion to direct the verdict since there is no jury to render a verdict. If the motion is denied, an exception is taken but it is not possible, as in the case of a jury trial, to make an affirmative motion that the case go to the jury on the facts. There is no summing up, but again the court may hear the arguments of counsel on the evidence. The judge's charge to the jury, exceptions to the charge and the requests to charge, the deliberation of the jury and everything that relates to verdicts are eliminated. There is no motion to set aside a verdict and for a new trial, nor is there a motion for a hearing in the first instance by the appellate court. 

§ 421. The Decision of the Court. 

At the end of a trial before the court without a jury, the court renders a decision which takes the place of a jury's verdict and in some measure also of the judge's charge. 

In connection with the decision, procedure exists which takes the place, in a way, of the requests to charge and exceptions to the judge's charge and his rulings on requests to charge. 

The decision is not the same as an opinion; it is a statement by the trial judge of his findings of fact and his conclusions of law with respect to the case. These findings

9. That all the remaining notes became due and were duly protested and the total amount of said notes and the judgment taken on the note of November 9, 1915, is $529.06, and defendant, W. X., is indebted to the plaintiff in said amount. 

10. That plaintiff was a creditor of the defendant, W. X., at the time of the sale of his place of business, namely, September 9, 1915, within the meaning of the Bulk Sales Act, to the amount of the notes due June 9th and September 9th, and no more. 

11. That the plaintiff was a creditor of the defendant, W. X., on and after November 23, 1915, but not within the meaning of the Bulk 

Sales Act. 

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW. 

1. That the question submitted for the court's consideration is answered in the negative. 

2. That the defendant, W. X., is entitled to a judgment dismissing the complaint herein upon the merits, with costs and disbursements. to be taxed by the clerk of this court. 

3. I direct that judgment be entered accordingly.

Dated, New York, February 7, 1917.

§ 423. Requests to Find. 

It is customary for attorneys after a trial before a court, to submit to the court at the close of the trial or within such time thereafter as may be allowed by the court, proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law. These are called

TRIAL BY THE COURT OR REFEREE WITHOUT A JURY 

Danc requests to find.18 Such requests to find take the form of a proposed decision. It is necessary that the court shall rule upon these requests by noting upon the margin, the manner in which each request has been disposed of. Such words as "found," "refused" and "found as modified," etc., indicate the marginal notations of the court upon such requests.¹9 

It is not too late to submit these requests after the decision has been filed and judgment entered thereon,20 but if submitted thereafter the findings made thereon can not be inconsistent with the findings and decree previously made and entered. 

§ 424. Filing Decision. 

The decision must be in writing and filed in the clerk's office within sixty days after the final adjournment of the term where the issue was tried.21 In the City Court, a decision need not be made unless a party requires it.22 If the decision is not filed within the time specified, either party may move at a special term for a new trial upon that ground. 

If the decision has not been filed when the motion is heard, the court must make an order for a new trial, either absolutely, or unless it is filed within a time specified in the order.23

§ 427. In General.¹ 

There are four distinct motions for a new trial. In some measure these motions overlap each other, but the motions themselves are distinct. These motions are respectively: (a) A motion on the minutes of the trial judge. (Sec. 549 

C. P. A.) (b) A motion in the appellate court for a new trial where the trial was by jury. (c) A motion at special term, and (d) A motion after the jury trial of specific questions in an equity action. (Sec. 553 C. P. A.) 

These motions will be discussed in order.

1. The Civil Practice Act has not changed the practice with respect to motions for a new trial to any appreciable extent. Such changes as [ 507 ] have been made will be noted in connection with each of the motions discussed in this chapter.

§ 428. Motion for New Trial Upon Judge's Minutes - Introduction. 

This motion was discussed in the chapter on trials by jury. 

It needs, however, a little further treatment than was given to it there. 

§ 429. The Same - When and to What Extent Applicable. 

This motion is applicable only after a trial by jury. The judge's minutes are the stenographer's record. There are two sections in the Civil Practice Act relating to this motion.³ 

The first section applies to common-law actions tried by a jury. The second section applies to equity actions where a jury trial is ordered on framed issues, and the court is bound by the verdict.

In equity actions where a jury is called in, the court is sometimes bound to follow the jury's verdict and sometimes such verdict is merely advisory and the court may disregard it if it chooses. In all equity cases where a jury trial is 

2. Judiciary Law, § 305; Rule 223. 

3. Civil Practice Act, § 549, for merly Code § 999 omitting the last sentence thereof which related to appeals from such order and substituting in the place thereof the following: "A minute of the decision of the presiding judge denying a motion for a new trial shall be made, but an order need not be entered unless the party aggrieved desires to take a separate appeal therefrom." 

This last sentence hanges the practice which formerly existed in connection with appeals from judgments and from orders denying a motion for a new trial made on the judge's minutes at the trial. The practice heretofore has been to enter an order denying the motion for a new trial, even though the motion was made at the close of the trial and denied thereat and an exception taken to the denial, and such motion, denial and exception appear in the stenographer's minutes of the trial. This last sentence of § 549 

quoted above makes unnecessary the entry of a formal order upon the denial of a motion for a new trial when the motion is made at the close of the trial itself and decided thereat. The only occasion now for the entry of an order upon the denial of a motion for a new trial made at the close of the trial is found where an appeal is to be taken from the order itself and not from the judgment entered in the action.

The other Civil Practice Act section relating to this motion is 553, formerly Code § 1003, in substance and in part. The joint legislative committee's note upon the changes made in the Code section by § 553 of the Civil Practice Act, follows: 

"Code § 1003, first sentence and first clause of second sentence, without change of substance, omitting the reference to § 970. The second clause of the second sentence is omitted; covered by general clause providing that upon motion for a new trial upon appeal an error in a ruling of a trial court must be disregarded, if a substantial right of any party shall not thereby be affected. Last sentence included in separate rule, ante.❞

ordered issues are framed for the jury to pass upon. The jury's verdict in all such cases is a special verdict. Such verdict is binding on the court where the statute gives to the parties a jury trial as a matter of right, but it is not binding on the court where it can order a jury or refuse to order one in its discretion.*

The cases where the court is bound by the jury's verdict are enumerated in section 309, ante. To illustrate, in a divorce action, where adultery is an issue the court must upon application of either party, order a jury trial; it has no discretion in the matter," and in such case the verdict of the jury is binding on the court. But in an ordinary equity case the court may, in its discretion, direct a jury trial and in that case it is not bound by its verdict. 

Now, when the court is bound by the verdict, the motion on the judge's minutes for a new trial is to be treated exactly as in a common-law action and the law stated in section 549 of the Civil Practice Act applies. In such cases, if a new trial is ordered it must be a new trial of all of the issues raised by the pleadings. But when the court is not bound to adopt the jury's verdict it may, in granting a new trial upon his minutes, grant it as to a part of the issues only and deny it as to the remainder. This explains the language used in section 553 of the Civil Practice Act. 

§ 430. The Same - Grounds for the Motion. 

The grounds for this motion are distinctly stated in sec tion 549 of the Civil Practice Act. No other grounds will lay the foundation for it."

These grounds apply to all equity actions where a jury is used as well as to actions at law.

§ 431. The Same - When the Motion Must Be Made and the Procedure. 

The motion must be made at the same term of the court at which the trial is had.' It has already been pointed out in the chapter on trials that the motion may be made at the close of the trial. It may, however, be made afterward on a notice of motion provided it is made at the same term of court. The grounds relied on should be distinctly stated whichever way it is made, and it is the practice in making the motion not only to specify the particular grounds relied upon, but to state generally that the motion is made upon all the grounds stated in section 549 of the Civil Practice Act. 

If the motion is not made at the close of the trial, an affidavit and notice of motion, or an affidavit and order to show cause may be used in making the motion. Since the motion must be made before the trial judge, the need for the affidavit is not very apparent. As, however, the motion must be made at the same term at which the trial took place, an order to show cause is sometimes necessary. Then too, in an order to show cause a stay may be had of the entry of judgment and of all proceedings. The affidavit is made by the attorney and states the facts of the trial and how it terminated, and the grounds of the motion and the reasons for asking for an order to show cause and that no previous application for the relief sought has been made. 

The order to show cause also should recite the grounds and contain the provision for a stay of proceedings pending the determination of the motion.

When the motion is determined, whether it grants or refuses a new trial, the order must specify the grounds on which the motion was made and the grounds on which it was decided, except when the motion was made on exceptions taken during the trial, or, presumably, on exceptions deemed taken during the trial.8

In the progress of a trial many exceptions are taken (or deemed taken by statute) to the admission or exclusion of evidence and to the rulings of the court on the various motions made. It sometimes happens that the court is doubtful of the legality of its rulings and would be glad to have the court to which an appeal from the judgment would be taken pass on these rulings before the judgment is entered. The motion now under consideration provides the means for accomplishing this end. 

§ 433. The Same Where Trial Was by Jury. 

The motion for a new trial in the court to which an appeal would be taken from a final judgment in the action where the trial was by jury is sometimes called a motion for a new trial on exceptions to be heard in the first instance in the appellate court. The phrase "in the first instance" is the significant thing here. It is used in the Civil Practice Act sections and in Rule 220 in connection with this motion. 

Hearing exceptions "in the first instance" simply means hearing them before the entry of judgment. The exceptions are ordinarily heard on the appeal from the judgment where
