§ 435. The Same - After the Entry of the Order. 

The order, as has been said, entitles the party who applied therefor to make a motion in the appellate court for a new trial on the exceptions taken or deemed taken. It is obvious that the appellate court cannot pass on the exceptions during the trial without the record of the trial or such part of it as will enable it intelligently to pass upon the exceptions to the trial judge's rulings. Whether the whole record or a part of it only will be required depends upon the nature of the exceptions which are to be reviewed. If the exceptions to be reviewed relate merely to the admission or rejection of evidence, the whole record would not be necessary to enable the appellate court to pass upon such exceptions. All that would be required would be such part of the record as will disclose the basis for the rulings of the trial judge to which the exceptions relate. On the other hand, if the exception is to a ruling of the court in denying a motion for a direction of a verdict or for a non-suit at the close of all the evidence, the appellate court would be quite unable to determine whether the ruling of the trial judge was correct or incorrect unless the entire record of the trial was presented on the motion for a new trial. Rule 

220 provides that the order which directs the exceptions to be heard in the first instance in the appellate court: "entitles the party applying therefor, to move in the appellate division for a new trial, after due notice, and on a case made and settled containing the exceptions and so much other matter, only, as may be necessary or appropriate to enable the appellate division to decide the motion.

If only a portion of the record of the trial is used on the motion and not the entire record, it is common to refer to the portion of the record used as a bill of exceptions. If 17

the entire record of the trial below is required it is called 16 a case.

The papers which are used on this motion in the appellate court must be printed. They consist of the pleadings, the minutes of the trial or such part of them as is necessary, and the order sending the case to the appellate court. There shall be prefixed to them a statement showing the time of the beginning of the action or proceeding and of the service of the respective pleadings, the names of the original parties in full, and any change in parties if such has taken place. 

There shall be added to them the opinion of the court below or an affidavit that no opinion was given, or if given, that a copy could not be procured. These papers shall constitute the record in the appellate court." 

The adverse party must be given an opportunity to propose amendments to the case or bill of exceptions. He may want more of the record printed in connection with an exception. The practice is for the party making the motion in the appellate court to serve upon his adversary a proposed case within the time provided by the rules.18 The adverse party has ten days thereafter within which to propose amendments to such case or bill of exceptions. If there is a dispute between them, either party may on four days' notice submit the proposed case and the proposed amendments to the trial judge for settlement of the same. He may allow or disallow the amendments proposed and the resulting case or bill of exceptions is said to be settled." 

This is filed in the clerk's office and the party making the motion causes the same to be printed, and unless the parties stipulate that the papers so printed are true copies of the original, the clerk must certify that they are true copies by comparing them with the original on file.20 

Regulations are made in the rules also for the printing

The procedure with reference to making the case or a bill of exceptions on this motion for a new trial in the appellate court is the same as it is when an appeal is taken from the judgment.22

It must not be forgotten that this is a motion for a new trial and all that the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court or other appellate court can do is either to grant the motion for a new trial or deny it.23

If the motion is granted, the appellate court by order directs that the verdict be set aside and a new trial be granted. If the motion is denied, the judgment may be entered on the verdict as if the motion for a new trial had not been made; but not until after the entry of the order of the appellate court denying the motion and the service on the attorney for the adverse party of a copy thereof with notice of entry.24 § 436. Motion for a New Trial in the Appellate Court After Inter locutory Judgment Is Entered. 

A motion for a new trial in the appellate court may also be had after a trial by the court, but in such case it is limited to actions wherein an interloctuory judgment is entered.25

An interlocutory judgment is one that does not finally dispose of the case but requires something further to be done before final judgment can be entered. An action to partition real property results first, if successful, in a decree or judgment directing a sale of the premises and provides for the application of the proceeds. A final judgment is entered after the sale is had confirming the referee's report thereon. The same thing is true in accounting actions. The first judgment, which is interlocutory, simply directs that the defendant account and the final judgment is entered on the report of the referee if one is appointed to take the account. 

21. Rules 235, 236. 

22. Rule 230. See Chapter XXXVII. 

23. Civil Practice Act, § 550; Mat thews v. American Cent. Ins. Co., 154 

N. Y. 449. 

24. Civil Practice Act, § 499, Martin v. Platt, 131 N. Y. 641. 

25. Civil Practice Act, § 551, Cramp v. Dady, 153 App. Div. 913; 138 N. Y.

S. 1112.

Now, in this class of actions a motion for a new trial may be made after the entry of the interlocutory judgment in the court to which an appeal from the judgment might be taken.26 The motion is made upon exceptions, express or implied." Whether a case or a bill of exceptions, or a case containing exceptions, is necessary depends upon the same principles that govern the motion for a new trial to be heard in the first instance by the appellate court after a jury trial. 

The proceedings with relation to notice of argument in the appellate court, the making of a case, and printing and filing the papers are governed by the same rules as on that motion.

The appellate court may grant a new trial or deny it, but on this motion even if the appellate court deny the motion, it may nevertheless modify the interlocutory judgment to make it conform to the law.28 Where the trial is by the court without a jury, there is no constitutional inhibition upon the modification of the decree of the lower court, and the appellate court therefore is not limited to granting or denying the motion for a new trial, but may modify the judgment of the court below so that a new trial will be unnecessary. 

§ 437. Motion for a New Trial to Be Made at Special Term.29 

The motion for a new trial at special term overlaps the motion for a new trial on the judge's minutes. It may be made for any of the grounds upon which such a motion may be made if made at the same term, but it may also be made on other grounds. The additional grounds which will lay the foundation for a motion for a new trial at special term are the following:

§ 441. The Same Failure to File a Decision. 

Where a trial takes place before the court it is necessary that the court should file its decision within sixty days after the final adjournment of the term at which the trial took place."2 

If the court fails so to file its decision, either party may make a motion for a new trial upon the ground at special term, and if, when the motion comes on to be heard the decision has not been filed, it is obligatory upon the court to make an order for a new trial either absolutely or unless the decision is filed within the time specified in the order.¹³

For example, if the motion is made on newly discovered evidence it should be made promptly after such evidence is discovered. § 443. Motions for a New Trial After the Trial of Specific Questions in an Equity Action. 

If in an equity action a jury is called in to aid in the determination of the issues of fact and some of said issues are submitted to the jury for determination, the trial judge may in his discretion direct a new trial as to some of the framed issues and refuse it as to others.51 In such case if there are remaining issues to be tried by the court, a motion for a new trial as to the issues which were specifically referred to the jury and tried by it may be made at the term where the remaining issues of fact are tried, and if all of the issues were referred to the jury a motion for a new trial may be made at the term where a motion for final judgment is made on the jury's findings.52 

If specific questions were referred to a referee instead of to a jury for determination, a motion for a new trial of those issues may be made at any time before the hearing of a motion for final judgment or the trial of the remaining issues of fact is had.58

§ 444. Defined and Classified. 

A judgment is the determination of the rights of the parties in an action.¹

Judgments are variously classified. 

1. There are interlocutory and final judgments. An interlocutory judgment determines some rights in the action but does not finally end the suit. Such judgments are only found in equity actions or in statutory actions of an equitable nature. It may, for instance, direct a conveyance of real estate and an accounting of the rents, leaving open until after the accounting is had the direction for final relief. It may direct a sale of real property by a referee and await the report of the referee before finally directing the distribution of the proceeds. The final judgment is the complete determination of the rights of the parties and leaves nothing further to be passed upon. 

2. Judgments are also classified into judgments in personam and in rem. The distinction between these two classes is given in chapter VII.³ 

3. Judgments are also either declaratory or coercive. A declaratory judgment rests content with the declaration of the rights of the parties which is final and binding as such, but does not undertake to compel the parties to perform the obligations resulting from the declaration. A coercive judgment carries into effect the determination of the rights of the parties by authorizing the use of force to place the parties in possession of them, or restrains interference with rights which have been determined.* 

4. Judgments are also classified into judgments by default and judgments after trial. From the point of view adopted 

1. Civil Practice Act, § 472. 

2. Civil Practice Act, § 472. 

3. See §§ 107 and 108. 

4. See chap. XXVIII, post, for illustration.

in this chapter, this is the important practical classification for consideration. This classification needs no definition but it is important because of the difference in the procedure necessary to enter and file such judgments. 

It happens not infrequently that there are several defendants and some of them default while others appear and stand trial. Provision is made in the Civil Practice Act for taking judgment against or for one or more plaintiffs or defendants and if the action is one in which the defendants are severally liable a judgment may be taken on the default of one or more and the action continued as to the others. It is important to note, however, that in actions at law there can be but one judgment for one action and before a judgment is entered against one defendant the action should be severed, otherwise the judgment entered against one will bar the further prosecution of the action against the others." 

5. There are also judgments by confession and judgments on submitted facts.

§ 446. The Same - Explanation of the Forms. 

No particular form for a judgment is prescribed in the Civil Practice Act. Generally speaking a judgment shall be entered in such form as may be required by the nature of the case and by the recovery or relief awarded; it shall refer to the verdict, decision or report that authorizes it, and state its result; but it shall not set out the provisions thereof, nor of the pleadings nor other papers in its recitals. 

In uncontested cases the facts upon which the jurisdiction depends must be stated.15 

Like an order, it should begin with a title or special term caption depending upon whether a court directs its entry or its entry is directed by a judge of the court, or made without direction by the clerk pursuant to law. Then follow the recitals which state such part of the preceding history of the case as authorizes its entry under the law. In uncontested cases this will require the recital of the jurisdictional facts, but in cases where there has been a trial the important facts to be recited are the verdict, the decision or the referee's report. The recitals in the judgment resemble, in a measure, the recitals in an order. Finally there comes the directory part of the judgment which states the rights declared or the coercive relief granted. It is signed by the clerk.106 The judgment need not be signed by the judge, and his signature is no part of it. "It is only where an interlocutory judgment is rendered with a direction that the final judgment be settled by the court or referee, that the signature of the judge or referee to the final judgment is required. ""17

§ 447. Judgments by Default Classes of. 

There are two classes of default judgments. The first class may be entered by the clerk without application to the court. The second class requires an application to the court and a direction from the court before the clerk can enter such judgments. A direction from the court is made by an order or a decision.20 When there is more than one defendant in an action at law and one or more but not all of the defendants is in default, care must be taken, if judgment is to be entered against some but not all of the defendants, that the action be severed before the entry of judgment otherwise the judgment will bar the prosecution of the action against the remaining defendants.21 

§ 448. Default Judgments Which the Clerk May Enter. 

To enable the clerk to enter judgment without an application to the court the following prerequisites must exist: 

1st. The complaint must demand judgment for a sum of money only. 

2nd. The action must be on contract. 

3rd. The sum demanded must be fixed by the terms of the contract or capable of being ascertained by computation only.22 

4th. There must have been personal service of the summons or its equivalent. Its equivalent is a notice of appearance.23 

5th. A complaint or a notice stating the sum of money for which judgment will be taken in case of default must have been served with the summons.24

6th. The defendant must have made default in appearing or in pleading.25

§ 449. The Same - Procedure Before the Clerk. 

The clerk is a ministerial officer. He must have before him proof of the existence of all of the prerequisites enumerated in the last section sufficient to satisfy the requirements of the statute before he can enter the judgment. The procedure before the clerk therefore consists merely in furnishing this proof.

Proof of those facts except the amount of the judgment is supplied (a) In case defendant has not appeared, by an affidavit of the service of the summons and of a copy of the complaint or the notice and an affidavit that the defendant has not appeared; and (b) In case defendant has appeared, by affidavit of service of the summons or of the appearance only and also an affidavit of defendant's default.27 

Proof of the amount of the judgment is supplied: (a) By the verified complaint, if there is one, for defendant's failure to answer admits both plaintiff's right of recovery and the amount28 stated in the complaint, and (b) If the complaint is not verified, or if a notice only was served with the summons the clerk must assess the amount of the judgment. This is done by an oral examination of the plaintiff under oath or by means of other competent proof, e. g. a verified complaint. In case the action is on an instrument for the payment of money the clerk may make the assessment by computing the amount due upon the instrument.29

§ 450. The Same - Taxation of Costs. 

81 Plaintiff in such cases is entitled to costs and the amount thereof must also be ascertained by the clerk, added to plaintiff's claim and included in the judgment. In case the default is in appearance and the defendant is, therefore, entitled to no notice, plaintiff should prepare a statement of his claim including the costs32 and submit it to the clerk with a proposed judgment. The clerk will see that the statement of costs conforms to the statute and will include the total thereof in the judgment. If the defendant has appeared, a bill of costs should be made out in advance and served upon the attorney for the defendant with notice of the time when the clerk will tax such costs. Two days' notice is required if the attorneys reside or have their offices in the same city, otherwise five days' notice is required. The clerk will enter the judgment taxing the costs and include them without such notice where a defendant has appeared, but in that event the plaintiff must serve upon the defendant's attorney a copy of the bill of costs as they were taxed by the clerk, together with a notice of retaxation, similar to the notice of taxation, and on the return of the notice of retaxation, if the amount of the costs as taxed by the clerk is excessive it must be reduced and the judgment must be corrected correspondingly." 83

Where any of the prerequisites enumerated in section 448, ante, are wanting, application must be made before the court for judgment in case of default. It will be convenient to classify such default cases into those where the summons was personally served while some or all of the other prerequisites are wanting, and those where the summons was served otherwise than personally. 

§ 452. The Same - Where An Application is Made.35 

In any county where a separate special term for the granting of motions only or for the transaction of ex parte business is regularly held, as for example in New York and Kings counties, the application shall be made to such special term as the local rules may provide.86

In counties not falling within such description, the application may be made at any special or trial term. If the defendant appear but default in pleading, notice must be given to him of the applications and in New York county the application would be brought on before Special Term, Part I. If the default was in appearing, it would come on before Special Term, Part II.89 Rule 191 requires the application to be made to the court but the Civil Practice Act permits an application in such cases to a judge unless one or more defendants have appeared and one or more have not, in which case the application, in the absence of consent, must be made to the court.40

§ 455. Default Judgments Where the Defendant Is an Infant. 

No matter what the character of the action may be, or whether the judgment is taken before the clerk or before the court, if the defendant is an infant and has made default, the judgment cannot be entered against him until twenty days have expired after the appointment of a guardian ad litem for him.62 

§ 456. Judgment by Confession. In General.03 

"Judgments are daily entered in our courts without process, declaration or appearance, and without the intervention of the court or even an attorney and without proof of any authority from the defendant except that inferred from his signature to the statement. 1164 This is possible by means of a simple method known as judgment by confession. All that is necessary is a written statement signed and verified by the defendant setting forth the amount, nature and consideration of the liability, and authorizing the entry of judgment therefor.65 Upon filing this statement, judgment may be entered before the clerk of the court; and such judgment has all the force and effect of a judgment in an action."7

§ 457. The Same - The Statement. 

"Prior to the Code, the usual mode of obtaining judgment by confession was by bond and warrant of attorney. The bond was counted upon in the record, and the judgment was upon that, as the ground of indebtedness:''73 

But this quickly led to "Fraudulent practices by debtors to shield their property, by creating fictitious liens upon it by means of judgments confessed to confidential friends. ''74

And so, in order to protect creditors of the defendant against such a fraudulent combination of the parties to the judgment, a provision was inserted in the Code, and is now contained in the Civil Practice Act, requiring the defendant to make, sign, and verify a statement as to the debt or liability." § 459. Entry and Enforcement of Judgment. 

One need not wait until the liability is accrued before entering judgment upon such a confession, but may do so immediately, or at any time within three years after the statement is verified. But a judgment can not be entered thereupon after the defendant's death. Armed with the statement and a form of judgment for the amount confessed, one may go to

JUDGMENTS AND INCIDENTAL PRACTICE RELATING THERETO. 

the county clerk of the county of which the defendant was a resident at the time of making such statement, and thereupon the clerk must enter a judgment for such sum. Costs must be taxed to the amount of fifteen dollars, and disbursements.82 

If the sum, for which judgment is confessed, does not exceed three thousand dollars, and interest from the time of making the statement, and if the defendant at the time of making such statement was a resident of the City of New York, a city court judgment thereon may be entered in like manner before the clerk of the city court, if one chooses.83 The judgment may be docketed and enforced against property, in the same manner and with the same effect as a judgment in an action in that court, "and each provision of law relating to a judgment in an action and the proceedings subsequent thereto apply to a judgment thus taken. ""84

Although judgment may be entered in this manner upon amounts not yet due, execution may be issued only for the collection of the sum which has become due. "The execution must be in the form prescribed by law for an execution upon a judgment for the full amount recovered; but the person whose name is subscribed to it must indorse thereupon a direction to the sheriff to collect only the sum due, stating the amount thereof, with interest thereon, and the costs of the judgment. *

When further sum becomes due, an execution in like manner, may be issued for the collection thereof; and successive executions may be issued as further sums become due.' '85

If, in disregard of this provision, the execution is endorsed with a direction to the sheriff to collect more than the amount actually due, a subsequent execution creditor, since his lien might be thereby impaired, may have it set aside in so far as it directs the sheriff to collect anything in excess of the sum presently due. 80

"Notwithstanding the issuing and collection of such an execution, the judgment shall remain as security for the sum or sums to become due after the execution is issued. 9987

§ 460. Judgment upon Submission of Agreed Facts-In General. 

In some controversies, there is no dispute concerning the facts, but the question about which the parties differ is as to a legal right. As early as 1848, a statutory remedy was provided by which questions of law in such cases could be decided and the rights of the parties finally determined without litigation.º⁹

The parties may submit the controversy to the court upon the agreed facts; when the requisite papers are filed, the controversy becomes an action, is tried by the court, and judgment rendered therein. Thus the delay and trouble incident to preparing and serving legal process and formal pleadings are avoided.90 

§ 461. The Same Who May Submit. 

Any party of full age and of contractual capacity may take advantage of this procedure.91 No board or officer may submit a controversy to the courts which might result in a money judgment against the state; for such judgment would be ineffective inasmuch as no action may be brought against the state directly or indirectly save by its consent." 

§ 462. The Same What Controversies May Be Submitted. 

A controversy in order to be thus submitted, must be "real" and such as "might be the subject of an action.''⁹³ 

This proceeding can not be used as a means of obtaining the opinion of the court upon a mooted question of law, even though the answer thereto might be a guide to future action or aid in the determination of a law suit not yet commenced.94 

Such abstract questions can not be made the subject of an action. The controversy must "arise out of some act done or threatened, which the court could relieve a party from or

The controversy submitted can not be one which calls for the granting of an order or writ of certiorari or mandamus, for such a controversy is not one "which might be the subject of an action."""" However, the relief demanded may be either legal or equitable.¹ 

§ 463. The Same - Necessary Papers. 

The necessary papers are a submission and an affidavit." 

The submission must be in writing, and acknowledged or proved and certified, in like manner as a deed to be recorded in the county where it is filed. It should be made to a court of record which would have jurisdiction of an action brought for the same cause.* It must present a casestatement of the facts upon which the controversy depends and a claim to relief. It must also include a statement that the parties agree upon that statement of facts, and a stipulation that the controversy be submitted to the court for its determination. A memorandum opposite the title to the effect that it is a case agreed upon in a controversy submitted without action, is not sufficient for this purpose." The submission must set forth the relief demanded by either party and the general nature of the judgment to be entered.' A submission providing that judgment may only be rendered in case of a decision in the plaintiff's favor will be dismissed, for the action however decided must terminate in a judg-

§ 466. Judgments After Trial-In General. 

As was shown in. the chapter on trials, the court may grant defendant's motion for judgment dismissing the complaint at different stages in the progress of the trial.28 Judgments may also be had at the close of a jury trial based upon the verdict obtained, and at the close of a trial before the court

JUDGMENTS AND INCIDENTAL PRACTICE RELATING THERETO. 

or referee based on the decision of the court or the report of the referee. 

§ 467. The Same - On the Dismissal of the Complaint. 

If the complaint is dismissed on motion in the course of the trial, an extract from the minutes showing the termination of the action will suffice as a direction to the clerk to enter judgment dismissing the complaint, tax the costs and insert them therein.29

The effect of such a judgment depends upon the stage of the trial at which the motion therefor was granted. If the complaint was dismissed before the close of the plaintiff's case, the judgment is not a bar to a new action for the same cause unless the judgment declares that it is rendered upon the merits. If the dismissal takes place at the close of the plaintiff's case or after all the evidence is in on both sides, it is an adjudication upon the merits and bars a new action unless the court dismisses the complaint without prejudice.30 

This section changes materially the law as it existed under the Code. There is no change so far as a dismissal before the close of the plaintiff's case is concerned, for in that event both under the Code and under the Practice Act, the judgment is not one on the merits unless the judgment expressly so declares. Under the Code, however, a dismissal of the complaint at the close of plaintiff's case or of the whole evidence was not on the merits unless the judgment so declared.31 

The rule is reversed under the Civil Practice Act for there the judgment is on the merits unless it is declared to be without prejudice. 

§ 468. Judgment After Trial By Jury-On General Verdict. 

The clerk of the court where the trial took place will, after a jury trial, furnish to the successful party an extract from the minutes which will state the amount and character of the verdict. This, presented to the clerk where the judgment is to be entered, will be sufficient authority for him to enter the judgment.82

JUDGMENTS AND INCIDENTAL PRACTICE RELATING THERETO. 553 § 469. The Same On Special Verdict. 

Either party may make a motion for judgment based on the special verdict of the jury. The motion is made at special term.33 

In an action triable by the court where one or more specific questions of fact arising on the issues have been tried by a jury, judgment may be taken on the application of either party. If all the issues of fact in the action are determined by the findings of the jury, or if part only of them have been tried by the jury and the remaining issues of fact have been determined by the decision of the court or a report of the referee, an application for judgment on the whole issue may be made at special term as on a motion. The application in such case would be based upon the special verdict of the jury or upon such special verdict combined with the decision or report as the case requires. If, however, some of the issues are tried by a jury and the remaining issues are not yet disposed of, application for judgment may be made on the whole issue at the term of the court where the remaining issues are tried, and if the remaining issues are tried by a referee, the referee in his report may give directions for the judgment.** 

§ 470. The Same - After Verdict Subject to the Opinion of the 

Court.

In a case where the trial judge might have directed a verdict but is doubtful about the law governing the case, he may direct the jury to render a verdict subject to the opinion of the court to which an appeal would be taken from a judgment rendered in the action. In such a case a motion for judgment is made in the appellate court on a case settled by the trial judge. This is not a motion for a new trial on exceptions heard in the appellate court in the first instance, but is a motion for judgment. On the determination of the motion judgment is entered by the clerk on the order of the appellate court. It differs from a motion for a new trial in the appellate court in that on such a motion the power of the appellate court is limited to granting or denying a new trial. 35

§ 471. Judgment After Trial by Court or Referee. 

"Except where otherwise expressly prescribed by law, judgment on the report of a referee after a trial by the referee of the whole issue of fact, or on the decision of the court on the trial of the whole issue of fact without a jury, may be entered by the clerk, as directed therein, on filing the decision or report. 7736 The phrase "except where otherwise expressly prescribed by law" is illustrated in matrimonial actions where the judgment may not be entered on the referee's report in case a referee other than an "Official Referee" was designated to hear and determine the issues, but such report must be confirmed by the court and a judgment must be rendered by the court, and in actions for a divorce a special direction must be given by the court for the entry of judgment."7 

In actions brought for judgment annulling a marriage or divorcing parties, an interlocutory judgment is first entered upon the decision of the court and this becomes final as of course after the expiration of three months unless the court or referee otherwise directs.38 

§ 472. The Entry of Judgment After Motion Made Therefor Prior to the Trial. 

We have seen that motions as incidental practice connected with pleadings, may be made for judgment dismissing a complaint or a cause of action therein or in a counterclaim, or a defense in an answer, and a motion may be made for judgment on one cause of action, counterclaim or defense, while the party may plead to another.39 It might easily happen that judgment would be directed on one cause of action, counterclaim or defense on the determination of a motion of this kind, while an issue of fact arising on some other cause of action, counterclaim or defense still remained to be determined. It might be, too, that a motion for judgment dismissing the complaint would be denied and the defendant fail, within the time allowed, to answer. Other situations may also arise where the entry of judgment becomes somewhat complicated. To meet situations of this kind various provisions are found in the Civil Practice Act and in the 40

§ 473. The Judgment-Roll. 

The clerk on entering judgment must immediately file the judgment-roll. The attorney for the successful party prepares it, except that the clerk must attach thereto the necessary papers which may be on file in his office.45 46 The judgment-roll shall consist, except where other special provision is made by law, of the following papers: the summons, the pleadings or copies thereof, admissions, the final judgment, and the interlocutory judgment, if any, or copies thereof, and each paper on file, or a copy thereof, and a copy of each order which in any way involves the merits or necessarily affects the judgment. The original pleading. where an amended pleading is served should not be included.*7 

Incidental motions, such as motions for extension of time to plead, or for bills of particulars which do not affect the judgment should not be included. If a defendant has appeared, neither the summons nor proof of its service becomes a necessary part of the judgment-roll¹8 But if a judgment is taken by default, the affidavit showing service of process and the default is required since they establish the jurisdiction of the court or the lack of it," and if the summons were served by publication upon a non-resident, all the papers necessary to show jurisdiction in the court must be included in the judgment-roll.

§ 474. Lien of Judgment for Money. 

50 A judgment for money is a lien for ten years from the filing of the judgment-roll upon the real property which the defendant has or may acquire within the ten years and which is located in any county where the judgment is docketed." 51 The lien is extinguished after the ten years, but in case the judgment debtor dies within the ten years it continues for two years after his death notwithstanding the fact that the ten-year period may have expired in the meantime." The lien may be revived after the ten years by issuing an execution against the property and filing at the same time with the clerk of the county where the property is situated a notice subscribed by the sheriff describing the judgment, the execution and the property levied upon. The lien of the judgment is revived only as to the specific real property described in the notice. The time during which a judgment creditor is stayed by an injunction or other order, or by 

50. No judgment is a charge upon the real property of any person unless and until he is designated by his name in a docket of such judgment in the office of the clerk in the county where such property is located. C.

§ 475. The Same - When the Defendant Is Sued by a Fictitious Name. 

A judgment obtained where the defendant was sued by a fictitious name does not become a lien on any one's property, but on such notice as the court may direct, such judgment may be amended by substituting for the fictitious name the real name of the defendant, and the judgment thus becomes a lien on the debtor's property. The ten-year period, however, begins to run from the time of the original docketing of the judgment and not from the time it was amended.62

§ 477. Motions To Correct Judgments.63 

The only errors which the trial court can correct by amendment of the judgment are "Clerical errors or a mistake in the entry of the judgment or the omission of a right or relief to which a party is entitled as a matter of course. 764 Thus where there is an apparent ambiguity in the findings of the trial court which is plainly the result of some inadvertence or omission, as where in an action to restrain the defendant from operating its elevated railroad in certain streets in front of plaintiff's premises, the trial court decided in plaintiff's favor, but in one finding of fact said that the street in question was opened by the city and "Henceforth continuously has been and now is kept open and approved for a public avenue" although subsequent findings show the defendant's obstruction thereon, the trial court properly amended the finding quoted above by adding "except as hereafter found. ''65

Judgments may be corrected to make them conform to verdicts, decisions and reports. Thus the phrase "on the merits" may be stricken out of a judgment by motion where the record shows that the judgment was not in fact on the merits. Again where the judgment was by mistake entered against defendants as individuals when it should have been entered against them in their representative capacity it may be corrected." Likewise when a verdict for money "recom-

Such error if there was one cannot be corrected on appeal. Likewise in an action for replevin where the jury awarded damages for the value of the property in question and for the detention thereof in one sum, and the clerk in entering judgment divided that sum into two separate amounts, a motion to correct the judgment would be the proper procedure." 

But it must be remembered that the trial court has 68 "no revisory or appellate jurisdiction to correct by amendment error in substance affecting the judgment. It cannot, by amendment, change the judgment in matter of substance for error committed on the trial or in the decision, or limit the legal effect of it to meet some supposed equity subsequently called to its attention or subsequently arising. It cannot correct judicial errors either of commission or omission. Those errors are, under our system of procedure, to be corrected either by the vacating of the judgment or by an appeal."'70

Thus in an equity action where costs are discretionary with the court, a judgment which allows no costs to either party cannot on a motion to correct it, allow costs to plaintiff since "A provision withholding or awarding costs is a substantive part of a judgment in an action in equity and cannot be amended. ''¹ 

And if the trial court does amend the judgment in this way where the defendant has defaulted in the action, and cannot, therefore, appeal, the proper remedy for such defendant is to move in the first instance to vacate the judgment.72

result that they cannot well be corrected, the judgment itself may be vacated because of them. 

The irregularities referred to are necessarily those arising in practice and consist of some step or proceeding taken in the prosecution or defense of an action, which is without authority of law, or contrary to some rule of practice. 9974 76 The irregularity which will warrant a vacation of the judgment must not affect a substantial right." Where, for example, in an action against partners upon a partnership obligation separate judgments are entered against each of the defendants instead of a joint judgment against all of them, there is presented an irregularity which should be relieved by a motion to vacate. This defect in the judgment is technical merely and does not affect any substantial right of the adverse party. Likewise where there are two classes of defendants in an action, those belong to one of such classes. being jointly liable, and those of the other class being severally liable, if the plaintiff's attorney on entering judgment against the defendants severally liable who have made default, by mistake and inadvertence, enters judgment against one of the defendants jointly liable, who was also in default, the court has power to relieve the plaintiff from such mistake by vacating the judgment as to the defendant jointly liable." If a judgment in an action is irregular because it should not have been entered in favor of defendants who were not served or who had not appeared in the action, the remedy is by motion to set aside or vacate the judgment."

§ 482. Procedure in Correcting and Vacating Judgments. 

Judgments are corrected or vacated by motion. If the motion is based on mistake, inadvertence, surprise or excusable neglect, or if it is based on irregularity, the motion must be made within one year after notice of the entry of the judgment." If the motion is made to vacate the judgment for error in fact it must be made within two years from the filing of the judgment-roll, except that in case the defendant is an infant, or is insane, or is in prison on a criminal charge, the time of his disability is not a part of the two years. The time cannot, however, in any event be extended for more than five years on account of such disability nor in any case more than one year after the disability has been removed.""

§ 484. In General. 

"The Supreme Court shall have the power in any action or proceeding to declare rights and other legal relations on request for such declaration whether or not further relief is or could be claimed, and such declaration shall have the force of a final judgment. Such provisions shall be made by rules as may be necessary and proper to carry into effect the provisions of this section."" 

While this provision relates specifically to judgments and is found in the Civil Practice Act in the article on judgments, it has been thought wise to treat the matter separately at this point in the development of the subject because a declaratory judgment, like any other judgment, is reached only through the conventional steps in an action. The complaint must disclose in its prayer for relief that a declaratory judgment is sought, and the allegations necessary to state a sufficient cause of action where this kind of relief is contemplated, will often differ from the allegations required for an action seeking the usual judgment. The earlier, therefore, that we comprehend the nature of the action seeking declaratory relief, the more comprehensive will be our understanding of other provisions of the Practice Act relating to the matter and yet to be discussed. 

1. 473 of the Civil Practice Act., cf. Rules 210-213, inclusive. And see two excellent articles in 28 Yale L. J.

2. Rule 210. [587]

§ 485. Declaratory Judgments Defined. 

A declaratory judgment is one which declares the existence of a right but prescribes no coercive measures for its enforcement. It will declare that A has a right to B's house but will not decree that B convey his house to A. It will declare that A has a right to sub-let the premises without the consent of the landlord, but it will not order the landlord to refrain from interfering with the sub-tenant's possession. It is a declaratory, as distinguished from a coercive decree.

It is common, however, in actions seeking declaratory judgments to find a demand for coercive relief as well as a request for a declaration of rights. The coercive relief thus sought is called consequential relief or simply further relief. 

The latter term is used in the New York statute. The former is the English term. In such case the judgment entered may at the same time be both declaratory and coercive. 

§ 486. Declaratory Judgments - History of. 

There are sporadic cases in the reports both in the United States and in England prior to any general statute authorizing declaratory judgments, where what were in effect declaratory judgments were made, though they were not so denominated.*

In 1883, Rule 5 of Order XXV, was enacted in England and the regulations therein contained exist to-day. That rule introduced into English practice an innovation of a very important kind. In 1893 this rule was supplemented

§ 487. A Digest of a Number of Cases Where Declaratory Judg ments were Sought.11

Perhaps the best way to give an idea of the scope and purpose of the section of the Practice Act now under consideration is to digest a number of recent cases where declaratory judgments were sought. The cases are numbered for convenience. 

Case 1. In Francis v. Ferguson,12 a declaratory judgment was rendered declaring that a certain covenant in a lease did not prevent the assignment thereof by the plaintiffs. In that case, the plaintiffs as executors of the lessee, entered into an agreement with the defendant for the transfer of the lease to him, but the defendant refused to complete the agreement on the ground that the lessor did not consent to the assignment. The question was whether a provision of the lease against assignment, followed by a covenant at the end of either public or private interests will be materially promoted by a declaration of the right or duty in advance of any actual or threatened invasion of right or default in duty. The judgincut rendered in such an action shall bind all the parties thereto and be conclusive and final as to the rights and duties involved. Section 2. This act shall take effect upon passage and publication."

This represents a type of controversy most common in an action for a declaratory judgment, viz.: where it is desired to determine the exact force of a clause in a lease or a similar document.13 The declaratory judgment action is particularly valuable in such cases because it frequently permits a determination of rights in advance of a serious breach or in advance of the expiration of a lease. 

Case 2. In Finch v. Unity Fee Co.,¹ a judgment was asked declaring the rights of the various parties under a certain restrictive covenant affecting a portion of the plaintiff's premises, which, it was claimed, was claimed, had been abandoned, and which owing to change in the neighborhood was no longer needed, and as alternative relief the plaintiffs asked, in the event the court should find that the covenant was still operative, that there should be judgment holding the erection and maintenance of a building on an adjoining parcel to be in violation of the covenant and that the building be ordered removed. The court upheld the covenant and granted to the plaintiff the alternative relief asked, directing the removal of the buildings from the parcel in question and enjoining the further maintenance of a building thereon.

The granting of such alternative or "coercive" relief in this case is an excellent example of the "further or consequental relief" referred to in Rule 211 of the Rules of Civil 

Practice.

In this case a cause of action of the usual type for damages existed, but plaintiff would have had to move out of the premises to maintain the action advantageously. And without the declaration, the subtenant, if he attempted to move in, would have been subjected to a great deal of physical inconvenience in addition to the mental uneasiness attendant upon buying into, a law-suit. In any event, plaintiff's resort to a declaratory judgment action eliminated the risk that moving out and instituting an ordinary action would have involved; and it provided a swifter and far less troublesome remedy than would have been used had plaintiff sought to avail herself of the defendant's breach by moving out, of, the premises and suing for damages. 

The following is the history of a parallel case under the old procedure.16 The plaintiff was a lessee of certain premises belonging to the defendant. The lease contained a provision restricting plaintiff's right to assign or sub-let without the landlord's consent. Plaintiff, desiring to assign the lease to W and being unable to get the landlord's consent, assigned to W without it, but the sub-lease was conditioned upon the undisputed and undisturbed possession of W for a period. W went into possession. The landlord gave notice of termination of the lease, rejected W as a tenant and notified W that the supply of steam and hot water would be discontinued. W vacated the premises, the tenant resumed possession. He refused to pay rent. The landlord brought this summary proceeding to recover possession of the premises. The tenant counterclaimed in the summary proceeding for damages sustained through the landlord's breach of this covenant of the lease by refusing to give his consent to the sub-letting. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the tenant in the sum of $7,045.19. Thereafter the case was reversed.

What cause of action plaintiff would have in such a case if a declaratory judgment action were not available is difficult to comprehend.

Alderton," the plaintiff agreed to procure a purchaser for certain properties of the defendant and the defendant agreed that plaintiff would be paid “handsomely" if a sale was effected, and when, as and if defendant received the purchase money from the buyer, but not a cent if no sale resulted from plaintiff's efforts. A sale to one M resulted on April 9, 1926. M paid $1,000,000 in cash and $400,000 additional by delivering to defendant a third mortgage due April 9, 1931. Plaintiff demanded $80,000 for his services, but defendant would only offer $6,000, so on May 28, 1929 plaintiff instituted this action for a declaratory judgment to have it declared that plaintiff's services were worth $80,000 and that plaintiff had a lien to that amount on the $400,000 that M was to pay on April 9, 1931. The trial of this action occurred on July 2, 1930. On April 9, 1931 M's obligation on the $400,000 third mortgage was extended to 1936. 

The Court of Appeals held that a declaratory judgment would not lie, because plaintiff was not entitled to any lien by his agreement, and on May 28, 1929 when suit was brought plaintiff's commissions were not yet payable and there had been no breach by defendant. The court pointed out that under the guise of a declaratory judgment the plaintiff was seeking to secure an equitable lien on a fund upon which he had no right to a lien, legal or equitable, and that there was nothing to prevent the plaintiff from bringing his action at law for services rendered, when the due date arrived. 

Crane, J. stated at pages 304-305: "His (plaintiff's) work and labor created a debt due him from the defendant, and to collect this debt his action at law was adequate.

Lord Strudale, M. R., said: 1 "There is no doubt now that actions can be brought for declarations, and the court can make declarations although no consequential relief is asked. That was so decided in Dyson v. Attorney General, 

(1911) 1 K. B. 410, Burghes v. Attorney General, .(1912) 1 Ch. 173, and Guaranty Trust Co. v. Hannay & Co., (1915) 2 K. B. 536. It is very useful jurisdiction and especially so in cases of a commercial character; but it does not at all follow that a declaration ought to be made in all cases. I think, speaking for myself, that there has been too great a tendency of late years to ask for declarations on every possible point. I have considerable doubts whether this was a case in which a declaration ought to have been made. As I say, the point was not taken" (by the Attorney-General) "and therefore, I only wish to say that I must not be taken as giving an opinion that this was a proper case in which to make such declaration." 

It may safely be said now that a person against whom no claim has been made cannot obtain a declaration that no such claim exists. In a recent leading cases where such was the situation, in refusing to take jurisdiction Swinfen Eady, M. R., said: "It is claimed ** that although no right of the petitioners has been interfered with and no claim made against them and although in their view they have no claim against Booth, they are entitled to come into Court to ask for a declaration that Booth has no claim against them in respect of the matter in question. I have pointed out the fact that he had not made any claim. Under those circumstances are they entitled to come and have it determined that he has no claim. In my opinion they are not; and none of the authorities to which reference has been made justify the advancing of such a claim."

Judge Eve said: 

"I agree. 

So soon as it was demonstrated that no specific right had been asserted and no claim formulated the Court had, in my opinion, no jurisdiction to deal with the petition in the way in which it has been dealt with."

§ 489. Constitutionality of Section 473 of the Civil Practice Act. 

A similar law was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of the state of Michigan. 33 It seems obvious from a consideration of the facts in such case that the Michigan court could have declined to entertain jurisdiction on the ground that the case was moot and thus have made it unnecessary to pass on the constitutionality of the act itself. Moot cases may arise under any act and if the act is to be declared unconstitutional because a moot case has arisen under it, few acts will stand. 

But the majority of the court went further and declared the act unconstitutional on the ground that it attempted to confer non-judicial powers upon the court. It can hardly be said, however, that in cases where a conventional action might have been brought but the plaintiff or defendant rests content with a demand for a declaration of rights the moderation of the demand strips the inquiry of its judicial character. The nature of the inquiry is the same whether the right to consequential relief exists or not. In each case the effort is to ascertain what the facts are which have already transpired and apply to them when ascertained some recognized principle of law that will determine the rights of the parties in the given case. For instance, Justice Field said in distinguishing a judicial from a legislative act.³ 34 66 The one determines what the law is, and what the rights of the parties are, with reference to transactions already had; the other provides what the law shall be in future cases arising under it." 

Another point which the Michigan court seemed to emphasize in declaring the power conferred by the act nonjudicial is that unless the court in pronouncing judgment has the power to enforce rights as well as declare them, its act in rendering judgment is not a judicial one. The case most

35. 219 U. S. 346. The reliance of the Supreme Court of the state of Michigan upon the Muskrat case to sustain its view that the Michigan statute was an unconstitutional enactment has been commented upon by Chief Justice of the United States

(219 U. S., p. 361.) It was not because the question was the determination of the validity of an Act of Congress but because this question did not arise in an actual controversy, that the court found itself without power to determine it. Had there been an actual controversy, the question of the validity of an Act of Congress, or any other question properly brought before the court, could have been determined. 

But in the absence of an actual controversy, neither that question nor any other could be properly determined by the court. It was pointed out that the power to decide upon the constitutional validity of a statute existed only when the court was called upon to determine an actual controversy. It was said that the whole purpose of the law there in question was to determine the validity of the class of legislation, not in a suit arising between parties concerning a property right necessarily involved in the decision, but in a proceeding against the Government in its sovereign capacity. The United 

States was to be made a defendant, but it had no interest adverse to the claimant's, the suit being brought solely to determine the validity of the legislation in question. “I do not think, therefore, that it distinguishes the Muskrat case to say that it related to the determination of constitutional questions, for this fails to state the ground upon which the court found itself unable to determine the constitutional question. I think that the paragraphs relating to the Muskrat case should be changed, and particularly that portion which states the distinction between the Muskrat case and the proposed legislation. I do not think it should be said that probably legislation, conferring a power to determine the validity of an Act of Congress, should be within the rule in the Muskrat case. 

The question will be whether there is a 'case' or actual 'controversy,' and if there is not, it may be assumed that the statute would be held to be invalid whether or not it extended to the determination of the constitutional questions. The point of distinction, it seems to me, should be, and it is sufficient to state, simply that the proposed legislation is intended to deal only with actual controversies and proposes that where there is an actual controversy between litigants the court may render a declaratory judg ment."

§ 490. Pleadings in Actions Seeking Declaratory Judgments. 

The main difference in pleadings in actions seeking declaratory judgments from the pleadings in the conventional action will be found in the prayer for relief. The prayer for relief in the complaint shall specify the precise rights and other legal relations of which a declaration is requested and whether further or consequential relief is or could be claimed. If further relief be claimed in the action the nature and extent of such relief shall be stated." An illustration of the character of the request for a declaration will be found in the cases digested in section 487, ante, and in the notes relating thereto."

The statement of the cause of action will not differ at all from such statement in the cases where the conventional type of action exists, for the same allegations will be required to sustain the right to a declaration which are required to sustain a conventional action. In cases, however, where no conventional type of action exists but where the court may nevertheless make a declaration of right, the statement of the cause of action will be the same, as far as it goes, as if the conventional right of action existed but it will not go so far. 

In the action seeking declaratory relief it will stop short of the conventional action. To make a conventional cause of action out of one seeking declaratory relief merely, a tender would have to be alleged or a demand and refusal or some other culminating allegation which would perfect the conventional cause of action but which is not required in a cause of action seeking declaratory relief.

§ 491. Provisional Remedies - Introduction. 

The usual course of an action is marked by the summons, the pleadings, the trial and the judgment. Many circum- [587]

ARREST. 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES 

stances may present themselves, however, in which the action pursued in the usual way would not furnish an adequate remedy. One who has defrauded another may be about to leave the country. He would not mind being served with a summons merely. A non-resident who has property within the state, if served with a summons, might remove his property out of the jurisdiction and ignore the summons. Parties to a contract may have a dispute over its interpretation and irreparable damage might be done if either were permitted to act upon his own interpretation before a judicial determination of the instrument was had. A defendant in possession of mortgaged premises may during the progress of the litigation for the foreclosure of the mortgage collect the rents and leave the interest, taxes and charges unpaid, neglect repairs and let the property so run down that it will not bring enough on a foreclosure sale to satisfy the mortgage indebtedness. Many other situations might be cited to show the need for extraordinary remedies to meet the demands of justice. The remedies provided for such needs are called provisional remedies. They are arrests, injunctions, attachments and receivers. 

§ 492. The Same - Availability Of. 

It is possible for a plaintiff if one of these remedies will not afford sufficient relief to pursue two or more of them at the same time.¹ In the ordinary case, however, the plaintiff should be required to elect between two provisional remedies at the time of application therefor." They are available to a defendant in connection with a counterclaim, or a claim against a co-defendant, and for the purpose of applying such remedies in such a case the plaintiff is deemed a defendant and the defendant the plaintiff.³ 

§ 493. The Same Jurisdiction. 

These remedies may ordinarily be instituted to accompany the summons and before its service and from the time of granting such remedy the court acquires jurisdiction and has control of all the subsequent proceedings. Yet such jurisdic-

§ 494. Arrests Classes Of. 

There are two kinds of arrests in civil actions. One is confined to equity actions and one principally to actions at law. Each is governed by a distinct section of the Civil 

Practice Act. Section 826 defines the cases where an arrest in a civil action at law is possible, and section 827 states the circumstances which will authorize an arrest in an equity action. These two sections must not be confused. They differ in their origin, in the evidence required to support the arrest under them, and in the character of the tribunal which may grant the order." 

6. Idem. City of New York v. Staten 

Island Midland Ry. Co., 110 Misc. 

695; 181 N. Y. S. 124. 

7. See Mun. Ct. Code §§ 25 and 139 § 495. The Same Origin Of. 

Section 826 traces its origin to the common law practice of imprisonment for debt. There, it made little difference whether the debtor was an honest man who met with reverses or a dishonest one who defrauded his creditors. 

Beginning with the Stillwell Act in 1831, an intent may be read from the statutes which have been passed from time to time by the legislature relating to this remedy, to restrict its use to actions sounding in tort and to such contract actions as are peculiar in their character, or allege fraud in contracting or incurring the liability. 

Section 827 traces its origin to the old chancery writ of ne exeat. The means of enforcing decrees in equity was by proceedings in contempt and required generally the presence of the defendant to be effective. When, therefore, an equity action was begun or contemplated, and it was brought to the attention of the chancellor that the defendant was about to leave the country, the writ of ne exeat (let him not depart) was issued, the defendant arrested, and his departure prevented. The writ of ne exeat is abolfor an example of an "arrest" provision in an inferior court.

A. D. 219; 175 N. Y. S. 342.

There are ten subdivisions to this section, each one of which enumerates a distinct type of action where an order of arrest may be had. These subdivisions briefly stated include the following actions: 

1. To recover a fine or a penalty. Illustrations of actions of this type which will support an arrest are hard to find.¹² 

A positive dictum is found in a recent case,¹³ but the subdivision has had little practical use. 

2. To recover damages for a personal injury. "A personal injury includes libel, slander, criminal conversation, seduction and malicious prosecution; also an assault, battery, false imprisonment or other actionable injury to the person either of the plaintiff, or of another.'"14

An action for a separation based on the husband's cruel and inhuman treatment, however, does not fall within the purview of this subdivision.¹º 

3. To recover damages for injury to property. "Injury to property is an actionable act, whereby the estate of another is lessened, other than a personal injury, or the breach of a 916 contract.

§ 827, a number of actions under which an arrest might be obtained which were actions at law. These were transferred by the amendment of that year to § 549 of the Code which corresponds with Civil Practice Act, 

§ 826, the purpose being as stated by Mr. Throop in his note to the section to confine § 550 of the Code to those cases where the former writ of ne exeat might issue.

5. To recover damages for misconduct or neglect in office or in a professional employment. Illustrations for this subdivision are difficult to find because they are usually located under some other subdivision at the same time and are considered under such other subdivision.21 

6. To recover damages for fraud or deceit. The term fraud is used twice in section 826 of the Civil Practice Act, once in subdivision 6 and once in subdivision 10 of the act. 

The fraud or deceit contemplated in subdivision 6 relates to tort actions for fraud or deceit. Here is contemplated an action based upon a false statement of a material fact made with knowledge of its falsity and with intention to deceive the adverse party who in turn must have been deceived thereby to his damage. The fraud contemplated by subdivision 10 is limited to fraud practiced in contracting or incurring the liability or the actual or contemplated removal or disposition of one's property with intent to defraud creditors. 8. To recover money received or to recover property or damages for the conversion or misapplication of property by a person acting in a fiduciary capacity. 9. To recover money, funds or property held or owned by the state or some subdivision, department or portion thereof where the defendant obtained it without right or to recover damages for so obtaining such money. This subdivision is self explanatory. Public funds are involved here. 

10. In an action upon contract, express or implied," other than a promise to marry, where it is alleged in the complaint that the defendant was guilty of a fraud in contracting or incurring the liability or that, since the making of the contract or in contemplation of making the same, he has removed or disposed of his property with intent to defraud his creditors, or is about to remove or dispose of the same with like intent. The fraud contemplated here must be perpetrated in connection with a contract and it must be found: (a) in contracting or incurring the liability, or (b) in the removal or disposition of property with intent to defraud creditors.

An action, for example, based upon a wrongful discharge from employment, even though the complaint alleges fraud in the making of the contract, does not set forth a cause of action for an arrest under this subdivision. If, however, a person is induced by fraudulent representations to buy a business for a sum of money, part in cash and the balance in notes secured by a purchase money chattel mortgage, and he brings an action to recover the full amount of the purchase price, a case is presented authorizing an arrest for fraud in the making of the contract and the right to the arrest is not defeated because equitable relief is sought in the way of declaring null and void the bill of sale and the notes.³¹

The removal or disposition of property which will authorize an arrest under this subdivision must be such as discloses an intent to defraud creditors. Thus where a debtor on the eve of a general assignment cancelled upon his books without consideration, an old account against one who was insolvent, the arrest under this subdivision was held improper since the intent to defraud was lacking. The cancelled debt was not property within the purview of the statute and the entry in the books did not amount to a transfer or disposition of it.32

In all actions under any of the subdivisions of section 826 the character of the action alone determines the propriety of the order of arrest. No extraneous circumstances need exist or be shown.

§ 497. Actions Where an Order of Arrest May Issue Under Section 

827.33 34 An equity action which requires the defendant to act rather than refrain from action will lay the foundation for an arrest under this section, but in all cases extraneous circumstances must exist before the order may issue. The extraneous circumstances are: (a) The defendant must be a non-resident, or, being a resident, must be about to depart from the state, and (b) By reason of such non-residence or departure danger must exist that a judgment or order requiring the performance of the act will be rendered ineffectual. 

The equity actions which will support the order of arrest under this section are the same as would support the issuance of the old writ of ne exeat, hence an arrest may be had under this section in actions for divorce and separation. The purpose of the arrest under this section is to insure the presence of the party in the state to answer the decree of the court and thus enable the court to enforce its decree which it otherwise might be powerless to do."

§ 498. General Restrictions on the Issuance of Arrest Orders. 

There are many situations which would, under the lan guage of sections 826 and 827 of the Civil Practice Act authorize an arrest, but because of restrictive provisions found in the law, the arrest is not authorized in the particular case.

The following restrictive provisions are of this character: (a) If a cause of action in which an arrest might be had is reduced to a domestic judgment, such judgment merges the original cause of action and if a suit upon the judgment thereafter becomes necessary, an arrest may not be had therein, but if such judgment be obtained in a court of another state an arrest may be had in the action thereon provided the original cause of action was founded upon fraud or deceit or for the price or value of property obtained thereby.s

§ 500. Necessary Papers to Procure an Order of Arrest Under Section 826 of the Civil Practice Act. 

The necessary papers to procure the order of arrest under section 826 of the Civil Practice Act are:51 

(a) An affidavit, (b) An undertaking, and (c) In three cases a complaint. These three cases are enumerated in subdivisions 7, 8 and 10 of section 826 and relate to actions for the recovery of a chattel or for the recovery of money or property converted or misapplied by a person acting in a fiduciary capacity, and actions upon contract where there was fraud in incurring or contracting the liability.

§ 501. The Same The Affidavit. 

52 Proof, on the application for an order of arrest, may be made by affidavit or by such other written evidence as the rules permit. As the right to the arrest under section 826 of the Civil Practice Act is determined by the nature of the action alone and does not depend upon any extraneous circumstances, the main function of the affidavit is obviously to set out the facts which will constitute a cause of action of a kind found in some one of the ten subdivisions of that section. The facts alleged in the complaint, however, are ultimate facts. The affidavit setting forth the cause of action should state the evidence supporting the ultimate facts required to state the cause of action in the complaint. Thus where the plaintiff stated in his affidavit that he knew the matters alleged "from facts and evidence in his possession". but did not disclose such facts and evidence, the affidavit was held insufficient. tion it is not sufficient for the plaintiff to allege in his affidavit that the defendant "wrongfully, maliciously, and without probable cause procured his arrest and prosecution before a magistrate, by whom he was discharged.'

Such affidavit should but does not present evidentiary facts. 

The court said: "The plaintiff accuses defendant of malice, but states no fact indicating it, nor does he fulfill the burden of proving absence of probable cause, for his assertion is not evidence. Were the facts real or apparent, such as would justify a reasonable man in the belief that he had lawful grounds for invoking the interposition of the magistrate? That cannot be known, as no facts are stated. ''55

Moreover, the affidavit should present competent proof of the facts constituting the cause of action. The affidavit, therefore, should be made by a person who knows the facts of his own knowledge, and if made on information and belief, the supporting affidavits of those who are the sources of the information should be attached or at least the details of the evidence which the source furnishes should be given.50 A supporting affidavit, however, which it is highly improbable that the plaintiff could obtain may be dispensed with." An affidavit made positively and not on information and belief will not be sufficient if the facts disclosed in it show that the affiant did not in fact have such positive knowledge."8 

This is especially true of affidavits made by attorneys. "It is the court or the judge making the order, and not the attorney, who must be convinced that there is sufficient ground for the order of arrest. Nor are the deductions made by the affiant from papers and statements in his possession, but which he does not produce, of any probative force. They are merely the conclusions of the affiant, but when courts and judicial officers are asked to act upon affidavits founded on information and belief, they must be furnished with the sources of the information in order that they may draw their own conclusions. § 502. The Same-The Undertaking. 

Before plaintiff can procure an order of arrest he must provide a written undertaking to the effect that if the defendant recovers judgment, or if it is finally decided that the plaintiff was not entitled to the order of arrest, the plaintiff will pay all costs which may be awarded to the defendant and all damages which he may sustain by reason of the arrest not exceeding the sum specified in the undertaking which must be at least equal to one-tenth of the amount of bail required by the order and not less than two hundred and fifty dollars.62 If there are two defendants, separate undertakings must be filed by the plaintiff. One undertaking which runs to the defendants jointly is insufficient." 

Security is not necessary, however, where the action is brought under subdivision 9 of section 826, that is, where the state or a subdivision thereof is the plaintiff.**

§ 505. The Same The Order. 

The order of arrest under section 826 of the Civil Practice Act may be granted either by the court in which the action is brought, or a judge thereof or any county judge." The order may be directed either to a sheriff of a particular county, or generally to the sheriff of any county." The body of the order must recite the ground or grounds on which it is granted." It must require the sheriff forthwith to arrest the party against whom it is directed, if found within his county, to hold him to bail in a specified sum, and to return the order with his proceedings thereunder as prescribed by law.' The order shall be subscribed by the attorney for the party obtaining it and, unless granted by the court shall also be signed by the judge."3 72 73 The attorney by endorsement on the order, or if granted by the court upon the copy thereof delivered to the sheriff, may fix a time within which the defendant must be arrested. 

In such case he may not be arrested afterward under the same order unless the time be extended by the court." 74

§ 509. The Same - The Undertaking. 

As the order under section 827 of the Civil Practice Act can be granted only by the court, an undertaking on the part of the plaintiff may be dispensed with and, if it is required, its form and the security to be given thereunder must be such as the court prescribes." Its form will be the same as that given where the application is made under section 826.78 

§ 510. The Same The Complaint. 

There is no specific requirement that a complaint should constitute a part of the necessary moving papers on an application for an order of arrest under section 827 of the Civil Practice Act. It is required, however, before an order of arrest can be granted under that section that there be "an action wherein the judgment demanded requires the performance of an act, the neglect or refusal to perform which would be punishable by the court as a contempt." 

A complaint shows what the judgment demanded is and furnishes the best evidence of such demand. It is, therefore, a desirable paper if not absolutely essential on the application for the order. It was held to be a necessary paper on an application for an order of arrest in an action for a divorce and the court in that action refused to accept the statement on the summons that the action was one for divorce as a sufficient statement of the character of the judgment demanded.79 

76. See § 501, ante, and cases cited in connection therewith. 

77. Civil Practice Act, § 836.

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES § 512. The Arrest Under Either Section. 

After the order is signed, if it is a judge's order, the original is delivered to the sheriff. If it is a court order, a certified copy thereof is delivered to the sheriff. In either case the papers upon which the order was granted with the undertaking, if any, must be delivered to the sheriff. The sheriff should be provided with an extra set of these papers. 

When he arrests the defendant, pursuant to the terms of the order, the sheriff delivers to the defendant a copy of each of the papers. The sheriff takes the defendant into his custody and keeps him there until discharged by law.82 

Within ten days after the defendant is arrested if he does not give bail, or if he gives bail within ten days after the justification of the bail, the sheriff must file with the clerk the order of arrest,- or where it was granted by the court the certified copy thereof delivered to him—with his return thereon endorsed, the papers upon which the order of arrest was granted, and the undertaking given on the part of the plaintiff. 83 

§ 513. Filing the Papers. 

Whether the application is made under section 826 or section 827 of the Civil Practice Act, the papers on which the order was granted must be filed within ten days after they have been served upon the defendant, and it is the duty of the attorney who procured the order to see that they are so filed. 

A failure to comply with this requirement gives the right to the opposing party to move to vacate the order .6 and the same shall be vacated by the court or judge granting it, unless for proper cause shown, time to file the petition or affidavit shall be extended. 9784

§ 515. Motion to Vacate the Order of Arrest, etc.- When Made. 

If the arrest were made under section 826 of the Civil Practice Act, the motion to vacate may be made at any time before final judgment or at any time within twenty days after the arrest. The same rule applies to the motion to reduce the bail or increase the security. If the arrest were made under section 827 of the Civil Practice Act the motion to vacate may be made at any time within twenty days after the arrest, but the application to increase the security may be made at any time before final judgment.87

Under either section, however, if the application to vacate is based upon the insufficiency of the complaint the motion may be made at any time after the complaint is served.88
