§ 518. The Same - Conditions Imposed in Granting the Order to 

Vacate.

If the court decides to vacate the order there is a possibility that a subsequent action on the part of the defendant against the plaintiff for false imprisonment may result. The court may prevent this by vacating the order conditionally, the condition being that no subsequent action for false imprisonment be prosecuted. The court has a right to vacate the order conditionally excepting where the right of the defendant to have the order vacated is absolute and does not rest in the discretion of the court. In the latter case no condition can be imposed.95

§ 520. Defendant's Compliance With the Order-In General. 

A defendant who has been arrested a. May remain in custody while the action takes the usual course. b. May give bail. c. May make a deposit of money in lieu of bail, or d. He may give an undertaking for the liberties of the jail. 

We shall take up these matters in order. 

§ 521. The Defendant May Be Discharged By Giving Bail. 

The defendant may procure his liberty by giving bail. An opportunity must be afforded him to do so "at any hour of the day or night." Moreover, reasonable opportunity must be afforded him to send for and procure bail before being committed to jail.⁹" 97 Bail may be given at any time from the moment of the arrest to the entry of judgment and afterward until the defendant is in contempt where the order was issued under section 827 of the Civil Practice Act, or until an execution against his person has been issued if the order was granted under section 826 of the Civil Practice Act.98

§ 527. Undertaking for Jail Liberties.36 

38 The undertaking must be executed by the prisoner and one or more sufficient sureties, resident householders or freeholders of the county in a penalty of at least twice the sum at which the sheriff was required to hold the defendant to bail and it contains the condition that the person so in custody shall remain a prisoner and shall not at any time. or in any manner escape or go without the liberties of the jail until discharged by the due course of law." The provisions relating to the justification of the surety on such an undertaking are similar to those on the justification of an undertaking given by bail excepting that the times for giving notice and justification vary slightly. The sureties may surrender the prisoner in a manner somewhat similar to the surrender. when bail is given for the defendant." It should be noticed that the undertaking given to secure the liberties of the jail is not as in the case of an undertaking given by bail security that the defendant will obey the orders of the court or deliver the chattel to the plaintiff or pay the sum recovered in the action or render himself amenable to any mandate that may be issued to enforce final judgment against him in the action, but is security merely that the defendant shall remain a prisoner and shall not at any time or in any manner go without the liberty of the jail until discharged by due course of law.40

The sheriff makes a full return of his proceedings upon the order of arrest forthwith or upon the opening of court on the first day thereafter when it is in session.50 If the plaintiff does not appear within one hour after that return, a judgment dismissing the complaint with costs must be rendered. If the plaintiff is present, but the defendant does not attend in person within that time, the defendant's default must be entered. If both appear, issue must be joined by either written or oral pleadings. Either party can demand a jury trial at that time,5¹ and in such case, the cause may be given a preference upon the calendar.52

The issue must be appointed to be tried within six days after such joinder unless both parties assent to a longer time, or unless, in the case of a jury trial, there is no term of court at which it could have been had within six days. And the trial cannot be adjourned without the consent of both parties, beyond three calendar months from the joinder of issue.53

§ 529. Introduction. 

The general purpose of provisional remedies is, as has been seen, to take such steps at the beginning of an action or during its progress as will render the judgment sought more effectual if obtained. The provisional remedy of arrest seeks to accomplish this, as already shown, by holding the defendant in jail either to prevent his escape from the [621]

INJUNCTION. 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES 

jurisdiction of the court before the final judgment is entered or to compel him before his release to provide means for satisfying the judgment if one is obtained against him. 

The injunction seeks to make the ultimate judgment effectual, if obtained, by restraining the defendant, during the pendency of the action, from doing things which would, if permitted, render the judgment, if and when obtained, of no avail, or less completely effective. If, for example, the defendant during the pendency of a foreclosure action is about to remove fixed machinery from the mortgaged premises and thus depreciate the security out of which the mortgage might be satisfied an occasion for an injunction restraining such acts would be presented.¹ 

§ 530. The Provisional Remedy of Injunction Distinguished from Injunctions Generally. 

In discussing the provisional remedy called the injunction we are by no means entering upon a discussion of the general subject of injunctions. The ordinary injunction is simply a judgment obtained in one kind of an action in equity. If, for example, a plaintiff brings an action to restrain a defendant from using his premises for a purpose forbidden by restrictive covenants in his deed and is successful in such action, a judgment will be entered enjoining the defendant from so using the premises in question. Such a judgment is an injunction and it may be obtained by prosecuting the action in the ordinary way and no provisional remedy need be ,involved in the suit. Similarly nuisances that are continuous in their operation may be enjoined by a judgment in equity obtained through an action prosecuted in its ordinary course."

Injunctions contained in judgments obtained as a result of an action in equity are permanent injunctions and such injunctions are not the subject matter of this chapter. Their discussion is found in works on equity. The injunctions which are provisional remedies and which are discussed here, are injunctions obtained at the outset of the action or

in the course of its prosecution and before the final judgment and are called temporary injunctions or injunctions pendente lite. They are issued by the court or judge upon affidavits setting forth the facts, and in this respect they are clearly distinguishable from final or permanent injunctions which are only granted after a trial on the merits, at which the oral testimony of witnesses is taken. A temporary injunction may be made permanent by the final judgment obtained in the action or it may be dismissed if the plaintiff is unsuccessful.* 

§ 531. Classes of Injunctions. 

Whether the injunction be temporary or permanent it may be classified as mandatory or prohibitive. A mandatory injunction directs the performance of an act while a prohibitive injunction directs the defendant to refrain from its performance. The distinction is often merely a matter of form. 

If a defendant has been furnishing water or electricity to a plaintiff to enable the latter to run his factory and the defendant threatens to cut off the supply it would make little difference in substance whether an injunction directed the defendant to continue the supply of power or prohibited him from cutting it off, although the former would be mandatory and the latter prohibitive in form. In determining the propriety of a temporary injunction it is necessary to look beyond the form and into the substance of the matter.

5. Ward v. Kelsey, 14 Abb. Pr. 106.

A temporary injunction will not be granted requiring the defendant to tear down chimneys and reconstruct them in accordance with the Building Code, since the effect of such injunction would be, not to maintain the situation in status quo, but to determine the litigation. Byrnes v. Kaufwein Realty 

Co., Inc., 206 A. D. 306; 200 N. Y. S. 

§ 532. Purpose of a Temporary Injunction.

Where a mandatory temporary injunction would in effect be a determination of the litigation, it should not be granted prior to a trial on the merits, nor will such an injunction be granted where it gives the same relief which it is expected to obtain by judgment, unless plaintiff's right thereto is clear. Judge Taft" states the purpose of a temporary, which he calls a preliminary, injunction more basically as follows: "The office of a preliminary injunction is to preserve the status quo until, upon final hearing, the court may grant full relief. Generally this can be accomplished by an injunction prohibitory in form, but it sometimes happens that the status quo is a condition not of rest, but of action, and the condition of rest is exactly what will inflict the irreparable injury upon complainant, which he appeals to a court of equity to protect him from. In such a case courts of equity issue mandatory writs before the case is heard on its merits.""

The language quoted is adopted by the Court of Appeals of this state.Ⓡ 

If the temporary injunction sought goes farther than the preservation of the status quo and seeks relief which would alter the existing situation it should be denied or at least limited to the preservation of the status quo. For example, an electrical company had a contract with a subway company under which it had already strung and was operating wires in the defendant's subway and claimed the right to additional space for its wires by the terms of its contract with the subway company. It seeks a temporary injunction asking first that its present occupancy be not interfered with and second that the defendant be compelled to grant it the additional space to which it deems itself entitled. The court granted the relief first sought as it preserved the status quo but denied the second demand for relief saying

§ 533. Authority of the Court to Grant a Temporary Injunction. 

There is no inherent power in a court of equity to grant a temporary injunction. Such power is statutory¹¹ and a careful examination of the provisions of the Civil Practice Act must be made to determine in what cases such relief may be given.

§ 538. Additional Requisites When the Application is Made Under Section 878. 

Under section 878 of the Civil Practice Act an injunction may be obtained even in a common law action, but in addition to showing a good cause of action and no adequate redress at law, certain extrinsic facts must be proved before the injunction will issue. There are two subdivisions to this section and they cover two distinct cases. Under subdivision 

1 the extrinsic circumstances necessary to be shown are: a. That the defendant is doing or procuring or suffering to be done or threatening or is about to do or to procure or suffer to be done an act in violation of plaintiff's right respecting the subject of the action, and b. That such fact tends to render the judgment ineffectual. 

Under subdivision 2 the extrinsic facts which must be shown are: a. That the defendant threatens or is about to remove or to dispose of his property, and b. That he is doing this with intent to defraud the plaintiff. 

The first subdivision applies to actions which have a specific subject-matter and as common law actions for the recovery of money only do not have any specific subject-matter, an injunction under the first subdivision can never be obtained in such an action.26 Thus where plaintiff bought a drug store and gave in part payment several promissory notes and before the notes became due he discovered that the defendant had been guilty of deceit in representing the pono v. Y. S. 128. A defendant was enjoined from disposing of corporate stock delivered to him as collateral security, where the right to sell was debatable.

§ 539. When and By Whom an Injunction May Be Issued Under Either Section 877 or 878. 

Section 818 of the Civil Practice Act provides that the injunction order, as in the case of the other provisional remedies of arrest and attachment, may be granted to accompany the summons. This section, however, contemplates the issuance of an ex parte injunction order by a judge or court. 

It was formerly the practice to obtain an order to show cause containing an interim restraining order, effective until the hearing of the motion, which was served on the defendant simultaneously with the summons. This practice, however, can no longer be followed in view of the recent amendment of section 882 of the Civil Practice Act effective September 1, 1930. The section as amended reads as follows: 

35. Broadfoot v. Miller, 106 Misc. 

455, 458; 174 N. Y. S. 497; Sherwood "The order may be granted only upon notice. Where an application for an injunction is made upon notice either before or after answer, the court or judge may enjoin the defendant until the hearing and decision of the application, but only upon such notice as the court or judge in its or his discretion may direct. 

The effect of this amendment would seem to be to abolish the ex parte injunction order. As a result, the usefulness of the remedy in a large number of cases has been greatly diminished. It depended for its efficacy upon the speed and secrecy of its issuance. As notice of the application must now be given, the defendant will be forwarned and forearmed. 

Under the present wording of section 882 it would seem that the attorney who now seeks to obtain an injunction order can at most serve with his summons a notice of his application for the injunction order, such notice being given by the ordinary notice of motion, or an order to show cause without an interim restraining order. After the action has once been commenced, the injunction may be issued at v. Fred O. H. Fincke Co., Inc., 187 

N. Y. S. 755. 

36. Disbrow v. Garcia, 52 N. Y. 654.

INJUNCTION. 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES 

any time upon notice, but it may not be made after final judgment." The word "final," as used here, however, has been construed to mean a final determination of the litigation and an injunction has been continued during the pendency of an appeal.38

The constitutionality of section 882 as amended has not yet been definitely tested. The effect of the recent amendment is particularly problematical with respect to the court's power to grant a stay under section 167 of the Civil Practice

The rules which the section in question authorizes do not relate to injunction orders however; they relate to warrants of attachments and orders of arrest. The statutory exceptions apply to injunctions seeking to restrain state officers. Such injunctions can be granted only by the Supreme 

Court. They also extend to actions suspending the general or ordinary business of a corporation or suspending the officers thereof from office,"¹ and to similar orders relating to joint stock associations," which injunctions may be issued only by the court in which the action is brought. There are also other exceptions.48 40 An injunction order, however, granted by a judge is enforceable as an order of the court so that there is little difference between the orders except in the application therefor."

§ 540. Papers Necessary on Application for Injunction. 

If the application is made under section 877 of the Civil Practice Act the papers necessary in applying for the injunction are: a. The summons, b. The complaint, c. An affidavit, d. An undertaking, and e. A notice of motion or order to show cause. 

If the application be made under section 878 of the Civil Practice Act the papers necessary in making the application are the same as under section 877, with the single exception that no complaint is required although one may be used.*

§ 541. The Same The Complaint. 

Under section 877 of the Civil Practice Act the injunction order depends upon the nature of the action and not upon extrinsic circumstances, and the complaint is therefore required to show that the action is of the proper kind." An affidavit alone will not suffice for this purpose.18 As has already been shown, the cause of action must be one entitling the plaintiff to a permanent injunction.19 It follows from this that the complaint must demand in its prayer for relief a permanent injunction restraining the defendant from the continuance of the acts complained of.50 The complaint must, moreover, state that the continuance or commission of the act complained of would "produce injury to the plaintiff' and it is not sufficient that the accompanying affidavit so state since under section 877 of the Civil Practice Act the right to the injunction must appear upon the face of the complaint. Moreover, the complaint must show that the injury will result in substantial damages if the injunction is not granted, and a showing that normal damages will 51

§ 542. The Same The Affidavit. 

The affidavit is required whether the application be made under section 877 or 878 of the Civil Practice Act although the need for the affidavit is not so manifest when the application is made under section 877. Under that section it is conceivable that the complaint if verified might make unnecessary the use of the affidavit. The danger, however, in attempting to rely upon the complaint is that it contains statements of ultimate facts which may be made on information and belief while the application for the preliminary injunction should show the evidence supporting the ultimate facts stated in the complaint and should be made so far as practicable on the knowledge of the affiant, or if made on information and belief, the sources of such information should be shown and the affiant should "set forth the alleged facts reported to him by the individual having the personal knowledge of the facts, and as to written papers on which he relies, they or extracts therefrom should be submitted. § 543. The Same - The Undertaking. 

60 Except in the case of a municipal corporation or a public officer acting on its behalf," the plaintiff on applying for an injunction must give an undertaking for the protection of the defendant. For actions generally, the rule is that this undertaking "shall be to the effect that the plaintiff will pay to the party enjoined, such damages, not exceeding a sum specified in the undertaking, as he may sustain by reason of the injunction, if the court finally decides that the plaintiff was not entitled thereto." Damages covered by such an undertaking are limited to those incurred solely or principally because of the injunction. They would not cover attorney's fees for a trial of the action and an appeal therefrom, although they would include attorney's fees involved in a motion to vacate the injunction.62 Where the injunction order stays the trial of an action at law after issue has been joined therein the undertaking must be to the effect that the party will pay all damages and costs which may be recovered in the action stayed by the injunction. If the stay is sought in such a case after verdict, report or decision and before final judgment thereupon, a sum of money sufficient to cover the sum awarded by the verdict, report or decision and the costs of the action must be paid into the court in which the action is commenced, or an undertaking given in lieu thereof," and if the injunction is sought after judgment in such a case the full amount of the judgment including interest and costs must be paid into court, or an undertaking in lieu thereof must be given, and this must be given in addition to the undertaking to pay the party enjoined all damages and costs which may be awarded to him by the court in the action in which the injunction order is granted." First Department, by a divided court refused to reverse an order of the

§ 545. The Same The Order. 

The order may be either a judge's order or a court order" except where it seeks to enjoin state officers from the performance of a duty imposed by statute or suspending the general and ordinary business of a corporation or restraining corporate officers from the performance of their duties when it must be a court order.73 

The order does not differ from other orders except that it must briefly recite the ground or grounds upon which it was 

In compliance with this requirement of the order the mere statement that the commission or the continuance of the acts. complained of during the pendency of the action would produce injury to the plaintiff, thus using the language of the statute, is not sufficient." Where, however, the order recites the several acts of the defendant complained of and this recital is followed by a statement in the language of the statute the grounds are sufficiently stated.7 

The order should also contain a specific statement of the acts sought to be restrained with sufficient clearness for a layman to understand what he is expected to do or refrain from doing."

§ 546. Service of the Order. 

Where the injunction order is granted by the court, it must be served by delivering a certified copy thereof; where it is granted by a judge, it must be served by showing the original order and delivering a copy thereof. Service of the order upon a corporation may be made as prescribed by law for making personal service of a summons upon a corporation. 

Copies of the papers upon which the order was granted must be delivered with the copy of the order.**

§ 548. Persons Bound by the Injunction Order. 

In terms the Civil Practice Act authorizes an injunction against the defendants only, not against the whole world. 

Therefore, an injunction order which purports to restrain "all other persons having knowledge of the injunction" is inoperative beyond restraining the defendants.87 Persons, however, who are not parties to the action may be bound by an injunction if they have knowedge of it provided they are servants or agents of the defendant, or act in collusion or in combination with them.88 Thus agents and employees of the manager of a theatre are bound by an injunction against their employer to restrain the presentation of a play at the theatre, and an injunction against the city of New York will bind members of the common council of the city.⁰⁰ An injunc- 89

§ 549. Vacating or Modifying the Injunction Order-In General. 

A motion to vacate or modify the injunction order may be made either on the original papers or upon new proofs or both.92 

§ 550. The Same On the Original Papers. 

Section 897 of the Civil Practice Act provides that where an injunction order is granted without notice, the party enjoined may apply, upon the original papers, for an order vacating or modifying the injunction order. Such application, the section further provides, may be made to the judge or justice who granted the order, or who held the term of the court where it was granted, or to a term of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, without notice. As under the amendment to Civil Practice Act section 882, injunction orders can no longer be granted without notice, it would seem that the provisions of section 897 referred to are practically obsolete and that the party enjoined ordinarily can no longer move to vacate or modify the injunction order, except upon notice. It is conceivable, of course, that a judge might inadvertently sign an injunction order although no notice had been given to the party enjoined. Such an improvident order could be vacated by the same judge, without notice, under section 897.

Where the application is made upon notice, the court or judge, in furtherance of justice, may allow the plaintiff to supply new proof to supersede or supply defects in the original proof and may amend the order to conform to such proof.93 

§ 551. The Same On New Proofs. 

If the defendant moves to vacate or modify the injunction order on new proofs he must always give notice of such

§ 552. The Determination of the Motion to Vacate or Modify. 

The court may grant or deny the application to vacate. 

If the motion is founded upon the original papers the denial of such motion does not prejudice a subsequent application seasonably made founded upon new proofs. Moreover if the complaint was not used by the plaintiff in obtaining the injunction order the denial of a motion to vacate the injunction on the original papers does not prejudice a subsequent application seasonably made after the receipt of the complaint, and founded upon a failure of the complaint to set forth a cause of action sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to the injunction order. Where the application to vacate or modify the injunction order is made upon notice the court may vacate the original order or modify it in some particulars, or it may require new and additional security to be given by the plaintiff; and if it finds that the alleged wrong or injury to the plaintiff is not irreparable and is capable of being adequately compensated for in money, it may vacate the injunction order upon the defendant's executing an undertaking in such form and amount and with such sureties as the court or judge directs, conditioned to indemnify the plaintiff against any loss sustained by reason of vacating such injunction order. Upon a motion to vacate an injunction, a verified answer on the part of the defendant may be used but it will have only the effect of an affidavit.* 3

§ 553. Defendant's Damages Where an Injunction Order is Mis takenly Granted.

If the injunction order is vacated or if on the trial of the action the defendant wins the suit and it is thus established that the plaintiff was not originally entitled to the injunction, the defendant may recover damages from the plaintiff. 

The undertaking given on the granting of the injunction order is to that effect. The damages are those which 5

Thus in an action brought to determine the rights of the parties to a wall claimed by plaintiff to be a party wall, which the defendant had begun to tear down together with the premises of which it composed a part so that a new building might be constructed, plaintiff obtained a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from tearing down the wall which occasioned delay in the completion of defendant's building. The defendant on winning the suit was allowed as his damages a. Loss in rent of the building. b. Increased cost of labor and material. c. Counsel fees on a motion to dissolve the injunction and on appeal from the order of dissolution. The attorney's fees which are allowed, however, are limited to those connected with the injunction order and the efforts of the defendant to dissolve it. They do not include attorney's fees for the trial of the action as that has no necessary connection with the preliminary injunction. They do include, however, attorney's fees incurred upon a reference to assess damages resulting from an injunction. 555. General Nature of. 

It was seen in the discussion of the provisional remedies of arrest and injunction that the defendant had to be within the jurisdiction before such provisional remedies could be made use of. Attachment is a remedy by means of which, whether the defendant is within the jurisdiction or outside of it, if he has property within the jurisdiction such property may be seized and held by the court to the end that the judgment which may ultimately be obtained be made effectual. 

This is the principal object sought by attachment. It is in the main a proceeding in rem, a proceeding against the property and not a proceeding in personam although jurisdiction may be had both in personam and in rem if the defendant is within the jurisdiction and is personally served with process therein. 

1. Carr v. Corcoran, 44 A. D. 97; 

60 N. Y. S. 763; National B'way Bank v. Sampson, 179 N. Y. 213. Shipman

Questions of jurisdiction are therefore common in the application of this provisional remedy. Where, for example, a resident of the State of Ohio brought an action in the courts of New York against a resident of the State of

Pennsylvania and procured a warrant of attachment and served the same upon a debtor of the defendant who also resided in Pennsylvania although he was served with the warrant in the State of New York, the question involved was whether the court had any kind of jurisdiction at all in the premises. It had no jurisdiction in personam and whether it had jurisdiction in rem or not depended upon whether the property of the defendant, which consisted of the indebtedness owing to him by the person upon whom the attachment was levied, was within the State of New York at the time the warrant was served and thus gave the court jurisdiction in rem. It was held that the situs of the debt was in Pennsylvania, the residence of the debtor and this being true the court had no jurisdiction either in rem or in personam and the attachment was void.¹ v. D. & H. Co., 219 A. D. 312; 219 N. Y. 

S. 628, affd. 245 N. Y. 567 cf. Farmers 

Loan & Trust Co. v. Minnesota, 280

§ 556. In What Actions Attachments of Property May Be Had. 

1. A warrant of attachment may not be had except in actions to recover a sum of money as a tax or as damages."

This limits the use of the remedy to actions at law. An action in equity will not lay the foundation for a warrant of attachment. Consequently in actions for the specific performance of a contract or for the possession of specific property or for the foreclosure of mortgages warrants of attachment may not be obtained. Even an action against an heir on a note made by his ancestor to charge real property of the ancestor in the hands of the heir will not support an application for a warrant of attachment since the action is equitable in its nature in that it seeks to acquire a lien upon real property." 

But if an action has merely the appearance of an equitable action though the basis of it is in reality an action for money a warrant of attachment may issue.' "It is undoubtedly the general doctrine that the remedy of the beneficiaries of a trust against a trustee where the trust is open and continued and the accounts of the trustee have not been settled and adjusted and a balance ascertained is in an action for an accounting in equity and that an action at law, either for money had or received or in any other form, will not lie in the first instance, but it is otherwise where the trust has been closed and settled and the balance ascertained."

A warrant of attachment may be granted in the latter stage of such an action.8 

U. S. 204; Harris v. Balk, 198 U. S. 

215, Cohen v. Enterprise, 214 A. D. 

238.

§ 557. Joinder of Actions. 

If a cause of action in which an attachment may be obtained is joined with one in which it may not, the plaintiff loses his right to an attachment altogether because of such joinder. 

In this respect the effect of joinder is the same in attachment cases as it is in cases where an order of arrest is sought.19 

§ 558. Grounds for the Attachment. 

In the preceding sections the classes of action were set forth where an attachment might be had, but the nature of the action alone is not sufficient to cause the warrant to issue.

Usually there is no difficulty in determining who is a non-resident but one is not a non-resident within the meaning of this section who actually resides here even if he has a legal residence in another state. The section was intended to supply a method for the collection of a debt by appropriating property of the debtor found within the state when proceedings against the debtor personally are impossible or liable to be made ineffectual, and thus it allows the use of the process in rem when process in personam can not be secured. Two things are necessary to establish this ground for the attachment. The first is that the defendant must either have departed from the state or be concealing himself within it. 

The second is that such departure or concealment must have been effected with the intent of defrauding creditors or to avoid the service of a summons. Either departure from the state or concealment in it will suffice for the first extrinsic fact in this connection, and it is not necessary that the plaintiff establish which of the two alternatives exist in his par-

A statement therefore, in the affidavit that the defendant has departed from the state of New York with intent to defraud his creditors or keeps himself concealed therein with like intent is not defective on the ground that the statement is made in the disjunctive. These two grounds may be stated in the alternative. 66 'Otherwise the clause can be of but little benefit, for where the debtor has secreted himself either by departing from the state or by hiding himself within the state, the creditor, if compelled to establish which, will in most cases be powerless to do so for reasons which are obvious.''24 

Mere departure from the state or concealment within it, however, is not enough. It must likewise appear that such concealment or departure is prompted by an intention to defraud creditors. Intention to defraud is a difficult thing to establish and must necessarily be established indirectly. 

Direct proof of the fact can rarely be obtained and when it is established it must ordinarily be inferred from circumstances. The following will illustrate the characteer of the evidence by means of which the intention to defraud is established: "The affidavits show that Dr. Lyman was not to be found on the twenty-second or twenty-third of March at his home or office or through his attorney, and that contradictory messages had been given as to whether he was away or was at home sick, and the office boy said he had come into the office for something and gone away at once; that persons to whom he owed money had searched for him in vain; that the paper had published an account of his absconding, and his attorney had failed to throw any light upon the subject or even to arrange for an appointment, and the sheriff had not succeeded in executing an order of arrest." 

The circumstances thus disclosed were sufficient to make out a prima facie case of intention to defraud creditors.25

The mere statement in an affidavit that the defendant had said that as soon as he could get the money he "would clear out of New York" and that he never would get into business there again is not sufficient to show fraudulent intent as such statements are as consistent with innocence as with guilt.26

In the City Court of the City of New York, the plaintiff is entitled to a warrant of attachment in all cases in which he would be entitled to it in the Supreme Court upon showing facts as are required to be shown therein.27 c. That the defendant, if a natural person or domestic corporation, has removed or is about to remove property from the state with intent to defraud his or its creditors, or has assigned, disposed of or is about to assign, dispose of or secrete property with the like intent or if the defendant is a domestic corporation that no person can be found within the state after diligent effort upon whom a summons can be served.

This subdivision differs from the preceding subdivision principally in that under this subdivision it is the property which is being removed or concealed and not the defendant. 

Under both subdivisions the intention to defraud creditors must exist, but in the preceding subdivision coupled with such intention the defendant must either have departed from the state or secreted himself within it, while in this subdivision it is the property which is departing from the state or being secreted within it. It should be also noted that prospective removal of property as well as the actual removal thereof is contemplated and also a prospective assignment, disposal or secretion of property as well as an actual disposal of or secretion of it will suffice.

Under the former subdivision the departure of the defendant from the state or his concealment therein might be set out as has been shown in the alternative.28 Under this subdivision it is not permissible to allege that the property has been removed or has been assigned or secreted or concealed in the alternative.20

The reason for permitting the alternative statement with reference to the defendant himself while not permitting it with reference to his property is stated as follows: "The removal of property with the intent to defraud creditors is one ground, and the assignment of it with like intent is another; but they are based upon different facts and both cannot well be included in or established by the same facts, whilst under the other

The necessity for stating evidence to support the requisite allegations for the cause of action requires especial attention in actions where the damages are unliquidated. It is sufficient for a complaint simply to state that the plaintiff suffered damages to an extent specified. The affidavit used on an application for an attachment, however, must set forth the evidence from which such damages may be inferred. Thus in an action for a breach of contract where the damages consisted of a loss of a large number of shares of the common stock of a corporation without par value, and the only evidence of the value of said shares set forth in the moving affidavit was the opinion of a stock broker, the court said:

The plaintiff had resold the salmon before the time for its delivery and sets forth in his affidavit upon which he procured a warrant of attachment the price at which he had resold the salmon and calculated the difference between the contract price and resale price of the salmon and set it forth in his affidavit as the damages suffered by him. He did not, however, set forth the fact that there was no market price on the salmon at the time and place of delivery. The court vacated the warrant of attachment because in the absence of the latter statement the correct measure of damages would have been the difference between the contract and market value of the salmon at the time and place of delivery. On the trial of this action the proper measure of damages was presented. See 

131 A. D. 572; 116 N. Y. S. 71, affd. on the opinion below, 199 N. Y. 518.

The warrant of attachment set forth the breach of the contract and damages sustained by stating that the defendants returned to the plaintiff 4300 skins out of those delivered to them upon examination of which by the plaintiff he discovered that 2000 thereof were improperly dyed and dressed, in that they contained black spots, were burned and damaged by being torn and that the dyeing and dressing done by the defendants were performed in an improper and unworkmanlike manner and that the skins in the condition in which they were returned were unmerchantable. The lower court vacated this warrant of attachment for insufficiency of the affidavit in showing the damages sustained by the plaintiff but the Appellate Division reversed the lower court and sustained the warrant¹8 on the authority of Haebler v. Bernharth, and quoted from that case the following statement: "The difference in the value of different kinds of merchandise is in very many, perhaps in most cases mere matter of opinion. The allegation in the complaint that the damages were the sum stated is an averment of a fact in form, but really of the opinion of the plaintiffs that the damages were so much, and this they verified."

"The court say: 'We think the papers presented to the judge upon which the attachment was granted contain some evidence to establish the necessary jurisdictional facts and justified the granting of the writ.' In other words there was some evidence to establish the facts necessary to confer jurisdiction, and therefore the Court of Appeals would not interfere. The only question was whether there was any evidence tending to establish the facts conferring jurisdiction. The question before the General Term on an appeal from an order granting or denying a motion to vacate an attachment, is whether there was not only some evidence tending to establish the facts, but sufficient evidence to justify the granting of the writ; the jurisdiction of the two courts on appeals being essentially different,one weighing the evidence, the other only seeing whether there is any evidence to support the necessary allegations. The case cited, therefore, has no effect upon the question now before the court. 1950 The Court of Appeals in a recent case cites the Haebler case with approval and says: "Even in an action for unliquidated damages where evidentiary facts must be stated with some degree of particularly to show a liability of the defendant for the amount stated, in order that the court may say, prima facie, that more than nominal damages have been sustained, complaints and affidavits, general in their terms and open to criticism on the ground that facts are loosely stated, have been upheld on applications to vacate, made, not by the defendants, but by other attaching creditors, where it could be fairly said that the allegations of fact were not "vague and inconclusive." The only question is whether the affidavits conferred jurisdiction to grant the warrant. (Steuben Co. Bank v. Alberger, 78 N. Y. 252, 258; Haebler v. Bernharth, 115 N. Y. 459, 464, 465.) Meticulous particularity in pleading the facts which must be shown by way of evidence to establish a cause of action is neither necessary nor proper. It bewilders the real issue and furnishes no safeguard against imposition or oppression. ''51

§ 563. The Same The Affidavit - Statement as to Counterclaims. 

In actions to recover damages for breach of contract, the affidavit must show that the plaintiff is entitled to recover a stated sum over and above all counterclaims known to him.52 

The omission of such statement is a fatal defect in the affidavit.53 This statement regarding counterclaims should be made positively. If it is made in an argumentative way it is not sufficient. Thus where the plaintiff alleges that he "is entitled to recover the sum of $6,000 with interest over and above all counterclaims known to him inasmuch as set forth in the foregoing paragraphs the defendants owe him $6,000 as commission, plus interest from September 20, 1919; and none of the defendants has claimed to have any counterclaim against the plaintiff.' the affidavit was declared argumentative and insufficient for that reason." 54

This statement as to counterclaims may be made in the language of the statute. If the action is brought by an assignee it is not necessary that the affidavit state that the plaintiff is entitled to recover a stated sum over and above all counterclaims known to the assignor.""

The following quotation from the opinion written in a recent case where an injunction was sought will illustrate the principal thus stated. The requirements so far as the method of stating facts is concerned do not differ in an application for a warrant of attachment from those in an application for an injunction. "The complaint is supported by an affidavit made by one of the members of the firm of attorneys of record for the plaintiff. He states as the reason why the affidavit is made by him and not by plaintiff, that plaintiff is a foreign corporation 'and that there is no officer of said corporation at present within the city or State of New York' and 'that his knowledge and information has been obtained from conversations with plaintiff's officers, and officers and agents of the defendant American Foreign Banking Corporation, and a representative of defendant, E. R. Sherburne Company, and also from contracts, letters and other documents actually in possession of deponent.' There is, however, nothing in the affidavit to show what the contents of the contracts, letters or other documents were upon which affiant relied, nor are there any extracts therefrom submitted. There is no statement in the affidavit indicating what any of the officers or agents of the plaintiff had stated about the matter. 

In other words, the allegations are simply the affiant's conclusions of alleged facts derived from persons, documents and papers without disclosing the contents of the papers or the information or the substance thereof given to him, excepting only that he states that 'Mr. H. M. 

Blinn, secretary of plaintiff company,' notified him 'that it (referring to the Sherburne Company) takes the position that it has the right to substitute vessels indiscriminately under the contract. 

There is no evidence that any such indiscriminate substitutions were made. Sherburne Company has evaded and declined to give plaintiff' information as to 'when the steamers designated cleared from the Island of Java because it did * * not have contracts for sugar on any of the designated ships and was merely speculating on the market, in derogation of plaintiff's rights to have the vessels designated.'

§ 567. The Same - The Warrant. 

The warrant of attachment corresponds with the order in an application for an injunction or an arrest. It may be granted by the court or by a judge thereof."

The warrant may be directed either to the sheriff of a particular county, or generally to the sheriff of any county. 

It must require the sheriff to attach and safely keep, so much of the property within his county, which the defendant has, or which he may have at any time before final judgment in the action, as will satisfy the plaintiff's demand with costs and expenses. The amount of the plaintiff's demand must be specified in the warrant, as stated in the proofs on which the warrant was granted. If the plaintiff believes that the defendant has property in different counties and that it will be necessary to levy upon the property of the defendrant of attachment could be granted only by a judge (Code § 638).

In the City Court of the city of New York a warrant of attachment must be executed by a sheriff and not by a city marshal.70

The manner of attesting and issuing the warrant, whether granted by the court or a judge may be regulated by rules." 

The present requirement is that a warrant of attachment against property must be subscribed by the plaintiff's attorney, and, except where it is granted by the court, by the judge. If granted by the court, the warrant may be subscribed by a judge holding the term or may be issued by the clerk, pursuant to order, under the seal of the court. Where it is subscribed by such judge the failure to enter an order therefor shall not invalidate the warrant.72 

§ 568. Filing of Papers. 

The plaintiff procuring the warrant must cause the affidavits, and the papers comprising the proof upon which it was granted to be filed in the office of the clerk within ten days after the granting thereof." The failure to file the papers, however, can not affect the validity of the attachment," but the opposing party may move to vacate the attachment for failure to file such papers and the warrant shall be vacated by the court or judge who granted it unless for proper cause shown time to file the papers shall be extended.75 

§ 569. The Levy. 

After the warrant is procured it is delivered to the sheriff together with copies of the papers upon which it was granted and with these the sheriff proceeds to make the levy. He "must execute the warrant immediately, by levying upon so much of the personal and real property of the defendant, within his county, not exempt from levy and sale by virtue of an execution, as will satisfy the plaintiff's demand, with the costs and expenses." The sheriff is the judge of how much he shall levy upon. He is responsible if there is sufficient property and he fails to levy upon enough to satisfy the plaintiff's demand, but if he takes too much the defendant may apply to the court for an order compelling the sheriff to release some of the property seized."

The manner of making the levy is stated in section 917 of Civil Practice Act. There are four subdivisions in that section. Generally speaking the first directs how a levy is made on real property; the second upon such personal property as is capable of manual delivery; the third upon personal property of an intangible nature and not capable of manual delivery; and the fourth principally upon property in the nature of an equitable interest where an action may be brought by the sheriff in aid of the attachment to set aside conveyances of property made for the purpose of defrauding creditors in order that legal title may be restored to the defendant and the levy thereafter made in accordance with the first three subdivisions of the section. 

§ 570. The Same - How the Levy Is Made on Real Property. 

The levy is made upon real property of the defendant by filing with the clerk of the county where it is situated a notice of the attachment stating the names of the parties to the action, the amount of plaintiff's claim as stated in the warrant and a description of the particular property levied upon. The notice must be subscribed by the plaintiff's attorney adding the office address, and must be recorded and indexed by the clerk." Anybody who acquires the property thereafter takes it subject to the lien of this attachment.80 

§ 571. The Same-On Personal Property Capable of Manual Delivery. 

It is necessary for the sheriff in making the levy upon personal property capable of manual delivery to take the same into his custody. Then he must deliver to the person from whose custody he took the property, a copy of the warrant and of the affidavits upon which it was granted. A bond, promissory note or other instrument for the payment of money is included under this subdivision with property capable of manual delivery and such instruments must be levied upon in the same way that tangible personal property

Actual custody on the part of the sheriff is necessary for a valid levy under this subdivision.88 

The fact that the goods and chattels have been fraudulently assigned by a debtor to hinder, delay and defraud creditors does not excuse the sheriff from taking such goods into his actual custody when making a levy thereon.84 

Where a promissory note was held by an agent, the sheriff sought to levy upon the same. He demanded possession of the note but the agent refused to surrender it. The sheriff thereupon obtained an order from the court requiring the agent of the defendant to deliver the note into the possession of the sheriff. In the meantime, however, the defendant debtor had assigned the note. The sheriff obtained possession of the note under his order but it was held that he had no lien upon the note either by virtue of the original demand since he did not take the note into his custody or by his subsequently obtaining the custody of the note as at that time the same was not the property of the defendant.85

§ 572. The Same - On Intangible Personal Property. 

To make a valid levy upon personal property which is intangible and not capable of manual delivery, the sheriff must leave a certified copy of the warrant and a notice showing the property attached with the person holding the same. 89 Debts owing to the defendant are of this character, but the situs of the debt must be within the state when the levy is made and a non-resident debtor of the defendant who comes within the state does not thereby bring property of the defendant within the state and subject it to a levy under a warrant of attachment. The situs of the debt owing to the defendant is the residence of the debtor.90 The United States 

Supreme Court on the contrary, has ruled that a debt is transitory in character and follows the person of the debtor so that it may be levied on by garnishee process against the debtor even though his stay in the state is temporary.91 A bank account of the defendant may be thus levied upon if the debt is here. To effect a levy on intangible property a certified copy of the warrant must be left with the person holding the property. An ordinary copy of the warrant is not sufficient.* 

A notice showing the property attached must also be left. 

A general notice by the sheriff that he attaches all property, debts and effects and all rights and shares of stock etc., in the possession or under the control of the individual served is usually sufficient," but the property sought to be levied upon may be so circumstanced that such a notice would not satisfy the requirements of the statute. Thus where such general notice was given to a trust company but the property of the defendant had not been deposited in the trust company in defendant's own name but had been deposited in the name of "Estate of Kate B. Russel, William H. Russel, administrator" the general notice did not reach this fund although the defendant William H. Russel was the owner and the sole owner of the money thus deposited. The bank was not bound to know this and in declaring that the notice was insufficient the court said: * * * "The notice given does not contain a specification of any par ticular property belonging to the defendant. It does not in terms. or otherwise, point out that the money standing in the account to the credit of Mrs. Russel's estate is the property or money or claim or debt sought to be attached. 

Nothing can be inferred in aid of the levy from the mere fact that verbal information was given to one of the officers of the trust company that the fund sought to be attached was the money standing to the credit of the Russel estate. The officers of the trust company were not obliged to look further than the notice to ascertain what property was sought to be attached."'

Service of the Summons After Granting of a Warrant of Attachment. 14 The warrant of attachment may be issued and a levy made thereunder prior to the service of the summons. The court acquires jurisdiction of the property seized under a valid levy and has control of all the subsequent proceedings.¹ 

Nevertheless, jurisdiction thus acquired is conditional, and liable to be divested in a case where the jurisdiction of the court is made dependent by a special provision of law upon some act to be done after the granting of the provisional remedy.15 Where the summons was not served prior to the granting of the warrant personal service thereof must be made upon the defendant against whose property the warrant is granted within thirty days after the granting thereof; or else before the expiration of the same time service of the summons by publication must be commenced, or service thereof must be made without the state pursuant to an order obtained therefor as prescribed by law;10 and if publication has been or is thereafter commenced, the service must be made complete by the continuance thereof."

If within the thirty days after the granting of the warrant the summons is not served or the publication thereof commenced, the jurisdiction which was acquired by the court on the levy under the warrant is lost. Referring to the necessity of serving the summons within thirty days after the granting of the warrant the Court of Appeals of this state said: "Here is a plain condition on which the vitality of the attachment depended; and it has not been complied with. § 578. Claims of Third Parties to Attached Property.. 

Parties other than the defendant sometimes claim ownership of the property which has been attached. Such persons have two courses open to them. They may take proceedings to procure the possession of their property or they may rest content with merely asserting their claim thereto without securing possession thereof. § 580. The Same Trial by the Sheriff of Third Party's Claim. 

When a third party has put in a claim to attached property the sheriff in his discretion, may empanel a jury to try the validity of the claim." The finding of the sheriff's jury is not conclusive on the question of whether the defendant or the third party has title to the property attached. The purpose of the trial is not to determine that question. The procedure is intended for the protection of the sheriff. If the sheriff's jury finds that the title to the property is in the claimant the sheriff is released from the obligation of continuing the levy upon the property, unless the plaintiff gives an undertaking with at least two sufficient sureties to the effect that the sureties will indemnify the sheriff to the amount therein specified which must be not less than twice the value of the goods and effects and damages as deter-. mined by the jury and two hundred and fifty dollars in addition thereto against all damages, costs and expenses in an action to be brought against him by the claimant or his representative or assignee by reason of the levy upon, the detention or sale of any of the goods or effects by virtue of the attachment.20 If the undertaking is given the sheriff may detain the goods or effects as the property of the defendant: .30

The inquiry before the sheriff's jury is a perfunctory matter. 

As a usual thing no evidence is taken and no witnesses heard. 

The affidavit of the claimant alone is read. The jury usually finds for the claimant as a matter of course. As the purpose of the proceeding is for the protection of the sheriff this usual finding of the jury is easily understood. If they should find for the defendant, however, such finding does not prejudice the claimant's right to bring an action to recover the property or the value thereof. After the jury has found for the claimant and the sheriff has required of the plaintiff the undertaking as a condition of continuing the levy, and the plaintiff has furnished such undertaking, the sheriff files the same and serves upon the claimant and the plaintiff's attorney a copy of the undertaking with notice of justification of the sureties thereof. If the claimant is not satisfied with the sureties he may appear at the time and place specified in the notice, which must be not less than two nor more than five days after the service of the notice, and examine the sureties who must attend there and testify on oath before a judge of the court concerning their sufficiency. If the claimant requires it such examination must be reduced to writing and subscribed by the sureties. If the judge finds the sureties sufficient, he must annex the examination to the undertaking, endorse his allowance thereon and cause the said undertaking together with the examination of the sureties to be filed with the clerk. Thereupon the sheriff is relieved and discharged from all liability by reason of the detention and taking of the property seized.92 

§ 581. The Same-Discharge by Third Party Claimants of Per sonal Property from Attachment.

A third party claimant of property levied upon under a warrant of attachment may at any time before such goods or effects shall have been sold under execution issued upon any judgment recovered by the plaintiff in the action wherein such goods or effects were attached apply to the judge who granted the warrant, or to the court, for an order to discharge the attachment. Upon such application the claimant must give to the sheriff an undertaking with two sufficient sureties who must justify in double the value of the property 

31. Civil Practice Act, § 926. 

32. Civil Practice Act, § 925.

claimed. The undertaking must be conditioned to the effect that in an action to be brought on the undertaking the claimant will establish that he was the owner of such goods and effects at the time of the levy thereon and that in case of his failure to do so he will pay the sheriff the full value of the property so attached with interest to date thereof together with the costs of the action.33

The undertaking must be filed with the clerk and a copy thereof with a notice of such filing must be served upon the plaintiff's attorney who may within three days thereafter give notice to the sheriff that he excepts to the sufficiency of the sureties. Thereupon the sureties must justify in like manner and upon like notice as bail upon an arrest. If the plaintiff does not except to the sureties he is deemed to have waived all objection to them. The sheriff is responsible for the sufficiency of the sureties until after justification and may retain possession of the property attached until such time.35 

§ 582. The Discharge of a Vessel from Attachment by Third Party 

Claimant In General. 

When a vessel has been attached the procedure by which a claimant thereto may discharge the same from the levy differs slightly from the procedure in such cases where other property is attached. A distinction is made between domestic vessels and foreign vessels. The general scheme for discharging the vessel is the same as in the case of other property. A claimant thereto must assert his claim. The vessel is then appraised and in the case of a domestic vessel, if the claimant desires the use of the vessel, it is necessary for him to bond it; that is, it is necessary for him to furnish an undertaking which will take the place of the vessel as plaintiff's security. In the case of a foreign vessel if a claimant asserts an interest therein the burden is upon the plaintiff if he desires the sheriff to continue the levy to furnish an undertaking to the sheriff as in the case of personal property generally.

§ 586. Actions by the Sheriff or by Plaintiff and Sheriff Jointly. 

Where property has been attached by the sheriff which is tangible, but the possession of which the sheriff has been unable to obtain, or where the property is intangible, the sheriff, subject to the direction of the court or judge, may maintain an action in his own name or in the name of the defendant to reduce such property to possession." 48 Like- wise the plaintiff by leave of the court or judge may bring or continue such actions in the name of himself and the sheriff jointly, but by his own counsel and at his own expense." 

The actions contemplated here include actions to set aside fraudulent transfers by the debtor of his property where the debtor and the party to whom the fraudulent transfer was made are the defendants. Such actions, however, as a rule are not maintainable until after the plaintiff has reduced his claim against the defendant on which the attachment was issued to judgment." 50

§ 588. The Motion to Vacate on the Original Papers. 

Any defect or omission in the affidavit upon which the attachment is procured will furnish a basis for a motion to vacate the attachment, made upon the original papers. Thus if an affidavit fails to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action under section 902 of the Civil Practice Act; or if it fails to set out any ground that would satisfy the requirements of section 903; or if the action be on contract, and the affidavit fails to state that the claim asserted exists over and above all counterclaims known to the plaintiff; the motion to vacate should be granted; and it is not sufficient the Bowe case for it would violate the fundamental law to require the defendant to pay the sheriff for having seized and held his property against his will and without any fault on his part in the case. However, where the defendant discharges the levy he simply substitutes an undertaking for the goods and the validity of the levy is not by that proceeding questioned. 

The section as it now reads in the 

Civil Practice Act, requires the de fendant to pay the costs, charges and expenses to the sheriff in the case of a discharge but not in the case of an annullment of the attachment or on its vacation.

§ 589. The Same — Amending the Original Papers on Such Motion. 

On the motion to vacate an order of arrest or an injunction order, the plaintiff may be allowed to amend the papers upon which the order was procured."* On the motion to vacate a warrant of attachment, however, the same liberality in permitting an amendment in the papers on which the warrant was procured is not always permissible. No question of jurisdiction can arise in procuring an order of arrest or an injunction order since jurisdiction in personam is obtained at the time of the service of such orders.65 On a motion to vacate them therefore no jurisdictional question can arise, the sole question being, have the statutes being complied with which prescribe the situations in which an arrest may be obtained or an injunction order granted. In attachment proceedings however it often happens that the only jurisdiction which the court acquires is jurisdiction in rem since an attachment may be obtained prior to the service of the summons and thereafter the summons may be served by publication. If the defect in the papers upon which the warrant of attachment was obtained is so serious that the court never acquired jurisdiction in rem the court can not allow an amendment to the papers on which the warrant was obtained since if it has no jurisdiction at all in the premises it is powerless to do anything in the matter." But if the defect in the papers is a mere irregularity, as distinguished from a jurisdictional defect, then the court should allow an amendment. The fact that the affidavit on which the warrant of attachment is based contained statements on affiant's information and belief without showing the sources 66

Republic, 234 N. Y. 372.

65. See 88 109 and 110, ante. 

66. Dexter and Carpenter Inc. v. 

Lake and Coal Corp., 198 A. D. 760; 

188 N. Y. S. 623.

thereof is a mere irregularity. Before an amendment of the original papers can be allowed, therefore, the court must ascertain whether it has any jurisdiction at all in the premises. 66a To give the court jurisdiction, however, it is not necessary that all the details be found in the moving papers which would be necessary to sustain the warrant on a motion to vacate. When the only question before the court for determination is whether it has or has not jurisdiction, the "meticulous particularly in pleading the facts which must be shown by way of evidence to establish a cause of action is neither necessary nor proper. 9967 If the ultimate facts are set forth which show a cause of action of the proper kind and the damages suffered and the grounds for the attachment, the jurisdictional requirements of the affidavit are satisfactory and such an affidavit may on a motion to vacate the warrant of attachment be amended by supplying the details of evidence necessary to support the ultimate facts alleged."

§ 591. The Same - Renewal of Motion to Vacate or Modify. 

The complaint is not a necessary moving paper on the application for the warrant of attachment. It may be served later. The mere fact that the defendant has made a motion to vacate the warrant of attachment prior to the service of the complaint and such motion has been denied will not prejudice his right to make a subsequent motion after the complaint has been served founded upon a failure of the complaint to set forth any of the causes of action furnished in sections 902 or 904 of the Civil Practice Act."2

§ 593. Before Whom the Motion May Be Made. 

If the motion is made on the original papers it must be made to the court excepting where the warrant was granted by a judge out of court in which case the motion may be made to the same judge in court or out of court. If the motion to vacate is made on new proofs it must be made to the court except that if the warrant was granted by a judge out of court it may be made to any judge of the court.82 

§ 594. Notice of Motion When Neccssary. 

If the motion to vacate is made upon new proofs or is made before the court on the original papers notice is necessary. 

If it is made on the original papers to the same judge who issued the warrant, it may be made with or without notice in the discretion of the judge before whom the application comes.

15. Answer "Yes" or "No":

X, a resident of Kings County, sued Y in the Supreme Court, New York County, for breach of promise. Y was a resident of

Y left, designating no person upon whom process could be served in his behalf. Five months later, X attached ten lots worth $1,000 each that Y owned in Nassau County and served Y by publication, the published summons containing a notice that in the event of default, judgment would be taken against Y for $100,000. On 

August 1, 1928, judgment was thereupon entered before the clerk, who informed X that her demand was too large and who entered judgment for only $50,000, over X's objection and exception. Y learned of the judgment by written notice exactly one year after his telephone call. On February 2, 1931, the day Y returned to the

U. S. A., Y appeared specially and moved to vacate the judgment on the ground that the Court had no power to attach his property or to enter a default judgment against him on service by publication. 

Y appeals from the judgment.

(a) The Supreme Court, New York County, had power to entertain the action even though neither plaintiff nor defendant resided in New York County. (d) X had valid grounds for serving Y by publication. (e) A warrant of attachment was validly issued against 

Y's lots. (f) The clerk had power to enter a default judgment in this case.

§ 597. Introduction. 

The last of the provisional remedies for consideration is the receivership. It may be necessary during the pendency of an action to place property which is the subject of the action in the custody of a person designated by the court and thus preserve it until the rights of the parties thereto are [695]

· RECEIVERS. 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES 

determined at the trial. Such a person is called a receiver. 

His function is "to take the care and custody of the property and administer it during the litigation and to hold it to answer the final judgment in the action."" He is "an officer, or, as he is sometimes called, the 'hand' of the court.'' Ordinarily, "A receiver is an indifferent person between the parties to a cause appointed by the court to receive and preserve the property or fund in litigation pendente lite when it does not seem reasonable to the court that either party should hold it." Ordinarily, too, "He is not the agent or representative of either party to the action, but is uniformly regarded as an officer of the court, exercising his functions in the interest of neither plaintiff nor defendant but for the common benefit of all the parties in interest. 274 There are, however, some cases where a receiver acts only for the party who had him appointed.¹ª 

1. Weeks v. Weeks, 106 N. Y. 626, 631. 

2. People ex rel. Attorney General v. 

The Security Life Insurance Co., 79 

N. Y. 267, 270. 

3. Devendorf v. Dickinson, 21 How. 

Pr. 275. 

4. Cory v. Long, 43 How. Prac. 497; 

Osborn v. Heyer, 2 Paige 342; Curtis

Like all the other provisional remedies the appointment of a receiver is incidental to and a subordinate step in an action. It is not an end in itself but is ancillary to a principal suit." 

§ 598. The Receiver and Other Provisional Remedies. 

When a plaintiff secures an attachment he secures a lien upon the defendant's property and if he is successful in the action the lien will inure to his own benefit. A receiver, however, ordinarily holds the property in custodia legis, where the receivership order does not otherwise provide, and when the action is finally determined the property will be applied not in satisfaction of the claim of the plaintiff only, but of all others who may establish a right to share therein. An attachment can not be had excepting in a law suit where the action is for a money judgment. A receiver is usually not available excepting in actions in equity. An attachment is often resorted to as a provisional remedy for the purpose of giving the court jurisdiction where jurisdiction in perv. Leavitt, 1 Abb. Pr. N. S. 274; Brown v. Northrup, 15 Abb. Pr. sonam can not be had because of the non-residence or nonavailability of the defendant for the personal service of the summons. If defendant has property within the jurisdiction, the attachment will give the court jurisdiction over it and the action may proceed to judgment on the service of the summons by publication. The appointment of the receiver is, however, essentially a proceeding in personam and although it may in some cases proceed in rem such use of the remedy is not common."

The remedy is more drastic than an injunction. When the court grants an injunction concerning property it restrains the parties to whom it is addressed from interfering with the property. Such persons are not physically prevented from interfering with the property but they are liable to punishment for contempt of court if they violate the injunction order. Where a receiver is appointed, however, he takes the property into his own custody and thus removes the danger of interference. The right to an injunction to restrain the disposal of property, however, necessarily involves the right to have a receiver appointed therefor.' As the appointment of a receiver of property is a more drastic remedy than the granting of an injunction relating thereto, the former will not be adopted where the latter affords adequate protection to the parties concerned."

The distinction between the receivership and an arrest is obvious. Under the latter provisional remedy the defendant himself is taken into the custody of the law and held pending the action that he may be ready to respond to any judgment that may be entered therein; while in the case of a receivership the property instead of the party is taken into the custody of the law and held to await its final disposition after the trial of the action.

"974. Receivers, generally. In addition to the cases where the appointment of a receiver is specially provided for by law, a receiver of property which is the subject of an action in the supreme court or a county court may be appointed by the court, in either of the following cases: 

1. Before final judgment, on the application of a party who establishes an apparent right to, or interest in, the property, where it is in the possession of an adverse party and there is danger that it will be removed beyond the jurisdiction of the court, or lost, materially injured, or destroyed. 

2. By or after the final judgment, to carry the judgment into effect, or to dispose of the property, according to its directions. 

3. After final judgment, to preserve the property during the pendency of an appeal.

The word 'property,' as used in this section, includes the rents, profits, or other income, and the increase, of real or personal property."

The initial phrase of this section suggests that, besides the receivers contemplated by the section itself other provisions are found in the law authorizing the appointment of receivers. The receivers contemplated by the section itself are the old equity receivers, sometimes called common law receivers and chancery receivers, and the language of this section constitutes a declaration of the practice that existed in equity prior to its adoption or the adoption of the Code section which preceded it with regard to the appointment of receivers. The section, therefore, suggests the first classification of receivers into equity receivers and statutory receivers, and these are discussed in the next succeeding section. 

A comparison of the three subdivisions of the section quoted above will reveal that under the first subdivision the appointment of the receiver takes place before judgment and under the second and third subdivisions it takes place after judgment. Strictly speaking the receiver appointed before judgment and pursuant to the provisions of the first subdivision is the one contemplated when the provisional remedy is considered and he is often called, for that reason, a receiver pendente lite.10 Such receivers are the ones principally considered throughout this chapter. 

Although the receivers contemplated by the second and third subdivisions of section 974 of the Civil Practice Act are appointed after judgment or continued thereafter, they are nevertheless, equity receivers just as those who are, appointed 

10. Clark on the Law of Receivers, page 19.

699 RECEIVERS. under the first subdivision of section 974 and the usages and rules of equity pertaining to equity receivers apply generally to them." Although their appointment takes place after judgment they are not properly called permanent receivers. The latter term is applied only where the receiver is appointed for the full term of the litigation and distributes the property at the close thereof to those who may be entitled thereto. His activities are not limited to the preservation of the property pending the litigation. A receiver of an insolvent corporation appointed to distribute its assets on the winding up of its affairs pursuant to section 117 of the General Corporation Law, or a receiver appointed under section 106 of the Stock Corporation Law is a permanent receiver. 

The receivers contemplated by the second and third subdivisions of section 974 will be briefly discussed in later sections of this chapter.¹2 § 600. Equity Receivers and Statutory Receivers. 

Receivers are either equity receivers, sometimes called chancery receivers and common law receivers, or statutory receivers. The equity receivers are the ones contemplated when the provisional remedy is under consideration. Such receivers were appointed by the courts of chancery before any statutes were passed authorizing their appointment, and the cases in which such receivers might be had and the rules regulating their appointment and governing their conduct were well settled before the Code of Civil Procedure was adopted in 1849. The Code provisions merely codify those well established rules,18 and the Civil Practice Act sections¹¹ continue the law as found in the Code.

§ 603. The Same-An Action Must be Pending and the Application 

Must be Made by a Party Thereto.

The appointment of a receiver pendente lite is never an end in itself. It is merely an incident in the course of an action. The action itself must have some other objective than the appointment of a receiver. Before application can be made for the appointment of a receiver the main action to which such appointment is an incident must be pending.29

Moreover, the application must be made by a party to the action. In O'Mahoney v. Belmont,3° a receiver was appointed without the application of any of the parties to the suit and seemingly against their wishes by the receiver's own solicitation. The court said: "Where such a right exists it is usually called in exercise upon the application of one or more of the parties in interest. While the court may upon its own motion nominate a receiver where the case requires it, such a proceeding cannot according to the regular practice be inaugurated and conducted by outside parties, who have no connection with the case, or interest in the subject-matter of the litigation. A person not having any interest cannot propose a receiver, and it is contrary to the orderly and regular proceedings of a court of justice to allow a stranger to participate in a motion for such an appointment. (Attorney-General v. Day, 2 Mad., 246; Edwards on 

Receivers, 22.)” 

29. Civil Practice Act, § 974. Em pire Trust Co. v. Kermacoe, Misc. 

266 N. Y. S. 685. 

30. 62 N. Y. 133, 142.
