§ 604. The Same - The Property Must be the Subject Matter of the Action. 

Section 974 of the Civil Practice Act specifically limits the appointment of a receiver to "property which is the subject of an action." This requisite excludes the possibility of having a receiver appointed in a great number of actions and limits the remedy for the most part to actions in equity. 

In common law actions for money a receiver can not be appointed, for such actions have no specific subject matter. 

In O'Mahoney v. Belmont,32 the court said: "The action was in reality for money had and received by the defendants, and if any liability existed, it arose from the purchase of bills of exchange of the defendants which had been delivered, and it is claimed were lost. It was not a legal claim for any specific property or fund which belonged to the plaintiff, but in reality an ordinary action to recover money. There is no principle which sanctions the appointment of a receiver in such a case, and it is entirely without a precedent to uphold it."

Thus where an action is brought to recover damages for fraud, deceit and misrepresentation on the part of the defendants as stockbrokers by which they induced the plaintiff to place moneys and a bond in their hands to be used in the purchase and sale of stock, the gravamen of the action is fraud and deceit and no receiver can be appointed. "There is no claim made for any specific property. The action does not involve property as such but is founded altogether in tort. 77 33 

31. Shubert v. Laughlin, 122 A. D. 

701; 107 N. Y. S. 708. 

32. 62 N. Y. 133, 142.

The ordinary common law actions that have a specific subject matter are replevin and ejectment. This requisite therefore excludes the possibility of a receiver in practically all common law actions excepting those two, which will be con-

77 N. Y. S. 574.

sidered later, and confines the appointment of a receiver to equitable actions like foreclosure, partition, dower, specific performance, actions for injunctions and the like. Replevin actions and actions in ejectment so far as the specific requisite now under consideration is concerned, might have a receiver appointed in them for they have a specific subject matter. 

Receivers, however, are seldom appointed in such actions because such actions fail to satisfy other conditions prerequisite to the appointment of a receiver and especially the one which denies the use of the remedy where any other adequate remedy provisional or otherwise may be had.³*

The requisite here under consideration is scrutinized carefully by the court and statutory actions which might on a casual examination seem to have a specific subject matter often on more careful examination are found not to have it. 

Thus the subject of an action to determine the validity of the probate of a will brought under a statute 35 which provided that the law "shall be confined to the question whether the writing produced is or is not the last will * of the testator," is not the property devised by the will, but it is the validity of the will; and, therefore, the court can not appoint a receiver to preserve such property pendente lite.30

In ejectment actions a receiver is seldom appointed for the reason that the plaintiff has other adequate remedies against loss or damage to the property. § 609. Clauses in Mortgages Authorizing the Appointment of a 

Receiver.

Mortgages often contain a clause whereby the mortgagor consents to the appointment of a receiver in any action to foreclose the mortgage and sometimes the clause authorizes the appointment without notice and without regard to the adequacy of any security for the debt. It has been contended that such clause being an agreement between the parties makes it incumbent upon the court to appoint a receiver in cases falling within its purview. It is now well 

Y. S. 446. Where, however in an action seeking an injunction adequate relief may not be had by the injunction, a receiver may be appointed, N. P. 

Bank v. Goddard et al 131 N. Y. 494; see section 639 post for a discussion of this case.

settled, however, that such clauses cannot control the court in the exercise of its discretion. The court will take such clause into consideration on the application for a receiver and will give weight to it as an agreement between the parties but it is not bound to specifically enforce it. In the leading case of Eidlitz v. Lancaster,62 Van Brunt, P. J., said: "It is true that the mortgage contains a receiver clause; but it is well established that the existence of such a clause gives the mortgagee no absolute right to the appointment of a receiver, the action for foreclosure being a proceeding in a court of equity; but that such a clause is to be considered among the other features of the case in determining the propriety of granting a motion for the appointment of a receiver."

Such clauses will not, therefore, dispense with the necessity of showing on the application for the appointment of a receiver the facts required in other cases before an appointment may be had but is to be used with other facts to aid in influencing the court in the exercise of its discretion. 63 Sometimes receivership clauses operate in favor of the mortgagor as where the clause provides for the appointment of a receiver on notice and a situation develops wherein a receiver might be appointed, in the absence of the clause, ex parte. § 610. The Appointment of a Receiver by or after Final Judgment.85 

A receiver may be appointed by or after final judgment, to carry the judgment into effect or to dispose of the property according to its directions. Illustrations of a receivership created for this purpose are not common but the power in the court to appoint a receiver for the purpose indicated is unmistakable. Thus in an action for an accounting between several partners who had entered upon a joint enterprise to buy certain lands and organize a corporation to take title thereto, each to contribute to the enterprise and take stock in the corporation in return for such contribution, it appeared that one Barnes who managed the enterprise fraudulently caused to be issued to himself most of the stock of the corporation and refused to transfer the same. 

The trial resulted in an interlocutory judgment in favor of the plaintiffs directing defendant Barnes to account and a final judgment was ultimately entered requiring the corporation to appoint an annual meeting and elect officers and the stock issued in Barnes' name was required to be transferred in different amounts to the plaintiffs. Though this judgment was affirmed by the Court of Appeals neither the corporation nor Barnes did as it required and on motion the Supreme Court entered an order appointing a receiver to carry into effect the final judgment by making the transfer of stock therein directed and by holding a meeting for the election of directors. The order appointing the receiver also ordered the persons having in possession the franchises, property, records and seal of the company to surrender the same to the receiver. On an appeal from this order the court said: 67

615. The Affidavit. 

The affidavit must show that the five prerequisites required by section 974 of the Civil Practice Act and discussed in the preceding sections 85 exist.

It must show that an action is pending in either the supreme or county court; 86 that such action has a specific subject matter and that the receivership is sought for that subject matter. It must also show that plaintiff has a right to or interest in the property; 88 that it is in the possession of the adverse party," and that there is danger that it will be removed beyond the jurisdiction of the court, or lost, materially injured or destroyed."⁰

If a verified complaint is used as one of the moving papers it will show the character of the action and whether it has a specific subject matter or not, and, if it has, it will show what that subject matter is. It will also show what plaintiff's interest in the property is and whether the defendant has it in his possession. Ordinarily the allegations in a verified complaint which are made on information and belief must be supplemented by an affidavit made by the source of the information when a provisional remedy is sought; but where the application for a receiver is made on notice and the adverse party thus has opportunity to contradict the allegations in the moving papers, the necessity for such supporting affidavits is not apparent and is not insisted on by the courts.91

Plaintiffs will not consent to this inequitable arrangement and in order to protect their security are compelled to begin this foreclosure action and to ask for the appointment of a receiver of the rents pendente lite.

There is a five-story "walk up" apartment house on the premises with small apartments for twenty families and I am informed by my inspector, who made the inspection of said premises, Harry H.

Taxes amount to the sum of $550.50 for the second half of 1917, which are still unpaid.

This foreclosure action promises to be a protracted action because of the numerous and widely scattered defendants. It is probable that some are infants and that the summons herein will have to be published against certain of the defendants. With interest and taxes alone amounting to about $3,500.00 a year, it is apparent that unless a receiver of rents is appointed, the amount due plaintiff at the time of sale under foreclosure (with the costs and expenses) might add 10% to the amount due on the principal of the mortgage. I verily believe that under present market conditions, the premises are not sufficient security for that amount and that the plaintiff should not be required to wait for months while the temporary administratrix is collecting and withholding the rentals which should be applied to the upkeep, expenses, taxes and the mortgage interest.

§ 617. The Order. 

The order must be made by the court whether obtained ex parte or on notice.93 The recital part of the order enumerates the papers upon which the application is made with such

elaboration as the taste of the attorney may determine. The directory part of the order should contain the following: 1. A blank space for the name and address of the receiver to be appointed. 

2. A designation of the property over which the receivership is sought.** 

3. A provision that the receiver before entering upon his duties file with the proper clerk a bond to the people with sufficient sureties in a penal sum which should be left blank in the form of order for the determination of the court, and conditioned upon the faithful discharge of his duties.95 

4. A provision defining the duties and powers of the receiver. With regard to this provision it is customary to use the phrase "with the usual powers." These powers are defined in the ordinary case by rule 175 of the rules of Civil Practice which authorizes the receiver to do a number of things without other or further special direction of the court. 

5. A direction to those in possession of the property over which the receiver is appointed to deliver the same to the receiver.

It is not considered proper in the order appointing a receiver to provide that the receiver may bring a particular action or actions generally or defend them, since some investigation by the court as to the propriety of beginning each particular action or defending it is contemplated before the authority to begin the action or defend it is conferred.ºº

§ 619. The Receiver's Bond. 

After the receiver is appointed and before entering upon his official duties, he must execute and file a bond to the people in a penalty fixed by the court, judge or referee in the order by which he was appointed and conditioned upon the faithful discharge of his duties as receiver.98 The bond is not void if it runs to the plaintiff instead of to the people but may be enforced as a common law bond." The "proper clerk" is the clerk of the county in which the action is triable.¹ The amount of the bond is determined by the court making the appointment and should bear some relation to the extent of the property placed in the receiver's custody. Even a receiver appointed in a matrimonial action is required to execute and file a bond for the faithful discharge of his duties.2

§ 621. Powers and Duties of Receiver-In General. 

As stated before, a receiver pendente lite is merely a custodian of the property during the pendency of the action. 

He acquires no title to the property committed to his charge.* 

He is entitled merely to the possession of the property as an officer of the court. He takes the property as he finds it subject to attachment liens or otherwise and preserves it." 

He can do very little without a special order or direction from the court. He is the representative of the court and if the necessity arises for action with reference to the property he makes application to the court for instructions and direction with reference to the matter. 

§ 622. The Same-Taking Possession of the Property. 

The receiver should take possession of the property if he can do so peaceably. The order appointing him is sufficient authority for this. The practice is for the receiver to serve a certified copy of the order appointing him, together with a written demand for the possession of the property upon the person or persons having possession thereof. If possession is refused on such demand contempt proceedings may be

If the person having possession of the property holds it under a claim of right thereto the receiver may, with the permission of the court, begin an action against such person to determine his right to the property, or such person may be made a party to the suit in which the receiver was appointed and an order extending the receivership to such property made; then if the party still refuses to turn over the property to the receiver contempt proceedings will lie against him. 

Once in possession of the property it is the duty of the receiver to retain such possession. Even a sheriff who had made a levy upon the property prior to the appointment of the receiver is not authorized to take the property out of the possession of the receiver and sell it under such execution. It is otherwise if the property never came into the possession of the receiver.10 Likewise an attachment of the property in the hands of the receiver can not be made without the permission of the court.¹¹

§ 624. The Same - Bringing Actions and Defending Them. 

Rule 175 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that "Unless restricted by the special order of the court, every receiver of the property of a debtor may sue for and collect all the

He may sue also in the name of the debtor, 14b where it is necessary or proper for him to do so; * * * He is not to be allowed for the costs of any action brought by him against an insolvent from whom he is unable to collect his costs, unless such action is brought by permission of the court, or by consent of all persons interested in the funds in his hands. 

It is obvious from the foregoing quotation from the rule, that a receiver may without special leave of the court sue for and collect all the debts, demands and rents belonging to such debtor. This is not, however, authority to bring actions generally and is limited to the types of actions thus enumerated. Indeed, it is wiser for the receiver to obtain permission from the court to bring even the actions indicated in the rule since he becomes personally liable for costs where judgment is recovered against him,15 and he receives no costs even if he is successful provided the defendant is insolvent unless he has obtained leave from the court to begin the action.16 Even where the receiver applies to the court for leave to bring an action he must show on such application that he has sufficient property in his actual possession to secure the person against whom the action is to be brought for any costs which he may recover against the receiver; otherwise the court may require the receiver to give a bond conditioned for the payment of such costs.17

The receiver would have to obtain leave of the court to bring an action other than those indicated in the quotation above from Rule 175, as for example an action of ejectment,18 or an action to declare a conveyance of a mortgage or the assignment thereof void for fraud.19 If leave is given to bring an action the receiver may sue, however, in a court other than the one in which he is appointed.20

§ 625. The Same - Dealing with Tenants and Making Leases. 

"Without notice, he may apply for an order that the tenants of any real property belonging to the debtor shall pay the rents and profits thereof to the receiver. He may be permitted by the court to make leases from time to time. He may be permitted to make repairs necessary to the preservation of the property; but, without leave of the court, he shall not make improvements or substantial repairs to real property."22

Prior to the adoption of the Civil Practice Act a receiver might without obtaining leave of the court make leases from time to time for terms not exceeding one year. This has been changed by the rule quoted above and now permission of the court is necessary in all cases irrespective of the length of the term, before a receiver may make leases of the property. This regulation makes less likely the leasing of the property by the receiver for a term that would extend for an unreasonable period beyond the termination of the litigation. If a lease would extend unreasonably beyond the termination of the litigation it is not for that reason void altogether. The lease in such case will not be sustained eyond the termination of the litigation but the lessee must be indemnified.23 The part of Rule 175 quoted above indicates that the receiver may make necessary repairs without leave of the court for the preservation of the property, but that he can not make substantial repairs or improvements without such leave. The permission thus given to the receiver to make necessary repairs is construed strictly."

§ 626. The Same-Disposing of Property. 

"It shall be his duty, without unreasonable delay, to convert the debtor's personal property into money. * * * By leave of the court, he may sell desperate debts and other doubtful claims of personal property, at public auction, giving at least ten days' public notice of the time and place of such sale; or by like leave he may compromise and settle such as are unsafe or of doubtful character. 9727 As the receiver pendente lite has no title to the property he cannot sell the same without direction from the court, and if the property is not of a perishable character it should be sold.28 If the title to the property is. in dispute and third parties claim it, no order should be granted directing a sale of such property.² 29 "It is not a justification for taking away and selling a man's possessions under such circumstances to tell him that he may assert his claim against the proceeds just as well as against the property.' In Brush v. Jay, the court said: "The authority of the court over such assets of the firm, as are either admitted by the pleadings or are judicially determined to be in the firm, is undoubted; but the power to order a sale of all property in the possession of a firm, which, in the usual course of business is frequently the custodian of the property of others, upon the mere fact of such possession, is not, we think, sustainable upon reason or authority, and its exercise is likely to produce manifest and irreparable wrong and injustice.

§ 628. The Same - Accounting. 

The receiver pendente lite is continued after judgment merely for the purpose of settling his accounts and distributing the property in his hands to those designated in the final judgment. 84 In presenting his accounts as receiver he must give notice to the sureties upon his official bond," and his accounts shall not be "passed, settled or allowed" unless such notice shall have been first given. 36

§ 630. Relation to Provisional Remedies. 

2 Replevin is not one of the provisional remedies. It has, however, some of the characteristics of one. It is a common law action to recover a chattel but incident to its prosecution the chattel may be seized and held to wait the outcome of the litigation. It is not essential to the prosecution of the action that the chattel be seized, that is replevied. The action may proceed without such seizure. In such case replevin is an ordinary action. The right to seize or replevy the property before the commencement of the action or during its progress is the feature of this action which makes it resemble the provisional remedy of attachment. An attachment, however, may be had in almost any kind of an action seeking a money judgment, while the seizure of the chattel in replevin is limited to that particular type of action where the object sought is the recovery of the specific chattel — not money although it is possible to get the value of the chattel in the action if the chattel itself is not recoverable. As in the case of an attachment, the seizure of the property may be had in advance of the service of the summons.* In the case of an attachment, however, the summons must be personally served or its service by publication commenced within thirty days thereafter, while in the case of seizure by replevin no time is specified for the commencement of the action thereafter." 

§ 631. The Same - Jurisdiction. 

1. The provisions of the Civil Prac tice Act relating to replevin are the same in substance as those of the Code of Civil Procedure except that § 1011a, relating to the disposition of perishable goods is new, having been added to the Civil Practice Act by the Laws of 1921, chapter 199. 

2. Civil Practice Act, § 1116, Crocker- 

In the case of provisional remedies, the court has jurisdiction from the time of the granting of the provisional remedy and may control all subsequent proceedings, although the summons be not served.' Where a chattel is replevied before the service of the summons, the seizure is regarded "as equivalent to the granting of a provisional remedy for the

11 purpose of giving jurisdiction to the court and enabling it to control the subsequent proceedings in the action." In the case of a provisional remedy jurisdiction acquired by the granting of the remedy in advance of the service of the summons is conditional and is liable to be divested where some affirmative action, required by law to retain it, is not taken." 

Where, for example, a warrant of attachment is granted and a levy made thereunder in advance of the service of the summons and no step is taken to effect the service of the summons within the next thirty days, the jurisdiction acquired by the court on the granting of the warrant is divested and the whole proceeding is void ab initio.10 In the case of a seizure through replevin, however, no affirmative act is required to retain jurisdiction and jurisdiction continues unless divested by affirmative action of some one opposing the litigation. In Kurzweil v. Story and Clark 

Piano Co. certain pianos were replevied. The defendant was never served with a summons and never appeared in the action. Nevertheless, the plaintiff procured a judgment. The defendant thereafter sued the plaintiff to recover the money paid on account of the purchase price of the pianos before they were replevied. The validity of the judgment which had been obtained in the replevin action was considered by the court. If such judgment was void for lack of jurisdiction in the court it could be attacked collaterally.12 If the court had jurisdiction such judgment although irregular for want of service of the summons is binding until set aside by direct attack in the same action.18 It was held that the court in the replevin suit had jurisdiction over the subject matter because the seizure in that action was "equivalent to the commencement of the action for the purpose of determining whether the plaintiff is entitled to maintain the action or the defendant is liable thereto," and therefore the collateral attack in the pending action was not available.15

§ 633. The Same - Election of Remedies- Consistency. 

It has often been contended that the commencement of the action of replevin bars one's right thereafter to prosecute for the same cause an action for trespass or conversion and vice versa.24 

The theory is that these remedies are inconsistent, because in replevin title to the chattels is presumed to continue in the plaintiff, while in conversion, title passes to the defendant and the plaintiff rests content with the damages for the wrong. For these reasons, it is said that the election to prosecute one of these types of action bars plaintiff's right later to pursue the other.25 The weight of authority, however, is to the contrary. By this contrary view one joint tort feasor may be pursued in conversion, another in replevin and both actions may proceed at the same time. Even the entry of a judgment against the one sued in conversion before the action in replevin is started against the other, does not bar the replevin action, unless and until the judgment in the conversion action is fully satisfied. A judgment in conversion does not effect a transfer of title to the property converted and replevin therefore is still open to plaintiff against any other person who may have the property or contributed in the tortious conduct.26 In Cramer v. Brownell27 plaintiff sued in replevin for the recovery of a horse from the defendant. The defense was that prior to the commencement of the suit, plaintiff had sued one Wilson to recover damages for converting the horse in question and that such suit constituted an election of a remedy inconsistent with the pending action and was a bar thereto. The trial court adopted

Linde Co., 162 A. D. 543; 147 N. Y. S. 1045.

On appeal to the Appellate Division, Woodward, J., said: "In this we are of the opinion that the learned court erred to the prejudice of the plaintiff's rights; that the plaintiff is not bound to rely upon her cause of action against Wilson, but may exhaust her remedy against any one who has wrongfully taken and withheld her property, though she cannot receive the mare and her damages for retention, and then continue the prosecution of the action against Brownell. She is entitled to recover as against either or both of them, and the payment of one judgment will discharge both, but until there is a judgment, and until such judgment has been paid, the plaintiff, as against tort feasors, is not within the doctrine of election. He may, under certain circumstances, waive a tort and proceed in assumpsit, in which case he would be barred from asserting an action sounding in tort (7 Ency. of P. & Pr. 371), but trespass, trover and replevin all proceed upon the theory of continued ownership in the injured party, and are not inconsistent remedies. (7 

Ency. of P. & Pr. 371, and authorities cited.)" 28 The judgment in this case was affirmed by the Court of Appeals.2 

§ 634. Relation of Replevin to Contract Actions - Inconsistency. 

A person who sells goods for cash and delivers the property to the purchaser before receiving the money may replevy the goods from the purchaser, the theory being that the purchaser obtained the possession by fraud and that plaintiff never parted with his title. If, however, instead of replevying the goods the plaintiff sued for the purchase price, he may not thereafter maintain an action in replevin since by suing for the purchase price he has affirmed the title to the goods in the defendant and has made a binding election."" 

28. 222 N. Y. 705. A distinction is made between actions based on the joint and several liability of joint tort feasors thus expressed and those based on contracts imposing joint and several liability. In the latter cases the principle is thus stated by the Court of Appeals: "I think there is a radical difference in principle between a joint and several obligation evidenced by an expressed contract or arising by implication from the facts proved, and a joint and several liability on the part of several tort feasors. A joint and several obligation based on a note, bond or other written contract, or one arising out of an implied contract, is a well known kind of obligation, and its legal meaning has come to be that each one is liable to a separate suit, or that all are liable to a joint suit, and in no other way can they be held. (Russell v. McCall et al., 141 N. Y. 437, 452; see also Cramer v. Brownell, 166 A. 

D. 456, 458; 151 N. Y. S. 1001)."

§ 635. Who May Maintain the Action for Replevin. 

32 Replevin is a possessory action and any one who has a present right to possession of the chattel may maintain it.30 

This is true whether plaintiff's property in the goods is absolute or qualified and whether he was deprived of his possession thereof by a wrongful taking or a wrongful detention.³¹ 

The right to possession is the issue to be determined." The owner may, of course, replevy the goods if he has a present right to the possession of them. But one who by contract with the owner has a right to the possession of the chattel may maintain replevin against the owner. So also one who has a lien on the goods may replevin them from the owner.34 33 In Baker v. Hoag certain goods were lost in a canal boat sunk in tide water, and plaintiff who was not the owner later recovered part of the goods by dragging the canal boat to the shore. The owner took the goods without the consent of the plaintiff who brought replevin against the owner and successfully maintained it. It was held that he had a lien on the goods and therefore a right to possession until his lien was satisfied. He had no general property in the goods but he had a sufficient special property in them to entitle him to their immediate possession. § 637. What Property May be Replevied. 

Real property may not be replevied. The action of ejectment must be resorted to to recover the possession of real estate. Personal property only may be reached by replevin. 

It is difficult often, however, to determine whether certain property is personal and replevinable or is real property and is not. The substantive law relating to fixtures is involved here. Thus, standing timber is real property, but when severed from the land the logs become chattels and may be replevied.53 On the other hand, personal property may become so attached to real estate that it will lose its character as personalty and become real property. In such case it may not be replevied. Thus, bricks may be made into a house. Generally speaking the intention of the parties as between themselves governs in the determination of the question whether the chattel has become a part of the realty. In the absence of other proof the mode of annexation will control. As was said by Rapallo, J., in the case of McRea v.

Central National Bank of Troy:54 

52 "The mode of annexation may, it is true, in the absence of other proof of intent, be controlling. It may be in itself so inseparable and permanent as to render the article necessarily a part of the realty, and in case of less thorough annexation the mode of attachment may afford convincing evidence that the intention was that the attachment should be permanent; as, for instance, where the building is constructed expressly to receive the machine or other articles, and it could not be removed without material injury to the building, or where the article would be of no value except for use in that particular building, or could not be removed therefrom without being destroyed or greatly damaged. 

51. Van Slooten v. Dodge, 145 N. Y. 

327; Reimers v. Schmitt, 68 A. D. 299, 74 N. Y. S. 122. 

52. Smith v. Benson, 1 Hill 176.

Special circumstances, however, often enter into the determination of the intention of the parties. The relation of landlord and tenant between them may be material in ascertaining their intention with regard to chattels used on the 

53. Johnson v. Elwood, 53 N. Y. 433, ef. Church v. Grossi, 124 Misc. 192. 

54. 66 N. Y. 489.

REPLEVIN. 

premises, or the parties may specifically set forth their intention with regard thereto, which is a common thing in a conditional sales agreement. Thus a tenant who places machinery in a leased building for the purpose of manufacture or trade contemplated in the lease, may remove it.55 If, however, the tenant does not remove the chattels on the termination of the lease, or renews the lease without reserving the right to remove the chattels they become fixtures. Again, the vendor of a chattel may enter into an express contract with the vendee that the same shall retain its character as personal property even though it be annexed to the realty. The parties are permitted to enter into such a contract and their intention thus expressed will control subject only to the limitation that where the subject or mode of annexation is such that the attributes of personal property cannot be predicated of the thing in question, as where the property could not be removed without practically destroying it, or where it is essential to the support of that to which it is attached, the chattel becomes a part of the real estate notwithstanding the expressed intention of the parties to the contrary.58 While the expressed intention of the parties will control to the extent just stated as between themselves, bona fide purchasers or encumbrancers of the premises without actual or constructive notice of such agreements are not affected thereby and as to them the manner of annexation is the controlling feature in determining the character of the property in question.50 50

§ 639. The Same Identification Necessary. 

The personal property which may be made the subjectmatter of an action in replevin must be capable of specific identification. As a rule, therefore, money is not subject to replevin. If, however, money is identifiable replevin will lie for its recovery." 66 

A change in the form of the goods does not necessarily defeat the right of replevin. If the identity of the original materials can be established a change in the form of the goods, wrought by labor or skill, will not defeat replevin, as where plaintiff's corn is converted into whiskey, his logs into lumber or his leather into shoes." The difficulty of identifying the specific property sought is also experienced where there is a confusion of goods as where grain of different owners is commingled. In such case no owner can identify his own. Where, however, the property is alike in quality and value and is divisible by weight or measure, the plaintiff may take out his share by replevin.68 If the grain of the plaintiff can not be separated from that of the defendant, the defendant who is guilty of the confusion must suffer the loss. The difficulties which may arise out of a confusion of goods are well illustrated in the case of N. P. Bank v. Goddard. There a firm of clothing manufacturers, pursuant to a plan to defraud, had, by false representations, procured materials from different sources and manufactured the same into clothing. Cloth purchased from one vendor had been combined with the linings of another and the buttons of a third. On the discovery of the fraud, the bank, which had loaned money to the firm and was one of its victims, attached the entire stock of clothing. Whereupon those who had sold materials to the firm rescinded the sales on account of the fraud and brought separate actions in replevin against the sheriff and the fraudulent vendees to recover the specific 70

§ 640. Restrictions on the Right to Maintain the Action. 

The Civil Practice Act, assuming the right to maintain the action, rests content with a statement of when the action can not be maintained." It specifies three classes of actions whereunder the general principles heretofore discussed, replevin would lie but in which by statute the action can not be maintained. These are: "1. Where the chattel was taken by virtue of a warrant against the plaintiff for the collection of a tax, assessment or fine issued in pursuance of a statute of the state or of the United States, unless the taking was, or the detention is, unlawful."

If a collector of a tax or fine seized the property of A in an attempt to satisfy a tax against B, the taking would be unlawful and replevin may be resorted to."2 Such is not the kind of seizure protected by the section. If, however, the ownership of the property is not disputed and the regularity of the proceeding alone is questioned, replevin will not lie unless it is apparent upon the face of the warrant for the collection of the tax or fine that it was issued without jurisdiction." "2. Where it was seized by virtue of an execution or a warrant of attachment against the property of the plaintiff or of any person from or through whom the plaintiff has derived title since the seizure thereof, unless it was legally exempt from such seizure or is unlawfully detained." 

71. Civil Practice Act, § 1089. 

72. L. S. & M. S. Railway Co. v. 

Roach et al., 80 N. Y. 339. 

73. Hudler v. Golden, 36 N. Y. 446.

REPLEVIN. 

745 74 This limitation prevents the plaintiff from replevying from the sheriff his own goods, which were taken on execution against him, or by virtue of an attachment against his property, but it will not prevent the plaintiff from replevying his own goods from the sheriff mistakenly taken by the sheriff in satisfaction of an execution or warrant of attachment against a third person."

It should be observed that while goods held by the sheriff under an execution may be taken from his possession by replevin at the instance of a third party claimant, goods held by the sheriff under a writ of replevin may not be taken from his possession under an execution against the defendant in the replevin action." The reason is that the judgment creditor can only claim through the title of his debtor and the property having been lawfully removed from the possession of the latter and being held in the custody of the law for final adjudication, he can not disturb that custody. "3. Where it was seized by virtue of an execution or a warrant of attachment against the property of a person other than the plaintiff and at the time of the commencement of the action the plaintiff had not the right to reduce it into his possession." 

The present wording of this subdivision makes it possible for a plaintiff, who has parted with his property by reason of the fraudulent representations of the vendee, to rescind the sale because of the fraud and replevin the goods even though at the time of the commencement of his replevin action the sheriff has them in his possession under an execution against the vendee. As the section was originally worded the rescission of the sale because of the fraud had to take place prior to the seizure under the execution, otherwise plaintiff could not replevy the goods." An amendment of the Code section, which has been superseded by subdivision 3 of section 1089, effected by the laws of 1894, chapter 305, substituted for the phrase "at the time of the seizure" which was contained in the section prior to that time, the phrase "at the time of the commencement of the action" which is now found there. This renders the decision in Wise v. Grant, supra, obsolete. 

74. Frost v. Mott, 34 N. Y. 253; 

Johnson v. Carnley, 10 N. Y. 570. 

75. First National Bank of Oswego v. Dunn et al., 97 N. Y. 149. 

76. Wise v. Grant, 140 N. Y. 593.

§ 641. When the Sheriff May be Required to Replevy. 

The plaintiff may require the sheriff to replevy a chattel when the summons is issued or at any time afterward and before the service of a copy of the defendant's answer, or where judgment is taken by default for want of appearance or pleading, before the entry of final judgment." 

§ 642. Necessary Papers. 

It should be noted here that the action of replevin may be maintained without any seizure of the chattels which constitute the subject-matter thereof. In such case the action of replevin is prosecuted like any other action, that is to say, the summons and complaint are served upon the defendant, and the subsequent steps follow the course of an ordinary action. If, however, the chattel is seized, or replevied at the commencement of the action or thereafter as indicated in the preceding section, the necessary papers to effect the seizure require careful attention. 

These are:79 . a. An affidavit, b. A requisition, and c. An undertaking. 

They will be considered in order. 

§ 643. The Same - The Affidavit. 

The contents of the affidavit is prescribed in section 1096 of the Civil Practice Act.80 It is well in drawing the affidavit to follow as nearly as practicable the subdivisions of that section. 

It should state: 

1. That the plaintiff is the owner of the chattel and if that be the fact such allegation will suffice without more, since ownership imports the right to possession. Plaintiff, however, may without being the owner maintain replevin and in such case the affidavit should state that plaintiff is entitled to the immediate possession of the chattel. In the latter case such allegation will not suffice but must be followed by a state-

That is to say it must state the authority of the agent or attorney to represent the plaintiff. It must also state what allegations, if any, are made upon the affiant's information and belief, and it must set forth the grounds of his belief as to all matters not stated upon his knowledge and the reason why the affidavit is not made by the plaintiff.97 

In showing the grounds of his belief the affiant must set out the evidentiary facts which induce his belief and not merely the ultimate facts which summarize the evidence. 

The following criticism by Mr. Justice Greenbaums of the affidavit submitted by an attorney for defendant to obtain the return of a replevied check applies equally well to the affidavit of an attorney for plaintiff used in procuring the seizure. 

96. Civil Practice Act, § 1110. 

97. Civil Practice Act, § 1110. 

"The affidavits upon which the attorneys for the defendant seek to obtain a return of the replevied check are, in my opinion, insufficient. The authority of the attorneys to represent the defendant is not disclosed, and the authority of the clerk of defendant's attorneys is still less apparent. But, assuming that the affiant was authorized to make the affidavit, it appears here that the grounds of his belief are stated to be 'letters and other communications received' from the father of the defendant, who resides in Michigan, and 'conversations had with and communications received from' a former attorney of the defendant in another action between the same parties concerning the matter which is the subject of the present action, without setting forth copies of the letters or the substance of the conversations or communications. It is not enough to state the sources of information to be statements, conversations and letters made by, had with, and received from, third parties, but the statements, conversations and letters themselves must be given in order that the court may determine whether they justify the conclusion drawn by the affiant. Matter of Bronson, 78 Hun, 351; Ladenburg v. Commercial 

Bank, 87 id. 269, 275; Steuben Co. Bank v. Alberger, 78 N. Y. 252.

It is not made apparent how the father or former attorney is possessed of the information or facts upon which the affiant relies. Where an affidavit is made on information and belief it is essential that the information should appear to be competently derived and the sources thereof must be disclosed in such a way as to enable the court to decide upon the probable truth of the statements and the authenticity of the jurisdictional facts. Murphy v. Jack, 142 N. Y. 215.”

§ 645. The Same - The Requisition. 

The requisition is a writing addressed generally to the sheriff of any county or to the sheriff of the particular county where the chattel is found requiring such sheriff to replevy the chattel described therein. It is endorsed upon or annexed to the affidavit and subscribed by the attorney for the plaintiff. It is deemed the mandate of the court. In the Municipal 

Court of the City of New York, the requisition must be endorsed by the court or a justice thereof, and must be issued by the clerk. 2 § 646. The Same-Form of Affidavit on Replevin and Requisition.

Office & P. O. Address, § 647. The Same - The Undertaking. 

The undertaking to be delivered to the sheriff with a requisition to replevy a chattel must be executed by at least two

REPLEVIN. 

sureties who must be approved by the sheriff. It must be to the effect that the sureties are bound in a specified sum, not less than twice the value of the chattel, as stated in the affidavit, for the prosecution of the action, for the return of the chattel to the defendant, if possession thereof is adjudged to him, or if the action abates or is discontinued before the chattel is returned to the defendant; and for the payment to the defendant of any sum which the judgment awards to him against the plaintiff. This undertaking secures the defendant's costs and a separate bond for that purpose is not required though plaintiff be a non-resident or a foreign corporation. But it inures only to the benefit of the defendant whose possession of the chattel is invalid and a defendant brought into the action by order of the court cannot claim under it. If the plaintiff fails in the action but does not return the chattel to the defendant, the value of the chattel and not the penalty specified in the bond is the measure of the sureties' liability,' and while the undertaking provides that the sureties will pay to the defendant any sum which the judgment awards to him against the plaintiff this would not cover a judgment awarded to the defendant on a counterclaim which had no connection with the replevied chattels.

§ 649. How Chattel to be Replevied. 

"If any chattel described in the affidavit is found in the possession of the defendant or his agent, the sheriff to whom an affidavit, requisition and undertaking are delivered, as prescribed in the foregoing sections of this article, must replevy it forthwith by taking it into his possession. He thereupon without delay, must serve on the defendant a copy of the affidavit, requisition and undertaking, by delivering the same to him personally if he can be found within the county; or, if he cannot be so found, to his agent, if any, from whose possession the chattel is taken; or, if neither can be found within the county, by leaving the copy at the usual place of abode of either with a person of suitable age and discretion. If any chattel described in the affidavit is secured or concealed in a building or inclosure, the sheriff must publicly demand its delivery. If it is not delivered pursuant to the demand, he must cause the building or inclosure to be broken open and must take the chattel into his possession. "'9 9a While it has been held that if the sheriff cannot find the chattel, though the defendant has it in his possession, an order of the court may be obtained requiring defendant to turn it over to the sheriff and punishing him as for a contempt if he refuses to do so, it has also been decided that the court has no power inherent or otherwise in the absence of statute, summarily to order a defendant in a replevin action to come in and disclose information as to the location of the goods to be seized."b

§ 650. The Defendant's Courses. 

The defendant from whose possession the chattel or chattels have been replevied has two courses open to him. He may except to plaintiff's sureties," or he may reclaim the chattel or chattels.12 In either case he must act within three days from the time when the chattel was replevied.13 If he takes neither course the sheriff must deliver the chattel to the plaintiff or answer to him for damages and a penalty of two hundred and fifty dollars, unless in the meantime a third party claims it, and even if plaintiff's sureties become insolvent thereafter he has no redress.¹ 14 15 

§ 651. The Same - Exception to Plaintiff's Sureties and Justifica tion Thereof.

If defendant decides to take exception to the plaintiff's sureties, he must within three days after the chattel is replevied serve upon the sheriff a notice that he excepts to them. Where the defendant has not appeared, the notice must be subscribed either by him or by his agent or attorney. 

The person so subscribing the notice must add to his signature his office address as prescribed by law with respect to a notice of appearance. Within ten days after service of such a notice the plaintiff's attorney must serve upon defendant's attorney or, if the defendant has not appeared, upon the sheriff, notice of the justification of the sureties. If the notice of justification is served upon the sheriff he must serve it immediately upon the person whose name is subscribed to the notice of exception in the mode prescribed by law for the service of a paper upon an attorney in an action.16

The justification of the sureties must take place either in the county where the chattel was replevied or in the county where one of the sureties resides. It takes place in the manner

§ 653. Sheriff's Disposition of the Chattel. 

The sheriff who has replevied a chattel must retain it in his possession, keeping it in a secure place until the person who is entitled to the possession thereof is ascertained when he must deliver it to such person, upon request and payment of his lawful fees and necessary expenses for taking and keeping it.26 This does not mean that the sheriff must retain possession until a final judgment is obtained in the action. 

The person entitled to possession of the chattel under this provision is determined in a very short time. The plaintiff is entitled to the possession of the chattel in each of the following cases unless a third party claims possession thereof. (a) If the defendant neither excepts to the plaintiff's sureties nor requires the return of the chattel within three days after it has been replevied.27 (b) If the defendant excepts to the plaintiff's sureties and the plaintiff thereafter procures through the justification of his sureties, the allowance of his undertaking. (c) If the defendant reclaims the chattel but fails within three days after service of the reclamation notice to serve notice of justification of his own sureties on the undertaking given by him or having given such notice his sureties fail to justify thereafter.20

§ 655. Claims of Third Persons. 

41 At any time before a chattel which has been replevied is actually delivered to either party, if a person not a party to the action claims as against the defendant a right to the possession thereof existing at the time when it was replevied, an affidavit may be made and delivered to the sheriff in his behalf, stating that he makes such a claim; specifying the chattel or chattels to which it relates, if two or more chattels have been replevied, and the claim relates only to part of them; and setting forth the facts upon which his right of possession depends." This method of procedure is not exclusive however. The third party may on his own application be made a party defendant in the action and assert his claim as such, or he may resort to other means recognized by law for procuring his rights. In case the third party claimant decides to assert his claim by filing an affidavit stating the same with the sheriff, he may maintain an action against the sheriff if the sheriff turns the chattel over to the plaintiff." 

The sheriff, in his discretion, before he delivers to the plaintiff, may, to avoid such liability, serve upon the plaintiff's attorney a copy of the affidavit, with a notice that he requires indemnity against the claim. If the indemnity is not furnished within a reasonable time after the plaintiff becomes entitled to the delivery of the chattel, the sheriff, in his discretion, may deliver the chattel to the claimant, without incurring any liability to the plaintiff by reason of so doing."" 42 If the plaintiff furnishes the indemnity it will consist of a written undertaking running to the sheriff executed by at least two sureties to the effect that they will indemnify him against any liability for damages, costs or expenses to be incurred in an action brought against him by the claimant, not exceeding a sum to be specified in the undertaking, which must be at least five hundred dollars and not less than the actual value of the chattel claimed, and two hundred and fifty dollars in addition thereto.15 Before delivering the chattel

§ 656. Return by the Sheriff. 

The sheriff within twenty days after he has delivered a chattel replevied by him to a party entitled to the possession thereof, or to a third person as indicated in the last two sections must file with the clerk the plaintiff's affidavit and the accompanying requisitions with a return stating in what manner he has executed the latter. If he fails to do so either party may require him so to do within ten days after service of a notice to that effect or to show cause at a term of the court designated in the notice why he should not be punished for a contempt of the court. This notice may be served at any time before final judgment except that it can not be served on the part of the defendant before answering.50 

§ 657. Second and Subsequent Replevin. 

Where the sheriff has replevied a part only of a chattel or of two or more chattels described in the plaintiff's affidavit and has served upon the defendant the papers required upon such a replevin, the plaintiff at any time before the service of a copy of the defendant's answer or before judgment by default for want of an appearance or pleading may require the same or any other sheriff to replevy any other part thereof. For that purpose he must deliver to the sheriff an affidavit containing the same allegations and a requisition and undertaking with respect to the part yet to be replevied as if the action were brought to recover that part only. The proceedings are exactly the same as if the former replevin had not been made."

§ 658. Replevin Where Order of Arrest Has Been Granted. 

The two remedies, arrest and replevin, can not be in full operation at the same time. Where a defendant has been arrested pursuant to an order of arrest, a subsequent replevin can not be made of a chattel with respect to which the order was granted. Similarly, if the defendant has not been arrested a subsequent replevin of a chattel with respect to which the order was granted supersedes the order.52 

§ 659. Service of the Summons in Replevin. 

As was stated heretofore, the action in replevin may be begun by the service of a summons without replevying the chattel and proceed in the usual course of the ordinary action. When the chattel is replevied before the commencement of the action it is customary to deliver the summons to the sheriff with the affidavit, undertaking and requisition and service of the summons is made upon the defendant at the same time that the chattel is replevied and the other papers are delivered to him. Thereafter the defendant's appearance and the pleadings proceed in the usual way. It is possible, however, that the sheriff may not be able to serve the summons at the same time that he requisitions the chattel. He may requisition the chattel from defendant's agent but the service of the summons must be made upon the defendant, and delivery thereof to the agent will not suffice. No time is fixed by the statute within which the summons must be served after the chattel has been replevied. In this it differs from the case where property is attached by the sheriff, for in such case service of the summons must be made or service by publication begun within thirty days after the granting of the warrant." 54 53 

§ 660. Pleadings in Replevin- The Complaint. 

There are special rules in relation to some of the statements to be made in the complaint in a replevin action which permit pleading certain legal conclusions, and a brief discussion of the allegations of the complaint and the manner of stating them is therefore desirable. The necessary allegations in such a complaint are:

761 (1) Plaintiff's ownership of the chattel or facts from which the right to possession without ownership is established. If ownership is relied on the statement that plaintiff was, at the time when the action was commenced or the chattel was replevied as the case may be, the owner of the chattel or that it was then his property is sufficient as a statement of title, without more, since ownership imports the right to possession. If the right to possession by virtue of a special property is relied on it will not do simply to state that plaintiff, at the time when the action was commenced or the chattel replevied, had a right to the possession of the chattel, but the facts which show such right must be set forth in the usual way. 56 It is important that plaintiff should determine at this point whether he will rely upon general ownership or a special property to establish his right to possession, which is the issue to be established, not only because as just shown a different rule applies in the manner of asserting the right to possession in the two cases, but for the further reason that a claim of ownership is a waiver of a lien which carries with it the right to possession, since such claim is inconsistent therewith," and if at the trial plaintiff fails to establish ownership when he has alleged it he will fail altogether in his action.58 (2) The wrongful taking or detention of the chattel by the defendant. If the complaint contains a sufficient statement of the plaintiff's title, a general allegation that the defendant wrongfully took the chattel, is sufficient without setting forth the facts showing that the taking was wrongful. If, however, the taking of the chattel is not complained of but the action is founded on its wrongful detention, the complaint must set forth the facts showing that the detention was wrongful.” A complaint which simply alleges that the defendant wrongfully took the chattel is satisfactory but a complaint which alleges simply that the defendant wrongfully detained the chattel is not. To the latter allegation must be added a statement of the facts and circumstances connected with the detention

§ 661. The Same The Answer. 

70 The answer in a replevin action should conform to the general rules of pleading. Under a general denial the defendant puts in issue plaintiff's title and his own wrongful detention. Under it he may prove title to the chattel in the nature of general ownership in a third party without connecting himself with such title," but he cannot under it show title in the nature of a special property in a third person without connecting himself with such interest. If it becomes necessary for defendant to allege ownership of the chattel in himself or in a third person at the commencement of the action or when the chattel was replevied such allegations are made as plaintiff makes them in his complaint." Likewise, if his defense rests on the right of possession by virtue of a special property, the facts upon which the special property depends must be set forth as the plaintiff sets forth similar allegations in his complaint.72

§ 663. The Same - The Damages. 

The damages which are to be stated in the verdict, report or decision may contemplate two distinct elements. First the deprivation of the use of the chattel and second, injury to or depreciation of the chattel while it was in the possession of the adverse party. In the absence of any proof that the damages suffered by being deprived of the use of the chattel are more or less than the interest or its value during the period of its wrongful detention such interest will presumptively measure this element of damages.81 Such would be the measure of damages where the property detained consists of merchandise kept for sale, grain and all other articles of property useful only for sale or consumption. But the same measure of damages would not generally furnish the owner an indemnity in case the property claimed has a value for use, or, in other words, a usable value, such as horses, cows, carriages, boats, auto trucks, etc.88 The verdict will state such damages down to the time of the trial but it sometimes happens that the unsuccessful party by appeal delays the satisfaction of the judgment during the pendency of the appeal. The successful party is entitled to interest on the value of the chattels during this interval as an element of

§ 664. The Same - The Value of the Chattel. 

The value of the chattel must be determined and stated in the verdict, report or decision. The value contemplated here is the value at the time of the trial.88 If there is a difference between the value of the property at the time of the trial and that at the time of the wrongful detention the successful party gets the benefit of the appreciation, as he should, since the property is determined to be his; and in case of a depreciation the successful party recovers it also but he gets it as an element of the damages. The value of the chattel, however, in contemplation here means the value of the successful party's interest in the same. If his interest is that of the owner then the value is the reasonable market value of the chattel, but if his interest is only a special interest then the value of the chattel is the value of that interest merely; that is, the value of the right of possession.⁹0

767 There are two cases in the nature of exceptions where the value of the chattel need not be fixed in the verdict, report or decision, but the verdict, report or decision in such cases must set forth the reason why the value of the chattel is not fixed therein. Both of these cases contemplate a recovery by the defendant in the replevin action. These exceptions are: 

1. Where the plaintiff is the general owner of the chattel, but it was rightfully distrained doing damage, and its value is greater than the damages sustained by the defendant by the injury for which it was distrained, in which case the damages must be fixed. 

2. Where the plaintiff is the general owner of the chattel but the defendant had a special property therein and the value of the chattel is greater than the value of the special property, or the sum charged upon the chattel by reason thereof, in which case the value of the special property or the sum so charged must be fixed.

§ 665. The Same For Part of Several Chattels. 

Where the action is brought to recover two or more chattels, the verdict, report or decision may award to one party one or more distinct chattels which can be identified and set apart from the others, and the residue to the other party. The final judgment rendered thereupon must award to each party the same relief with respect to the finding in his favor as if separate judgments were rendered; except that where each party is entitled to an absolute award of a sum of money against the other, the smaller sum must be deducted from the greater and the balance only must be awarded." to satisfy his claim in trust for the true owner." § 666. Final Judgment in Replevin. 

Final judgment for the plaintiff in an action of replevin must award to him possession of the chattel recovered by him. with his damages, if any, and costs. If he has possession of the chattel already such a judgment gives to the plaintiff his full recovery. 1. The law relative to executions and proceedings to punish for contempt is the same under the Practice Act as it was under the Code. The Reviser's note on the subject of executions found in the report of the Joint Legislative Committee, page 349, reads as follows: "The subject of 'Executions' 

in the Code of Civil Procedure covers sections 1362 to 1495. Practically all of these sections have been here retained in the form of statute law. The provisions relating to executions against the person and execution against property affect the rights of the individual so intimately and so few of these provisions might properly be the subject of rules, that it has been determined to keep the entire subject together in the form of statute. 

The objections to our existing system of court practice are directed against the procedure in an action up to the time of obtaining judgment. 

The objections relate to the method of pleading, to the trial, to incidental motions and proceedings, and to the delays which may be interposed before the judgment is actually obtained. The method of obtaining satisfaction of a judgment by execution is well defined, has been in successful operation for many years, and is not the subject of criticism from either the courts or the members of the profession. 

It may also be noted that the sections of the code relating to executions are very infrequently amended and that most of them have stood in their present form without any change since their orginal enactment as part of the code, so that they cannot be said to be the subject of constant legislative amendment. These sections have stood the test of years of trial and under them personal and property rights have been settled with but comparatively little litigation. The sections are for the most part well drafted, their language is clear and unambiguous, [773]

ENFORCEMENT OF JUDGMENTS BY CONTEMPT PROCEEDINGS § 669. Enforcement of Judgments in General. 

Generally speaking, judgments are enforced by executions and by contempt proceedings.2 These means of enforcing judgments will be considered in this and the next succeeding chapter. The remedies thus afforded, however, are inadequate to enforce successfully many judgments and other proceedings are required and provided to supplement them. 

Such other proceedings are called proceedings supplementary to execution or supplementary proceedings. These will be considered in the second succeeding chapter. Beside executions, contempt proceedings and proceedings supplementary to execution an equitable action called a judgment creditor's action is sometimes necessary to reach the assets of the debtor. For example, a person may have procured an ordinary judgment for a sum of money. Contempt proceedings will not apply to enforce this judgment at all. In the first instance an execution is the only available remedy. An execution, however, will, generally speaking, reach only tangible personal property and real estate. The judgment debtor may have money owing to him from responsible people but an execution will not reach such property. Supplementary proceedings must be resorted to in such case to make available such property. The judgment debtor may, however, have during the pendency of the action and in anticipation of the judgment, without consideration and for the purpose of defrauding his creditors, divested himself of the legal title to property, although the beneficial interest therein still belongs to him. Even supplementary proceedings may not be adequate to reach such property and apply it to the satisfaction of the judgment. A judgment creditor's action against the judgment debtor and another prosecuted by the receiver in supplementary proceedings or by the judgment creditor to cancel a fraudulent conveyance and resore the legal title of the property to the judgment debtor and thus make available an execution against it may be necessary." and because of their very nature and purpose they are here set forth as a part of the proposed practice act with but few and unimportant changes in wording." With respect to punishment for contempt in Supplementary 

Proceedings, see sec. 800 C. P. A. and 

Judiciary Law, sec. 753.

§ 670. Judgments Enforceable by Executions. 

"Sec. 504. Enforcement of judgment by execution. In either of the following cases a final judgment may be enforced by execution: 

1. Where it is for a sum of money in favor of either party; or directs the payment of a sum of money. 

2. Where it is in favor of the plaintiff in an action of ejectment or for dower. 

3. In an action to recover a chattel, where it awards a chattel to either party.' 978 This language obviously contemplates common law actions. They are enforceable by execution. Yet it would be erroneous to infer that none but common law actions are enforceable by execution. The general rule is that any judgment equitable or otherwise that directs the payment of a sum of money is enforceable by execution. Thus in Harris v. 

Elliott et al., Harris, who was assignee in trust of a certain mortgage to secure payment of money to a firm, had, after such payment, a balance in his hands as trustee and brought an action in equity to ascertain the amount thereof owing to defendants. A judgment was obtained decreeing that he "pay within five days to the defendant Wheeler the sum of $1170.” Plaintiff refused to make payment and a proceeding was brought to punish him for contempt. The court held that such judgment was one directing the payment of a sum of money, was enforceable by execution and was not enforceable by contempt proceedings. It was urged in that case that because the money was not immediately payable the county clerk of New York County had refused to docket the judgment against the plaintiff. The court said, however, that "The clerk, therefore, should have docketed the judgment, and being a ministerial officer, could have been thereunto compelled by mandamus." and that 

(Cit- "The judgment being docketed the defendant at the expiration of the time given could have issued an execution.” ing Cases.)

Likewise a direction for the restitution of moneys paid upon a judgment which has been set aside upon motion or reversed upon appeal is, in effect, a judgment for a sum of money and is enforceable by execution.12

§ 671. Exceptions to the Rule That Requires Judgments for Money to Be Enforced by Execution. 

There are two exceptions to the rule which requires judgments for a sum of money to be enforced by execution. They are both authorized by statute. They are the following: 

1. In matrimonial actions judgments directing the payment of alimony although they are for the payment of moneys are enforceable by contempt proceedings. This exception is authorized by express provision of the statutes relating to matrimonial actions.16

The right to enforce by contempt proceedings judgments in such actions, however, does not apply to costs directed to be paid by such judgments." There is a limit moreover to the extent of the imprisonment under contempt proceedings to which a defendant in a matrimonial action may be subjected. 

Section 72 of the Civil Rights Law formerly limited the period of imprisonment for nonpayment of alimony awarded by final judgment in matrimonial actions to three months where the amount ordered to be paid was less than five hundred dollars, and to six months where it was five hundred dollars or over. § 672. Judgments Enforceable by Contempt Proceedings. 

Except in the cases discussed in the last preceding section where the judgments may be enforced either by executions or contempt proceedings any judgment that is enforceable by execution must be so enforced. This leaves for enforcement by contempt proceedings the judgments enumerated in sec tion 505 of the Civil Practice Act. 

Under the first subdivision of that section final judgments which can not be enforced by execution are enforced by contempt proceedings. The following judgments would be so enforced under this subdivision and illustrate the meaning thereof: 

A judgment for a mandatory injunction requiring defendants to remove the part of their building which overhangs the plaintiff's lands,25 a judgment requiring the removal of a nuisance, a judgment requiring the delivery of a conveyance and a cancellation of its registration," a judgment requiring the return and cancellation of a note,28 or the delivery of a mortgage," or requiring the removal of an obstruction from plaintiff's land." 80 Under the second subdivision where the judgment is final and part of it can not be enforced by execution, the parts not so enforceable are enforceable by contempt proceedings.

§ 674. Manner of Enforcing Judgments by Contempt Proceedings -In General. 

There are two kinds of contempts, private contempts and public contempts, sometimes called civil contempts and criminal contempts.2 In the first of these classes the authority of the court is lent to the suitor for his safety: 41 "The authority is exerted in his behalf as a private individual, and the fine imposed is measured by his loss and goes to him as an indemnity; and imprisonment, if ordered, is awarded, not as a punishment, but as a means to an end, and that end the benefit of the suitor in some act or omission compelled which are essential to his particular rights of person or of property. The second class of contempts consists of those whose cause and result are a violation of the rights of the public as represented by their constituted legal tribunals, and a punishment for the wrong in the interest of public justice, and not in the interest of an individual litigant. In these cases if a fine is imposed its maximum is limited. by a fixed general law, and not at all by the needs of individuals; and its proceeds when collected go into the public treasury and not into the purse of an individual suitor. ''48

The contempt proceedings resorted to in the enforcement of judgments are civil contempts. 

Contempts punishable civilly.-A court of record has power to punish, by fine and imprisonment, or either, a neglect or violation of duty, or other misconduct, by which a right or remedy of a party to a civil action or special proceeding, pending in the court may be defeated, impaired, impeded, or prejudiced, in either of the following cases :-

§ 675. Prerequisites to the Enforcement of Judgments by Contempt Proceedings. 

Before proceedings can be instituted properly for the enforcement of a judgment by contempt proceedings a certified copy of the judgment must be served upon the defendant together with a demand that he perform the act or acts required by its terms.45

In addition to this, facts must exist which show that a "right or remedy of a party may be defeated, impaired, impeded or prejudiced. 9946 The demand must be made by or on behalf of the person to whom the obligation is owing." Ordinarily facts exist which show that a right of the party has been "defeated, impaired, impeded or prejudiced" when the judgment has not been performed by the defendant after demand. § 676. The Same - In Judgments Requiring Payment of Alimony. 

Contempt proceedings for the enforcement of judgments requiring the payment of alimony differ from such proceedings for the enforcement of other judgments in two particulars. In addition to the usual prerequisites it must appear “presumptively, to the satisfaction of the court, that payment cannot be enforced by means of the sequestration of his (defendant's) property or by resorting to the security, if any, given as prescribed by Statute." The statutory provisions relating to sequestration and security in such cases are found in section 1171 of the Civil Practice Act. On the other hand "no demand of any kind upon the husband shall be necessary in order that he be proceeded against and punished for failure to make any such payment or to pay any such installment.""48

§ 677. Necessary Papers to Enforce a Judgment by Contempt Proceedings. 

The papers which must be prepared to enforce by contempt proceedings the performance of a judgment are: a. An affidavit, and b. Either an order to show cause or a warrant to attach the offender.49

The affidavit should be entitled as the action is where it is begun by an order to show cause; if the proceeding is otherwise begun it may be entitled either in the name of the people or as the action is entitled.50 It must show the facts referred to in either one or the other of the two preceding sections and the proof of these facts must be full and complete. The statute authorizing the enforcement of judgments by contempt proceedings is strictly construed in favor of the defendant who can not be adjudged guilty of contempt unless all the requirements made by the statute are fully satisfied."¹ 

On applications to punish in contempt proceedings a defendant for noncompliance with a judgment for the payment of alimony no demand need be shown, but the affidavit on such an application must show either "an adjudication that payment of the alimony and counsel fee can not be enforced by sequestration proceedings or by resorting to the security if any was given,52 or facts from which the court may be satis fied that sequestration or the giving of security would be ineffectual. 53

§ 678. Service of Papers. 

The order to show cause or warrant together with the affidavit upon which the order or warrant was procured must be served upon the defendant personally, and not merely upon the attorney." Where the proceeding is begun by a warrant of attachinent the sheriff brings the offender before the court who issued the warrant and an undertaking may in the discretion of the court, be required of him for his appearance on the day set for the hearing of the application to commit him for contempt."* 

§ 679. The Hearing Upon the Return of the Warrant or Order. 

Upon the return of the order to show cause or warrant the issues before the court for determination are simply a. Whether the proceeding was brought on regularly in accordance with the foregoing sections, and b. Whether there has been an actual contempt and if so what excuse the offender has to offer for its commission."5 

If the proceeding was brought on by an order to show cause the issues are determined as upon any other motion. 

If the matter was brought on by a warrant and the accused denies the offense charged against him the accused has a right to have the charge against him set forth in interrogatories specifying the facts and circumstances of the offense and to these interrogatories he must make written answers under oath within a reasonable time."7 

§ 680. Determination of the Application.
