The final order must specify the acts to be done and the amount of money to be paid, and it is insufficient to refer to any other order for this purpose." It must adjudge that the misconduct or violation of duty was such that it might have defeated, impaired, impeded or prejudiced a right or remedy of a party and that it either was calculated to do so or did so; but it is not necessary to show actual loss. Moreover, if the order omitted such adjudication it can not be amended by inserting it later."¹

The order under discussion is a determination of a proceeding to punish as for a civil contempt and should be distinguished from the order which determines a proceeding as for a criminal contempt since in the latter order the particular circumstances of the offense must be set forth therein.72 

§ 681. The Commitment. 

If the proceeding was begun by an order to show cause a certified copy of the final order referred to in the last paragraph is sufficient authority for the sheriff to commit the prisoner in accordance with its terms. If, however, the proceeding was instituted by a warrant of attachment it will be necessary to prepare a warrant of commitment based on the final order to enable the sheriff to carry out the provisions of the final order."

The imprisonment may continue until the defendant has performed the acts for which he was committed and paid the fine imposed, but after he has performed the act he can not be imprisoned for more than three months for the nonpayment of the fine, if the fine imposed is less than five hundred dollars nor more than six months if it exceeds five hundred dollars. Problems. 

1. Can a person be held in contempt of a court that has no jurisdiction of his person? (Ebsary v. Ruby, 256 N. Y. 406.)

§683. Introduction. 

The first five sections of the preceding chapter relating to the enforcement of judgments by contempt proceedings should be read in connection with this chapter as they are really introductory to both chapters. The first note in the preceding chapter will show that no change of any substantial character has been made by the Civil Practice Act in the practice that prevailed under the Code and the cases therefore which expound the code sections relating to executions are applicable in interpreting the sections of the Civil Practice Act relating thereto. The judgments which are enforceable by execution have been shown in section 670 of the preceding chapter.

In treating the subject of execution, it will be convenient to discuss first, the subject generally, giving forms of the various types of executions which will illustrate the general discussion; then there will be taken up in order executions against property, executions against the person and finally executions against earnings or income of the judgment-debtor. 

The larger subdivision of this chapter will therefore be the 

---

A. EXECUTIONS GENERALLY INCLUDING FORMS. 

§ 684. Executions - Nature Of. 

An execution is the process of the court from which it is issued,¹ by means of which its judgments are enforced. It is directed to the sheriff or to the coroner if the sheriff is interested,² who is the officer of the court to enforce its process. It must intelligently describe the judgment and require such officer to enforce or satisfy the judgment as the circumstances of the particular case require. The manner of enforcing or satisfying the judgment varies with the character of the judgment. If, for example, the judgment is one in ejectment or for the recovery of a chattel, the sheriff or officer will be required by the execution to deliver the possession of the property to the party entitled thereto. If the judgment is for the recovery of money, the execution will require the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of the personal property of the judgment debtor and if that is insufficient out of his real property. The classes of executions and the forms thereof required for particular cases are discussed in the following sections. 

§ 685. Kinds of Executions. 

"There are four kinds of execution as follows: 

1. Against property. 

2. Against the person.

Team of 3. For the delivery of the possession of real property with or without damages for withholding the same. 

4. For the delivery of the possession of a chattel, with or without damages for the taking or detention thereof."7

These are the regular and well established kinds of executions. Where, however, the sheriff returns an execution against property unsatisfied, authority exists under the direction of the court for the issuance of an execution against the wages, debts, earnings, salary, income from trust funds or

2. Civil Practice Act, § 636. 

3. Schley v. Andrews, 225 N. Y. 110, 114. In the City Court of the City of New York, executions are levied by the sheriff or a city marshal (City Ct. 

Act, § 28). Cf. the present language of C. P. A. Section 775, subdivision 4. 

4. Civil Practice Act, § 640.

profits due and owing to the judgment debtor or which thereafter may become due and owing to him provided they equal or exceed twelve dollars per week, and the judgment may be satisfied out of such income at a rate not to exceed ten per cent thereof. The regular types of execution will be discussed first in the following sections and the execution against wages, salary, etc., will be discussed later." 

§ 686. General Requisites of an Execution. 

There are certain general requisites which all forms of execution must possess and these give the skeleton form of execution. 11 a. In whose name issued. Executions are issued in the name of the people of the state. Since the execution is a process of the court 10 it must conform to the usual requirements of process. Under the Code " a writ or other process had to issue in the name of the people of the state. That section of the Code has not been incorporated in the Civil Practice Act or elsewhere and this requisite, therefore, has not the same statutory sanction that it had under the Code. 

It is believed, however, that this general requisite which characterizes other writs, 12 will attach to this form of execution. b. To whom addressed. It is directed to the sheriff unless he is a party or is interested, in which case it must be directed to the coroner, or the court in its discretion may by order direct it to be issued to a disinterested adult resident who must, to make his designation effective, file a bond to the people for the faithful performance of his duties under the execution.18 c. The recitals of the execution. The execution must intelligently describe the judgment stating the names of the parties in whose favor, and against whom, the time when and the court in which, the judgment was rendered, and if it was rendered in the supreme court, the county in which the judgment roll is filed.14

§ 687. Requisites of an Execution in Particular Cases. 

In addition to the general requisites discussed in the preceding section, there are special requisites for each class of executions. a. An execution against property must specify among its recitals the sum recovered or directed to be paid, and the sum actually due when it is issued. It must specify a day from which interest upon the sum due is to be computed and a failure to insert such interest date will enable the defendant to satisfy the execution by paying the face of the judgment without the interest.23 If all the parties against whom the

In the recital part of such an execution, if the judgment roll is not filed in the clerk's office of the county to which it is issued, a statement must be inserted of the time when the judgment was docketed in that county.25 If a warrant of attachment has been levied, that fact should appear among the recitals.2 26 The directory part of such execution must substantially require the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of the personal property of the judgment debtor, and if sufficient personal property can not be found, out of the real property belonging to him at the time when the execution was docketed in the clerk's office in the county or at any time thereafter.27 If a warrant of attachment has been levied on property of the defendant, and the defendant is a non-resident or a foreign corporation, and the summons was served upon him or it, without the state, or otherwise than personally, and the judgment debtor has not appeared in the action, the execution must require the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of the personal property attached since jurisdiction in rem alone exists in such case. In any other case where a warrant of attachment has been levied upon the property of the defendant, the direction to the sheriff is that he satisfy the judgment out of the personal property attached, and if that is insufficient out of other personal property of the judgment debtor, if both are insufficient out of the real property attached, and if that is insufficient out of the real property belonging to him at the time when the judgment was docketed in the clerk's office of the county or at any time thereafter.28 In the latter cases the court has personal jurisdiction.

If the execution is against any heir or representative, a tenant or trustee, it must in its directory part require the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of the real or personal property in the hands of the executor, administrator, heir, devisee, legatee, tenant or trustee,20 otherwise the individual property of such persons will be held by the execution.29a

(d) Form of execution against joint debtors. 

The form of an execution where a judgment is obtained against a number of defendants jointly liable is the same as the form of execution where there is but a single defendant save only that in the directory part of the execution the command to the sheriff may be that he should satisfy the judgment "out of the personal property of the said judgment debtors, or any of them." Such a requirement is not essential to the execution since the sheriff is empowered to satisfy an execution against joint debtors without any such direction out of the joint property of the joint debtors, or out of the individual property of any one of them.36 

Judge Earl, in the case of Saunders vs. Reilly,37 quoting from Lindley on Partnership said: "Athough the writ of execution on a joint judgment must be joint in form, it may be levied upon all or any one or more of the persons named in it,' and that the consequence of this is, that the sheriff may execute a writ issued against several partners jointly, either on their joint property or on the separate property of any one or more of them or both on their joint or their respective separate property.' 999 If, however, the summons was not personally served on any one or more of such defendants, and they have not appeared in the action the attorney for the judgment creditor must endorse upon the execution a direction to the sheriff containing the name of each defendant who was not summoned and restricting the enforcement of the execution as against such defendants to the joint property owned by them with the other defendants. The endorsement in such case would read as

§ 690. Form of Execution Against the Person. 

An execution against the person of the defendant can not be issued unless and until an execution against his property has been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied,43 except where the judgment debtor is actually confined without having been

B. EXECUTIONS AGAINST PROPERTY § 691. Executions Issued As Of Course. 

The party recovering a final judgment, or his assignee, may have execution thereupon without any application of the court and as a matter of course in the following cases: 46 (a) If the judgment debtor is living an execution may issue as of course any time within five years after the entry of the judgment. It should be noted that the death of the judgment creditor does not alter the rule, for the representatives of the deceased, who are entitled to act, may issue the execution within the five year period the same as if the creditor had lived, but in such case the execution must be endorsed with the name of the person issuing it. For the purpose of reckoning the five year period the day on which the judgment is docketed must be excluded from the calculation.48 (b) An execution may be issued as of course after the expiration of the five year period provided an execution was issued within the five year period and was returned wholly or partly unsatisfied or unexecuted.49 (c) Where the judgment debtor is dead, but during his life time conveyed real estate in fraud of his creditors or any of them, and any judgment creditor of such deceased, against whose judgment such conveyance shall have been declared fraudulent by the judgment and decree of any court of competent jurisdiction, may enforce his said judgment against such real property with like effect as if the judgment debtor were living, and it shall not be necessary to obtain the leave of any court or officer to issue such an execution.50 In such case the person issuing the execution shall annex thereto a description of the real estate and shall endorse the execution with the words "issued under Section 655 of the Civil Prac- 

46. Civil Practice Act, § 650. The phrase at the opening of section 650 "except as otherwise specially prescribed by law" refers to the cases where leave of courts must be obtained before issuing the execution and those cases are enumerated in the next section.

§ 692. Executions Issued by Leave of Court. 

In the following cases execution can be issued only by leave of the court: 51 53 (a) After the lapse of five years from the entry of a final judgment if within the five years no execution was issued and returned wholly or partly unsatisfied or unexecuted, an order of the court granting leave to issue an execution must be obtained.52 The theory is that if no execution is issued upon a judgment for five years from its entry, a presumption of payment arises and this presumption must be rebutted by evidence before the execution may issue. Leave is obtained when the presumption is overcome, but the debtor must be given an opportunity to be heard.54 If leave is granted the execution issues, if denied plaintiff may apply for leave to sue on the judgment and thus determine whether the same was or was not paid.54 The granting or withholding of leave is in the discretion of the court and the exercise of such discretion is not reviewable on appeal to the court of appeals.55 

If, however, an execution is issued without leave after the lapse of five years, such execution is not void but voidable and must be set aside on motion.56 

51. Civil Practice Act, § 655, sub division 6. The purpose here is to prevent preferences among creditors where the assets in the hands of the executor or administrator may not be sufficient to pay all claims of the class to which the judgment creditor belongs."4 

§ 693. Necessary Papers and Procedure in Obtaining Leave to Issue Execution After Lapse of Five Years. 

The papers required to obtain an order of the court permitting the issuance of an execution where the judgment debtor is living but more than five years have elapsed since the entry of judgment are (a) An affidavit, and (b) A notice of motion or an order to show cause. 

The affidavit should show the character of the judgment and the date of its entry and docket; that it has not been paid; the amount due thereon; that no execution has been issued thereon within five years; whether the debtor is a resident of the state or a non-resident and where he resides.

The notice of motion is required by section 653 of the Civil Practice Act and must be served personally upon the judgment debtor if he is a resident and personal service can be made upon him with reasonable diligence. The ordinary notice of motion will suffice in such case. 99 65 An order to show cause is simpler where the judgment debtor is a non-resident or being a resident cannot be served personally within the state with reasonable diligence for the reason that, in such cases, the manner of giving notice must be "as the court directs. The order to show cause makes possible the submission to the court in the first instance of the manner in which notice should be given under the circumstances shown by the affidavit, and the procedure after the order to show cause is signed simply carries out the plan contained therein. 

§ 694. Necessary Papers and Procedure in Obtaining Leave When the Judgment Debtor Died Since the Entry of Judgment. 

A distinction must be made in applying for leave to issue an execution after the death of the judgment debtor between an execution for the delivery of possession of real property and one for the collection of a sum of money. The procedure in the former case is governed by section 651 and in the latter case by sections 654 and 655 of the Civil Practice Act. 

(a) If the judgment is for the recovery of possession of real property the necessary papers are (1) An affidavit, and (2) Notice of motion.

§ 695. Delivery To and Receipt By Sheriff of Execution. 

76 The first step after an execution is prepared is to place it in the hands of the sheriff. It cannot be said to be issued until it is delivered to the sheriff. On delivery when so required, the sheriff without compensation, must make a memorandum in writing specifying the names of the parties etc., as required by the Civil Practice Act, and the sheriff upon receipt of the execution must endorse thereon a memorandum of the day, hour and minute when received." Upon delivery, the fee for receiving and returning the execution together with the mileage should be paid for the sheriff is not obliged to execute the mandate if this is not done.78 

The sheriff is bound by the directions of the attorney delivering the execution although the power of the sheriff cannot be enlarged by improper directions.70

§ 697. Effect on the Title of Bona Fide Purchasers Before Levy. 

"Sec. 683. The title to personal property, acquired before the actual levy of an execution, by a purchaser in good faith, and without notice that the execution has been issued, is not affected by an execution delivered, before the purchase was made, to an officer, to be executed.'' 86 87 To acquire a good title, however, a purchaser of goods and chattels from a judgment debtor after an execution is delivered to the sheriff, must in fact be a purchaser in good faith. 

One to whom the goods and chattels of the judgment debtor are assigned in payment of a pre-existing debt is not such a purchaser. The consideration for the purchase must be a fresh one. Thus a person who was possessed of a chattel mortgage upon the property of the judgment debtor before the judgment was obtained or before the execution thereon was delivered to the sheriff loses his lien, if after the delivery of the execution to the sheriff he takes a new mortgage upon the chattels in exchange for the old one which was about to expire, provided, of course, a levy is made upon the goods during the life of the execution. If a mortgagee desires to continue his lien to the exclusion of the lien of the execution he must file the statement required by section 

235 of the Lien Law or otherwise comply therewith.88

§ 699. Order of Preference Among Executions. 

"Sec. 680. Where two or more executions against property are issued out of the same or different courts of record against the same judgment debtor, the one first delivered to an officer to be executed has preference, notwithstanding that a levy is first made by virtue of an execution subsequently delivered; but if a levy upon and sale of personal property has been made by virtue of the junior execution, before an actual levy by virtue of the senior execution the same property shall not be levied upon or sold by virtue of the latter." 8 66 'Sec. 681. Where there are one or more executions and one or more warrants of attachment against the property of the same person, the rule prescribed in the last section prevails in determining the preferences of the executions or warrants of attachment; the defendant in the warrants of attachment being, for that purpose, regarded as a judgment debtor."

Under the sections quoted above it would be apparent that priority of delivery of the execution to the officer rather than priority in the entry of judgment or in making a levy upon the goods determines who is entitled to first claim upon the proceeds of the sale.

In Pach v. Gilbert 10 Pach had obtained a warrant of attachment and the sheriff on December 30, 1887, levied thereunder upon a stock of dry goods belonging to Orr. On the same day the judge who granted the warrant made an order vacating it and the sheriff thereupon released the levy. On January 3, 1888, Orr confessed judgment in favor of certain creditors and executions on these judgments were placed in the sheriff's hands. On January 4th the sheriff levied on the stock of dry goods belonging to Orr. On January 12th Pach obtained an order setting aside the order vacating the warrant of attachment. While the warrant of attachment, the order vacating it and the order setting aside the order of vacation were in his hands, and on January 16th, the sheriff sold the property of the judgment debtor under the executions issued January 4th. The sum realized on that sale was more than sufficient to pay the amount for Pach's claim which was subsequently reduced to judgment and execution thereunder delivered to the sheriff, but the proceeds of the sale were by the sheriff wholly applied on the executions issued on the judgments confessed January 3d. Pach there- 

8. Civil Practice Act, § 680. 

9. Civil Practice Act, § 681. 

10. 124 N. Y. 612.

upon sued Gilbert, the sheriff, for damages. In holding the sheriff liable, the court said after quoting the then statute which corresponds with the Civil Practice Act sections quoted at the beginning of this section: "Thus by statute it is made the duty of a sheriff to give preference in the application of proceeds of a sale under junior executions to a prior warrant of attachment although no levy be made thereunder. 

As the warrant of attachment in question came first into his hands, and the effect of the last order made was to give it vitality as of the date when delivered to him it should have been treated in the application of the proceeds of the sale as if he had neglected to make a levy under it, but had instead levied and sold under executions subsequently issued. This the defendant did not do. He has, therefore, failed in his attempt to show in mitigation of damages that the plaintiff was not injured by his action."

The question of prior rights to the proceeds of a sale of property sold under an execution frequently arises where one or more levies thereunder have become dormant. A levy under an execution becomes dormant when the execution creditor instructs the sheriff not to proceed further. Any direction by the execution creditor to the sheriff which suspends the lien or delays the enforcement of the levy renders the execution dormant against subsequent creditors or bona fide purchasers.¹¹ "However veiled may be the direction; however much it may be founded on a humane desire to protect the debtor; if it is tantamount to a mandate or instruction to the sheriff to withhold the execution of his process during the interim that he accedes to this demand, the levy ceases to be effective" and is dormant. Where a levy thus becomes dormant subsequent levies have a prior right to the proceeds of a sale of the goods levied upon notwithstanding the prior delivery to the sheriff of the execution which has become dormant. 

In Excelsior Needle Co. v. Globe Cycle Works,12 M and W 

obtained a judgment against the defendant for upwards of three thousand dollars damages and costs and execution was promptly issued to the sheriff and a levy made upon the stock, tools, chattels, machinery and fixtures in the manu- 

11. Excelsior Co. V. Globe Cycle 

Works, 48 A. D. 304; 62 N. Y. S. 538; 

Sage v. Woodin, 66 N. Y. 578; Storm v. Woods, 11 Johns. 110. 

12. 48 A. D. 304; 62 N. Y. S. 538.

facturing plant and store occupied by the defendant in the city of Buffalo. Eight other executions on judgments recovered on the same day were also delivered to the sheriff and like levies made by him in pursuance of these executions. A week later all of these execution creditors united in sending a written direction to the sheriff to release the levy upon all the property except machinery and fixtures. The letter to the sheriff said: 66 you are to retain your levy under said executions upon the machinery and fixtures only, for the present, but the Globe Cycle Works are not to be interfered with in the possession of their premises for the use of the machinery and fixtures." 

The sheriff was also told to withdraw his deputies. He did so. The Cycle Company continued to run its manufactory and its store selling its goods until its personal effects were nearly all disposed of and the entire property, including the plant and manufactory, only brought on a public sale four thousand dollars, although at the time of the levy the plant alone was claimed to be worth sixty thousand dollars. During the interval while the levy was thus made dormant by the directions of the judgment creditors to the sheriff, the Excelsior Company obtained two judgments aggregating upwards of two thousand dollars against the Globe Cycle Works and issued execution thereon to the same sheriff who levied upon the stock, wheels, tools, machinery, etc., of the defendant. 

Other judgments were obtained also and like the judgments of the Excelsior Company executions thereon were issued to the sheriff. The sale then took place and four thousand dollars was realized.

M and W on behalf of the other judgment creditors at whose direction the levy had become dormant, claimed a prior right by reason of the priority of their executions to the four thousand dollars thus recovered. The court said: "The law is quite clear that the object of the execution is to enforce payment of the judgment debt, and not to convert such execution into a security upon the property and still allow the judgment debtor to prosecute his business regardless of the lien of the execution. As was said in Freeman on Executions (Sec. 206): In other words it is not the mere issuing or delivery of the writ which creates a lien; but an issuing and delivery for the purpose of execution. The execution of a writ for the purpose of making or keeping it effective as a lien cannot stop with a mere levy upon the property.

If the officer is instructed by the plaintiff not to sell till further orders, the lien of the execution and levy becomes subordinate to that of any subsequent writ placed in the officer's hands for service.''' 

§ 700. Property Subject to Levy-Real Estate.13 

Real property is subject to levy under an execution, but personal property must be applied first in satisfaction of the judgment and real property can be applied only when sufficient personal property cannot be found by the sheriff.¹ 

Leases of land where the unexpired term is five years or more is real property in this connection.15 Real property held in trust may be levied upon where by reason of the invalidity of the trust the law vests the estate in the beneficiary.16 But real property which is mortgaged cannot be sold under an execution issued upon a judgment recovered for the mortgage debt or any part thereof," and to prevent a levy upon such property under such circumstances, the attorney who subscribes the execution must indorse thereon a direction to the sheriff not to levy it upon the mortgaged property or any part thereof describing therein the property.18 A judgment debtor who has a contract for the purchase of real property has not, however, a leviable interest in real property.¹9

§ 702. The Same - Where a Warrant of Attachment Has Been Issued. 

Where a warrant of attachment has been issued in an action and a levy made thereunder, the execution issued on a judgment obtained by the plaintiff in such action reaches the property attached.36 The lien of the execution in such case supersedes the lien of the attachment.37 As a warrant of attachment reaches intangible property of the judgment debtor as well as tangibles the execution in such case reaches intangible personal property of the judgment debtor. Where jurisdiction in rem only is obtained in such an action the attached property alone is subject to levy and other real or personal property of the debtor is beyond the reach of the execution.39 It is otherwise if jurisdiction in personam is obtained.40

It is not so clear now that joint property may be seized by the sheriff to satisfy an individual judgment of one of the judgment debtors. Formerly it was the law that on an execution against one partner the joint property of the partnership could be seized by the sheriff but he could sell only the interest of the partner therein. Such interest consists only of what would come to the judgment debtor out of the choses in possession after the debts of the firm had been satisfied. The purchaser of the interest became a tenant in common with the other partners.42 It is believed that this procedure has been somewhat modified by section 54 of the Partnership Law and that now an order of the court is necessary to enable a judgment creditor of a partner to receive the interest of such partner in the firm. Such an order is called a "charging order" under the Partnership Law, which authorizes the court to appoint a receiver of the judgment debtor's share of the profits that may accrue to him from the partnership.43 41 Joint property may be seized under a warrant of attachment levied upon the interest of one or more of the partners, however, and the other partners may get relief from the seizure by giving an undertaking to the effect that they will pay to the sheriff, on demand, an amount not exceeding the sum specified therein in case judgment is recovered against the defendant or defendants whose interest in the partnership has been levied upon.44 When property levied upon under a warrant of attachment has been thus restored to the partnership no levy can be made upon such property by virtue of an execution against the individual property of one

§ 706. Claims of Third Persons to Property Levied Upon Under an 

Execution.

If personal property levied upon as the property of the judgment debtor is claimed by or in behalf of another person, as his property, an affidavit may be made and delivered to the sheriff in behalf of such person at any time while such property, or the proceeds thereof, are in the sheriff's possession stating that he made such a claim, specifying in whole or in part the property to which it relates, and in all cases stating the value of the property claimed and the damages if any over and above such value that the claimant will suffer in case such levy is not released. If under such circumstances the sheriff deliver the property to the claimant and it ultimately turned out that the property belonged to the defendant, the sheriff would be liable to the plaintiff for the damages suffered by him for the release of the levy.58 On the other hand, if the sheriff retain the property and it ultimately turns out that the goods belong to the claimant, the sheriff would be liable to the claimant for the damages which he might suffer. To relieve himself from liability under such circumstances the sheriff may in his discretion empanel a jury to try the validity of the claim.59 

56. Scott v. Morgan, 94 N. Y. 508, 515. 

§ 707. The Same - Procedure in Determining Third Party Claims. 

Ordinarily the sheriff empanels a jury to determine whether the defendant or the claimant has title to the property. If the jury find that the property belongs to the claimant the sheriff

may relinquish the levy unless the judgment creditor gives him an undertaking to the effect that the sureties thereon will indemnify him to an amount not less than twice the value of the property in damages as determined by the jury, and two hundred and fifty dollars in addition thereto against all damages, costs and expenses in an action brought against him by reason of the levy upon, detention or sale of the property by virtue of the execution. If such undertaking is given, the sheriff must retain the property as belonging to the judgment debtor. If the property is found to belong to the defendant, the levy is continued by the sheriff in which case, of course, no undertaking is required. 60 

§ 708. Effect of the Jury's Findings. 

It is well settled that the action of a sheriff's jury in determining a claim of title to property seized by a sheriff under execution or attachment, is not a judicial determination and is not subject to review by motion or otherwise. It is not conclusive upon any one as to the title claimed, and its only office is to afford jurisdiction to the sheriff for surrendering the property to the claimant who had sued out the execution or the attachment.63 Such being the law, it seldom happens that a sheriff's jury finds for any one but the claimant as a matter of practice. If they found for the defendant such finding would not prejudice the right of the claimant to bring an action to recover the property so levied upon or damages by reason of the levy, detention or sale. The only way, therefore, that the sheriff's jury can protect the sheriff is by finding for the claimant which it usually does.

§ 713. Sheriff's Certificate of Sale. 

The sheriff on the sale must make out, subscribe and acknowledge before an officer authorized to take the acknowledgment of a deed, duplicate certificates of the sale 

1. The name of each purchaser and the time when the sale was made.

4. The whole consideration money paid."

The sheriff must, within ten days after the sale, file one of these duplicate certificates in the clerk's office and deliver another to the purchaser. A failure to file or deliver the certificates within ten days, however, is not a ground for vacating the sale.

§ 716. The Same By Creditor. 

If the judgment debtor or other person referred to in the preceding section does not exercise his right of redemption within one year from the sale, a judgment creditor or mortgagee whose judgment or mortgage is a lien upon the property sold, may within the next three months, redeem by paying the sum of money which was paid upon the sale with interest at seven per cent from the time of the sale. He must at the same time execute a certificate of satisfaction in whole or in part of his judgment or mortgage.20 Creditors may within three months redeem from one another. 

If the second redeeming creditor's lien is subsequent to that of the first redeeming creditor he must reimburse the first redeeming creditor the sum paid by him to redeem the property with interest at seven per cent from the time of the first redemption and also pay him the sum specified in the certificate of satisfaction executed by the first redeeming creditor upon his redemption." If the second redeeming creditor's lien is prior to that of the first redeeming creditor, he need not pay the sum specified in the latter's certificate of satisfaction.22 Other redemptions by creditors are affected in the same manner.23 The leading case of Benton v. Hatch 24 gives the history of these statutes relating to redemptions and furnishes a concrete illustration of their application in a rather complicated situation.

If a redemption took place on the last day of the fifteen months, twenty-four hours after such redemption is allowed for any creditor to redeem from any other redeeming creditor.25 Such final redemption must take place at the sheriff's office.20 In other cases, the redemption money may be paid to the purchaser or creditor from whom the redemption is effected, or to the sheriff.27

§ 718. The Sheriff's Deed. 

"Immediately after the expiration of fifteen months from the time of the sale, except where a redemption has been made on the last day of the fifteen months, and, in that case, immediately after the expiration of twenty-four hours from the last redemption, the sheriff who made the sale must execute the proper deed or deeds in order to convey to the person or persons entitled thereto the part or parts of the property sold which have not been redeemed by the judgment debtor, his heir, devisee or assignee. The deed conveys to the grantee therein the right, title and interest which were sold by the sheriff. After the same shall have been recorded for twenty years in the county where the real estate is situated, it shall be presumptive evidence of the facts therein stated."'1

§ 719. Liability of Sheriff and Execution Creditor for Wrongful 

Levy.

A wrongful levy may impose liability upon the sheriff or the execution creditor.

The sheriff is liable if he proceeds to make a levy under an execution that is void upon its face, but if its validity is not thus apparent and the sheriff is ignorant of its infirmity he is not liable.36 Where, however, the sheriff proceeds after being apprised of the infirmity of the writ he is liable. The sheriff is also liable, as has been shown, when he seizes property belonging to a third party under a valid execution against the judgment debtor, or seizes property of the judgment debtor which is exempt by law from levy under an execution.38 

The execution creditor is liable where the execution is void in fact but valid on its face, as where it is issued on void or satisfied judgments. The apparent validity of the writ protects the sheriff but the execution creditor is liable as a trespasser.39

If the execution is voidable merely and not void no liability attaches to acts thereunder before such process is set aside. The execution creditor may indemnify the sheriff for continuing a levy after a claim is made of ownership of the property by a third person and the liability of the sheriff is thus passed on through the bond of indemnity to the obligors thereon, but such liability is limited by the terms of the bond. Thus in Bowe v. Wilkins et al.,41 attached property was claimed by a third party and the attaching creditor procured a bond of indemnity to be given to the plaintiff for taking and detaining the property under the warrant. The sheriff continued to hold the property even

The third party claimant of the property brought action in conversion against the sheriff and recovered thereon. The conversion proved being the refusal to turn over the property to the claimant after the warrant had been vacated. The sheriff thereafter tried to hold the obligors on the bond of indemnity, but it was held that the bond only indemnified the sheriff for continuing his detention of the property up to the notice of the vacating of the warrant, that the sale of claimant's property under the execution was a conversion not chargeable to the indemnitors under the bond of indemnity, the court continuing said: "There is no evidence that these defendants ever knew one word as to where the money came from to pay a judgment in an action to which they were not parties, and none that any orders were given by anyone to the sheriff as to what property to levy on. Issuing an execution without any direction as to how it is to be enforced or as to what property is to be taken, implies only an authority to do a lawful act pursuant to its command (Welsh v. Cochran, 63 N. Y. 

181), and the knowledge of the attorney, in the execution as to where the money came from which he took from the sheriff, there being no proof of like knowledge by the plaintiffs in the execution, when they received the money from him, would be no ratification even as to them, of the prior illegal act of the sheriff in refusing to surrender the goods, much less on the part of these defendants, being equally ignorant. (Clark v. Woodruff, 83 N. Y. 518.) "

C. EXECUTIONS AGAINST THE PERSON. 

§ 720. In General. 

In effect an execution against the person is simply imprisonment for debt. Under the common law a judgment debtor could be put in jail for his debt and there left until the debt was paid. Not only that, but while in jail he had to maintain himself.42 

42. As an eminent English judge puts it in Manby v. Scott, 1 Mod. 124, 132: "If a man be taken in execution and lie in prison for debt, neither the plaintiff at whose suit he is arrested, nor the sheriff who took him, is bound to find his meat, drink, or clothes, but he must live on his own, or on the charity of others; and if no man will relieve him, let him die in the name of God, says the law, and so may I." Quoted in People ex rel. 

Levine v. Shea, 201 N. Y. 471.

The rigor and extent of an execution against the person have been modified by statutory enactments from time to time, yet the judgment debtor is still kept in custody at his own expense.13 If, however, he makes oath that he is unable to support himself, the county will support him.** 

§ 721. In What Actions Possible. 

An execution against the person is possible only in the classes of actions enumerated in section 826 of the Civil 

Practice Act. This will appear from the following discussion: 

It is provided in substance in section 764 of the Civil Practice Act that an execution may not issue against the judgment debtor unless (a) The judgment is one enforceable by execution, and (b) The action was one in which an order of arrest might have issued during its pendency." 

It follows that if the judgment is enforceable by contempt proceedings no execution against the person may issue."

The actions in which an order of arrest may issue are specified in sections 826 and 827 of the Civil Practice Act. Under section 827, however, an arrest may be had only in 47 "an action wherein the judgment demanded requires the performance of an act; the neglect or refusal to perform which would be punishable by the court as a contempt," etc.

It seems clear, therefore, that no execution against the person may be had where the action falls under section 827 of the Civil Practice Act, which leaves section 826 thereof as the only section containing an enumeration of actions. whose judgments may be enforced by an execution against the person. To get a body execution in an action in the 

Municipal Court of the City of New York where a summons is served without a verified complaint the summons must bear an endorsement substantially as follows: "Plaintiff claims defendant is liable to arrest and imprisonment.''47a 

§ 722. The Same - Subdivision 2 of Section 764 Meaningless. 

In all of the actions enumerated in section 826 of the Civil Practice Act the nature of the action gives the right to the arrest since no extrinsic facts must be shown under that section to secure the order, while they must be shown under sec ecution see §§ 670 and 672 and chap ter 34 ante.

Civil Practice Act. 

The second subdivision of section 764 begins with the words "in any other case. There are no other cases where an order of arrest may be had, except those contemplated by section 827 of the Civil Practice Act, and as we have just shown in the preceding section, these are enforceable by contempt proceedings and not by execution, and therefore no body execution may be had in such actions. Subdivision 2 of section 764 is, therefore, meaningless-although no adjudicated case seems to say so--and will be disregarded in the following discussion relating to executions against the person. 

§ 723. The Same The Action Must Actually Be One Contemplated by Section 826 of the Civil Practice Act and Not Merely Colorably So. 

51 The action whose judgment may be enforced by an execution against the person must actually be one of the type contemplated in section 826 of the Civil Practice Act and not merely so in form. Thus an execution against the person may be resorted to in the enforcement of a judgment obtained in an action for conversion of personal property, or of promissory note,50 or of rents collected, or of the proceeds of a sale of goods by a factor after demand.52 But an ordinary action for money due under a contract is not transformed into an action for conversion by alleging that the "defendant embezzled and controverted to his own use. plaintiff's share of the commissions," since the word embezzled and controverted under the circumstances are mere legal conclusions and may be disregarded. A judgment obtained in an action for the breach of a fiduciary relationship may be enforced by an execution against the person.54 

But where the complaint as a whole does not show that the defendant was acting in a fiduciary capacity the mere injection into the complaint of the statement that the defendant was acting in a fiduciary capacity will avail nothing. Thus, an 53

§ 724. Executions Against the Person of the Plaintiff. 

If the action is one in which an execution against the person is allowable, it makes no difference in whose favor the judgment in such action is obtained. If the plaintiff fails in his action, and a judgment is entered against him for costs, the defendant may have an execution against the person to enforce it.50 Likewise, where the plaintiff succeeds, but on account of the smallness of the verdict the defendant becomes entitled to costs, and the costs exceed the verdict so that defendant obtains a judgment against the plaintiff, such judgment may be enforced on behalf of the defendant by an execution against the person. The right of the defendant to arrest the plaintiff upon a body execution depends solely upon the right of the plaintiff to have the defendant arrested had the judgment been against the defendant instead of against the plaintiff.58 57 

§ 725. Limitations on the Right to an Execution Against the Per son - General Rule.

Even though the action be one in which an execution against the person is allowable, there are certain limitations upon the judgment creditor's right to resort to it. 

The general rule is that an execution against the person of the judgment debtor can not be issued until an execution against his property has been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied. Moreover, if the judgment debtor be a resident

To lay the proper foundation for an action against the bail, an execution against the property of the defendant must have been issued to the sheriff of the county in which he was arrested and returned by that sheriff wholly or partly unsatisfied, and if the defendant is a resident of the state and his arrest was effected in some other county than that of his residence an execution against his property must have been issued in the county where he resides. § 726. The Same-Exceptions to the General Rule. 

While it is the general rule that an execution against the property of the judgment debtor must have been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied before an execution against his person may be issued there are two exceptions to such rule. 

An execution against the person may be issued without having previously issued an execution against property in the following cases: a. Where the judgment debtor is actually confined, without having been admitted to the liberties of the jail, by virtue of an execution against his person issued in another action, or of an order of arrest or a surrender of his bail in the same action, an execution against his person may issue in the first instance.65 b. An execution against the person of the judgment debtor may by leave of the court issue while an execution against his property issued in the same action remains unreturned."" 

§ 727. The Same - Where the Defendant Is a Woman. 

In addition to the limitations on the right to issue an execution against the person discussed in the two preceding sections, if the judgment debtor be a woman an execution against her person can not issue unless an order of arrest has been granted and has not been vacated." Before an order of arrest can be procured against a woman defendant, except in a case where the order can be granted only by the court, the action in which it is obtained must not only be one of those specified in section 826 of the Civil Practice Act, but must be for wilful injury to person, property or character. To secure, therefore, an execution in such a case against the person of a woman (leaving out of consideration cases where the order can be granted only by the court), 68 (a) The action must be one specified in section 826 of the 

Civil Practice Act. 

(b) In such action a recovery of damages must be sought for willful injury to person, property or character. the damages suffered by the plaintiff by reason the escape and the insolvency of the defendant is a defense. 

Where the sheriff is liable as bail the insolvency of the defendant is no defense and could not be shown in mitigation of damages. Buczynski v. 

Anderson, 174 A. D. 790, 161 N. Y. S. 

697; Smith v. Knapp, 30 N. Y. 581. 

65. Civil Practice Act, § 766; Smith v. Knapp, 30 N. Y. 581.

67. Civil Practice Act, § 765. 

68. Civil Practice Act, § 829, See 

§ 498, ante.

(c) An order of arrest must have been issued in said action and must have been executed and not vacated. 

The case of Allen v. Fromme " well illustrates the difference in practice with relation to men and women defendants in this connection. Allen had brought an action for conversion against Mary A. Becket, who was engaged in the storage business. The alleged conversion was based upon the refusal of Mary A. Becket to deliver certain personal property, held by her in storage, unless the cartage and warehouse charges on the same were paid. Plaintiff claimed the right to the property without the payment of such charges. The action resulted in a judgment for the defendant for costs. Thereupon her attorney Fromme issued an execution against the person of Allen under which he was taken into custody and restrained of his liberty for six months. 

An application had been made to vacate the execution which was denied in the lower court but granted on appeal. Thereupon Allen begins this action against the attorney for false arrest, claiming that as the original action was against a woman defendant where no willful injury to property, person or character was alleged no execution against her person could have issued in that action had the plaintiff been successful, and consequently no body execution could legally have issued against the plaintiff on the defendant's success. 

The Court of Appeals sustained this view and reversed the lower court's dismissal of the complaint for failure to state a cause of action.70 

§ 728. Effect of Imprisonment Under an Execution Against the 

Person. 

At common law the imprisonment of the judgment debtor was deemed to be a satisfaction of the judgment so that there no longer remained any judgment upon which an execution thereafter could issue. This rule has been expressly changed by statute for now it is provided that notwithstanding that the judgment debtor has been imprisoned under an execution and subsequently discharged, the judgment creditor "has the same remedy against the property of the person imprisoned which he had before such execution or mandate was issued; but the 

69. 195 N. Y. 404. 

70. See also Stewart v. Smith, 186 

A. D. 755, 175 N. Y. S. 468; Gray v. 

Breckheimer, 193 A. D. 231, 183 N.

prisoner shall not be again imprisoned upon a like process issued in the same action or arrested in any action upon any judgment under which the same may have been granted."71

The present rule is that an imprisonment under an execution of a person is a satisfaction of the judgment so long only as the imprisonment continues. The judgment is not thereby absolutely extinguished, but the imprisonment bars the creditor from all other actions while the debtor is in custody." 

The imprisonment surrenders the lien of the judgment upon the real estate of the defendant and the plaintiff while the imprisonment continues can neither bring an action on the judgment nor enforce collateral securities for its payment. 

The release of the prisoner upon an undertaking given by him for the liberties of the jail, does not alter the effect produced by his imprisonment, since the judgment debtor is still considered to be imprisoned," but if he escapes from prison the lien of the judgment is restored and he may be imprisoned under a new execution or an execution against his property may be issued the same as if he had never been taken and imprisoned under an execution against his person."4 

§ 729. Effect of the Consent of the Judgment Creditor to the Release of the Judgment Debtor from Imprisonment.

After a judgment debtor has remained in custody by virtue of an execution against his person for the space of thirty days, the judgment creditor may serve upon the sheriff a written notice requiring him to discharge the judgment debtor from custody by virtue of the execution. The sheriff must thereupon discharge him. In such case another executio against the person of the judgment debtor can not be issued upon the judgment, but the judgment creditor may otherwise enforce the judgment as if the execution from which he was discharged had been returned without his having been taken.

§ 730. The Term of Imprisonment. 

No person shall be imprisoned within the prison walls of any jail for a longer period than three months under an execution, or any other mandate against the person to enforce the recovery of a sum of money less than five hundred dollars in amount, and where the amount is five hundred dollars or over, such imprisonment shall not continue for a longer period than six months.78 No person shall be imprisoned for a longer period than six months upon any execution or other mandate against the person, and no action shall be commenced against the sheriff upon a bond given for the jail liberties by such person. It shall be the duty of the sheriff in whos custody any such person is held to discharge such person at the expiration of said respective periods without any formal application being made therefor. The statute also provides that these limitations on the term of imprisonment to three months or six months respectively likewise limit a commitment for contempt of court in the nonpayment of alimony or counsel fees, but this provision has been expressly superseded by section 1172 of the Civil Practice Act, where each installment of alimony may constitute a separate basis for 79

D. EXECUTIONS AGAINST EARNINGS OR INCOME § 731. History of Executions Against Earnings or Income. 

Executions against property are in general limited to tangible personal property of the judgment debtor and to his real estate. In 1903, there was introduced into the law a new type of execution. It is an execution against wages, debts, earnings, salary, income from trust funds or profits. 

It was originally limited in its application to judgments recovered wholly for necessities sold or work performed in a 88

§ 733. What Are Wages, Debts, Earnings, Salary, Income from Trust Funds or Profits of the Judgment Debtor Amounting to Twelve Dollars Per Week. 

Wages, salary and earnings contemplate compensation for services rendered. Earnings is a more comprehensive term than wages and includes any pecuniary benefit added to wages paid." Thus a judgment debtor who works for forty-five dollars per month and board, which is estimated to be worth three dollars and a half per week, earns more than twelve dollars per week, and is subject to a salary execution." But forty-nine dollars per month and unascertained value of a right to live in a house with his sister in consideration for his furnishing food, light and fuel to her do not authorize the issuance of an execution against the judgment debtor.99 

Again, compensation due to a lecturer for the board of education represents "if not wages or salary certainly earnings.'"

The terms wages, earnings and salary have been liberally construed. An implied contract of services comes within the statute if the reasonable value of the service exceeds the weekly minimum of twelve dollars required by the statute," and where the judgment debtor is employed as a salesman on commission and is paid one thousand dollars a month in advance of the rendition of his services, with the understanding that at the end of the year if it be found that his commissions exceed such payments he shall receive the excess, and if they are less the overpayment shall be charged against future commissions, the one thousand dollars per month received by the judgment debtor constitute wages, earnings or salary within the contemplation of the statute. The term debt seems to add very little to the terms wages, earnings and salary which may be considered debts after they are earned. Accrued alimony is not a debt within the meaning of this section. The payment of alimony is not the payment of a debt but the performance of a duty.*

Income from trust funds may be reached but where a trust is created for the benefit of a debtor and his family and the trustee was to receive the rents, income and profits and itself apply them to the support of the judgment debtor, and whatever was not needed for his support the trustee was directed to pay over to other persons, it was held that there was no income of a trust fund due and owing to the judgment debtor or which under the trust ever could become due and owing to him. Where a trust fund has been created and the income payable to the settlor's divorced wife for the support of herself and their three children, a garnishee execution issued to enforce collection of a judgment against the wife should be directed only against one-fourth of the income from the fund and should not cover the whole thereof." While section 684 of the Civil Practice Act provides the only method for reaching an accruing salary there may be other ways of reaching the income from a trust fund." The term profits represents the advantage or gain resulting from the investment of capital or the acquisition of money beyond the amount expended - a pecuniary gain.¹º 10 Therefore, a voluntary payment made to a wife from a husband who was living apart from her, though it consists of one hundred and fifty dollars monthly, can not be reached by garnishee execution for it is not a profit any more than a gift is, and it is not a debt, for while the husband is liable for the support and maintenance of his wife he is not in the absence of a decree indebted to her in any sum whatever, and, of course, such payment does not fall under the terms of wages, debts, earnings or salary."

§ 734. Application for Order Directing Issuance of Garnishee Execution - To Whom Made. 

12 The judgment creditor may apply to the court in which the judgment was recovered or to a judge or justice thereof for the order directing the issuance of an execution against wages, salary, etc.¹ The statute not only authorizes the court in which the judgment was recovered to issue the order but provides that "the court having jurisdiction of the same may do so.15 This empowers a justice of the supreme court, or a county judge of the county where the action is triable or in which the attorney for the applicant resides to issue the order.16 In New York county where there is no county judge a justice of the City Court may make or modify such an order." It was held, however, under the Code that a county judge had no statutory power to issue a garnishee execution in a supreme court action.18 Orderly practice seems to require that this order should be applied for, however, in the judicial district where the judgment debtor lives.¹º 

§ 735. Necessary Papers. 

The necessary papers upon which the application for an order directing the issuance of a garnishee execution may be made are: An affidavit, sometimes a notice to the judgment debtor and sometimes to the person from whom the judgment is to be collected, and the proposed order. The requirements of the affidavit and the proposed order are sufficiently shown in the two following sections.

§ 740. The Presentation of the Execution. 

The execution is delivered to the officer named in it. Such officer will be the constable, if the execution is issued under the direction of a justice of the peace; a marshal, if issued by direction of the Municipal Court of the City of New York or a judge thereof; the city marshal, if issued under the direction of the City Court of the City of New York or a judge thereof; the sheriff, if issued out of the County Court or the Supreme Court or by a judge or justice thereof. The officer should present the execution personally to the employer, trustee or person from whom the judgment is to be collected. If such person be a corporation the execution is presented to an executive officer or some agent of the corporation whose duties are of sufficient importance to make it reasonably proper that the process will be brought to the attention of the corporation.28 If a question arises as to the 

28. Sharke v. Beckwith, 227 N. Y. 42.

sufficiency of such presentation, the determination of such question would seem to be one for the jury in any action brought against the corporation for failure to comply with the terms of the execution.29 

§ 741. The Effect. 

Upon presentation to the party to be charged therewith such an execution constitutes a lien and continuing levy upon the wages, earnings, debts, salary, income from trust funds or profits due or to become due to said judgment debtor to the amount specified in the execution.30 In case the party served with the execution be any city or county official of the state or board of education of any city, and the judgment debtor shall resign or be dismissed before such execution is satisfied and such employee be reinstated or re-employed the execution lapses and no further deduction shall be made thereon unless such reinstatement or re-employment occur within ninety days after such resignation or dismissal.³¹ 

Such execution, moreover, in any such case if filed in any department of such city, county or board within five days prior to the date on which payment of wages, debts, earnings and salary are paid shall not become a lien against the wages, debts, earnings and salary that are payable on the said payroll but shall become a lien upon the wages, debts, earnings and salary which shall become due and owing to the judgment debtor thereafter.82

§ 744. Introduction. 

As executions reach, generally speaking, only legal interests in real estate and tangible personal property, it becomes important to inquire into the ways and means of reaching other property which the judgment debtor may have and of applying it to the satisfaction of the judgment. The debtor may have claims against third parties. He may have an interest in real or personal property which he has fraudulently conveyed to avoid an execution. He may in general have many choses in action as distinguished from choses in possession, none of which are reachable by execution but which nevertheless are valuable and inquiry will be directed in this chapter into the ways and means of reaching such property and applying it to the satisfaction of the judgment. 

Then too, the debtor may have tangible assets which neither the creditor nor the sheriff has discovered and some form of procedure is needed to disclose such property and apply it to the satisfaction of the judgment. 

The only form of procedure furnished by common law for the enforcement of a judgment was the execution, and after that remedy was exhausted, equity stepped in and through the instrumentality of a creditor's bill sought to give the relief desired. 

This latter proceeding was often attended with great delay and expense and was generally unsatisfactory. Accordingly, certain statutory remedies have been devised which were intended in part at least as a substitute for the creditor's bill and have for the most part superseded that process.¹ 

1. Importers & Traders Natl. Bank v. Quackenbush, 143 N. Y. 567, 571 and cases cited; Lissner v. Toplitz, 86 

A. D. 1; 83 N. Y. S. 423, aff'd 177

N. Y. 559. 28

JUDGMENTS-SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

These statutory remedies are summary in character and comparatively speedy in producing results. They are special proceedings as distinguished from actions and are denominated in the Civil Practice Act "Proceedings Supple mentary to Execution."" Nevertheless, they are held to be proceedings in an action for the purpose of determining where papers are to be filed¹ and orders in them of some courts of limited jurisdiction may be served anywhere within the state as orders in an action may be." 

§ 745. Remedies Provided. 

There are four distinct remedies provided for achieving the purpose described in the preceding section." While all of them have for their object, the discovery of property of the judgment debtor and the application of it to the satisfaction of the judgment, the first two and the fourth of these remedies seek to accomplish such result by an examination of the judgment debtor, while the third seeks to accomplish it by an examination of a third party. The distinction between the first and second of the remedies is that the first defers the examination until after the return of the execution and the consequent exhaustion of the legal remedies of the judgment creditor and is therefore a substitute for the former judgment creditor's bill in equity,' while the second seeks the examination before the execution is returned and is therefore a proceeding really in aid of execution and not a substitute for a creditor's bill. The fourth is a short cut, via subpoena, to the first or second. The remedies are distinct from one another by the express language of the statute and the third may be prosecuted either alone or simultaneously with either of the other three." Indeed by prosecuting the third remedy with one of the others, better results are often

§ 746. General Prerequisites That Must Exist Before Any of the Four Remedies May Be Resorted To. 

Before any of the remedies provided by sections 773 and 773a of the Civil Practice Act may be resorted to, the following prerequisites must exist:10 (a) A judgment must have been obtained that is enforcible by execution as distinguished from one that may be enforced only by contempt proceedings. These proceedings are supplementary to execution, not to contempt proceedings. (b) The judgment must have been rendered for a sum not less than twenty-five dollars. (c) The judgment must be one in personam as distinguished from a judgment in rem. (d) The execution must have been issued out of a court of record (except in the case of the fourth remedy). (e) It must have been issued either "1. To the sheriff of the county where the judgment debtor, at the time of the commencement of the special proceedings, has a place for the regular transaction of business in person; or, 2. If the judgment debtor is then a resident of the state, to the sheriff of the county where he resides; or, 3. If he is not then a resident of the state, to the sheriff of the county where the judgment-roll is filed, unless the execution was issued out of a court other than that in which the judgment was rendered, and, in that case, to the sheriff of the county where the transcript of the judgment is filed; or, 4. If the judgment was recovered in the Municipal Court of the 

City of New York, to a city marshal pursuant to sections one hundred and thirty and one hundred and thirty-five of the New York city municipal court code. If in the City Court, to a sheriff or a city marshal, pursuant to Sec. 28 of the City Court Act."

§ 748. The Same - The Judgment Must Be One in Personam. 

The statute requires either the debtor's appearance in the action or the personal or substituted service of the summons upon him therein.13 As a judgment in rem may be satisfied only out of the property subject to the control of the court, a proceeding to discover other property which could not, if discovered, be applied to the satisfaction of the judgment would be useless.14 Substituted service is sufficient to procure a judgment in personam and therefore will furnish a proper basis for this proceeding,15 and a judgment entered by confession answers this requirement. 16 

§ 749. The Same - The Execution Must Have Been Issued Out of a Court of Record.

Except in the case of the fourth remedy, the execution must have been regularly issued out of a court of record.¹ 

Therefore, an execution issued without leave of the court more than five years after the entry of the judgment will not lay the foundation for supplementary proceedings.18 Before proceedings supplementary to execution may be resorted to for the purpose of enforcing a judgment obtained in a justice court, a transcript thereof must be filed in the office of the clerk of the county in which the judgment was rendered. The judgment from then on is deemed the judgment of the county court of that county and may be enforced accordingly.10 The Municipal Court of the City of New York is now a court of record,20 and an execution issued out of it to a city marshal will lay the foundation for supplementary proceedings.2 21

§ 750. The Same - Residence and Place for the Regular Transac tion of Business in Person.

The residence contemplated in section 775 of the Civil Practice Act need not be the judgment debtor's permanent His temporary residence will satisfy the requirements of the statute." one. 23 A place for the regular transaction of business in person is not satisfied by the place where the judgment debtor does business only through an agent. A teacher regularly transacts business in person at the school house where she teaches, though an actor does not do so at the theatre where he is filling an engagement.25 24 The residence or place of business contemplated by the statute is the one existing "at the commencement of the special proceeding" and not the one that may have existed when the execution was issued if they should be different."" 

§ 751. The First Remedy - Possible Courses. 

The first remedy provided by subdivision 1 of section 773 of the Civil Practice Act makes possible two courses which the judgment creditor may pursue. He may apply for an order for the examination of the judgment debtor or he may apply for a warrant for the arrest of the judgment debtor. The former is the usual course and the latter is invoked only where there is danger that the judgment debtor may leave the State or conceal himself and thus avoid the examination even though in doing so, he places himself in contempt of the order." The purpose of the warrant for the arrest of the judgment debtor is to secure his presence for the examination. These remedies are not exclusive of one another. The creditor may start with either but though he start with the order he may resort to the warrant in addition thereto whenever the danger of the judgment debtor's departure or concealment becomes imminent.28

§ 752. Additional Prerequisites for the First Remedy Where an Order Is Sought. 

In addition to the general prerequisites enumerated in section 746, ante, which must exist before any of the three remedies authorized by section 773 of the Civil Practice 

Act may be invoked, the following prerequisites must exist when the first of these remedies is resorted to, that is, when it is sought to examine the judgment debtor after the return of the execution: 

(a) The execution must have been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied.29 (b) The application must have been made within ten years after the return of the execution.30 (c) The judgment creditor must have exhausted all of his remedies at law for the satisfaction of the judgment.³¹ 

The statute plainly requires the return of the execution against property wholly or partly unsatisfied and that the application shall be made within ten years from such return. 

It says nothing, however, about the exhaustion of legal remedies as a prerequisite. This latter requirement grows out of the nature of this remedy as a substitute for a creditors' bill in chancery. Before such a bill could be successfully maintained, the exhaustion of the creditors' remedies at law for the satisfaction of the judgment had to be shown³2 and this requirement attaches accordingly to the substitute.33 

In most instances compliance with the literal requirements of the statute will show the exhaustion of the legal remedies but when more than ten years have elapsed since the judg ment was rendered but less than ten since the return of the execution a case is presented which literally complies with the statutory requirements but in which nevertheless the remedy may not be had because the legal remedies are not exhausted. The judgment in such case has ceased to be a lien upon the real property and chattels real of the judgment debtor and in consequence the judgment creditor's remedy at law is not exhausted. He must therefore sue on the judgment, reinstate the lien and issue an execution on

Again if a supplementary proceeding is commenced in one county and a receiver is appointed therein who attempts to sell real property located in another county, to the sheriff of which latter county no execution had issued, his attempt may be frustrated because the legal remedies of the judgment creditor in that county have not been exhausted."5 

§ 753. Additional Prerequisities for the First Remedy - When a 

Warrant Is Sought.

If a warrant of arrest is sought instead of or in addition to the order not only the general prerequisites shown in section 746, ante, must exist and the particular ones enumerated in the last section but in addition to these the following must exist: (a) Danger must exist that the judgment debtor will leave the State or conceal himself." (b) There must be reason to believe that he has property which he unjustly refuses to apply to the payment of the judgment."

The judgment debtor may be a resident or a non-resident," but he must be in the state when the application is made as the statute requires a showing of danger that he "will leave the state." "Reason to believe that he has property" is not satisfied by inferences drawn from allegations that he has expensive habits."" 38 

§ 754. The Second Remedy-Possible Courses. 

There are two possible courses under the second remedy provided by subdivision 2 of section 773 as there are under the first remedy. The judgment creditor may proceed by applying for an order for the examination of the judgment debtor or for a warrant for his arrest.40 The choice between them is based on the same considerations as under the first remedy.¹

JUDGMENTS § 755. Additional Prerequisites for the Second Remedy. 

In addition to the general prerequisites enumerated in section 746, ante, which must exist before any remedy in supplementary proceedings may be invoked, the following prerequisites must exist before application may be legally made to examine the judgment debtor before the return of the execution. (a) The judgment debtor must have property which he unjustly refuses to apply toward the satisfaction of the judgment.42 Such property may consist of tangible property which the sheriff cannot clearly identify for the purpose of levying upon the same or it may be intangible property which the sheriff could not reach under an execution such as a bank account.¹ 44 43 (b) Prior to the amendment of C. P. A., § 780, in 1932 it was necessary to demand that such property be applied to the satisfaction of the judgment. Such demand was necessary to establish the injustice of the debtor's refusal to apply the property to the satisfaction of the judgment.5 Under the amended statute as it exists today such a demand is no longer necessary. This remedy is not like the first, a substitute for a creditor's bill, and, therefore, it is not necessary first to exhaust the legal remedies of the judgment creditor before applying for it.16 Neither does the ten year limitation prescribed for the first remedy," apply here.48

§ 757. Necessary Papers. 

The necessary papers for any of the three remedies provided by section 773 of the Civil Practice Act are an affidavit and an order. In the case of the third remedy, the examination of a third party, the judge may require that a notice be given to the judgment debtor of the subsequent proceedings such as the examination of the third party and the making of orders with respect to his property and before a receiver can be appointed he must require that such notice be given." In the case of the first two remedies, an affidavit and warrant may take the place of the affidavit and order or be had in addition thereto.55 § 758. § 760. The Same Affidavit for an Order Before Return of 

Execution. 

The requisites of the affidavit where the order is sought before the return of the execution are the same as those for the affidavit after the return of the execution, except with regard to the facts to be stated in the body thereof. The body of the affidavit in this case must show the general prerequisites enumerated in section 746, ante, and required by section 775 of the Civil Practice Act, and it must in addition state facts showing the existence of the particular prerequisites pertaining to this, the second remedy, which are enumerated in section 755, ante, and required by section 780 of the Civil Practice Act. In addition to these it must satisfy the requirements of Rule 61 of the Rules of Civil Practice.

§ 761. The Same -Form of Affidavit for Order Before Return of 

Execution. 68 The form of the affidavit for an order before the return of the execution is the same as the form of the affidavit for an order after the return of the execution, except that in the body of the affidavit, two differences exist. The first difference is that the statement to the effect that the sheriff has returned the execution wholly or partly unsatisfied is stricken out and the following statement is substituted: "That said execution has not been returned by said sheriff and said judgment is wholly unsatisfied."

The second difference between this affidavit and the former one is that there must appear in this affidavit a statement to the following effect, which does not appear in the affidavit for an order after the return of an execution: 19.... "That said judgment debtor has property consisting of (here state what the property is as fully as may be possible), which he unjustly refuses to apply to the satisfaction of the judgment and as deponent is informed and believes that on the ...... day of ... and after the issuance of the said execution a demand was made by .........."

The requisites of the affidavit used where an order is sought for the examination of a third person are the same as those required for the affidavit after the return of an execution except with regard to the facts to be stated in the body thereof.
