§ 765. The Same - The Order - What Judge May Make. 

Proceedings supplementary to execution must be instituted before a judge and not before the court. 76 Judgments rendered in the Supreme Court. 

A Justice of the Supreme Court in any part of the state may make the order on a Supreme Court judgment," but if the judgment debtor is a resident of the state or has an office within the state for the regular transaction of business in person, he cannot be compelled to attend without the county where he has such residence or place of business. A county judge of the county to which the execution was issued may also institute proceedings on such a judgment." The execution may be issued to any county simply by filing a transcript of the judgment with the county clerk of said county.

Judgments rendered in the County Court. 

The county judge of the county may of course make the order on a county court judgment, so may the special county judge or the special surrogate.75 Where it is shown by affidavit that each of these judges is absent from the county, or for any reason is unable or disqualified to act, a justice of the Supreme Court may make the order.76 A transcript of a county court judgment may be filed in the office of any county clerk in the state and execution issued thereon to that county. Thereupon the foregoing regulations will apply to such county the same as if it were the county where the judgment was rendered.

Judgments of the City Court of the City of New York. 

A justice of the City Court of the City of New York may make the order on such judgments." A transcript of a city court judgment may be filed and the judgment docketed in the office of the clerk of any county in the state and execution issued thereon to that county. Thereafter such judgment may be enforced by supplementary proceedings the same as if it were a county court judgment. 

Judgments of the Municipal Court of the City of New York. 

Where the judgment upon which the execution was issued was recovered in a Municipal Court of the City of New York, either special proceeding shall be instituted before a justice of the City Court of the City of New York.78 Such proceedings may now be instituted by a justice of the City court where the execution is issued to a city Marshal." 

A transcript of such judgment may be filed in the office of the clerk of the county where rendered80 and therein docketed after which the judgment is deemed a judgment of the Supreme Court and may be enforced accordingly.82

Justice Court Judgments. 

Since these courts are not courts of record, supplementary proceedings may not be instituted to enforce judgments rendered in them until a transcript thereof is filed in the office of the clerk of the county where rendered. Thereafter, however, such judgment is deemed a judgment of the County Court of that county and must be enforced accordingly.83

§ 770. Second and Subsequent Examinations. 

once fully. Further examinations are in the judge's dis- 

The judgment creditor has a right to examine his debtor cretion and in an application for the same it should be made to appear that the judgment debtor has acquired property since his last examination, that it remains in his possession or under his control, and is applicable to the payment of the judgment. § 772. The Examination — Where Held. 

If the judgment debtor or third party, required to attend and be examined, is, at the time of the service of the order upon him, a resident of the state, or then has an office within the state for the regular transaction of business in person, he can not be compelled to attend, pursuant to the order or to any adjournment, at a place without the county wherein his residence or place of business is situated."

§ 773. The Same - Conduct of. 

The examination proceeds under oath.98 The subject-matter thereof is the property of the judgment debtor. The sources of the judgment debtor's property may be inquired into," and its disposition ascertained. One special object of inquiry is whether any fraudulent disposition or concealment of property has been had or attempted.¹ 

On this issue the parties to the proceeding may be examined as witnesses on their own behalf and may produce witnesses as on the trial of an action and examine them." 

Witnesses must be compelled to attend by subpoena, and the subpoena should be signed by the judge or referee before whom the examination is being conducted.* 

To the end that the examination may be most searching a party or witness is not excused from answering questions on the ground that his examination will tend to convict him of the commission of a fraud, and answers made can not be used as evidence in a criminal action or proceeding against him.5 

§ 774. The Same - Adjournments of. 

Reasonable adjournments may be had from time to time."

§ 775. Referees in Supplementary Proceedings. 

The original order instituting the proceedings may designate therein a referee before whom the judgment debtor or third party is required to attend and be examined," or the judge to whom such order is made returnable may, at any stage of the proceedings, make an order directing that any other examination or testimony be taken by, or a question arising be referred to, a referee designated in such order.12 

The referee should not be an interested party, such as an attorney holding an unsatisfied judgment against the debtor.13 

The referee before entering upon an examination must subscribe and take an oath that he will faithfully and fairly discharge his duty upon the reference and make a just and true report according to the best of his understanding.¹4

At the conclusion of the examination he must certify to the judge to whom the order is returnable all the evidence and other proceedings taken before him.15 

§ 776. Judgment Creditor's Course When Property is Found - In 

General.

The course which the judgment creditor may follow when property of the judgment debtor is discovered on the examination, depends upon the nature of the property and its control. 

In the first place, certain property is exempt from these proceedings and may not be interfered with by them.10

Where property not exempt is discovered a receiver may always be appointed to take it over or sue for its possession and apply it according to law and under the direction of the court to the satisfaction of the judgment.' 17 It is not, however, always necessary that a receiver be appointed when property not exempt is discovered. § 778. The Same - Permissive Order. 

Where a person or corporation is indebted to the judg ment debtor, the judge by whom the order instituting these proceedings was granted or to whom such order is made returnable may make an order in his discretion permitting the person or corporation to pay to a sheriff designated in the order a sum on account of the alleged indebtedness not exceeding the sum which will satisfy the execution.82 This order is permissive and not mandatory. Its purpose is to enable a person who owes the judgment debtor and is willing to pay the debt, to make payment thereof to the sheriff without being subject later to an action by the judgment debtor for the recovery of the indebtedness. The effect of a payment made pursuant to a permissive order is a discharge of the indebtedness to the extent of the payment.33 

Such permissive order, however, must be made, if made at all, before the appointment of a receiver in the proceeding.34 

Notice of the application for the order to the person who is to pay the debt may be required or dispensed with in the discretion of the judge. The sheriff to whom the money is paid disposes of it as he would under an execution, unless a receiver is appointed when he turns it over to the latter after deducting his fees.36 35

§ 780. The Same-Appointment of Receiver. 

45a In any case where property of the judgment debtor is discovered a receiver may be appointed to apply it or to realize upon it and in cases not falling within the last two sections where permissive and mandatory orders may be made for the application of the property to the satisfaction of the judgment without a receiver, the appointment of a receiver is the only remedy afforded by supplementary proceedings for reaching and applying the property. Thus where a substantial dispute exists as to the title and right to possession of articles of personal property in the possession of a third party, and therefore a mandatory order may not be had, the appointment of a receiver is necessary since an action must be brought to recover possession of such property and a receiver is the proper party to bring such action.46

At least two days' notice of the application for the order appointing a receiver must be given personally to the judgment debtor unless the judge is satisfied that with reasonable diligence he can not be found within the state; in which case, the order must recite that fact, and may dispense with notice or direct notice to be given in any manner in which the judge thinks proper. If, however, a receiver is appointed on the return day of an order directing the judgment debtor to attend or be examined, or at the close of the examination then notice is not necessary.47 In some cases notice is required to be given to persons other than the judgment debtor. It is the duty of the judge conducting the proceeding to ascertain, if practicable, by the oath of the judgment debtor, or otherwise, whether a judgment creditor's action 48 or another special proceeding is pending against the judgment debtor. If either is pending and a receiver has not been appointed therein, notice of the application for the appointment of a receiver and of all subsequent proceedings respecting the receivership must be given in such a manner as the judge directs to the judgment creditor prosecuting it.40

§ 781. The Same Receiver Must Be Resident of the State. 

No person shall be appointed a receiver who is not a resident of this state, nor shall any person continue to act as a receiver after he has ceased to be a resident thereof, and the judgment creditor may apply to the court or judge that appointed such receiver, within thirty days after said receiver ceases to be a resident of this state, for the appointment of another person in his place, upon such notice to the persons interested as the court or judge may direct.50 

§ 782. The Same Bond of. 

A receiver in supplementary proceedings must qualify by filing a bond in the office of the clerk of the county where the judgment roll in the action is filed; or, if the execution issue out of a court other than that in which the judgment was rendered, in the office of the clerk of the county where the transcript of the judgment is filed." Although the language of section 812 of the Civil Practice Act would seem to indicate that a bond is not always required the receiver takes no title to the property of the judgment debtor until he has qualified by filing one." The form of the bond is the same as in the case where a receiver is appointed as a provisional remedy." 52 54 

§ 783. The Extension of a Receivership. 

Only one receiver of the property of a judgment debtor may be appointed. On the application for the appointment of a receiver therefore, the judge to whom the application is made must ascertain, if practicable by the oath of the judgment debtor or otherwise, whether another special proceeding or judgment creditor's action is pending against the judgment debtor." If such proceeding or action is pending and a receiver has not been appointed notice must be given to the judgment creditor prosecuting such action or proceeding. § 784. The Receiver in Supplementary Proceedings Compared With An Equity Receiver - Powers and Duties. 

A receiver in supplementary proceedings differs from an equity receiver appointed as a provisional remedy⁹ in several important particulars. In the first place, he acts for the benefit of the judgment creditor at whose instance he is appointed, and of those later supplementary proceedings to which the receivership is extended," while an equity receiver very frequently acts for the creditors generally."1 

Again, a general receiver takes no title to the property over which the receivership exists but is merely the custodian thereof," while a receiver in supplementary proceedings does take title to the personal property of the judgment debtor and. a qualified title to his real estate. While the powers and duties of the receiver are substantially alike in both cases** there is a special statutory provision" specifying the court which has control over the receiver in supplementary proceedings and indicating the manner in which he shall keep and settle his accounts.

§ 786. The Same As of what Date Title Vests in the Receiver. 

Ordinarily the title of the property of the judgment debtor vests in the receiver from the time the order appointing him is filed.80 Neither the title to property which the judgment debtor had at any time prior to this date 81 nor the title to property which subsequent to this date he acquires, vest in the receiver under the general rule. But this date varies with circumstances. 

a. The qualified title to real property vests in the receiver only from the time that the order or a certified copy thereof is filed with the clerk of the county where the real property is situated.83 b. Where the judgment debtor at the time when the order is filed resides in another county of the state, his personal property is vested in the receiver only from the time when a copy of the order certified by the clerk in whose office it is recorded is filed with the clerk of the county where he resides.84

The title of the receiver may, however, be made to reach back by relation or forward by extension for the benefit of the judgment creditor instituting the proceedings. The receiver's title extends back so as to include property of the judgment debtor owned by him at the date of the first step in the supplementary proceedings of which the judgment debtor had notice,85 and the title to property acquired by the judgment debtor subsequent to the filing of the order appointing a receiver vests in the receiver if supplementary proceedings, instituted by other judgment creditors at sub-

§ 787. Application of Proceeds by Receiver. 

Because a receiver in supplementary proceedings acts for the benefit of the judgment creditors who secures his appointment and not for the creditor generally, it is necessary for any other judgment creditor who desires to protect his rights to institute supplementary proceedings of his own, even though a receiver has already been appointed at the instance of a prior judgment creditor, and while only one receiver of the property of the judgment debtor may be appointed, an existing receivership, as already shown, may be extended to cover the later supplementary proceedings." 

The judgment creditors who are thus covered by the receivership are entitled to payment in full in the order indicated by their diligence in instituting the proceedings, and judgment creditors outside the receivership are not entitled to an order applying property in the possession of the receiver to their judgments.92 Any surplus in the hands of the receiver after payment of the judgments covered by the receivership should be restored to the judgment debtor. 

When subsequently acquired property of the judgment debtor comes into the possession of the receiver through the extension of the receivership to supplementary proceedings subsequently instituted no distinction is made between the 93

§ 788. Disobedience of Orders Contempts. 

Violation of legal orders made in supplementary proceedings is punishable as a contempt of court.95 A refusal on the part of a witness to obey a subpœna issued in a supplementary proceeding is not to be confused with a refusal to obey an order.96 Provision is made elsewhere for refusal to obey a subpœna.97 

Section 800 of the Civil Practice Act relates to punish ment for disobedience to orders.

The orders contemplated are not merely those which direct the judgment debtor or third party to attend and be examined but all other orders, even oral directions, made or given in supplementary proceedings.98 They include refusals to appear for examination," refusals to testify at the examination,' unless the refusal was not in the presence of the court,2 refusal to obey an injunction restraining the judgment debtor or third party from disposing of property,³ and a refusal to turn over property to a sheriff or a receiver.* 

§ 789. The Same - Punishment. 

The punishment for contempts under section 800 of the 

Civil Practice Act is prescribed in the Judiciary Law. Con tempts are there classified into criminal and civil and the refusal to obey orders in supplementary proceedings may be either depending upon the circumstances connected with the refusal. The punishment for criminal contempts may be a fine not exceeding two hundred and fifty dollars or imprisonment not exceeding thirty days, or both in the discretion of the court. Where a person is committed to jail for the non-payment of the fine, he must be discharged, however, at the expiration of thirty days so that even if fine and imprisonment are both imposed the limit of the imprisonment would be sixty days. Proceedings to punish as for a criminal contempt are not frequent in supplementary proceedings as in such cases the fine imposed does not inure to the benefit of the judgment creditor.?

Civil contempts are enumerated in section 753 of the Judiciary Law. In all cases of civil contempt a right or remedy of a party must be "defeated, impaired, impeded or prejudiced." Refusal to be sworn as a witness or to answer questions is enumerated in the list of civil contempts as well as in the list of criminal contempts, but the refusal must be contumacious to make it a criminal contempt.10

The punishment for civil contempts is of two kinds. (a) If an actual loss or injury has been caused to a party to an action or special proceeding by reason of the misconduct proved against the offender, and the case is not one where it is specially prescribed by law that an action. may be maintained to recover the damages for loss or injury, a fine sufficient to indemnify the aggrieved party must be imposed upon the offender and collected and paid over to the aggrieved party under the direction of the court. (b) Where it is not shown that such an actual loss or injury has been produced, a fine must be imposed not exceeding the amount of the complainant's costs and expenses and two hundred and fifty dollars in addition thereto, and must be collected and paid in like manner. In the former case (a) the fine may equal the amount of the judgment, while 11

§ 791. Corporations and Supplementary Proceedings. 

Supplementary proceedings are now applicable to corporations as they are to natural persons, and a receiver may be appointed for a corporate judgment debtor." Originally supplementary proceedings did not apply to corporations,18 but in the year 1908 the law was amended so as to include them. The language of the Civil Practice Act relating to supplementary proceedings does not specifically or otherwise exempt corporations from the provisions relating to the appointment of receivers of judgment debtors, but the corporation law itself provides for the appointment of receivers of domestic corporations and under such receivership a pro rata distribution of the assets of the corporation is made in case of insolvency. The rule in supplementary proceedings, which, briefly stated, is that the more vigilant judgment creditors are rewarded to the exclusion of the less. vigilant ones, seemed to conflict with the pro rata rule under the corporation law, and the Court of Appeals decided that the Legislature did not contemplate so radical a change in the distribution of corporate assets when it extended supplementary proceedings to corporations in 1908. 

Prior to the amendment of section 805 of the Civil Practice 

Act in 1934, a receiver of a debtor corporation had to be applied for under the provisions of the General Corporation 

Law, but that is no longer necessary.

§ 793. In General. 

If a party feels himself aggrieved¹ by errors in legal proceedings, he ordinarily has resort to one of two modes of correcting such errors. Where the error is one of form arising out of a failure to conform to the settled rules of practice of the court, the remedy is usually by motion. But where the error is committed by the court itself in making its adjudication, the remedy is either by vacating the judgment 

1. Matter of Dolphin, 240 N. Y. 89. In re Iroquois, 258 N. Y. 124; Jud.

Law, § 88. 

[901]

APPEALS. 

or by appeal to a higher tribunal to have the action of the lower court reviewed therein.¹ This right to appeal is not guaranteed by the Constitution, but is entirely statutory² and within the judgment of the legislature, and can be limited thereby.* This right can be waived by the parties, either expressly by stipulation," or impliedly, as by the acceptance of a benefit under the adjudication."

The details regulating the passage of a case from a lower to a higher court will now be considered. 

§ 794. Judgments and Orders Not Appealable 

In General.

An appeal must be from a judgment or an order; no appeal will lie from a decision of a court." 

Not every judgment or order of a lower court however is appealable to a higher tribunal. A party who has defaulted, cannot generally appeal from a judgment or order rendered or made upon his default, for he is deemed to have acquiesced therein, and is not in a position to question its validity. Nor can such a party appeal from an order denying his application to have that judgment or order set aside or modified, and thus accomplish by indirect means what he would not be permitted to do directly. The proper remedy in such a case is by motion to open the default,¹º or, under the new practice, by an application to extend the time fixed."

§ 795. Who May Appeal. 

Only a person who is aggrieved by a ruling, may appeal therefrom. If not a party to the action, the person desiring to appeal must not only be aggrieved, but must be entitled to be substituted in place of a party." A person is aggrieved, within the meaning of this provision, only when the adjudication has binding force against his rights, his person, or his property.15 An executor or a trustee under a will is not aggrieved by a judgment in regard to the disposition of property belonging to others, and cannot appeal therefrom when the real beneficiaries do not complain.16 But when an executor or trustee has a direct interest in the controversy, which is affected by the result, he may appeal," as in the case of an order imposing a transfer tax, for which he is made personally liable.18

Where the party to the record is merely a nominal one, and the real party in interest is the one aggrieved, or where since the judgment or order, there has been by death or in some other way a devolution of the entire interest or property involved in the litigation to some other party who has thus become the party aggrieved, such aggrieved party may

§ 796. Time to Appeal. 

If an appeal is not taken by the service and filing of a notice of appeal, and the giving of an undertaking when necessary, within a prescribed time, one loses his right thereto. A motion to dismiss an appeal attempted to be taken after the expiration of such time, will be granted.23 

Except in one instance, a court or judge has no power to extend the time fixed by law within which to appeal, no matter how meritorious the excuse for failure to appeal in due time.24 Where a party dies before the expiration of the time within which the appeal may be taken, the court may allow the appeal to be taken by the heir, devisee or personal representative of the decedent, at any time within four months after his death.25 The time to appeal can be extended by the parties by stipulation or can be waived, as where an attorney, after the expiration of the time limited, admits due service of the notice of appeal."

This time is ordinarily measured from the time of service upon the attorney for the appellant of a copy of the judgment or order appealed from, and a written notice of entry thereof.27 In the case, however, of the party who enters the judgment his time runs from the entry thereof. The following specifies the date from which the time begins to run in the various contingencies that may occur:28

§ 797. Notice of Appeal-In General. 

In order to perfect an appeal within the prescribed time, a written notice of appeal must be served, and in certain cases which will be discussed in connection with particular appeals, an undertaking must be given within that time. The notice of appeal must be served upon the attorney for the adverse party and upon the clerk with whom the judgment or order appealed from is entered.38 The adverse parties, within the meaning of this provision, include not only the plaintiffs in the case of a defendant appealing, or the defendants in the case of a plaintiff appealing, but also any parties on the same side whose interest in relation to the subject of the appeal is in conflict with the reversal of the order or decree appealed from, or the modification sought by the appellant." This notice is served upon the attorney in the usual way prescribed by statute and is served upon the Clerk by filing it in his office. It is proper to serve it upon the attorney who represented the adverse party in the proceedings in the lower court, or an attorney substituted in his place. If such attorney is dead, or if he has been removed and notice of removal has been served upon the appellant's attorney, but another attorney has not been substituted in his place, or if for any reason service of a notice of appeal upon the proper attorney for the adverse party, cannot be made within the state with due diligence, the notice of appeal may be served upon the respondent in the manner 40

45 An appeal may in some cases be taken directly from an order or interlocutory judgment as will be discussed later, in connection with particular appeals. § 801. Relief From Omission to Do Necessary Act in Taking 

Appeal. 

An appellant may sometimes be relieved from an omission to do an act necessary to perfect an appeal or to stay the execution of the judgment or order appealed from.53 In order to be thus relieved, he must have seasonably and in good faith served a notice of appeal therefor upon the clerk or upon an adverse party. If he has omitted however, through mistake, inadvertence or excusable neglect, to serve it upon the other, or to do any other act necessary to perfect the appeal or to stay the execution, he may apply to the court in which the appeal is taken or to the court to which the appeal is taken, for an order allowing him to supply the omission or permit an amendment.5 Such an order lies in the discretion of the court and may be made upon such terms as justice requires.' 55 Thus, where a party has served a notice of appeal seasonably and in good faith, but notice was returned by the attorney for the adverse party upon the ground that the paper upon which it was typewritten was not of the quality and weight required by the Code of Civil Procedure, he was allowed to serve the notice of appeal after the expiration of

§ 802. Orders and Interlocutory Judgments Reviewable on Appeal From Final Judgment or Order. 

Not all orders from which no separate appeal has been taken, may be reviewed upon appeal from a final judgment in an action or a final order in a special proceeding. Orders from which a direct appeal is not allowed, may not be reviewed in this manner. Moreover only intermediate orders may be thus reviewed, that is, orders made after the commencement of the action and before the entry of judgment. An order which is in effect merely a written authority to enter a final judgment or a final order, is not an intermediate order within the meaning of this provision." 

Furthermore, in order to be thus reviewed, the order must be such that it necessarily affects the final judgment or order such that, if reversed, it would take away the 62 63

An order denying a motion to strike out a defense of res adjudicata in defendant's answer is not reviewable on appeal from the judgment; such order does not necessarily affect the judgment dismissing the complaint, for the plaintiff might still urge upon the trial that the proofs offered by the defendant did not establish that defense. Dickinson v. Springer, 246 N. 

Y. 203, 208. 'There seems to be a conflict in the decisions upon the question whether an order of reference necessarily affects the final judgment, and is thus reviewable upon an ap-

APPEALS. 

911 foundation of the judgment, or make the trial or the judgment entered invalid or without support.65 Orders which merely relate to the pleadings or procedure in the action, such as an order to amend a pleading or for a bill of particulars, do not necessarily affect the final judgment." Likewise, an order substituting a plaintiff as the assignee of the former plaintiff in the action, has no relation to the final judgment and is not reviewable upon the appeal therefrom."7 

But an order made upon a motion for judgment upon the pleadings necessarily affects the judgment and may be included in an appeal from a final judgment, although the better practice in such a case is to appeal directly from the order before the entry of judgment." Where a motion is made before the entry of judgment to set aside a verdict and for a new trial upon the ground of the misconduct of a juror," or upon the minutes," an order denying that motion is reviewable upon appeal from the final judgment. 

After final judgment is entered, this is the only method of reviewing such an intermediate order or interlocutory judgment, for the right to a separate appeal therefrom does not survive the entry of final judgment."¹ 

§ 803. Review of Rulings Made During Trial. 

A direct appeal cannot be taken from mere rulings made during the course of the trial. But such rulings, if duly excepted to, may be reviewed upon an appeal from the judgment rendered after the trial. § 804. Case and Bill of Exceptions-In General. 

Upon an appeal, it is sometimes necessary to place before the appellate tribunal, the entire record or part of the record of the trial. If one is seeking to review only rulings of the court upon exceptions to the admission or rejection of certain testimony, one need present only the particular evidence objected to, together with such of the context as is absolutely necessary to aid the higher court in its determination as to the admissibility or inadmissibility of that evidence. 

The paper or set of papers containing such evidence is termed a bill of exceptions. 

Upon appeal from certain other rulings of the court, however, such as a nonsuit or the direction of a verdict, the entire record of the trial must be set forth; for, without such record, the appellate court could not decide whether there was sufficient evidence introduced to sustain the cause of action in the one instance, or sufficient evidence to go to the jury in the other instance." Where it is thus necessary to present all the evidence taken at the trial, the paper or set

§ 805. The Same When Necessary. 

A case or a bill of exceptions is, in general, necessary when a party intends to appeal from a judgment rendered after the trial of an issue of fact, or from an order granting or denying a motion for a new trial upon the minutes." However, where an issue of fact was tried by a Referee or by the court without a jury, and the only question to be brought up for review is whether the findings of fact authorize the conclusions of law and the judgment rendered thereon, the judgment roll is all that is needed to present this question.80 

If any other question is to be raised, however, such as the rulings upon the admission or rejection of evidence upon the trial, a case or a bill of exceptions is necessary.8¹ 

A motion for a new trial upon the ground of newly discovered evidence is peculiar in its nature, in that it depends merely upon extrinsic facts and not upon errors committed upon the trial. § 806. The Same Contents. 

85 The case or bill of exceptions must contain the evidence by question and answer, the objections thereto, the rulings of the court, and the exceptions of all parties to the record. 

Prior to 1913 it was proper to set forth the evidence in narrative form, but now it must be set forth in haec verba.84 However, if the parties agree on the facts proven, with the approval of the judge, they may insert these facts as agreed upon instead of the testimony. The opening and summing up or the remarks of counsel are not to be included unless so ordered by the judge or referee. Any remark or comment of the trial judge which has been duly excepted to and which it is desired to review may be contained therein.87 

Exhibits on a trial or voluminous documents used on a motion, need not be included at length unless the Judge or Referee so direct. If such a paper is directed to be included, there must be either a certificate of the clerk that the printed paper is a true copy of the original, or a stipulation by the parties to that effect. If the case or bill of exceptions does not conform to the rules thus laid down, the court before which it is brought for review, may order the same back for resettlement.89 

If it is desired to review a question of fact, a case is necessary containing all the evidence. Furthermore there must be annexed to the case a certificate of the trial judge that all the evidence is contained therein.90 If there is no such certificate, the facts will not be reviewed," for it will be presumed that sufficient evidence was offered to warrant the decision. § 807. The Same Settlement Thereof. 

2 When it is necessary to make a case or a bill of exceptions, a copy thereof must be served upon the opposite party within a certain prescribed time. If the trial was before the court or a referee, including trial by a jury of one or more specific questions of fact in an action triable by the court, the time limited for such service is thirty days after the party has been served with a copy of the decision or report, and of written notice of the entry of judgment thereon. If the trial was before a jury, and a motion is made for a new trial and not decided at the time of the trial, the time limited is thirty days after notice of the entry of the order on such motion; in other cases where the trial was before a jury, thirty days after service of a copy of the judgment and notice of entry. If a party omits to make a case within the time limited, he thereby waives his right thereto. The proper practice in such a case is to move in the appellate court for an order dismissing the appeal for failure to prosecute with due diligence.* The party served with a case or bill of exceptions may propose and serve amendments thereto within ten days after such service. § 808. Appeals From the Supreme Court to the Appellate Divi sion-In General.

As the most usual course for an appeal to take, is from the Supreme Court to the Appellate Division and from the Appellate Division to the Court of Appeals, these two steps will be here considered. 

§ 809. The Same - From Judgments. 

19 A final judgment rendered in the Supreme Court upon a trial may be taken upon appeal to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. A judgment not rendered at a trial, as a judgment entered upon an order dismissing an action for failure to prosecute, is not appealable, but the orders upon which a judgment rests are appealable, and upon their reversal, the judgment would necessarily fall.2º 21 An appeal from a judgment brings up for review questions of fact as well as questions of law, and this is true whether the trial was by a referee, by the court without a jury, or by the court with a jury. Prior to 1914, in the case of a jury trial, an appeal from the judgment brought up only questions of law, the facts being reviewable only upon an appeal from an order denying a motion for a new trial. But now, upon an appeal from the judgment, the appellant may make the claim that the verdict was against the weight of evidence despite the failure to move for a new trial.22

§ 810. The Same From Orders in an Action. 

The review of orders, upon an appeal from a final judgment, has been discussed.23 A separate appeal may be taken, if one chooses, from certain Supreme Court orders, if made in an action. Only orders made upon notice are appealable.25 It matters not, however, whether the order be a court order or a judge's order,20 or even whether it is made by a judge of a court other than the court in which the action is pending.27 A judge's order must be filed, however, before an appeal can be taken therefrom. A party wishing to appeal may, by application to a judge of the court to which the appeal may be taken, compel the filing of the order.28 

An order made preliminary to the bringing of an action may nevertheless be an order in the action, as in the case of an order for the publication of a summons. An order made upon a summary application after judgment, is deemed to have been made in the action within the meaning of this section. This latter provision has been applied to orders opening or setting aside judgments, and to an order denying a motion to vacate the satisfaction of a judgment.31 30 An order may be appealed from if it involves some part of the merits,32 or if it affects a substantial right. A "substantial right" does not refer merely to an absolute legal right, but to a matter of substance as distinguished from one of mere form. Thus an order though discretionary, may affect a substantial right, and hence may be reviewed upon appeal to the Appellate Division. The following are orders affecting a substantial right, and hence are appealable: An order granting leave to sue a receiver appointed in an 34

§ 811. The Same - From Interlocutory Judgment. 

A direct appeal may also be taken to the appellate division from an interlocutory judgment rendered at a special term or trial term of the supreme court or entered upon the report of a referee.50 Or such interlocutory judgment may be reviewed upon an appeal from the final judgment, as previously stated.51 

§ 812. The Same-Security to Perfect Appeal or to Stay Execu tion.

No security is required to perfect an appeal from the Supreme Court to the Appellate Division.52 However, upon an appeal from a final judgment, the appellant may in certain cases give security, and the giving of the security operaates as a stay of the execution of the judgment appealed from.53 No order is then necessary. In such a case, he must give all the security that is required, both to perfect an appeal to the Court of Appeals from a judgment of the same amount or to the same effect, and to stay the execution thereof. The judgments, the execution of which may be thus ipso facto stayed upon the giving of security, are the same as upon an appeal to the Court of Appeals; and the security to be given in each instance, will be considered in the discussion of appeals to the Court of Appeals. § 813. The Same - Where Appeals to be Heard. 

The appeal must in general be heard in the department embracing the county in which the judgment or order appealed from is made. However, where four justices of the 

Appellate Division are not qualified to sit in the case, or where the justices qualified to hear the appeal are equally divided and hence unable to render a decision therein, a party is entitled to an order transferring the appeal to another department to be there heard and determined.5 When the justice before whom an action was tried or who granted the order appealed from, is a member of the Department of the Appellate Division before which the appeal comes on for argument, a party may move for an order sending the appeal to an adjoining department. The granting of such a motion lies in the discretion of the court. Since 1915, the court has had also the discretionary power to grant an order directing an appeal to be sent to another department for hearing and determination, in any other case, where such an order would aid in the furtherance of justice."7

although the Appellate Division could reverse a judgment for errors of law or because the findings or verdict were against the weight of evidence, in case of such reversal, a new trial had to be granted. It had no power to render a final judgment in favor of the appellant, unless the facts were conceded, incontrovertibly established by record or otherwise, or found by the trial court. Division may reverse wholly or partly the judgment appealed from, and its power to order a new trial in such case, a new trial in an action against a single defendant can be granted only as to the whole action." Otherwise fragments of the same cause might be found, some in the court of original jurisdiction and others in the court of last resort. Where there are several defendants, however, and there is error affecting only one who has a separate defense, the judgment as to him may be reversed and a new trial ordered, leaving final judgment to stand as to the others."7

The right to a trial by jury is insured by the Constitution. 

Accordingly, when a trial has been before a jury, the appellate court cannot in general make its own findings of fact, but if it renders final judgment, this judgment must be rendered either upon the special finding of the jury or the general verdict. However, where, upon a motion to dismiss the complaint or to direct the verdict, or upon the submission of disputed questions of fact to the court for decision, the trial court errs by submitting the case to the jury, or in deciding a question of fact submitted to it, the Appellate Division may finally dispose of the case in the manner in which it should have been disposed of in the first instance."⁹ 

In such a case, the right to a jury trial never existed or has been waived. Where specific questions of fact or the assessment of damages has been submitted to the jury, pending the decision of a motion for non-suit or for the direction of a verdict, and thereafter such motion is granted, the Appellate Division may reverse the judgment entered thereon, and grant judgment on the special findings of the jury.70 

In such a case, the special verdict or general verdict must form part of the record."¹

§ 815. Appeals to the Court of Appeals In General. 

The appeals to the Appellate Division, which have been discussed in the preceding sections, are decided by four separate divisions or departments of the Appellate Court, and it is inevitable that their judgments, to some extent, conflict with each other. Hence, in order that the law of the entire state may be uniform, consistent and harmonious, a second appeal is, in certain instances, allowed. This appeal is to the Court of Appeals, the court of last resort in the state's judicial system.72 73 

§ 816. The Same - Jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals. 

The proper and necessary function of a court of last resort, is to settle the law; and so the jurisdiction of the 

Court of Appeals is limited, both by the Constitution and by the Civil Practice Act, to the review of questions of law, except in criminal cases where the judgment imposes the penalty of death, or in a civil case where the Appellate Division has made new findings of fact upon reversing or modifying a final determination of the court below and has rendered a final judgment or final order thereon." Controversy about the facts ends with the Appellate Division." The 

Court of Appeals must accept the facts as found in the Appellate Division, unless there is no evidence to support the verdict or finding. It cannot inquire into weight of evidence in favor of a verdict or finding." Nor can it review matters lying in the discretion of the lower court; for whether the court will exercise a discretionary power depends upon all the circumstances of the case, and thus involves a question of fact." But the question whether there is any evidence to support a verdict or a finding, or a refusal to find, or whether

However, not all questions of law may be reviewed by the Court of Appeals. Many questions of law necessitate a review of all the facts; for example, the court must review the entire record in order to determine whether there is any evidence to sustain a finding of fact or a verdict. At one time, all of such questions were appealable to the Court of Appeals. But that court became overloaded with work, much of which was outside of its primary function of settling the law of the state.80 Hence, a provision of law was enacted precluding the review of a unanimous decision of the Appellate Division that there is evidence to sustain a finding of fact or a verdict not directed by the court. This provision does not make the judgment entered on such a decision unappealable, but merely prevents the review of that particular question of law. § 817. The Same - From Final Judgments and Final Orders.

Accordingly, it has restricted the absolute right to appeal therefrom to the following cases: 89 1. Until the law was amended in 1917, permission to appeal was necessary in certain actions in order to appeal to the Court of Appeals from any unanimous decision of the Appellate Division, even though of reversal or modification. These actions included among others, actions for damages for personal injuries, actions to set aside a judgment or conveyance as in fraud of creditors, or actions to recover wages.98 But by amendment, this provision was omitted and accordingly such cases now fall within the general rules relating to appeals. 

§ 818. The Same - Appeals Directly From Lower Court in Case of Interlocutory Judgment or Order Refusing a New Trial. 

Most appeals to the Court of Appeals reach that court directly from the Appellate Division. But one notable case in which an appeal is allowed directly to the Court of Appeals from any court of record has already been pointed out, viz., the case in which the only question involved is one of constitutionality. In a few specified cases, appeals bringing up for review a determination of the Appellate Division, are allowed to the Court of Appeals from a final judgment rendered at a special or trial term, or pursuant to the directions contained in a referee's report. This is true in the following two classes of cases: 

1. Appeals to the Court of Appeals from final judgments rendered in the court below, after the affirmance, reversal or modification by the Appellate Division of an interlocutory judgment. 

2. Appeals from final judgments rendered in the court below after the refusal by the Appellate Division of a new trial."⁹ 

This provision allowing an appeal directly to the Court of Appeals is intended to save the time and expense otherwise incurred in the useless formality of a second appeal to the Appellate Division.

§ 819. The Same - From Order Granting a New Trial. 

A direct appeal to the Court of Appeals from an order of the Appellate Division is allowable as a matter of right in only one case, and then conditionally. If the Appellate 

Division has granted a new trial, a party may, instead of taking the new trial under the order of that court, appeal from such order to the Court of Appeals as a matter of right.' Where the Appellate Division affirms an order of the trial court granting a new trial, it is the same in effect as though the Appellate Division had itself granted a new trial, and may be thus appealed as of right.2 

But, in order to appeal from such an order a party must stipulate that, upon affirmance of that order by the Court of Appeals, judgment absolute shall be rendered against him.³ 

So, such an appeal lies only when the party obtaining a verdict or judgment is content, if he cannot sustain the appeal from such order, to fail wholly in his action or defense. 

Where the order is for a new trial unless the plaintiff will remit part of his verdict, he cannot appeal from that order without such stipulation; and if the order is affirmed, he loses the benefit of the alternative judgment for a reduced amount."

Under no circumstances can an appeal from an order granting a new trial be allowed without a stipulation to this effect."

Upon such an appeal, if the Court of Appeals determines that no error was committeed in granting the new trial, it must render judgment absolute against the party thus stipulating. If judgment absolute is thus awarded against the defendant, the effect is to award to the plaintiff the judgment which he is entitled to upon his complaint, without regard to any defense that has been interposed by the answer.Ⓡ 

The judgment is remitted to the court of original jurisdiction, and in that court, an assessment of damages or any other proceeding requisite to render the judgment effectual, may be had. In assessing the damages, the allegations of the complaint are required to be treated as true and as if no answer had been interposed, and the proceeding is similar to the taking of an ordinary inquest.10 A judgment absolute directed by the Court of Appeals upon stipulation is a bar to subsequent action between the same parties where the issues in both actions are identical.10a

PART V. 

A. A COMPLETE SET OF FORMS IN AN ACTION AT LAW. 

Smith v. Nassau Electric R. R. Co. 

1. Statement of Facts in the Action. 

Mrs. Helen Smith, age nineteen years, resides with her husband,

Edward Smith at No. 456-79th street, Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York. On March 14, 1930, at 8:30 p. m., Mrs. Smith boarded a Fifth avenue surface car at 79th street and Fifth avenue, Brooklyn, paid her fare and took a seat in the middle of the car on the right-hand side. As the car approached the intersection of 

Fifth avenue and 92nd street, Mrs. Smith arose from her seat, signalling the conductor that she wished to get off. The conductor, who was in the front of the car, rang the bell and Mrs. Smith went to the back platform. As she was in the act of alighting, with one foot on the ground and the other on the step of the car, the conductor again rang the bell and the car started, throwing Mrs. Smith to the ground. The car went on, but stopped after going twenty feet, due to the fact that two by-standers who saw the accident called to the conductor and rushed forward to Mrs. Smith's aid. 

Mrs. Smith's right leg was severely injured as a result of the accident, and she was taken home in a taxi. She received medical attention from her family physician, who had X-ray pictures taken of the leg. The pictures showed that a bone in the leg had been broken. 

Under the doctor's orders the leg was placed in a plaster cast and Mrs. Smith was confined to the house for over two months. In addition to the pain suffered by Mrs. Smith, it appears that her injuries in the opinion of her physician will be permanent in character, due to a shortening of the bone in her right leg, which causes her to walk with a limp. 

Mrs. Smith and her husband call on you and request that legal proceedings be instituted on her behalf against the Nassau Electric Railroad Company, a New York corporation, which operated the surface railway on which the accident happened. [938]

2. Petition for Appointment of Guardian ad Litem.

SUPREME COURT - KINGS COUNTY. 

In the Matter of the Application of 

HELEN SMITH, an infant over the age of fourteen years, for the appointment of a guardian ad litem.

TO THE SUPREME Court of THE STATE OF NEW YORK, Kings County : 

The petition of HELEN SMITH, respectfully shows: 

1. That petitioner is an infant over the age of fourteen years, to wit, of the age of nineteen years, and resides at No. 456-79th street, Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York, with her husband Edward Smith. 

2. That your petitioner is desirous of commencing an action in this court against the Nassau Electric Railroad Company, for the recovery of damages suffered by your petitioner as a result of bodily injury received by your petitioner through the negligence and carelessness of said Nassau Electric Railroad Company, its agents and employees in starting a trolley car, while your petitioner was in the act of alighting therefrom on March 14, 1930, at the intersection of Fifth avenue and 92nd street, Borough of Brooklyn, New

York City. Petitioner was thrown to the ground and severely injured without any negligence or carelessness on her part. The damages sustained by petitioner as a result of the negligence of the Nassau Electric Railroad Company, as your petitioner is advised and believes, amount to Thirty Thousand ($30,000.00) Dollars. 

3. That petitioner's husband, Edward Smith, is willing to act as guardian ad litem for your petitioner as appears by his consent which is presented on this application, and he is a person fully competent to understand and protect the rights of petitioner. 

4. No previous application for the relief herein asked has heretofore been made. 

WHEREFORE, Your petitioner prays that Edward Smith may be appointed guardian ad litem for your petitioner, for the purpose of bringing the action hereinabove described against the Nassau 

Electric Railroad Company for your petitioner.

Dated: September 5, 1930. 

HELEN SMITH, Petitioner.

8. Complaint. 

SUPREME COURT· - KINGS COUNTY. 

HELEN SMITH, an infant, by EDWARD SMITH, her guardian ad litem, Plaintiff, against 

NASSAU ELECTRIC RAILROAD COMPANY, Defendant. 

The plaintiff, complaining of the above-named defendant, by 

ROBERT GRACE, her attorney, alleges: 

First: That plaintiff is an infant nineteen years of age, that on the first day of October, 1930, EDWARD SMITH, the husband of plaintiff, was by an order of this court duly appointed guardian ad litem of said infant and authorized to institute and prosecute this cause of action.

Second: On information and belief, at the times hereinafter mentioned, the defendant was and now is a domestic corporation, organized and existing under the laws of the State of New York and at the times hereinafter mentioned, was engaged in the operation of a Street Surface Railroad, upon various streets in the Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York, including the line operating upon 

Fifth avenue, Borough of Brooklyn, City and State of New York. 

Third: That on or about the 14th day of March, 1930, the plaintiff was a passenger on one of the defendant's cars, then being operated by it upon said Fifth Avenue, Borough of Brooklyn, City and State of New York. 

Fourth: That near the intersection of Fifth avenue and Ninetysecond street, Borough of Brooklyn, New York City, plaintiff notified the conductor in charge of said car to stop the same at such intersection so that plaintiff might alight therefrom, and said conductor thereupon notified the motorman. That said car was thereupon stopped for such purpose and at the usual place, and plaintiff attempted to alight therefrom, but that through the negligence and carelessness of the motorman or conductor of said car or of both of them, said car was suddenly started while plaintiff was in the act of alighting therefrom and before she had reasonable opportunity fully to descend therefrom.

Fifth That in consequence of the aforesaid negligence and without fault or negligence on plaintiff's part, she was violently. thrown to the ground. 

Sixth: That by reason of the defendant's negligence as aforesaid, plaintiff suffered great bodily injury with accompanying pain and still continues to be sick, sore and disabled and as plaintiff is informed and believes her injuries as aforesaid, will be permanent, and she

FORMS. 

945 will be permanently disabled and caused to suffer continuous pain and inconvenience.

Seventh: That by reason of the defendant's negligence as aforesaid the plaintiff was obliged to and did necessarily employ medical aid and attendance for herself and has paid Five Hundred and Fifty ($550) Dollars for the same and will incur further liability for medicines and medical attendance. 

Eighth: That by reason of the premises, plaintiff has suffered damages to the extent of Thirty Thousand ($30,000) Dollars. 

STATE OF NEW YORK) COUNTY OF KINGS 

WHEREFORE, plaintiff demands judgment against the defendant for the sum of Thirty Thousand ($30,000) Dollars, together with the costs of this action.

ROBERT GRACE, SS.: 

Sworn to before me this 18th day of November, 1930.

GEORGE ENGLEMAN, Notary Public, Kings County 

Clerk's No. 26. Commission expires April 1, 1934. 

EDWARD SMITH, being duly sworn, says that he is the Guardian

Ad Litem above-named for the infant plaintiff, HELEN SMITH, that he has read the foregoing complaint and knows the contents thereof, that the same is true to the knowledge of deponent, except as to the matters therein stated to be alleged on information and belief, and as to those matters he believes it to be true. 

EDWARD SMITH.

12-b. Affidavit in Support of Motion. 

SUPREME COURT-KINGS COUNTY. 

HELEN SMITH, an an infant, by

EDWARD SMITH, her guardian ad litem, Plaintiff, against 

NASSAU ELECTRIC RAILROAD COMPANY, Defendant. 

STATE OF NEW YORK CITY OF NEW YORK SS.: 

COUNTY OF KINGS 

FREDERIC B. STEWART, Being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is the Assistant Secretary of the above-named defendant, which is a domestic street railroad corporation having its principal office at No. 85 Clinton Street, Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York. 

That this is an action for personal injuries and is brought by the plaintiff through ROBERT GRACE, ESQ., her attorney, whose office and post office address is at No. 165 Broadway, in the Borough of

Manhattan, City of New York, to recover the sum of $30,000 as damages for injuries alleged to have been received by the plaintiff on or about the 14th day of March, 1930. In her verified complaint, served on the defendant upon the 19th day of November, 1930, plain-

FORMS. 

949 tiff, after setting up the incorporation of the defendant, and the fact that it was a carrier of passengers, alleged that On or about said 14th day of March, 1930, as plaintiff was attempting to alight from one of defendant's cars on Fifth avenue, near the intersection of Fifth avenue and 92nd street, the said car suddenly started while plaintiff was in the act of alighting therefrom, and she was violently thrown to the ground. 

By reason thereof, plaintiff suffered great bodily injury with accompanying pain and still continues to be sick, sore and disabled, and she is informed and believes her injuries will be permanent, all to plaintiff's damage. 

That the allegations in the complaint are so general that they fail to show in detail or specifically, what plaintiff claims to be: 

1. A statement of injuries claimed to have been sustained by plaintiff, the nature, location, extent and effects of same; length of time plaintiff was confined to bed and house; what injuries it is claimed are permanent; what injuries it is claimed continue; the itemized amounts plaintiff paid for doctor's bills, hospital bills and medicines, and obligations incurred therefor. 

2. The nature of plaintiff's occupation, how long plaintiff was prevented from attending to her occupation, and what earnings plaintiff claimed to have lost as a result of the accident. 

3. An exact statement of the alleged negligent acts of the defendant's servants and particulars of any other negligent acts or omissions of defendant to which plaintiff attributes the accident. 

That by its verified answer herein the defendant denies all the material allegations of the plaintiff's complaint and that notices of trial have been served by both parties. 

Deponent further says, on information and belief, that the defendant, and its officers and agents, are entirely ignorant of the matter herein before more particularly mentioned, of which a bill of particulars is asked for herein. Upon information and belief, diligent effort has been made by the persons who have charge of this case to obtain the information asked for, but they have been unable to secure the same. That the facilities to obtain this information and the knowledge lie entirely with the plaintiff. That deponent does not believe and cannot form an opinion as to the matters with which this defendant is charged; that the complaint is so general that this defendant, through its officers and agents, does not know what it is charged with in regard to the matters before enumerated. 

That deponent has fully and fairly stated the case to GEORGE D. 

YEOMANS, ESQ., defendant's attorney herein, whose residence is at 

No. 30 East 38th street, New York City, that a verified bill of particulars of the plaintiff's claim for damages as indicated above is absolutely material and necessary for the defendant in order to investigate and properly prepare for the trial of this action, and enable it to make a defense and prevent surprise on the trial, as

FORMS. 

deponent is informed by said George D. Yeomans, attorney for the defendant, and as deponent verily believes. 

FREDERIC B. STEWART. 

Sworn to before me this 15th day of February, 1931.

WILLIAM J. MARTIN, Commissioner of Deeds, City of New 

York. Residing in the County of

Stewart, verified the 15th day of February, 1931, with due proof of service thereof, and upon the pleadings and all the proceedings heretofore had herein, and after hearing George D. FORMS.

PART V. 

FORMS. 

B. A COMPLETE SET OF FORMS IN AN ACTION IN EQUITY. 

(O'Neill v. Pilgrim Savings Bank.) 

18. Statement of Facts in the Action. 

JOHN O'NEILL, of Castlewellan, Ireland, writes to you in substance, as follows: "From 1920 to 1925 I resided in the United

States, returning to Ireland in December, 1925. My sister, Katherine 

Farrell and her husband, Arthur Farrell also resided in the United States from February, 1920, to July, 1928. They were not happily married, the husband abusing his wife and not supporting her. A number of times I advanced my sister sums of money to relieve her wants. In July, 1928, Katherine Farrell and her husband returned to Ireland. On or about July 25, 1928, Katherine Farrell gave to me a bank book showing that she had opened an account in the Pilgrim Savings Bank, 100 Chambers street, Borough of Manhattan, New York City, in the name of 'Katherine Farrell in trust for

John O'Neill.' She stated that it represented her earnings and that if anything happened to her she wished the money in the account to go to me, as I had done more for her than any one else and that she did not wish her husband to get a penny of it. The bank book shows that the account was opened on November 15, 1925, with a deposit of $100. A number of deposits were subsequently made and the present balance is $2,400. Katherine Farrell died at Castlewellan, Ireland, on March 23, 1929. The bank book remained in my possession at the time of my sister's death. Katherine Farrell died without a Will and no letters of administration have been issued on her estate.. After my sister's death I wrote to the Pilgrim 

Savings Bank notifying it of the foregoing facts. I requested payment to me of the credit balance in the account with accrued interest. The bank replied to my letter advising me that it had received a letter from Arthur Farrell in Ireland, claiming the monies in the account as his. The bank in its letter further stated that it would not pay the money to me, unless I produced from Arthur Farrell, a withdrawal of his claim to the moneys. This cannot be done.' 

O'Neill concludes his letter by stating that he wishes the proper proceedings to be taken in his behalf, to procure for him the balance in the account. [959]

22. Complaint.

SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK, COUNTY OF NEW YORK. 

JOHN O'NEILL, Plaintiff, against

The above-named plaintiff for his complaint herein alleges on information and belief:

First: That at all the times hereinafter mentioned, defendant was and now is a domestic banking corporation, organized and existing under the laws of the State of New York and having an office at 

No. 100 Chambers street, Borough of Manhattan, New York City. 

Second: That on or about the 15th day of November, 1925, one

KATHERINE FARRELL, a sister of the plaintiff, deposited with the defendant bank for the benefit of and in trust for the plaintiff, the sum of $100, and at the same time said KATHERINE FARRELL received from said bank its pass-book No. 500742, reading "KATHERINE FAR- 

RELL in trust for brother JOHN O'NEILL. 

Third: That thereafter and on or about the 25th day of July, 1928, KATHERINE FARRELL delivered said pass-book to plaintiff, who has ever since been and now is in possession thereof. 

Fourth: That thereafter and on or about the 23rd day of March, 1929, said KATHERINE FARRELL, died intestate and no administrator or other representative has ever been appointed of her estate. 

Fifth That after the deposit of the original sum in the account opened by her in trust for the plaintiff in the defendant bank, the said KATHERINE FARRELL from time to time deposited other sums of money in the said account, and that the total of these sums with accrued interest which still remains on deposit in the defendant bank in the same form as originally deposited now amounts to $2,400. 

Sixth: That plaintiff has heretofore demanded of said bank the payment to him of said sum, but payment thereof has never been received. That the defendant ARTHUR FARRELL, the husband of

KATHERINE FARRELL, makes some claim thereto and has demanded of said bank payment of such sum, and has notified said bank not to pay the same to said plaintiff. 

WHEREFORE, plaintiff demands judgment decreeing that a trust in the said sum of $2,400 and accrued interest was created by said KATHERINE FARRELL for the benefit of plaintiff, and became irrevocable upon her death, that the said fund is now the property of the plaintiff; that the defendant ARTHUR FARRELL has no right or title thereto; and that plaintiff have judgment excluding the said 

ARTHUR FARRELL, and the defendant bank from any interest in or

FORMS. 

963 to said trust fund and that the defendant bank be directed to pay said sum of money and all accrued interest to the plaintiff, and that plaintiff may have such other and further relief as may be just, with the costs of this action.

Farrell delivered the bank book to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff was in possession of the same at the date of the death of Katherine 

Farrell, the creator of the trust, on March 23, 1929. 

Third: That the prayer for judgment in the complaint herein asks that it be declared that a trust was created by Katherine Farrell for the benefit of the plaintiff and became irrevocable upon her death, that the said fund is now the property of the plaintiff, and that the defendants be adjudged not to have any right or title thereto, and that the plaintiff have judgment excluding the defendants from any interest in or to said trust fund, and that the defendant bank be directed to pay the fund to the plaintiff herein. 

Fourth: That as deponent is informed and believes, the defendant, Arthur Farrell, is the husband of Katherine Farrell, deceased, the creator of the trust; that said Arthur Farrell has made a demand upon the defendant, Pilgim Savings Bank, for the monies on deposit in the account hereinbefore referred to, which claim is in opposition to the plaintiff's claim as beneficiary of the said trust fund; that the sources of deponent's information as to the foregoing, are a letter received by deponent from the plaintiff, dated July 14, 1930, a copy of which is annexed hereto, and a letter written from Ireland by Arthur Farrell to the defendant Pilgrim Savings Bank, under date of May 15, 1930, the original of which is in the bank's possession but a copy of which is annexed hereto.

FORMS.

First: Where did your sister, Agnes Farrell, reside from the time of the opening of this account to the time of her death? 

Second: How many times did you see her during this period? 

Third: State each case specifically, giving date and place? 

Fourth: Did she on any of these occasions speak of this bank account?

Fifth: If so, state what she said in relation to this bank account upon each occasion when she spoke of it? 

Sixth: Did your sister, Agnes Farrell, ever refer to her husband, Arthur Farrell, in relation to this bank account? 

Seventh: If so, what did she say? 

Eighth: Have you seen Arthur Farrell since the death of your sister Agnes Farrell?

Ninth: If so, state the substance of any conversation you may have had with him?

SUPREME COURT NEW YORK COUNTY. 

JOHN O'NEILL, Plaintiff, against

Deposition of John O'Neill, the plaintiff above-named, produced. sworn and examined the 14th day of April in the year One Thousand 

Nine Hundred and Thirty-one at Downpatrick, in County Down,

Ireland, under and by virtue of an order of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, County of New York, in the above-entitled action, dated the 26th day of March, 1931; 

John O'Neill of Drumaroad, Castlewellan, County Down, Ireland, whose occupation is that of farmer, aged sixty-four years and upwards, being duly sworn and examined as a witness in his own behalf, doth depose and say as follows: 

First: To the first interrogatory, he saith, John O'Neill.

Second: To the second interrogatory, he saith, 64 years on 28th day of October, 1930.

Fifth: To the fifth interrogatory, he saith, farmer.

March, 1929, at Castlewellan, County Down, Ireland.

Tenth: To the tenth interrogatory, he saith, I witnessed her funeral pass my home on 25th March, 1929. 

Eleventh: To the eleventh interrogatory, he saith, Castlewellan, County Down, Ireland. 

Twelfth: To the twelfth interrogatory, he saith, yes. 

Thirteenth: To the thirteenth interrogatory, he saith, Arthur Farrell. 

Fourteenth: To the fourteenth interrogatory, he saith, no.

Fifteenth: To the fifteenth interrogatory, he saith, I know she did not. 

Sixteenth: To the sixteenth interrogatory, he saith, I know that no administrator has been appointed. 

Seventeenth: To the seventeenth interrogatory, he saith, yes. 

Eighteenth: To the eighteenth interrogatory, he saith, during the month of July in the year 1928.

Nineteenth: To the nineteenth interrogatory, he saith, from my sister Katherine Farrell. 

Twentieth: To the twentieth interrogatory, he saith, she said, “I want you to have the money deposited in this Bank Account, if anything should happen to me, for you are the only one has helped me or been good to me." 

Twenty-first: To the twenty-first interrogatory, he saith, no, on two or three occasions my sister Katherine Farrell said to me, "I am in need of money to buy clothing, for my husband gives me nothing. 

Let me have the Bank Book so that I can draw some money from the Bank and I will return it to you. In accordance with her request I gave her the Bank Book on three occasions and after she had drawn some money out she returned the Bank Book each time to me. On each occasion when she returned the Bank Book she said, "I want you to have any balance there is in the bank when I die, for my husband has never contributed anything to my support." 

Twenty-second: To the twenty-second interrogatory, he saith, yes.

ANSWERS TO CROSS-INTERROGATORIES. 

First: To the first cross-interrogatory, he saith, in 1925 my sister was at service in New York when she opened the Bank Account; she returned to Ireland in October, 1928, and resided in the same house as her husband in Castlewellan, County Down. I returned from Schenectady to Ireland in July, 1925, and went to reside with

FORMS. 

my brother Francis in Drumaroad which adjoins Castlewellan Townland. With the exception of periods when my sister was in the hospital or when she stayed with my brother and me, she resided in the house with her husband. 

Second: To the second cross-interrogatory, he saith, I saw my sister occasionally while she was in U. S. A. and prior to her emigration to America and for the last few years of her life I helped her financially. Since my return to Ireland I saw my sister frequently, Third: To the third cross-interrogatory, he saith, at Mass on Sunprobably two or three times a week. days and frequently she came down to our house on Sunday and week evenings and sometimes I went up to her place as the both houses are within a few minutes' walk of one another. 

Fourth: To the fourth cross-interrogatory, he saith, yes, on several occasions. 

Fifth: To the fifth cross-interrogatory, he saith, she always said that she wanted me to have whatever balance there was in the Bank Account at the time of her death for the reason that I had been good to her and helped her. On one of the occasions she asked me to give Fifty pounds to her niece on her marriage, and also to pay Five pounds to have Masses said for her. I have already paid these monies from my own pocket. 

Sixth: To the sixth cross-interrogatory, he saith, yes. 

Seventh: To the seventh cross-interrogatory, he saith, on several occasions she said she did not wish her husband to get any of the money; that it was her own hard earnings and none of it belonged to him; that ever since her marriage she had to support herself and that her husband treated her badly. 

Eighth: To the eighth cross-interrogatory, he saith, yes. 

Ninth: To the ninth cross-interrogatory, he saith, In the Spring of 1929 he came to me where I was working in my farm and showed me a letter he had from the Defendant Bank. I read the letter, which as far as I recollect stated I was the only person who could draw the money. I asked him for it. He declined to give it to me but later I got a copy of it. Since, I have met him several times on the road going to or coming from church but he never again referred to the matter, nor spoke to me. We were not on friendly terms owing to the treatment he gave my sister.
